title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text: Which treatment process changes a pollutant’s chemical form, and which transfers it into a stream that still needs to be managed?
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Learning goals

Match a chemical form to an appropriate treatment mechanism.
Calculate sequential load transfers and distinguish transformation from removal.
Use reaction stoichiometry to explain oxygen and alkalinity requirements.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Start with the target form
Particles, dissolved ions, neutral organic molecules, and microorganisms behave differently. Settling or filtration can remove particles while leaving many dissolved species. Coagulation changes particle interactions and can capture some colloidal or associated dissolved material. Sorption transfers selected molecules to a solid. A treatment choice must specify the target, its form, and a receiving phase; one generic removal percentage cannot apply to all pollutants.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Precipitation and sorption transfer material
Metal or phosphate precipitation depends on pH, free-ion activities, solid identity, and competing ligands. Coagulant hydrolysis can generate acidity; simplified \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+3H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s)+3H^+}\) shows why alkalinity matters. The actual precipitate and net reaction depend on conditions. Settled sludge retains the transferred element and requires management. A fall in water concentration is not elemental destruction.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Biological oxidation changes species
Aerobic organic oxidation consumes oxygen and produces inorganic carbon. Nitrification oxidises ammonium to nitrate, consumes oxygen, and generates acidity. Nitrate is still dissolved nitrogen. Denitrification can convert nitrate to N₂ when a suitable electron donor and conditions are present. These are chemical balances behind treatment functions, not a full reactor design or a promise of complete conversion in every plant.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Sequential percentages multiply
A second treatment stage acts on the mass entering that stage, not the original mass unless specified. If stage one removes fraction \(f_1\) and stage two removes \(f_2\) of the remainder, water retains \(M_0(1-f_1)(1-f_2)\). Keep separate balances for effluent, solids, gas, and transformed products. Adding percentage removals can exceed 100% and obscures where the material goes.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Disinfection and residuals
Disinfection addresses viable microorganisms; it does not automatically remove chemical contaminants. Oxidants can react with organic matter and create transformation products, so target inactivation and chemical byproducts need separate evaluation. This course explains the mechanisms and balances; treatment protocols, dosing, and performance criteria require the actual system and its operating evidence.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Worked example
Start with 10.0 mg of an element in a tracked water volume. Stage one transfers 60.0% to solids: 6.00 mg solid and 4.00 mg water. Stage two transfers 50.0% of the remaining water inventory: 2.00 mg more solid and 2.00 mg effluent. Total transfer is 80.0%, and 8.00 + 2.00 = 10.0 mg closes the element balance. This example assumes no gas or chemical-product stream.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 16: precipitation, coagulation, sorption, and balanced nutrient transformations.
EPA wastewater nutrient overview: Why treatment goals distinguish nitrogen and phosphorus pathways.
USGS phosphorus chemistry: The difference between adsorption, mineral formation, and transport.
EPA nutrient-control chemistry: the net oxidation and alkalinity balances in chapter 4 support the reaction examples; reactor-design sections are beyond this unit.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text:
1. Another sequence
Two stages each remove 30.0% of the entering water-phase mass. Start with 100 mg. Find final water mass and overall removal.






Hint





Multiply the two remaining fractions.









Worked solution





100 × 0.700² = 49.0 mg remains; 51.0% is removed from the water. The element still resides in the specified residual stream unless transformed/exported elsewhere.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text:
2. Coagulant acidity
Assume 0.0200 mmol/L Fe³⁺ undergoes the supplied hydroxide precipitation reaction completely. Calculate H⁺ generation and the equivalent alkalinity decrease.






Hint





Each mole Fe³⁺ produces three moles H⁺ in this representation.









Worked solution





H⁺ = 0.0600 mmol/L; alkalinity decreases by 0.0600 meq/L. Other reactions and species must be included for a real dosing calculation.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text:
3. Track nitrogen
A process changes 1.00 mmol/L NH₄⁺ into 1.00 mmol/L NO₃⁻, with no other nitrogen products. Has it removed nitrogen? What process could remove dissolved nitrogen as gas?






Hint





Compare nitrogen atoms across forms.









Worked solution





No: 1.00 mmol N/L remains. Nitrification changes form. Denitrification to N₂ can export nitrogen from water, subject to the donor, conditions, and gas-transfer boundary.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text:
4. Choose and justify
A water contains suspended clay, dissolved nitrate, and a neutral organic contaminant. Explain why filtration alone is not a complete treatment argument.






Hint





Match particle size and chemical form to mechanism.









Worked solution





Filtration can capture some particles depending on the medium and size, but dissolved nitrate and a molecular organic solute generally require other suitable mechanisms. Consider nitrate transformation/separation and contaminant-specific sorption or destruction, then account for residuals and products. No operating prescription follows from this generic example.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises
text:
Explore: where the phosphorus goes
Predict how much of 100 mg phosphorus reaches the effluent if three stages transfer 30 %, 40 % and 90 % of what enters each one. Is it 100 − 160 %? Then change one stage at a time and watch where the removed phosphorus ends up.


Reference case: 100 mg phosphorus through stages transferring 30 %, 40 % and 90 % of what enters each leaves 4.2 mg (4.2 %) in the effluent; 30.0 + 28.0 + 37.8 = 95.8 mg is in sludge.



E1. Choose Phosphorus plant. Check the three sludge amounts and the effluent by hand, then show that the four parts add up to 100 mg. Why is the “added percentages” value impossible?
E2. Choose Exercise 1 and compare with your answer to exercise 1. Then set stage 3 to 50 %. Does a third stage of 50 % halve the overall removal, or the amount left in the water?
E3. In the phosphorus plant, which single stage would you improve by 5 percentage points to lower the effluent most? Try each one. Then explain why the sludge total rises by exactly the amount the effluent falls.

Model conditions and hand check
Each stage transfers a fixed fraction of the mass that enters it to sludge; there is no gas or chemical-product stream, which suits phosphorus and metals but not nitrogen. The stage percentages are round constructed numbers, not data from a real plant. For the reference case, the fraction left is 0.70 × 0.60 × 0.10 = 0.042, so 4.2 mg of 100 mg reaches the effluent and 95.8 % is transferred: 30.0 mg, 0.40 × 70.0 = 28.0 mg and 0.90 × 42.0 = 37.8 mg to sludge. The notes’ worked example (10.0 mg, 60.0 % then 50.0 %) gives 2.00 mg in the effluent and 80.0 % overall. Nothing is destroyed: the sludge still has to be managed.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
About this lecture


Copper was mined at Falun in central Sweden for roughly a thousand years, until 1992. The mine is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its waste heaps are still chemically active: water draining them carries acid, sulfate and metals toward the lakes downstream.
Why does old rock keep making acid long after mining stops?
Today you will learn to:

balance pyrite oxidation: 4 H⁺ per FeS₂;
separate present pH from future acid-generating inventory;
close a neutralisation budget with a stated endpoint;
tell concentration from load.

Last lecture, soils consumed acid from finite stocks. Today a solid produces it.

 The Great Pit at Falun copper mine, Sweden. Photo: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Open with Falun. The mine was one of Europe’s most important copper sources for centuries, and the great open pit formed when old workings collapsed in 1687. The ore contained copper sulfides together with a great deal of pyrite, iron disulfide. Mining and roasting left large volumes of sulfide-rich waste around the town. That waste is the reason why water draining the area is still acidic and metal-rich today, decades after the mine closed. The striking point is the time scale: acid production does not stop when people leave. Contrast with last week’s soil lecture, where acid arrived from the air and soil inventories consumed it. Here the solid itself is the acid source.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: The colour of Swedish houses is mine chemistry
text:
The colour of Swedish houses is mine chemistry


 A Falu red cottage, Lysekil, Sweden. Photo: W.carter, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

The classic red paint, Falu rödfärg, is made from pigment recovered from the Falun mine’s weathered waste.
The pigment is mainly iron oxides. They formed when iron sulfide in the waste reacted with oxygen and water over centuries.
So the reactions that gave Swedish cottages their colour are the same ones that produce acid in the mine drainage.
Today’s question: what exactly happens when pyrite meets air and water, and how much acid does it make?


This is a nice way to make the chemistry familiar. Falu red paint has been produced from the Falun mine’s waste for centuries. The pigment consists largely of iron oxides formed by weathering of the iron sulfides in the waste. Ask students: if iron sulfide turns into iron oxide, where did the sulfur go, and what happened to the hydrogen balance? Some will guess sulfate, and that is right. The point of the lecture is to make that conversion quantitative. Two oxidations happen, sulfur and then iron, and both release hydrogen ions. Once the bookkeeping is clear, we can compare acid production with the neutralising minerals in the waste and see why the balance can shift over decades.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: Pyrite: stable underground, reactive in air
text:
Pyrite: stable underground, reactive in air


 Pyrite (FeS₂) crystals on a glass, photographed in Visby, Gotland. Photo: W.carter, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Pyrite, FeS₂, “fool’s gold”, is the most common sulfide mineral. Sulfur sits as the disulfide ion S₂²⁻, oxidation state −1 per S.
Deep in bedrock or under water, there is almost no oxygen, so pyrite can persist for millions of years.
Mining, road cuts and drained wetlands crush the rock and expose it to air and water. Crushing also creates vast new surface area.
Pyrite is common in ore waste, in some black shales, and in drained coastal acid sulfate soils around the Baltic.


Pyrite forms under reducing conditions, for example in marine sediments where sulfate reduction produces sulfide, the process you met in the redox unit. As long as it stays away from oxygen it is stable. The trouble starts when we move it. Crushing ore to recover copper and zinc leaves fine-grained waste with enormous surface area, piled in heaps exposed to air and rain. Mention that the same chemistry appears outside mining. Along the Swedish and Finnish Baltic coast, land uplift and drainage have exposed sulfide-bearing sediments, forming acid sulfate soils that release acid and metals to rivers. Road and tunnel construction through black shale can do the same. The chemistry is identical; only the setting changes.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Inside a waste heap

Pyrite oxidation needs oxygen and water together. Both enter from the surface, so most reaction happens in an outer oxidation zone. The products leave the heap as seepage.

Walk through the cross-section. Oxygen enters the heap mainly by diffusion and air flow through the pores. Rain and snowmelt infiltrate from the top. Where the two meet pyrite, it oxidises. Deep inside, oxygen is used up before it gets there, so pyrite survives. This geometry is the reason for one of the main remediation strategies: cover the waste with a dense layer such as compacted till, or flood it under water, to keep oxygen out. Seepage collects at the base and carries hydrogen ions, sulfate, iron and other metals released as the sulfide minerals dissolve. Copper and zinc sulfides in ore waste are usually less abundant than pyrite, but their metals ride along in the acid water.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Two oxidations, four hydrogen ions

Each step is a redox reaction that also releases H⁺. Step 1 makes 2 H⁺ and dissolved Fe²⁺. Step 2 oxidises the iron and precipitates it, releasing 2 more.

Go slowly through the two steps. In step 1, the sulfur in pyrite is oxidised from minus one to plus six in sulfate. Oxygen is the electron acceptor, and two hydrogen ions are released per pyrite. Iron is still in the plus two state and dissolved. In step 2, iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III). Iron(III) is very insoluble at all but low pH, so it hydrolyses and precipitates. The hydrolysis is what releases the extra hydrogen ions: water molecules bound to iron(III) give up protons. Fe(OH)3 is a teaching formula; real precipitates are ferrihydrite, goethite or schwertmannite. The overall result, four hydrogen ions per pyrite, is the number to remember for acid budgets.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Check the balance: exercise 1


\mathrm{FeS_2+\tfrac72O_2+H_2O\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2SO_4^{2-}+2H^+} \mathrm{Fe^{2+}+\tfrac14O_2+\tfrac52H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3+2H^+}
Add them and cancel Fe²⁺:
\mathrm{FeS_2+\tfrac{15}{4}O_2+\tfrac72H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3+2SO_4^{2-}+4H^+}

This is exercise 1, done together. Adding the equations and cancelling iron(II) gives fifteen quarters of oxygen and seven halves of water. Then check each row. Oxygen is the one students usually get wrong: on the left, fifteen quarters of O2 is seven and a half oxygen atoms, plus three and a half from water, eleven in total. On the right, three oxygen atoms in the hydroxide plus eight in two sulfates. Hydrogen: seven on the left from water, three in the hydroxide and four free ions on the right. Charge: two sulfates carry minus four, four hydrogen ions plus four. Encourage students to do this check every time they write a budget reaction.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Iron(III) speeds it up

Once drainage is acidic, dissolved Fe³⁺ itself oxidises pyrite, and iron-oxidising microbes regenerate Fe³⁺ from Fe²⁺. Acid drainage can accelerate itself.

The two-step equations give the stoichiometry, not the mechanism. At low pH, iron(III) remains dissolved and is a strong oxidant for pyrite. It reacts at the grain surface without oxygen being present there. The iron(II) produced is oxidised back to iron(III) by acid-loving microbes, such as Acidithiobacillus species, which gain energy from the reaction and need oxygen. Abiotic oxidation of iron(II) is slow at low pH, so the microbes greatly speed up the cycle. The net reaction is unchanged, so our four hydrogen ions per pyrite still holds. The practical lesson: it is much easier to prevent acid drainage from starting than to stop it once the waste has acidified.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: What the end point looks like
text:
What the end point looks like


 Iron-stained stream bed of the Río Tinto, Spain. Photo: Carol Stoker, NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

The Río Tinto in southwest Spain drains a sulfide belt that has been mined for thousands of years.
Its water is strongly acidic, often around pH 2, and rich in dissolved iron(III), which colours it red.
Few organisms beyond specialised microbes live there. The river is studied as an analogue for life in extreme environments.
This is the iron cycle of the previous slide running at full speed.


The Río Tinto is the textbook image of acid mine drainage. The Iberian Pyrite Belt has been mined since antiquity, and the river’s acidity and iron load are a mixture of natural sulfide weathering and the effects of mining. At pH around 2, iron(III) stays in solution and gives the deep red colour. NASA scientists have studied the river’s microbes because they live on iron and sulfur chemistry in conditions that resemble what might be found on other planets. Use the photo to emphasise that at this pH almost all neutralising capacity has gone, and the iron cycle runs freely. Falun’s drainage is far less extreme, but the same chemistry is at work.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Orange streams: iron precipitates downstream


 Iron hydroxide precipitate in a stream receiving acid drainage, Missouri. Photo: D. Hardesty, USGS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Where acid drainage mixes with less acidic stream water, pH rises and Fe³⁺ precipitates as orange iron hydroxide (“yellow boy”).
Two consequences:

Step 2 releases its acid here, in the stream, not in the heap. A seep can leave the heap at moderate pH and still acidify the stream.
The orange coating smothers the stream bed, and the fresh precipitate binds metals such as Cu, Zn and As.

Removing the orange solid does not remove the acid already released.


This photo shows step 2 happening in the open. Water from a mine seep can contain plenty of dissolved iron(II) at modest pH. As it flows downstream, it picks up oxygen, iron oxidises and precipitates, and the stream becomes orange. Each mole of iron that precipitates releases two moles of hydrogen ions into the stream. This is why pH alone at the seep can mislead. The water’s acidity includes the dissolved iron that has not yet precipitated, sometimes called mineral acidity. The precipitate is ecologically damaging because it coats gravel where invertebrates and fish eggs live. It also sorbs metals, which is useful but, as we will see, not necessarily permanent.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Present pH is a snapshot


A leachate pH tells you about the water now. It says nothing about:

the pyrite still unreacted in the waste (acid potential);
the calcite and other buffers still present (neutralisation potential);
how fast oxygen and water reach either.

Mine-waste assessment therefore compares two inventories, usually in kg CaCO₃ per tonne of waste: acid potential versus neutralisation potential.


Same pH, different futures. Two heaps both drain at pH 7 today. Heap 1 contains abundant calcite and little pyrite. Heap 2 contains the reverse, and its calcite is being spent. Only an inventory, not a pH reading, tells them apart.



This is the core idea of the lecture and mirrors last week’s soils. pH is a state. The acid potential and neutralisation potential are inventories. In practice, mining companies and regulators estimate them from total sulfur and from a titration of the waste with acid, a procedure called acid–base accounting. The unit, kilograms of calcium carbonate equivalent per tonne of waste, lets both sides be compared directly. A waste with neutralisation potential well above acid potential is unlikely to generate acid drainage; one with the reverse ratio probably will, eventually. The word eventually matters, and the next slide shows why a waste can look harmless for decades.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Neutral today, acid tomorrow

While calcite lasts, it neutralises the acid as fast as pyrite makes it, and drainage looks harmless. When calcite runs out, the acid potential that was there all along appears in the water.

This is a constructed illustration, not a model of Falun. One tonne of waste with one percent pyrite has an acid potential of about 333 equivalents. We gave it 150 equivalents of calcite and chose a slow first-order oxidation rate purely for illustration. For the first thirty years the drainage is neutral, because calcite consumes the acid as fast as it forms. Then calcite is exhausted and acid drainage begins, with most of the pyrite still unreacted. In reality rates depend on grain size, oxygen supply and temperature, and calcite can be used up locally along flow paths long before it is gone overall. The general lesson is robust: a neutral leachate today is not proof of a stable waste.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Neutralisation depends on the endpoint


For the CO₂* endpoint (acidic final water, carbon leaves as CO₂):
\mathrm{CaCO_3+2H^+\rightarrow Ca^{2+}+CO_2^*+H_2O}
For a near-neutral endpoint, bicarbonate stays in the water:
\mathrm{CaCO_3+H^+\rightarrow Ca^{2+}+HCO_3^-}
The same calcite can neutralise 2 or 1 equivalents per mole. Mine-waste schemes differ in which they assume, so always state the endpoint before you use a coefficient.




Students have seen the first reaction in the carbonate and soil lectures. The second one is new here and matters for mine waste. If the final water is near neutral, carbon remains as bicarbonate and each calcium carbonate takes up only one hydrogen ion. That is the same chemistry as the carbonate lecture’s predominance diagram: at pH 7 most dissolved carbon is bicarbonate, not CO2-star. Assessment schemes differ in which endpoint they assume, and the answer can change by a factor of two, so always state it. Ask students which endpoint is more cautious for judging whether a waste is safe. The near-neutral one is, because it credits each mole of calcite with less neutralisation.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: Calcite present is not calcite available
text:
Calcite present is not calcite available

In acid, iron-rich water, limestone grains become coated with iron hydroxide or gypsum. The calcite is still there, but H⁺ cannot reach it. Calcite in a layer the water does not pass through is equally useless.

This is a practical limit on any neutralisation inventory. When acid, iron-rich drainage meets limestone, the calcite dissolves at first, raising the pH. That pH rise makes iron(III) precipitate, and it precipitates on the nearest surface: the limestone itself. Sulfate-rich water can also deposit gypsum. The coating, called armouring, slows further dissolution dramatically. Passive treatment systems therefore try to keep oxygen out of limestone drains so that iron stays as dissolved iron(II) until the water has left the limestone. The same logic applies inside a heap: calcite away from the flow paths, or coated, is counted in an inventory but contributes little in practice. An inventory is a maximum, not a guarantee.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Worked example: closing the budget


0.0100 mol FeS₂ oxidises completely:

acid: 4 × 0.0100 = 0.0400 mol H⁺ eq
sulfate: 2 × 0.0100 = 0.0200 mol
CaCO₃ needed (CO₂* endpoint): 0.0400 / 2 = 0.0200 mol = 2.00 g

Exercise 2: only 0.0150 mol CaCO₃ is accessible. It neutralises 0.0300 eq, leaving 0.0100 mol eq of acid.




This is the worked example from the notes, followed by exercise 2. Walk through the left panel: forty millimoles of acid, half from each step, fully neutralised by twenty millimoles of calcite. With a molar mass of 100 grams per mole, that is two grams of calcium carbonate. The right panel is the shortfall: fifteen millimoles of calcite neutralise thirty millimoles of acid, and ten millimoles remain. Two cautions from the exercise. First, the residual is an amount, not a pH; to get a pH you need the water volume and the remaining acid–base equilibria. Second, this is a stoichiometric comparison, not a design dose. Real treatment adds a safety margin because rates, access and mixing are imperfect.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Check yourself


How many moles of H⁺ equivalents can 0.0050 mol FeS₂ generate, oxidised completely to Fe(OH)₃ and sulfate?
A seep leaves a heap at pH 6 with 20 mg/L dissolved Fe²⁺. Will the stream downstream necessarily stay at pH 6? Why?
A waste contains enough calcite to neutralise its acid potential at the CO₂* endpoint. Is it safe if the final water will be near neutral?
Name two reasons why calcite present in a heap might not neutralise the acid produced there.



Answers. One: four times 0.0050, so 0.020 mol of hydrogen ion equivalents. Two: no. The iron(II) will oxidise and precipitate downstream, releasing two hydrogen ions per iron. Twenty milligrams per litre of iron is about 0.36 millimoles per litre, so up to about 0.7 millimoles per litre of acid can appear in the stream, depending on its alkalinity. Three: not necessarily. At a near-neutral endpoint each calcite neutralises only one equivalent, so the same inventory covers only half the acid potential. Four: armouring by coatings, and calcite located away from the flow paths where acid is produced. Slow dissolution relative to flow is a third acceptable answer.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Concentration is not load




Load = flow × concentration.

Discharge A: 10.0 L/s × 2.00 mg/L = 20.0 mg/s Fe
Discharge B: 40.0 L/s × 1.00 mg/L = 40.0 mg/s Fe

B looks cleaner but exports twice as much iron, about 1.3 tonnes a year.
During snowmelt, concentrations often fall while loads rise. Judge a waste by its load to the receiving lake.


This is exercise 3, and it repeats the very first unit of the course: concentration and load answer different questions. A regulator who samples only concentration might judge discharge B as the smaller problem, yet it delivers twice the iron to the lake. Forty milligrams per second over a year is about 1.3 tonnes. Seasonal flow matters in Sweden. Snowmelt flushes the heaps, diluting the water, but the larger volume can carry out salts and metals that accumulated during the winter, so the annual load is often dominated by a few high-flow weeks. Remind students that these are dissolved loads. Iron leaving as suspended precipitate is a separate term that needs its own measurement.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Immobilised is not destroyed

Treatment often moves metals from water onto solids. The solid then needs conditions that keep it stable: enough alkalinity to keep pH up, and enough oxygen to keep iron oxidised.

Return to the water-treatment unit: precipitation and sorption transfer contaminants to solids, which become residuals. Here we ask how stable those residuals are. Iron hydroxide surfaces bind copper, zinc, lead and also anions such as arsenate and phosphate. If pH falls, hydrogen ions compete for surface sites and cationic metals desorb. If the solid becomes waterlogged and oxygen runs out, microbes reduce iron(III) to dissolved iron(II), and the carrier itself dissolves, releasing everything it held. This links ahead to the redox processes in the synthesis lecture. Any claim that a waste or sludge is safely immobilised must state the chemical conditions that keep it so, and how long those conditions will last.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: Back to Falun: a worked estimate
text:
Back to Falun: a worked estimate


Constructed: one tonne of waste rock with 1 % pyrite by mass.

FeS₂: 10 kg / 120 g/mol ≈ 83 mol
acid potential: 4 × 83 ≈ 333 mol H⁺ eq
sulfate: 2 × 83 ≈ 167 mol
CaCO₃ to neutralise: ≈ 17 kg (CO₂* endpoint) or ≈ 33 kg (near-neutral endpoint)

Multiply by the millions of tonnes of waste at an old mining district, and the century-long drainage makes sense.

 The Great Pit at Falun with its weathered, iron-stained rock and the town beyond. Photo: Arild Vågen, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Bring the numbers back to the opening case. The calculation is constructed, with round numbers, but it shows the scale. Ten kilograms of pyrite in a tonne of rock generates about 333 moles of hydrogen ion equivalents, which would need about seventeen kilograms of limestone at the carbon dioxide endpoint, or twice that if the water is to end near neutral. At Falun, centuries of mining left very large waste volumes. Oxygen reaches the pyrite slowly, from the surface inward, so the inventory is used up over centuries rather than years. That is the honest answer to the opening question: the acid comes from an inventory that is still far from exhausted, released at a rate set by access to oxygen and water.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Beyond mines: other leachates


The same reasoning, inventory + access + reaction, applies to other wastes:

Landfills: organic waste consumes oxygen. Leachate becomes reducing, rich in ammonium, dissolved organic carbon, Fe²⁺ and Mn²⁺.
Ash and slag: often strongly alkaline, with metals such as lead or chromium whose solubility depends on pH.
Acid sulfate soils: drained sulfide sediments behave like mine waste.

In every case, ask what is still in the solid, and what controls its release.


A useful template for any leachate

Which reactive solids are present, and how much?
What lets them react: O₂, water, low pH, microbes?
What neutralises or retains the products?
What flow carries the products out, and when?
What could change in 10 or 100 years?




Broaden the view so students see a method, not just a mine. Municipal landfills contain degradable organic matter. Microbes consume the oxygen, and leachate becomes strongly reducing, so iron and manganese dissolve and ammonium accumulates. Old landfills are therefore a reducing, not an acid, problem. Incineration ash is often very alkaline because of lime and oxides, and some metals, such as lead, are amphoteric and can dissolve at high pH as well as at low pH. Acid sulfate soils along the Baltic coast are a natural version of mine waste. The five-step template on the right works for all of them. It is also a good structure for the exam questions on leachate.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Pyrite gives 2 H⁺.” Only step 1. Iron oxidation and precipitation add 2 more: 4 H⁺ per FeS₂.
“Neutral leachate means a safe waste.” Calcite may simply not be exhausted yet.
“CaCO₃ always neutralises 2 H⁺.” That depends on the endpoint: 1 at near-neutral pH.
“Calcite present = calcite available.” Armouring and flow paths limit access.
“Lower concentration = smaller problem.” Compare loads.
“Metals on iron hydroxide are gone.” Low pH or reducing conditions can release them.


Go through these as a self-test, and ask students to justify each correction with a reaction or a number from today. The first mistake is the most common in budget calculations, often because students stop at the first equation in a textbook. The second and the last are the most important for environmental decisions: both treat a present state as if it were permanent. Mention that the same structure of mistakes reappears in the next lecture on organic contaminants. There, disappearance of a compound from water is often mistaken for destruction, when it may simply have moved to another phase. Keeping track of inventories in all phases is the shared habit.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Explore: acid potential versus neutralisation


Same pH today, different futures: when does the calcite run out?



Same pH today, different futures: when does the calcite run out?

Start with the worked example: one tonne, 1 % pyrite, 333 equivalents of acid potential, 150 equivalents of calcite, calcite gone after about 30 years. This is the lag-time figure made adjustable. Then switch to the near-neutral endpoint and to half the calcite coated: both halve the reachable neutralisation and bring the acid drainage forward, for different chemical reasons. Change the oxidation rate and ask students what moves: only the timing, not the totals. Finish with the calcite-rich heap, then lower the reachable share until it fails. The exercise page has the assumptions, a hand check and a static reference for printing.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Pyrite
FeS₂, S at −1; stable without O₂, reacts when exposed to air and water


Step 1
FeS₂ + 7/2 O₂ + H₂O → Fe²⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺


Step 2
Fe²⁺ + 1/4 O₂ + 5/2 H₂O → Fe(OH)₃ + 2H⁺, often downstream


Total
4 H⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻ per FeS₂


Fe³⁺ cycle
at low pH Fe³⁺ oxidises pyrite; microbes regenerate Fe³⁺


Inventories
acid potential vs neutralisation potential; pH is a snapshot


Lag
drainage can stay neutral for decades, then acidify


Endpoint
CaCO₃ neutralises 2 eq (CO₂*) or 1 eq (HCO₃⁻)


Load
flow × concentration; dilution can hide a large export


Immobilisation
sorbed metals return if pH falls or Fe(III) is reduced



Next: Organic contaminants and environmental fate. Where does a molecule go, and is “gone from the water” the same as “destroyed”? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Sailors in firefighting foam (AFFF) during a sprinkler test, 2006. Photo: US Navy, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Recite the chain once. Exposing pyrite to oxygen and water oxidises sulfur and then iron, giving four hydrogen ions and two sulfates per pyrite. At low pH, dissolved iron(III) and microbes accelerate the process. Whether drainage turns acidic depends on comparing two inventories, acid potential and neutralisation potential, and on access to them. A neutral leachate can hide a declining neutralising reserve. State the endpoint when you use calcite in a budget, judge discharges by load, and treat immobilised metals as conditionally stored. The photo previews the next lecture: firefighting foam contained PFAS compounds, which contaminated drinking water in Ronneby, Sweden. There the question is not acid but where an organic molecule goes.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text: If a contaminant disappears from water, is it removed from the environmental system or transferred onto a mobile particle?
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Learning goals

Explain pH-dependent surface charge and specific binding.
Close a water–solid mass balance using a supplied Kd.
Distinguish sorption equilibrium, finite capacity, and colloidal transport.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
A surface is chemically active
Oxide surfaces carry hydroxyl groups that can gain or lose protons. Schematically, \(\mathrm{>SOH+H^+\rightleftharpoons >SOH_2^+}\) and \(\mathrm{>SOH\rightleftharpoons >SO^-+H^+}\). Here >S denotes a surface site, not dissolved sulfur. Some clay charge arises from crystal substitutions and is less directly pH dependent. Surface charge influences electrostatic attraction, while specific ligand exchange can bind solutes beyond a simple opposite-charge picture.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Define a distribution coefficient
In a linear equilibrium approximation, \(q=K_dC_w\), where \(q\) is sorbed mass per dry solid mass (mg/kg), \(C_w\) is aqueous concentration (mg/L), and \(K_d\) is L/kg. State the measurement conditions. The coefficient can change with pH, competing solutes, and concentration. It is not a universal molecular constant and should not be applied outside its range without evidence.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Close the two-phase balance
For a closed bottle with water volume \(V_w\) L, dry solid mass \(m_s\) kg, and total solute mass \(M_T\) mg, \[M_T=C_wV_w+qm_s=C_w(V_w+K_dm_s).\] Thus \(C_w=M_T/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). The sorbed fraction is \(K_dm_s/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). The denominator has litre units in both terms. The model excludes degradation, wall loss, and non-equilibrium transport.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Capacity and competition
A linear model has no finite saturation plateau. A Langmuir teaching model, \(q=q_{max}bC/(1+bC)\), approaches a limiting capacity \(q_{max}\). Real surfaces can have several kinds of sites and hysteresis. Phosphate can bind to iron oxides, but competition, site occupation, mineral changes, and pH alter retention. A low-concentration Kd should not be extrapolated to unlimited loading.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Particles may move
Sorption onto settling solids can retain a solute locally, but sorption onto mobile colloids can assist transport. Operational filtration does not perfectly separate a dissolved molecular pool from every particle size. Particle settling, aggregation, and resuspension change the boundary fluxes. To claim removal, identify the destination and whether it remains outside the receiving water over the relevant timescale.



Predicted equilibrium water concentration as dry solid mass increases in a closed bottle.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Worked example
Distribute 1.00 mg between 1.00 L water and 0.0100 kg dry solid, with \(K_d=100\) L/kg. Then \(K_dm_s=1.00\) L, \(C_w=1.00/(1.00+1.00)=\mathbf{0.500}\) mg/L, and \(q=50.0\) mg/kg. Water contains 0.500 mg and solid contains 0.500 mg. The total stays 1.00 mg. Half is sorbed; none has been destroyed.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 14: surface protonation, a transparent linear balance, finite capacity, and colloidal mobility.
USGS phosphate retention: Mineral surfaces, finite adsorption, and phosphorus transport.
EPA sorption coefficients: Definitions and conditions for distribution coefficients.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
1. Double the solid
Repeat the worked example with 0.0200 kg solid, keeping all other inputs fixed. Find aqueous concentration and both inventories.






Hint





Use the full denominator, not a proportional guess.









Worked solution





Cw = 1/(1 + 100 × 0.0200) = 0.3333 mg/L. Water holds 0.3333 mg, solid 0.6667 mg. The sorbed concentration is 33.33 mg/kg and the total remains 1.00 mg.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
2. A loading limit
A solid has qmax = 20.0 mg/kg and dry mass 0.0100 kg. Can it bind 1.00 mg on those sites?






Hint





Multiply capacity by dry solid mass.









Worked solution





The maximum site inventory is 0.200 mg, so 1.00 mg cannot all bind there. More solid, other retention mechanisms, or a larger aqueous pool would be required.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
3. A desorption change
A new pH changes Kd in the original bottle from 100 to 10.0 L/kg. At equilibrium with the same total mass and volume, what is Cw?






Hint





Changing Kd redistributes the fixed inventory.









Worked solution





Cw = 1/(1 + 10 × 0.0100) = 0.9091 mg/L. Aqueous mass is 0.9091 mg and sorbed mass 0.09091 mg. Desorption raised the water concentration without adding total solute.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
4. Removal or transport?
A filtered sample loses metal while the unfiltered downstream sample does not. How could particles explain this observation?






Hint





Compare operational fractions and whether particles settle or remain mobile.









Worked solution





Metal may bind to particles excluded by filtration while remaining in the moving water-plus-particle system. Measure particle loads, size fractions, flow, and phase inventories. A filtered concentration decrease alone does not establish destruction or permanent retention.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
Explore: the two-phase bottle
Predict what happens to the water concentration if you double the solid while keeping the solute and water fixed. Then predict what a tenfold drop in Kd, for example after a pH change, does to the mass on the solid.


Reference case: 1.00 mg solute, 1.00 L water, 0.0100 kg solid and Kd = 100 L/kg give 0.500 mg/L in water and 0.500 mg on the solid.



E1. Choose Worked example, then Double the solid. Check both water concentrations by hand with Cw = MT/(Vw + Kdms). Why is the second one a third, not a quarter?
E2. Choose pH change: Kd falls to 10. How much solute moved from the solid back into the water? Was any solute added?
E3. Reset, then find the solid mass at which exactly half the solute is sorbed for Kd = 20 L/kg. Explain your answer using the idea of an “extra volume” Kdms.

Model conditions and hand check
For the worked example, Kdms = 100 × 0.0100 = 1.00 L, so Cw = 1.00/(1.00 + 1.00) = 0.500 mg/L. The water holds 0.500 mg, the solid 0.500 mg, and q = 50.0 mg/kg. With 0.0200 kg solid, Cw = 1/3.00 = 0.333 mg/L. With Kd = 10 L/kg, Cw = 1/1.10 = 0.909 mg/L.
The bottle is closed and at equilibrium. Sorption is linear (q = KdCw), so there is no capacity limit; a real solid holds at most qmax × ms. Kd is set by hand: the demo does not calculate how pH changes it. There is no degradation, loss to the walls, or competition from other solutes. The comparison curve uses a Kd ten times smaller than the current one.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Soil chemistry and retention
Soil chemistry and retention
section: Two soils, same pH, different futures
text:
Two soils, same pH, different futures


 A podzol profile: the pale, leached layer lies just below the surface. Photo: Ailith Stewart, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Imagine two forest soils, both measured at pH 5.0:

Soil A, a sandy podzol like the one in the photo, typical of much of Sweden’s forest land;
Soil B, a clay loam rich in organic matter.

Both receive the same acid deposition for decades. One keeps feeding calcium to its stream; the other soon releases aluminium.
Question for this lecture: what does a soil contain that a pH reading cannot show?


This is the puzzle we resolve by the end. A podzol forms in cool, wet climates on sandy parent material under conifers. Organic acids and water leach the upper mineral layer, leaving the bleached grey band you see in the photo, and deposit iron, aluminium and humus lower down. Such soils are common across Scandinavian forests. Ask students to predict which soil copes better with acid and why. Many will guess the clay soil, which is right, but ask them to say what exactly the clay contributes. The answer is an inventory of charged sites and the cations on them, plus sometimes minerals that neutralise acid. pH measures none of these directly. We will measure them by the end.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Soil is several reacting phases

Soil water is the phase that plants take up and streams receive. Its composition is set by exchange with minerals, organic matter and gas. Soil pH describes the water’s state under a stated method. It does not count what the solids can still deliver or absorb.

Give the big picture once. By volume, a typical loam is roughly half solids and half pore space, the pores shared between water and air depending on wetness. The proportions vary widely; the point is the reactions between phases. The soil gas often contains much more carbon dioxide than the atmosphere, because roots and microbes respire, which links to last week’s carbonate chemistry. Minerals weather and dissolve. Clay and organic surfaces exchange ions with the water. Water leaving the bottom of the profile carries the result to streams. The rest of the lecture focuses on one of these arrows, exchange with charged surfaces, and then asks what happens when acid arrives.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Where the negative charge comes from
text:
Where the negative charge comes from

Clay minerals carry permanent negative charge from ion substitution inside the crystal. Organic matter carries pH-dependent charge from acid groups that lose H⁺ as pH rises. Both kinds of charge attract and hold cations from the soil water.

Clay minerals are sheets of silicon, aluminium, oxygen and hydroxide. When a clay forms, an aluminium ion sometimes sits where a silicon ion should be, or magnesium replaces aluminium. Each such swap leaves the crystal one positive charge short, so the sheet carries a net negative charge that does not depend on pH. Organic matter is different. Humus contains many carboxyl and phenolic groups. These are weak acids, so at higher pH more of them have lost their proton and carry negative charge. That is why soil organic matter holds more cations in a neutral soil than in an acid one, and why a measured exchange capacity must state the pH of the test.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Cation exchange: ions trade places

Exchange moves ions between sites and solution without destroying any element. X stands for one unit of negative site charge. A divalent ion occupies two units.

Walk through the picture. On the left, four sodium ions sit on four negative sites, and one calcium ion is in solution. On the right, calcium has taken two sites and two sodium ions have moved into solution. Nothing has been created or destroyed, and the surface charge is still balanced. Write the reaction with X for one site charge, so calcium appears as X2Ca. The reaction is reversible and fast, typically minutes to hours. This explains a familiar observation: road salt can flush calcium and magnesium from roadside soils, because a large excess of sodium pushes the equilibrium the other way. Remember the key rule: count charge, not ions.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Which cation wins a site?


Two things decide what sits on the exchanger:

Selectivity. Higher charge and a smaller hydrated ion are held more strongly. A rough order is Al³⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Mg²⁺ > K⁺ > Na⁺.
Mass action. A large excess of a weakly held ion can still push others off. Road salt (Na⁺) flushes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from roadside soils.

So capacity (how many sites) and selectivity (who gets them) are different quantities.


Consequence for acid soils. Al³⁺ is held strongly. Once acid has released aluminium from minerals, Al³⁺ takes over sites that used to hold Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. The exchanger then stores acidity instead of nutrients.



Selectivity follows from electrostatics. A triply charged ion is held more strongly than a doubly charged one, and among ions of the same charge, the one with the smaller hydrated radius gets closer to the surface. The sequence on the slide is a common rough order. Real exchangers differ, and some clays hold potassium specifically. Mass action reminds us that exchange is an equilibrium. Even a weakly held ion wins sites when it is abundant enough. The box anticipates the acid story. In strongly acidified soils, aluminium dominates the exchanger. The soil has not lost its capacity, but its sites hold the wrong ions. That difference between capacity and occupancy is what we count next.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Counting exchange capacity


Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the total negative charge available for exchange, per kilogram of dry soil.
Unit: cmolc/kg, centimoles of charge.
1\ \mathrm{cmol_c/kg} = 0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ charge/kg}
Sand has almost none. Organic matter and swelling clays have a great deal. A few percent of humus can dominate a soil’s CEC.




The unit causes most of the errors, so slow down. A centimole of charge is one hundredth of a mole of charge. Calcium carries two charges, so one centimole of calcium ions is two centimoles of charge. The ranges in the figure are approximate typical values from textbooks. They vary with pH and the measurement method, so treat them as orders of magnitude. Two things stand out. Quartz sand contributes almost nothing. Organic matter has the highest capacity per kilogram, which is why the thin dark humus layer of a sandy forest soil can hold more exchangeable cations than the much thicker mineral horizon beneath. Swelling clays such as smectite also hold a lot.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Worked example: from charge to moles
text:
Worked example: from charge to moles

A 0.200 kg sample with CEC 10.0 cmolc/kg holds 0.0200 mol charge. If Ca²⁺ occupies half, that is 0.0100 mol charge, but only 0.00500 mol Ca, because each Ca²⁺ fills two sites.

This is the calculation in the notes, drawn out. Multiply the CEC by 0.01 to convert to moles of charge per kilogram, then by the mass. That gives twenty millimoles of charge, drawn here as twenty boxes. Half the boxes are occupied by calcium. Each calcium ion covers two boxes, so there are only five calcium units, five millimoles. The common mistake is to report 0.0100 mol calcium. Ask students to redo the calculation for magnesium filling all sites in 0.100 kg of soil with CEC 20, which is exercise 1. Stress the last caution from the notes: this is a capacity inventory. It does not mean all this calcium will enter the soil water at once.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Base saturation: what fills the sites
text:
Base saturation: what fills the sites




Base saturation is the share of CEC held by the base cations Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺ and Na⁺. The rest is mostly Al³⁺ and H⁺.
\text{BS}=\frac{\text{base cations (cmol}_c\text{/kg)}}{\text{CEC (cmol}_c\text{/kg)}}
Example: 9.00 / 12.0 = 75.0 %.
Our two soils have similar pH. Soil B holds about 8 times more exchangeable base cations than Soil A.


Base saturation answers who sits on the sites. The constructed soils in the figure both read about pH 5, yet Soil A holds 1.7 and Soil B about 14 centimoles of base-cation charge per kilogram. That is the hidden difference behind the opening puzzle. Exercise 2 asks for the base saturation of a soil with 9 out of 12 centimoles of charge occupied by base cations: 75 percent. Warn students about two misreadings. Base saturation is a property of the solid, not a statement that the soil water has the same ion ratio. And it does not set the pH uniquely: mineralogy, organic acids, selectivity and the measurement method all matter.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Check yourself


A 0.100 kg soil has CEC 20.0 cmolc/kg. If all sites hold Mg²⁺, how many moles of Mg is that?
Which holds more exchangeable charge: 1 kg of quartz sand or 0.1 kg of humus? Use the CEC ranges.
A soil has CEC 12.0 cmolc/kg and 3.0 cmolc/kg of Al³⁺ + H⁺ on the sites. What is its base saturation?
True or false: “This soil has pH 6, so its exchanger is full of calcium.”



Answers. One: 20.0 times 0.01 times 0.100 gives 0.0200 mol charge, and magnesium carries two charges, so 0.0100 mol magnesium. Two: sand at about one to five centimoles per kilogram gives one to five centimoles in total; humus at 150 to 300 gives fifteen to thirty for the tenth of a kilogram, so the humus wins by a wide margin. Three: base cations hold 12 minus 3, so 9, and base saturation is 75 percent, the same as exercise 2. Four is false. pH does not report the exchanger’s composition or size. A soil can read pH 6 with a small CEC and few base cations. Use this to move to acid inputs.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Acid arrives: three ways to consume it
text:
Acid arrives: three ways to consume it

Every pathway uses up something finite. Look at the bottom box: a cation can only leave the soil together with an anion. Sulfate from deposition is the vehicle that carries calcium out to the stream.

Acid deposition supplies hydrogen ions with sulfate and nitrate, as in the deposition unit. In the soil, the hydrogen ions are consumed in three main ways. Carbonate minerals dissolve if present. Hydrogen ions displace base cations from exchange sites. And in strongly acid soils, aluminium hydroxide minerals dissolve. Organic acid groups also take up protons, which we fold into exchange here. The bottom box is the key insight from catchment studies. Charge balance means that calcium cannot leave in drainage by itself. It needs an accompanying anion, and the sulfate from deposition is exactly that anion. Acid rain therefore drives calcium loss twice: by displacing it and by supplying its partner.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Which reaction dominates depends on pH
text:
Which reaction dominates depends on pH

As acid accumulates, soils move from one buffer range to the next: carbonate, then slow silicate weathering, then cation exchange, then aluminium. Each range holds the pH roughly steady while its inventory lasts. The ranges are approximate and overlap.

This classification of soil buffer ranges goes back to the German soil chemist Bernhard Ulrich in the 1980s. The pH limits are approximate, and different texts quote slightly different values, so do not memorise the decimals. The idea is what matters. While carbonate remains, pH stays near neutral. Without carbonate, silicate weathering supplies base cations slowly. When acid input outpaces weathering, the exchanger gives up its base cations, and the soil sits around pH 4 to 5. Below that, aluminium minerals dissolve, which neutralises acid but puts aluminium into the water. The arrow is a time arrow under continued acid load: a soil moves to the right when it exhausts each reserve.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Exchange buys time, not immunity

Without carbonate, each equivalent of acid removes one equivalent of base cations from the exchanger. Soil A runs out after 1.7 cmolc/kg; Soil B after 14.2. Until then their pH may look similar. Afterwards, aluminium takes over.

This constructed figure uses the two soils from the base saturation slide. Each equivalent of acid that is neutralised by exchange removes one equivalent of base cations, so the inventory falls in a straight line. Soil A has very little to lose and reaches the aluminium range quickly. Soil B can absorb about eight times more acid before the same happens. The figure deliberately ignores weathering, which slowly resupplies base cations, and uptake by trees, which also removes them. Make the key point explicitly. A soil that has resisted acid so far may simply be spending its reserve. Resistance to one acid pulse, or even to decades of deposition, does not guarantee indefinite protection.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: When the bases run out: aluminium
text:
When the bases run out: aluminium




\mathrm{Al(OH)_3(s)+3H^+\rightleftharpoons Al^{3+}+3H_2O}
Three H⁺ per Al³⁺, so free Al³⁺ rises 1000-fold per pH unit at mineral equilibrium.
Dissolved inorganic aluminium damages fish gills and fine roots. It was a main cause of fish loss in acidified Scandinavian lakes.
Model: gibbsite equilibrium, log K = 8.11 at 25 °C; free ion only.


The aluminium buffer neutralises acid, but at a price. The equilibrium constant expression contains the hydrogen-ion concentration cubed, so each pH unit changes the free aluminium concentration a thousandfold. The curve uses the equilibrium constant for crystalline gibbsite from standard tables. Real soils contain less ordered aluminium phases and organic complexes, so measured concentrations differ, often being higher in total. The thousandfold slope is the robust message. Biologically, inorganic aluminium precipitates on fish gills and disrupts salt balance, and it damages fine roots. In many acidified Scandinavian lakes, aluminium washed in from soils was as important as low pH itself. The metals unit covers how ligands change this picture.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Back to Hubbard Brook


 Gene Likens, co-founder of the Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study, beside a precipitation collector, 2015. Photo: Mariel Carr, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Long-term records showed large losses of exchangeable calcium from the forest soil. Lower sulfate deposition slowed the loss, but the exchanger refills only as fast as minerals weather.
In 1999 researchers spread a calcium silicate mineral over one whole catchment by helicopter to test the idea.
Constructed estimate: raise base cations by 1.0 cmolc/kg in the top 10 cm of 1 ha (≈ 1.0 × 10⁶ kg soil):
10 000 mol charge = 5000 mol Ca ≈ 200 kg Ca, or ≈ 500 kg CaCO₃.


Return to the opening case. The slow stream recovery at Hubbard Brook was explained by soil chemistry: the exchanger had lost much of its calcium during decades of acid deposition, and weathering resupplies it slowly. The calcium addition experiment applied the mineral wollastonite, a calcium silicate, to a whole small catchment, so the response of soil, trees and stream could be followed. The estimate on the slide is our own constructed calculation, not the experiment’s dose. Assume a soil density of one kilogram per litre. One hectare to ten centimetres is a thousand cubic metres, about a million kilograms. One centimole of charge per kilogram is ten thousand moles of charge, five thousand moles of calcium, about two hundred kilograms.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Retention is not the same as transport
text:
Retention is not the same as transport

A high CEC protects groundwater only if the solute meets the sites. Water in macropores can bypass most of the soil, anions are not held by cation exchange, and colloids can carry sorbed metals with them.

Students often treat CEC as a universal filter. It is not. First, exchange needs contact time: after heavy rain, water and anything dissolved in it can race down root channels, worm burrows and shrinkage cracks, reaching drains in hours. Second, CEC holds cations. Nitrate is hardly retained, and sulfate only by specific surfaces in some soils, which is why nitrate leaching is a classic problem. Third, small particles, colloids, can move through pores while carrying sorbed metals or phosphate. And erosion simply moves the solids, sites and all. To predict movement, combine chemical partitioning with water flow, residence time and particle transport. Redox changes in waterlogged soil add another layer, which we revisit in the synthesis.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Fast paths in a real soil
text:
Fast paths in a real soil


 Shrinkage cracks in drying clay, Gauteng, South Africa. Photo: Paul Venter, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Clay soils with high CEC shrink and crack when they dry. The next heavy rain runs straight down the cracks.
This produces a paradox. The soil with the most exchange sites can deliver a pesticide or phosphate pulse to a field drain within hours, because the water hardly touched those sites.
Fair tests of retention therefore report flow conditions, not only CEC and pH.
The next lecture applies the same thinking to waste heaps: what is inside matters, but so does how water and oxygen get in.


Use the photo to make the paradox concrete. Swelling clays, the same smectites with high exchange capacity, shrink when they dry and form crack networks. In agricultural clay soils, as in parts of southern and central Sweden, much of the water leaving the field after a heavy rain can pass through such cracks and through worm burrows to tile drains. Field studies of pesticides and phosphorus loss repeatedly show quick pulses after rain. The chemical capacity of the soil is real, but the water did not stay long enough to use it. This prepares the next lecture, where access of water and oxygen to a waste heap controls how fast its chemistry runs.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Back to the two soils: what to measure
text:
Back to the two soils: what to measure
