Same pH, different reserves. Soil A acidifies its stream soon; Soil B can neutralise about eight times more acid first.

 Podzol profile from Sweden, ISRIC World Soil Reference Collection. Photo: D. Creutzberg, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.


This answers exercise 4 and closes the opening puzzle. Before predicting how a soil responds to acid, measure its capacity under stated conditions, its base saturation, any carbonate or weatherable minerals, its organic matter, and how water moves through it. Equal pH is not evidence of equal buffering or equal retention. The values in the table are the constructed soils used throughout this lecture. The photo shows a real Swedish podzol profile kept as a reference in an international soil collection. Point out the bleached grey horizon that lost its iron and aluminium, and the darker layer below where they accumulated. These are exactly the soils where acidification caused the most damage.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Equal pH means equal buffering.” pH is a state; CEC, base saturation and carbonate are inventories.
“cmolc of Ca equals cmol of Ca.” Divide charge by 2 for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, by 3 for Al³⁺.
“Base saturation is the soil-water ion ratio.” It describes the solid’s sites.
“Exchange destroys the acid.” It moves base cations out and stores acidity on the solid.
“High CEC retains everything.” Not anions, not water in macropores, not colloids.
“A soil that resisted acid is safe.” It may have been spending a finite reserve.


Run through these as a quick self-test and ask students to explain each in their own words. The second is the most common calculation error in this unit, so ask for an example: 2.0 cmol of charge from aluminium corresponds to about 0.67 cmol of aluminium ions. The fourth is subtle. Exchange neutralises the water passing through, but the acidity has not disappeared. It now sits on the exchanger as hydrogen and aluminium ions, and the base cations have gone downstream with sulfate. The last one is the policy lesson from Hubbard Brook and from Swedish forest soils: a soil’s apparent resistance can hide a declining reserve that recovers only slowly.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Explore: same pH, different reserves


Soil B holds 14.2 cmolc/kg of exchangeable base cations, Soil A only 1.7. After 5.0 cmolc/kg of acid, Soil B still has 9.2 left; Soil A is buffering with aluminium.



Compare the two soils and add carbonate.

This is the inventory-depletion figure made interactive, using the two soils from the base saturation slide. Start with Soil B, then switch to Soil A at the same acid input: similar pH, but Soil A has already run out and aluminium is doing the buffering. Ask students to predict where the bases run out before pressing the preset. Then use the limed preset: each mole of CaCO3 adds two equivalents, and carbonate is spent first. Finally, raise CEC with fixed base cations to separate capacity from base saturation. Weathering, uptake and rates are left out, as in the figure. The exercise page has the model assumptions and a hand check.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Soil phases
minerals, organic matter, water, gas; soil water reflects exchange with all


Negative charge
permanent in clays (substitution); pH-dependent on organic matter


Cation exchange
2XNa + Ca²⁺ ⇌ X₂Ca + 2Na⁺; charge conserved, reversible


CEC
cmolc/kg; 1 cmolc = 0.01 mol charge; divide by ion charge for moles


Base saturation
base-cation charge / CEC; a solid property, does not fix pH


Acid response
carbonate → silicate weathering → exchange → aluminium


Carbonate
CaCO₃ consumes 2 eq H⁺ per mol; finite and access-limited


Aluminium
free Al³⁺ rises 1000× per pH unit; toxic to fish and roots


Leaching
cations leave with mobile anions such as SO₄²⁻


Transport
macropores, anions and colloids escape exchange



Next: Waste materials and leachate chemistry. Why does a mine waste heap keep producing acid for centuries? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Río Tinto, Spain: iron-stained stream bed from acid mine drainage. Photo: Carol Stoker, NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Recite the chain once. Soil solids carry negative charge, which holds cations. We count the capacity in charge units and convert to moles by dividing by the ion’s charge. Acid is consumed by finite inventories in turn: carbonate, weathering, exchange and then aluminium, with the released cation leaving together with sulfate. A soil’s pH does not reveal how much of its reserve remains, which is why Hubbard Brook and many Swedish streams recovered slowly. Finally, retention needs contact, so flow paths matter. The photo teases the next lecture. In mining waste, the chemistry runs the other way: the solid itself generates acid when air and water reach it, and the river turns red.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text: When oxygen runs low, why can iron, nitrogen, sulfur, and phosphorus change together even though not every element changes oxidation state?
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Learning goals

Balance a redox reaction using electron transfer.
Interpret electron-acceptor evidence without assuming a universal sequence.
Connect iron-phase changes to associated phosphate release.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Electron donors and acceptors
Organic matter can supply electrons as its carbon is oxidised. Electron acceptors such as O₂, nitrate, iron(III) solids, and sulfate are reduced. The oxidation and reduction half-reactions must transfer equal numbers of electrons. \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) is a useful carbon-oxidation bookkeeping form, not a claim that every substrate has that composition. Electron balance constrains possible stoichiometry; microbes and transport control the realised rate.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
A nitrogen contrast
Aerobic nitrification has net stoichiometry \[\mathrm{NH_4^++2O_2\rightarrow NO_3^-+2H^++H_2O}.\] Nitrogen is oxidised from −III to +V. In contrast, denitrification reduces nitrate to N₂; with a CH₂O donor one net form is \[\mathrm{4NO_3^-+5CH_2O+4H^+\rightarrow2N_2+5CO_2+7H_2O}.\] These net reactions omit biomass growth and intermediate pathways. Nitrification changes nitrogen form; denitrification can export nitrogen from water as gas.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Iron reduction changes a solid phase
text:
Iron reduction changes a solid phase
For goethite-like FeOOH, use the reduction half-reaction \[\mathrm{FeOOH(s)+3H^++e^-\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2H_2O}.\] The iron(III) solid becomes dissolved iron(II) under this simplified representation. If phosphate was retained on that solid, dissolving or restructuring it can release phosphate without changing phosphorus from oxidation state +V. Other solids, sorption sites, or precipitation reactions may retain some released solute.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Sulfur and strongly reducing conditions
Sulfate reduction can be written as \[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}+9H^++8e^-\rightarrow HS^-+4H_2O}.\] Sulfide can react with metals to form low-solubility solids, changing mobility again. Reduced sulfur can later reoxidise if oxygen returns. Thus anoxia does not mean every metal becomes permanently dissolved, and reoxygenation does not simply reverse every process at the same speed.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Interpret a redox sequence
A common conceptual progression is oxygen use, nitrate reduction, manganese/iron reduction, sulfate reduction, and methanogenesis. It is a guide to possible energy and availability constraints, not a universal timetable or a single set of pH-independent thresholds. Spatial microsites and transport allow processes to overlap. An electrode potential alone seldom identifies all active processes in a mixed natural sample; combine reactant loss with product formation and solid-phase evidence.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Worked example
In the supplied CH₂O–nitrate reaction, each nitrate N goes from +V to 0 and gains five electrons. Four nitrate ions therefore accept 20 electrons. Carbon goes from 0 in CH₂O to +IV in CO₂ and loses four electrons; five CH₂O units donate 20. Both sides contain 4 N, 5 C, 14 H, and 17 O atoms and have net charge zero. The donor ratio is 1.25 mol CH₂O carbon per mol nitrate in this model.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapters 10, 13, 15: balanced reactions and coupled carbon, nitrogen, iron, and sulfur examples.
USGS redox framework: Electron-acceptor patterns and the need for several indicators.
USGS organic-contaminant geochemistry: How organic inputs couple microbial electron transfer with changing water chemistry.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
1. Nitrification acid demand
Oxidise 0.100 mmol/L NH₄⁺ completely to nitrate using the supplied reaction. Find O₂ demand and H⁺ production.






Hint





Use the balanced coefficients 1:2:2.









Worked solution





O₂ demand = 0.200 mmol/L = 6.40 mg/L using 32.0 mg/mmol. H⁺ production = 0.200 mmol/L, corresponding to a 0.200 meq/L alkalinity decrease in the stated net model.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
2. Denitrification donor
Reduce 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate entirely to N₂ with the CH₂O model. Find organic carbon consumption and N₂ production.






Hint





Use five CH₂O and two N₂ for four nitrate.









Worked solution





Carbon consumption = 0.100 mmol C/L = 1.20 mg C/L using 12.0 mg/mmol. N₂ production = 0.0400 mmol/L. The carbon demand excludes biomass and alternative sinks.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
3. Check a half-reaction
Verify atoms and charge for FeOOH + 3 H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2 H₂O. What is reduced?






Hint





FeOOH contains one hydrogen and two oxygens.









Worked solution





Both sides have 1 Fe, 2 O, and 4 H. Left charge is +3 − 1 = +2, matching right charge. Fe(III) gains one electron to become Fe(II).
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
4. An anoxic sediment observation
Dissolved iron and phosphate rise while oxygen declines above a sediment. Give a coupled explanation and one reason it is not proven by correlation alone.






Hint





The carrier phase can change oxidation state while phosphate retains its own oxidation state.









Worked solution





Organic-matter oxidation can consume O₂ and support reduction of Fe(III) solids; associated phosphate can be released. Mixing, other mineral changes, and independent sources could also produce patterns. Use Fe(II), solid-phase, porewater, and time/flux observations to test the explanation.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
Explore: the electron-acceptor ladder
Predict the order in which oxygen, nitrate, iron(III) oxide and sulfate are used up as organic matter decomposes in a closed bottom water. When does phosphate first appear?


Reference case: 0.500 mmol C/L decomposed uses up 0.30 mmol/L O₂, 0.080 mmol/L nitrate and 0.20 mmol/L Fe(III) oxide, releasing 0.020 mmol/L phosphate and reducing 0.025 mmol/L sulfate.



E1. Choose Denitrification worked example. Check the carbon used and the N₂ formed against exercise 2.
E2. Choose Oxygen still present, then slowly raise the organic matter. At what amount of carbon is phosphate first released? Explain why the phosphate waits for oxygen and nitrate to run out, although phosphorus is never reduced.
E3. In Baltic bottom water, why does 2.00 mmol/L sulfate last so much longer than 0.20 mmol/L iron oxide? Use both the amounts and the electrons per acceptor. Then choose Low-sulfate lake water: what forms once sulfate is gone?

Model conditions and hand check
Each CH₂O carbon gives 4 electrons when it is oxidised to CO₂. O₂ takes 4 electrons, nitrate (to N₂) 5, Fe(III) (to Fe²⁺) 1 and sulfate (to HS⁻) 8. So the carbon needed is 1 mol C per mol O₂, 1.25 per mol nitrate, 0.25 per mol Fe(III) and 2 per mol sulfate. In the reference case, oxygen uses 0.300 mmol C/L, nitrate 0.100, and the iron oxide 0.050, a total of 0.450 mmol C/L. The remaining 0.050 mmol C/L reduces 0.025 mmol/L sulfate. For exercise 2, 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate needs 0.100 mmol C/L (1.20 mg C/L) and gives 0.0400 mmol/L N₂.
The starting amounts are constructed, per litre of bottom water, with the reactive iron oxide at the sediment surface counted in the same litre. The phosphate held on the oxide is set at 0.1 mol P per mol Fe and is all released as the oxide is reduced; none is sorbed again. Acceptors are used strictly in order. Manganese oxides, biomass growth, intermediates such as nitrite, and FeS formation are left out. Organic matter left after sulfate is gone forms CO₂ and methane (2 CH₂O → CO₂ + CH₄). Real sediments overlap the steps in space and time.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: Why PFAS do not go away
text:
Why PFAS do not go away

PFOS combines two unusual features: a fully fluorinated tail that hardly degrades, and an ionised head that keeps it in water. That combination makes it both persistent and mobile.

Show the structure and let students find the two parts. The tail is a chain of eight carbons, each carrying fluorine instead of hydrogen. Carbon–fluorine bonds are among the strongest in organic chemistry, and microbes have essentially no pathway to break this chain under environmental conditions. The tail repels both water and oils, which is exactly why these compounds are excellent in foams and coatings. The sulfonate head is a very strong acid, so in any natural water it is present as an anion. That is important for today. It means PFOS dissolves, moves with groundwater and does not simply stick to soil. Persistence plus mobility is what brought it to the Ronneby taps.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
A contrasting story: DDT


 DDT spraying in the US malaria eradication programme, 1958. Photo: CDC, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

DDT was the most widely used insecticide of the mid-20th century, in agriculture and against malaria mosquitoes.
Like PFOS it is persistent. Unlike PFOS it is neutral and very hydrophobic: it barely dissolves in water and collects in organic matter, sediments and fat.
Sweden banned most uses around 1970. DDT and its product DDE are still measurable in Baltic sediments and wildlife.
Two persistent compounds, two different destinations. Why?


DDT is the classic persistent organic pollutant and a useful contrast to PFAS. It was sprayed in huge quantities after the Second World War. Rachel Carson’s book Silent Spring in 1962 drew public attention to its effects on birds, and many countries banned agricultural use in the 1970s. Sweden was among the early countries to act. The key point for today is that DDT and PFOS share persistence but differ completely in where they end up. DDT goes to sediments, soil organic matter and the fatty tissue of animals. PFOS stays largely in water and binds to proteins. The difference comes from molecular properties we can describe with a few numbers. That is the rest of the lecture.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Where can a molecule go?

From water, a contaminant can sorb to solids, volatilise, be taken up by organisms, be exported, or be transformed. Only transformation changes the parent molecule. The others just move it.

This map organises the lecture. The central box is the dissolved parent compound. Four arrows move the same molecule to another phase or another place: sorption to particles and sediment, volatilisation to air, uptake into organisms, and export by flowing water. Each one lowers the dissolved concentration you would measure in a water sample, yet none destroys anything. Only the red arrow, transformation by microbes, sunlight or chemical reaction, changes the parent into products. This distinction will matter repeatedly. Today we quantify two arrows: sorption with a partition coefficient, and transformation with a first-order rate. Volatilisation and bioaccumulation use similar partition ideas, which we treat qualitatively.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Measuring phase preference: Kow




Shake a compound with octanol (an oily liquid standing in for fat and organic matter) and water. At equilibrium:
K_{ow}=\frac{C_\text{octanol}}{C_\text{water}}
The values span many orders of magnitude, so we use log Kow.

Polar groups (–OH, –COOH, charges) favour water: low Kow.
Large, nonpolar, chlorinated molecules favour octanol: high Kow.

Kow is a partition property. It is not a half-life and not a toxicity.


Octanol was chosen decades ago because it has a long hydrocarbon chain like lipids but one polar hydroxyl group, so it mimics the mixed environment of cell membranes and organic matter. In the picture, ten molecules sit in the octanol for every one in the water, so Kow is ten and log Kow is one. Real contaminants go far beyond that. Point out the warning in the last line. Students often assume a high Kow means a dangerous or persistent compound. Kow says only how the compound distributes between two liquids at equilibrium. It says nothing about how quickly the compound breaks down, or about what it does in an organism. Those are separate questions.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: The Kow scale for real compounds
text:
The Kow scale for real compounds

Each unit of log Kow is a factor of ten. DDT prefers octanol over water by roughly ten million to one. Ethanol slightly prefers water. Notice what is missing: PFOS has no meaningful Kow, because it is ionised and gathers at the oil–water interface.

These are rounded literature values, for orientation. Benzene, from petrol, has log Kow around two. The herbicide atrazine is similar, which is one reason it is found in groundwater. Naphthalene and lindane are in the middle. DDT is near seven, so it is about ten million times more concentrated in octanol than in water at equilibrium. That explains its accumulation in sediments and fat. PFOS is not on the scale. Surfactants sit at the boundary between phases instead of dissolving in one, so the octanol–water experiment does not give a useful number. This is a good example of a tool with clear limits. The next slide shows the other reason: ionisation.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Ionisation changes the problem




For an organic acid HA:
f_{HA}=\frac{1}{1+10^{\,\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}}
The same form as the carbonate fractions. For pKa = 4.50:

pH 4.50: neutral fraction 0.500
pH 6.50: 0.009901, about 1 %

The anion is far more water-loving. A Kow measured for the neutral form does not describe the total at pH 6.5.


This is exercise 2. The equation is the same Henderson–Hasselbalch logic as the carbonate unit, and students should recognise the shape of the curves. Each pH unit above the pKa reduces the neutral fraction tenfold. In most natural waters, between about pH 6 and 8.5, an organic acid with pKa 4.5 is almost entirely an anion. Many pesticides and pharmaceuticals are weak acids or bases, so their behaviour changes with pH. PFOS is an extreme case: its pKa is very low, so it is ionised everywhere in the environment. The neutral-form Kow then describes only a tiny fraction of the compound, and using it for the total would overestimate sorption badly.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Ionised does not mean unsorbed


Charged organic compounds still bind, but by different mechanisms:

Cations (many amine drugs, some pesticides) sit on cation exchange sites, as in the soil lecture.
Anions such as PFOS bind to proteins, to positively charged iron oxide surfaces, and at air–water interfaces.

So “ionised means mobile” is a tendency, not a rule.
Why PFOS ends up in blood, not fat: it binds to blood proteins such as albumin and is excreted slowly, over years.

 PFAS-containing foam on the Huron River, Michigan: surfactants gather at the air–water surface. Photo: MountainFae, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The notes warn against the rule that ionised compounds never sorb. Cationic organic compounds behave like the cations in last week’s lecture. They compete for negative exchange sites on clays and organic matter and can be held quite strongly. Anionic compounds avoid negatively charged surfaces but can bind to positively charged oxide surfaces at low pH, and to proteins. PFAS also concentrate at air–water interfaces, which matters in unsaturated soil; the river foam in the photo is a visible example. The last line connects to exposure. PFOS in humans binds to proteins in blood serum and is eliminated slowly, with half-lives of several years reported in the literature. That is why Ronneby residents still had elevated levels long after the clean water supply was restored.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: From Kow to sorption on soil: Kd = focKoc
text:
From Kow to sorption on soil: Kd = focKoc

For neutral hydrophobic compounds, the organic matter of a soil or sediment does the sorbing. Only that fraction counts. Two soils with the same compound can differ in Kd by a factor of 100.

Neutral hydrophobic molecules partition into organic matter much as they partition into octanol. The coefficient Koc describes this per kilogram of organic carbon and is a property of the compound. Multiplying by the organic-carbon fraction of a particular solid gives Kd for that solid. Exercise 1 does this: 0.02 times 5000 gives 100 litres per kilogram. The trap is units. A soil described as two percent organic carbon has foc 0.02, not 2. Using 2 gives a Kd a hundred times too high. Remind students of the conditions: this works for neutral compounds where organic matter dominates sorption. It is not valid for ions, for clean mineral surfaces, or for soot-like carbon.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: How much stays in the water?
text:
How much stays in the water?




At equilibrium, mass is shared between water and solid:
M = C_w V_w + C_s m_s,\qquad C_s = K_d C_w
C_w = \frac{M}{V_w + K_d\, m_s}
With 1.00 L water and 0.0100 kg solid:

U (Kd = 100): half in water, Cw = 0.500 mg/L
V (Kd = 10): 0.909 in water, Cw = 0.909 mg/L



This is the mass balance from the surfaces unit, applied to the fictitious compounds U and V from activity C. Each starts with one milligram of parent. The denominator is an effective volume: the water itself plus the amount of solid weighted by Kd. When Kd times the solid mass equals the water volume, half the compound is on each phase. That is U’s case: one hundred times 0.01 equals one. V has a ten times smaller Kd, so most of it stays in water. The figure shows the whole curve. Emphasise that sorption moves mass but does not remove it. The sorbed parent is still there and can return to the water if conditions change.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Persistence: a first-order rate




If transformation is first order with constant k and no new input:
M(t)=M_0\,e^{-kt},\qquad k=\frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}

U: t1/2 = 10 days. After 10, 20, 30 days: 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 mg.
V: t1/2 = 30 days.

The half-life describes how fast the parent disappears, under stated conditions. It says nothing about where the parent is.


First-order kinetics is the simplest persistence model. The rate of loss is proportional to the amount present, so each half-life removes half of what remains, regardless of the starting amount. Students have met this in radioactive decay. The half-lives here are stipulated for the fictitious compounds. Real half-lives depend strongly on conditions: temperature, oxygen, microbes, light and whether the compound is dissolved or sorbed. A pesticide may degrade in weeks in warm topsoil and persist for years in cold, anoxic groundwater. For PFOS, no relevant environmental degradation is known, so its effective half-life in groundwater is extremely long. Note again: the half-life is about identity, not location.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: Combining the two: the activity C model
text:
Combining the two: the activity C model

Assume rapid sorption equilibrium and the same k in both phases. Then the total decays exponentially and water concentration follows: C_w(t) = M(t)/(V_w + K_d m_s). V starts higher (less sorbed) and declines more slowly (longer half-life).

This is the model in fate.R. Two simplifications make it easy. First, sorption reaches equilibrium much faster than transformation, so the phase split stays constant. Second, the parent transforms at the same rate whether dissolved or sorbed, so the total follows one exponential. Water concentration is then just the total divided by the effective volume. The curves show two separate effects that are easy to confuse. V’s curve starts higher because V sorbs less. It falls more slowly because V persists longer. If only dissolved parent degraded, or exchange were slow, we would need a different kinetic model. The figure is a model prediction, not data, and the markers match the table in the exercise.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: Worked example: compound U at day 20
text:
Worked example: compound U at day 20




Start: 1.00 mg U, half on each phase, Cw = 0.500 mg/L.
After 20 days = two half-lives:

total parent: 1.00 × ¼ = 0.250 mg
water: 0.125 mg, so Cw = 0.125 mg/L
solid: 0.125 mg
transformed: 0.750 mg

The missing 0.750 mg is no longer U. It did not “go to the sediment”. What it became, the model does not say.


Work through the numbers from the notes. Two half-lives leave a quarter of the starting parent, 0.25 milligrams. The phase split is unchanged, so half is in water and half on the solid. The water concentration is 0.125 milligrams per litre, a quarter of the starting value. The three bands always add up to one milligram, which is the check students should do every time. The grey band is an accounting term. It records parent that has changed identity, nothing more. It is not a measured product, not proof that the compound was mineralised to carbon dioxide, and not a statement about toxicity. Exercise 3 extends this to day 30: total 0.125 milligrams and water 0.0625 milligrams per litre.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Check yourself


A soil has 3.0 % organic carbon. For Koc = 1000 L/kg OC, what is Kd?
An organic acid has pKa 4.50. Roughly what fraction is neutral at pH 7.0?
For U, double the solid mass to 0.0200 kg. What fraction of parent is now in water? Does the half-life change?
True or false: “Compound X has log Kow 6, so it will persist for decades.”



Answers. One: foc is 0.030, so Kd is 30 litres per kilogram. Two: pH 7 is 2.5 units above the pKa, so the neutral fraction is about one over 316, about 0.003. Three: the effective volume becomes 1 plus 100 times 0.02, which is 3 litres, so one third of the parent is in water. The half-life is unchanged in this model, because transformation acts equally in both phases. Changing Kd or the solid mass changes the split, not the persistence. That is exactly what the demo shows later. Four is false. Log Kow describes partitioning. Persistence needs a separate rate measurement. Some high-Kow compounds degrade quickly, and PFOS has no useful Kow at all but persists.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: A falling concentration is not a mechanism
text:
A falling concentration is not a mechanism

Three different processes give the same water result. To tell them apart, measure all phases (water, solid, gas) and look for products, with good analytical recovery, at matching times.

This is exercise 4. A water sample shows the parent concentration falling after sediment is added. Is it degrading? Not necessarily. In jar A, the parent simply moved to the sediment. In jar B, it became products. In jar C, it escaped to the headspace. Measuring only the water cannot separate these. The test is a mass balance: extract the solid and analyse it, trap or sample the gas, and look for expected products. Recoveries matter, because sorbed compounds are often harder to extract, and a poor extraction can look like degradation. Log Kow alone cannot answer the question, because it describes a preference, not a process that happened.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Transformation is not mineralisation

A disappearing parent can leave products that are more persistent or just as harmful. Only complete mineralisation to CO₂, water and inorganic ions removes the problem.

Two examples make this concrete. DDT loses hydrogen chloride to form DDE. DDE is more persistent than DDT in many environments and was the main cause of eggshell thinning in birds of prey. So the decline of DDT in an ecosystem did not mean the problem was solving itself. PFAS have a similar story. Some foams contained precursor compounds, which microbes or oxidation convert to terminal perfluoroalkyl acids such as PFOS and PFOA. These do not break down further under environmental conditions, so precursor transformation increases the amount of the most persistent products. The lesson: always ask what the products are before treating parent loss as good news.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: Partitioning into organisms: the sea eagle
text:
Partitioning into organisms: the sea eagle


 White-tailed eagles in Färnebofjärden National Park, Sweden. Photo: LG Nyqvist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Hydrophobic, persistent compounds partition into fat. Each step of a food chain eats much more than it retains, so concentrations rise up the chain: biomagnification.
Around the Baltic, white-tailed eagles at the top of the chain had very poor breeding success in the 1960s and 70s. DDE and PCBs were the main causes.
After bans on DDT and PCB, contaminant levels fell and the eagle population recovered. A clear case where chemistry explained, and policy fixed, a problem.


This brings partitioning into biology. An organism is partly an oily phase, so a compound with high Kow that is not metabolised accumulates in fat. Predators eat many prey and keep the persistent fraction, so concentrations increase at each level. In the Baltic the white-tailed eagle declined dramatically. Studies linked the reproductive failure to DDE and PCBs. Conservation work, including winter feeding with uncontaminated food, helped the remaining birds, but the long-term recovery followed the bans of DDT and PCBs and the gradual decline of these compounds in Baltic fish. Today the species is much more common again. It is a good story of chemistry, monitoring and policy working together.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
section: Back to Ronneby: putting the properties together
text:
Back to Ronneby: putting the properties together

Each step follows from a property: ionised, so weakly sorbed in low-carbon sand; not degraded, so it accumulates and travels for years; protein-binding, so it stays in people. A DDT-like compound would have stayed near the source.

Return to the opening question and answer it with today’s tools. Foam was used repeatedly on a training ground. The PFAS were ionised and the sandy soils contained little organic carbon, so sorption was weak and the compounds reached groundwater. With no relevant degradation pathway, a first-order half-life is effectively infinite, so the compounds accumulated and moved with groundwater toward the wells. The waterworks pumped them into the drinking water. In people, PFOS binds to serum proteins and is excreted slowly, so blood levels stayed high for years. Contrast with DDT: neutral and hydrophobic, it would have sorbed to soil organic matter near the source. Different properties, different destinations, different exposure routes.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Four separate questions








Question
Property or measurement
Example




Where does it go?
Kow, Kd = focKoc, pKa, volatility
DDT to sediment; PFOS stays in water


How long does it last?
half-life under stated conditions
U: 10 days; PFOS: no known degradation


Who is exposed?
pathway: water, food, air, soil
Ronneby: drinking water


What does it do?
toxicity, measured separately
DDE: eggshell thinning



A strong answer to one question never answers another. High Kow is not toxicity; low concentration in water is not low risk.

This table is the conceptual summary of the lecture and a template for exam answers. Partitioning tells you where a compound will be found. Persistence tells you how long it lasts. Exposure depends on where people or organisms meet the compound. Effect depends on biology and needs toxicity data. Many weak arguments merge these. For example, a low concentration in water may hide a large amount in sediment or fish. A short half-life may hide a toxic product. Ask students to apply the four questions to a compound they know, such as a pharmaceutical in wastewater, and say which they could answer from today’s numbers and which need new data.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Gone from the water means destroyed.” It may be sorbed, volatilised or taken up.
“High Kow means toxic” or “means persistent.” Kow is a partition property only.
“Ionised means it never sorbs.” Cations exchange; anions bind proteins and oxides.
“foc = 2 for 2 % organic carbon.” It is 0.02. A factor-100 error.
“Changing Kd changes the half-life.” In our model it changes only the phase split.
“Parent lost = problem solved.” Ask what the products are.


Run through these as a self-test. The first and last are the conceptual errors that matter most in environmental decisions. The fifth is the one the demo is built to expose. In the activity C model, transformation acts equally on both phases, so moving mass between them does not change how fast the total declines. In a real system where only dissolved parent degrades, stronger sorption would actually slow transformation, but that is a different model with different assumptions. Ask students to say which assumption they would change to make Kd affect persistence. Then move to the interactive demo, which lets them test each statement directly.

text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Fate map
sorption, volatilisation, uptake, export move the parent; only transformation changes it


Kow

Ionisation
f_{HA}=1/(1+10^{\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}); ions need their own sorption model


Sorption

Phase split
C_w=M/(V_w+K_d m_s); U: half in water, V: 0.909

Products
DDT → DDE; PFAS precursors → PFOS, PFOA; parent loss is not mineralisation


PFOS

Four questions

Next: Connecting air, catchments, and water. One catchment, all the course’s chemistry at once. Then the exercises, the notes and activity C.

 Cyanobacteria (Nodularia) bloom in the Baltic Sea, August 2015, false colour. Image: NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Recite the chain once. For any contaminant, first ask where it goes: partition coefficients and ionisation answer that, within their conditions. Then ask how long it lasts: a rate under stated conditions. Combine them with a mass balance, as in activity C, and keep every milligram accounted for. A falling water concentration needs evidence from all phases before it is called degradation, and degradation needs a look at the products. Ronneby and the Baltic eagles show the same tools explaining real events. The image previews the final lecture. Blooms in the Baltic are fed partly by phosphate released from sediments when oxygen runs out, which ties together redox, nutrients and catchment budgets.

text:
The CSV supplies fictitious neutral compounds U and V for a deterministic teaching model. It is not an experimental dataset. Constants are stipulated rather than estimated from observations. The script generates daily time values from 0 to 60 days. It calculates k_per_day = log(2) / half_life_days, the dimensionless remaining fraction, total parent mass in mg, water concentration in mg/L, solid concentration in mg/kg, both phase inventories in mg, and transformed-parent mass in mg.
Rapid equilibrium with fixed Kd and the same transformation coefficient in both phases permit the simple total-parent exponential. There is no input, export, volatilisation, changing volume, or product tracking. A slower exchange or a phase-specific degradation coefficient needs a different model. title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
About this lecture


When acid rain fell on southern Scandinavia, brown trout and salmon disappeared from many lakes and rivers. Researchers found that the acid itself was often not the main killer. The fish died from aluminium, washed out of the soil by the acid.
Yet in brown, humic lakes with the same pH and the same aluminium, fish often survived.
Today you will learn to:

see that a dissolved total is not the free ion;
describe complexation and hydrolysis, and tell them apart from redox;
use a one-ligand model to find the free metal;
test mineral saturation with the free ion, not the total.

Last lecture showed that dissolved organic matter carries binding groups. Today we use them.

 Brown trout (Salmo trutta), a species lost from many acidified Scandinavian lakes. Photo: Sam Stukel, USFWS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Start with the story. In the acid-rain decades, fish populations collapsed across southern Norway and Sweden. Field and laboratory work showed that aluminium, mobilised from soils by the acid, was a main cause of fish death, often more important than the low pH itself. Then add the twist that makes this a speciation lecture: in brown, humic lakes, fish often survived at the same pH and the same measured aluminium. The total was the same, so something else differed. That something is the chemical form of the metal. Remind students that the previous lecture introduced dissolved organic matter and its carboxyl and phenol groups. Today those groups become ligands.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Same total, different danger

Two constructed lakes have the same pH (5.0) and the same total dissolved aluminium. In the clear lake, most aluminium is present as small inorganic ions. In the brown lake, most is held by dissolved organic matter.
Question for this lecture: how can the same total hide such different chemistry, and how do we calculate the part that matters?

Present this as the puzzle that the rest of the lecture solves. The numbers are constructed but realistic: an acidified lake at pH 5 can carry several micromoles per litre of aluminium. Both lakes would give the same number on a standard laboratory report of filtered aluminium. The difference is what the aluminium is bound to. In the clear lake, the aluminium is mostly the hydrated ion and its first hydrolysis products. In the brown lake, organic matter binds most of it. Ask students to predict which lake is more dangerous for fish, and why. Most will guess correctly. The task today is to make that intuition quantitative.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
What does “dissolved metal” contain?

“Dissolved” usually means whatever passes a 0.45 µm filter. It is an operational definition. The filtrate holds the free ion, several kinds of complexes and even small colloids. One number sums them all.

Walk through the figure from left to right. The laboratory filters the sample, often through 0.45 micrometres, and reports everything in the filtrate as dissolved. That number is useful for mass balances. It does not tell you which species are present. The free aqua ion, hydroxo complexes, inorganic complexes with chloride, sulfate, carbonate or fluoride, complexes with organic matter, and nanoparticles small enough to pass the filter all count. For aluminium in acid waters, fluoride and organic complexes are important. When you read a metal concentration in a report, ask: which fraction is this, and which species might it contain? The rest of the lecture gives you tools to estimate the split.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: A metal ion in water is already a complex
text:
A metal ion in water is already a complex

A dissolved Al³⁺ ion is surrounded by six water molecules. Each donates an electron pair to the metal: the waters are ligands, the whole unit is a complex. Another ligand can replace a water (complexation), or a bound water can lose H⁺ (hydrolysis). In both cases aluminium stays at +III.

This picture is the foundation of the lecture. Writing Al3+ is shorthand. In water the ion is really hexaaqua-aluminium, with six water molecules arranged around it in an octahedron. The metal is an electron-pair acceptor, the water molecules are electron-pair donors. Two things can now happen. Another ligand, such as fluoride or a carboxylate group, can push out a water: complexation. Or a bound water can give up a proton to the solution, leaving a hydroxide ligand on the metal: hydrolysis. The highly charged metal pulls electron density from the water, which makes its protons easier to lose. Neither change involves electron transfer to or from the metal.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Ligands that compete with water

Natural waters offer inorganic ligands that bind with one atom, and organic ligands that can bind with two or more. A ligand that grips the metal with two arms forms a ring, a chelate. Chelates usually bind much more strongly. Dissolved organic matter carries many such groups.

Give the cast of ligands. Hydroxide, chloride, fluoride, sulfate and carbonate are common inorganic ligands. Each binds through one atom. Oxalate is a small organic example that binds through two oxygen atoms and closes a five-membered ring with the metal. That ring makes the complex much more stable, which is called the chelate effect. Humic and fulvic substances, the bulk of dissolved organic matter, carry many carboxyl and phenol groups. Pairs of neighbouring groups can act like chelating ligands. Their binding depends on pH, because the groups must lose their protons before they bind well, and on competition from other metals such as calcium. This is why the brown lake could hold most of its aluminium.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Four ways a metal changes form
text:
Four ways a metal changes form

Complexation, hydrolysis and precipitation all keep the oxidation state. Only redox moves electrons. Each process can change how mobile a metal is, so a change in mobility is not evidence of redox by itself.

Students often call every change in a metal “oxidation” or “reaction”. Separate four processes clearly. Complexation exchanges ligands. Hydrolysis is a special case where water itself becomes hydroxide by losing a proton. Precipitation forms a new solid phase. Redox transfers electrons and changes the oxidation state, as when iron(II) becomes iron(III). Only the last one changes the oxidation state, but all four can change whether a metal travels with water. Sorption to surfaces, the topic of the next lecture, is a fifth process that also keeps the oxidation state. When you explain a field observation, name the process and check whether an oxidation state actually changed.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
A one-ligand model


For one complex, \mathrm{M+L\rightleftharpoons ML}:
\beta=\frac{[\mathrm{ML}]}{[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{L}]}
The metal balance is M_T=[\mathrm{M}]+[\mathrm{ML}]=[\mathrm{M}](1+\beta[\mathrm{L}]), so
[\mathrm{M}]=\frac{M_T}{1+\beta[\mathrm{L}]}
Here [L] is the free ligand. The product β[L] decides the split: at β[L] = 1, half the metal is free.




This is the one calculation model of the lecture. We keep only two metal species, the free ion M and one complex ML. The constant beta has units of litres per mole, so beta times the free ligand concentration is dimensionless. Write the mass balance for the metal, factor out the free metal, and divide. The curve shows the free fraction, one divided by one plus beta L, against free ligand on a log axis. Point out the midpoint at beta L equal to one, and that one more factor of ten in ligand leaves only about nine percent free. The constants are concentration-based teaching values; activity corrections are ignored in dilute water.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Worked example: how much metal is free?
text:
Worked example: how much metal is free?


A fictitious metal: MT = 2.00 µmol/L, β = 1.00 × 10⁶ L/mol, free ligand [L] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

β[L] = 10⁶ × 10⁻⁵ = 10.0
[M] = 2.00 / (1 + 10.0) = 0.1818 µmol/L
[ML] = 2.00 − 0.1818 = 1.818 µmol/L

Check: 0.1818 + 1.818 = 2.00. Nothing was lost.
With ten times less ligand, β[L] = 1.00 and the metal splits 1.00 : 1.00.




Do the calculation slowly with the class. First form the dimensionless product: ten. Then divide the total by eleven to get the free metal, 0.1818 micromoles per litre. The complex is the rest. Always close the balance: free plus complexed must return the total you started with. The right-hand bar is exercise 1: reduce the free ligand tenfold and the product becomes one, so the metal is split evenly. The total metal is identical in both bars, but the free metal differs by a factor of five and a half. Connect this to the opening: a laboratory total of two micromoles per litre would look the same in both cases.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Check the ligand before you trust the answer
text:
Check the ligand before you trust the answer




The model asks for free ligand. That is safe only if the ligand is in large excess, so binding hardly uses it up.
Suppose total ligand LT is only 0.500 µmol/L. A claim of 1.818 µmol/L ML is then impossible: each ML uses one ligand. At most 0.500 µmol/L can be complexed, and at least 1.50 µmol/L of metal stays outside ML.
When ligand is scarce, write a second balance, L_T=[\mathrm{L}]+[\mathrm{ML}], and solve both together.


This is exercise 2 and an important habit. The simple formula hides an approximation: it treats the free ligand concentration as known and fixed. That works when ligand is plentiful compared with the metal, for example organic matter in a brown lake. When the ligand is scarce, the complex uses it up and the free ligand falls. A quick bookkeeping check catches the error. Every complex contains one ligand, so the complex can never exceed the total ligand. If someone substitutes the total ligand for the free ligand without checking, they can overestimate binding. Solving the coupled balances exactly is beyond today, but recognising the impossible answer is required.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Hydrolysis makes metal ions acids


 Río Tinto, Huelva, Spain. Photo: David Mata Verdejo, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

\mathrm{[Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+}\rightleftharpoons[Al(H_2O)_5OH]^{2+}+H^+}
The more charged and smaller the ion, the more strongly it pulls on its water, and the easier the proton leaves. For Al³⁺ the pKa is about 5. For Fe³⁺ it is about 2.
Spain’s Río Tinto drains sulfide ores that have been mined for thousands of years. Its water has a pH near 2 and carries iron(III), whose hydrolysis products colour the river red.


Hydrolysis means a metal ion behaves like a weak acid. Hexaaqua-aluminium has a first acid constant near ten to the minus five, similar to acetic acid. Iron(III) is a much stronger acid, with a pK near 2. This explains two everyday observations. Solutions of iron(III) or aluminium salts are acidic, which matters again in the water-treatment lecture, when we add these salts as coagulants. And when acidic, iron-rich water meets less acidic conditions, iron hydrolyses further and precipitates as red and orange oxyhydroxides. The Río Tinto is an extreme natural and mining-affected example, with very low pH. The colours are iron(III) species and their precipitates. Notice that hydrolysis releases protons: the water becomes more acidic as the metal hydrolyses.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Why acid water carries so much aluminium
text:
Why acid water carries so much aluminium

In equilibrium with solid Al(OH)₃, dissolved aluminium is lowest near pH 6. Below that, every pH unit raises Al³⁺ a thousandfold, because the solid takes up three H⁺. In this model, pH 5 water holds about thirty times more Al than at the minimum.

This is the key aluminium figure. Dissolving aluminium hydroxide uses three protons per aluminium, so the free Al3+ concentration in equilibrium with the solid rises by a factor of one thousand for each unit drop in pH. That is the steep red line. At high pH the solid dissolves instead as the aluminate anion. The total, the black curve, has a minimum near pH 6. The constants are approximate, and real soils hold aluminium in several solids and on clay exchange sites, so read the shape rather than exact numbers. The message for the lakes is clear. Acidification from pH 6.5 to 5 moves the water from the bottom of the curve onto the steep acid branch. Aluminium that stayed in the soil now comes out with the water.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Test saturation with the free ion
text:
Test saturation with the free ion


For a fictitious hydroxide, \mathrm{M(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons M^{2+}+2OH^-}:
[\mathrm{M^{2+}}]_{sat}=\frac{K_{sp}}{[\mathrm{OH^-}]^2}
With Ksp = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁶ and pH 9 ([OH⁻] = 10⁻⁵ mol/L): [M²⁺]sat = 1.00 µmol/L.
A water holds 10.0 µmol/L total with β[L] = 9.00. Free M = 10.0 / 10.0 = 1.00 µmol/L: exactly saturated.
Using the total would wrongly suggest a tenfold excess.

 Gibbsite, Al(OH)₃, the natural aluminium hydroxide mineral (museum specimen). Photo: TheUltimateGrass, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.


This is exercise 3. The solubility product only contains free ions, because only free M2+ and hydroxide take part in the equilibrium with the solid. Complexed metal is dissolved, but it is not M2+. First compute the free saturation concentration: ten to the minus sixteen divided by ten to the minus ten gives one micromole per litre. Then compute the free metal in the sample from the binding model. Ten divided by one plus nine is one, so the water is exactly at saturation. If you had compared the total, ten, with the saturation value, you would have predicted heavy precipitation that does not happen. The photo shows gibbsite, the real mineral form of aluminium hydroxide.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Complexation raises the dissolved total

At saturation the free ion is fixed by Ksp and pH. Each line adds complexed metal on top: dissolved total = [M²⁺]sat × (1 + β[L]). A strong ligand lets far more metal stay in solution beside the same solid.

Turn the previous result into a general picture. For each pH, the solid fixes the free ion. The complex adds more dissolved metal in proportion to beta L. With beta L equal to 99, the water can hold one hundred times more metal in solution than without ligand, even though the free ion is the same. This is why organic-rich waters often carry high dissolved iron and aluminium. It also explains why the brown lake can have the same total aluminium as the clear lake while having much less free aluminium. The lines fall steeply with pH because hydroxide is squared. The figure ignores hydrolysis and precipitation kinetics; it compares equilibrium states only.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Check yourself

Use the one-ligand model and the saturation rule.

MT = 5.0 µmol/L and β[L] = 4.0. What are free M and ML?
A report says “dissolved copper 3 µg/L”. Name three forms that could make up this number.
Iron changes from a dissolved complex to a solid hydroxide. Is this redox?
Two waters at pH 9 contain 10 µmol/L total M. One has β[L] = 0, the other β[L] = 9. Which is supersaturated with M(OH)₂?



Answers. One: free M is 5 divided by 5, so 1.0 micromole per litre, and ML is 4.0. Two: any three of the free aqua ion, hydroxo or carbonate complexes, organic complexes, and small colloids that pass the filter. Three: not necessarily. If iron stays iron(III), this is precipitation, not redox. Only if the oxidation state changes is it redox. Four: the water without ligand. Its free metal is 10 micromoles per litre, ten times the saturation value of one. The other water has a free metal of exactly one, so it is just saturated. Ask students to say which numbers they needed for each answer.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Back to the lakes: how aluminium harms fish
text:
Back to the lakes: how aluminium harms fish

Acid input dissolves aluminium from soil minerals and clays. Runoff carries inorganic Al to the stream. At the fish gill the water is less acidic, so aluminium hydrolyses and deposits on the gill surface, disturbing salt balance and breathing.

Now we can explain the opening story. Acid deposition supplies protons to the soil. They dissolve aluminium hydroxides and exchange aluminium off clay minerals, exactly the steep branch of the solubility curve. Runoff delivers inorganic aluminium to streams and lakes, often in pulses during snowmelt. The gill is the critical site. The fish’s gill surface has a different, typically higher pH than the acidic water, so the inorganic aluminium hydrolyses and polymerises right there and binds to the gill. Fish then lose control of their salt balance and have trouble taking up oxygen. Speak of a main mechanism rather than the only one; low pH itself also stresses fish. Aluminium bound to organic matter is far less able to do this.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Why the brown lake was safer
text:
Why the brown lake was safer


Return to the two lakes. Use the model with the lake numbers, treating organic matter as one ligand with β[L] ≈ 10 (constructed):

clear lake: β[L] ≈ 0, so nearly all 6 µmol/L Al is inorganic;
brown lake: free fraction = 1/11, about 0.5 µmol/L inorganic Al.

Same total, about ten times less of the harmful form.
Biological effect also depends on the organism, calcium and other ions. The model compares chemistry, not risk.




Close the loop with the same model we used for the fictitious metal. Treat organic matter as a single ligand with beta L of about ten; that is a constructed value chosen to show the effect, not a measured constant for humic aluminium. In the clear lake there is almost no organic ligand, so the six micromoles per litre are essentially all inorganic. In the brown lake one eleventh remains inorganic, about half a micromole per litre. The figure shows where each lake sits on the free-fraction curve. Stress the limits. Real toxicity depends on calcium, which protects gills, on fish species and life stage, and on fluoride and other complexes. The model ranks the lakes chemically; it does not predict how many fish die.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: A filtered metal rises as pH falls
text:
A filtered metal rises as pH falls

The oxidation state stays the same, so redox is not needed. Acid can desorb metal from particles, dissolve a metal-bearing solid, or protonate a ligand and shift the binding. Each mechanism predicts a different measurement.

This is exercise 4 and a typical exam question. Students should first rule out the assumption that something was oxidised or reduced, because the oxidation state was measured and stayed the same. Then list mechanisms that do not involve electron transfer. Protons compete with metal ions for surface sites, so acid pushes metal off particles. Protons dissolve hydroxides and carbonates, as in the aluminium curve. Protons also bind to the carboxyl and phenol groups of organic ligands, which weakens their hold on the metal. A good answer names a test for each: metal on the particles, the solid phase, and free versus total metal together with organic carbon. Correlation with pH alone cannot tell the three apart.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Metals from mines: a Swedish legacy
text:
Metals from mines: a Swedish legacy


 Stora Stöten, the great pit of the Falun copper mine, Sweden. Photo: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Copper was mined at Falun for about a thousand years. Today the mine is a World Heritage Site.
When sulfide ore meets air and water, it oxidises and releases acid and dissolved metals. Downstream, as the water is neutralised, iron and aluminium hydrolyse and precipitate as orange and white solids.
Those fresh solids have large, reactive surfaces that bind copper, zinc and lead. That is the next lecture.


Bring the chemistry home to Sweden. The Falun mine produced much of Europe’s copper in the seventeenth century, and its waste rock and slag still release metals to local waters. The red Falu paint used on Swedish houses is made from iron-rich mine residues, a reminder of how much iron oxide such sites produce. The chain is the same as in the Río Tinto. Oxidation of sulfide minerals produces sulfuric acid, which keeps metals dissolved. As the drainage mixes with other water, the pH rises, iron and aluminium hydrolyse, and their hydroxides precipitate. Those precipitates bind other metals on their surfaces, which can retain them or carry them downstream. Note that sulfide oxidation is redox, but the precipitation that follows is not.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Dissolved means free.” A filtered total includes complexes and small colloids.
“The metal changed form, so it was oxidised.” Complexation, hydrolysis and precipitation keep the oxidation state.
“Put total ligand into β[L].” The model needs free ligand; check that ligand is in excess.
“Compare the total with Ksp.” Saturation is tested with the free ion.
“Bound metal is harmless.” A dissolved complex can still travel, and it can release metal if conditions change.
“A free-ion calculation predicts toxicity.” It compares chemistry; biological effect needs more information.


These are the errors seen most often in exercises on this topic. Go through them and ask students to explain each correction in their own words, ideally with an example from today. The second one is the most persistent: students see colour changes or precipitates and call them oxidation. The fifth is subtle. Complexation can lower the free ion and reduce immediate toxicity, but a mobile complex can carry metal far downstream, where a change in pH or competition can release it again. The last reminds us that the free-ion idea is a good chemical guide, but toxicity depends on the organism, on competing ions such as calcium, and on exposure time.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Dissolved total
operational (filter); includes free ion, complexes, small colloids


Aqua ion
a metal ion in water is a complex with water ligands


Complexation
ligand replaces water; oxidation state unchanged


Chelate
ligand with two or more binding atoms; binds more strongly


One-ligand model
[\mathrm{M}]=M_T/(1+\beta[\mathrm{L}]), with free L in excess


Ligand check
ML can never exceed LT


Hydrolysis
bound water loses H⁺; Al³⁺ pKa ≈ 5, Fe³⁺ ≈ 2


Al solubility
lowest near pH 6; rises steeply in acid water


Saturation
compare the free ion with Ksp/[OH⁻]²


Acid lakes
inorganic Al harms fish gills; organic binding lowers it



Next: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption. Where do metals go when they leave the water? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Iron oxyhydroxides (limonite and goethite). Photo: Darla Sondrol, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.


The table is the revision sheet. Read the chain once more. A dissolved total is a sum of forms. The free ion is the part that takes part in mineral equilibria and that many organisms respond to most directly. Ligands, including dissolved organic matter, lower the free ion while keeping metal in solution. Hydrolysis and acidity control aluminium and iron. For the acid lakes, low pH released inorganic aluminium, and organic matter offered protection. The teaser photo shows iron oxyhydroxides, the orange solids that form when iron hydrolyses. Their surfaces bind metals, phosphate and organic molecules. The next lecture asks whether a metal that leaves the water has been removed, or has only moved onto a particle.

title: Week 5 demo: the connected catchment budget
text:
Model conditions
This is a constructed annual equivalent budget, not a dynamic lake model. Accessible capacity caps how much of the added acid can react; unused capacity is not credited as extra alkalinity. Residual acidity is subtracted from an explicitly supplied reference annual alkalinity export. The other terms stay fixed when one slider changes. A real change in water flow could also alter weathering, transport, and retention. A pH prediction requires inorganic carbon, gas exchange, and appropriate acid–base constraints. Use the closed-water demo for the separate pulse problem.

title: Week 5 demo: the connected catchment budget

Questions to try

Choose Worked binding case. Confirm that free plus complexed metal equals 2.00 µmol/L.

title: Week 3 demo: metal binding and saturation
text:
Hand check and static reference
For one complex, free M = total M / (1 + β[L]free), with β = 10⁶ L/mol. At total M = 2.00 µmol/L and free L = 10.0 µmol/L, β[L] is 10, giving 0.1818 µmol/L free M and 1.818 µmol/L complexed M.
At pH 9.00, hydroxide is 10⁻⁵ mol/L in the supplied approximation. With Ksp = 10⁻¹⁶, the saturation free-metal concentration is 1.00 µmol/L. At total M = 10.0 and free L = 9.00 µmol/L, that free concentration gives Ω = 1. Removing ligand at the same total gives Ω = 10.

The curves describe binding before any mineral reaction. A supersaturated state may favour precipitation, but the demo does not calculate precipitation, dissolution, rates, or a new equilibrium total. Hydrolysis, ligand protonation, competing ligands, and biological effects are omitted.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
One catchment, the whole course

Every unit appears here: deposition brings acid, soils neutralise most of it, carbonate chemistry sets the lake’s alkalinity and pH, metals follow pH, redox controls the sediment, and contaminants partition between water and sediment.

This is the map for today. It is a constructed teaching catchment of one square kilometre, the same one used in the deposition unit. Each numbered thread is a unit you have studied. We follow the threads in order. First, acid from the air. Second, the soils, which consume most of it. Third, the lake, where we convert an annual budget to an alkalinity. Fourth, aluminium and metals, which depend on how well the first three balance. Fifth, a separate set of sediment observations and a redox hypothesis. Sixth, the contaminant model from activity C. Keep asking at each step: what is measured, what is assumed, and what boundary does the number refer to?

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Thread 1: from smokestack to acid input
text:
Thread 1: from smokestack to acid input


 A coal-fired power station (Huntley Station, New York). Photo: Ken Lund, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

SO₂ and NOx are oxidised in air to sulfuric and nitric acid, then deposited wet or dry.
Deposition unit, worked example:

HNO₃: 0.0200 mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ × 1 eq/mol
H₂SO₄: 0.0100 mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ × 2 eq/mol
total: 0.0400 eq m⁻² yr⁻¹

Over 1.00 × 10⁶ m²: 40 000 eq/year of acid.
Counting in equivalents lets us add acids of different charge.


Recall the deposition unit. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are precursors; oxidation in gas and droplets turns them into sulfuric and nitric acid. Sulfuric acid supplies two equivalents per mole, nitric acid one. Multiplying the flux per square metre by the catchment area gives the annual input. Remind students of the caveat from that unit: deposited sulfate does not always arrive as free acid. Ammonia can neutralise it in the air, and ammonium deposition can later generate acidity through nitrification. In our budget we use the stated convention that all of it counts as acid. The power station photo is a reminder that this budget starts with fuel chemistry, and that cutting sulfur emissions was the effective long-term remedy.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Close the annual budget




\text{residual}=\text{input}-\text{neutralised}
40 000 − 30 000 = 10 000 eq/year
Convert to a flow-weighted concentration with the annual water export:
\frac{10\,000\ \text{eq/yr}}{5.00\times10^{8}\ \text{L/yr}}=2.00\times10^{-5}\ \text{eq/L}
= 0.0200 meq/L
Work in annual amounts first, then divide by water.


This is exercise 1, part one. The neutralisation term, 30 000 equivalents per year, is stipulated in this teaching budget. In a real catchment it would be estimated from weathering rates, changes in soil exchangeable cations and stream chemistry, each with uncertainty. The order of operations matters. First close the balance in annual amounts, where addition and subtraction are valid. Only then divide by the annual water volume. The units cancel to equivalents per litre, and multiplying by a thousand gives milliequivalents. Warn against a common shortcut: do not silently add an unmeasured retention or biological term to make a budget match an observation. If a budget does not close, that is information.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Thread 2: where the 30 000 eq went

The soil lecture’s three pathways: carbonate dissolution, cation exchange, and aluminium release. Exchange and weathering supply base cations, which leave with sulfate. Each pathway draws on a finite inventory.

Bring back the soil lecture. Most of the acid entering a catchment never reaches the lake as acid, because soils neutralise it. In a granite catchment without carbonate, the main terms are silicate weathering, which is slow, and cation exchange, which is fast but finite. The calcium and magnesium released leave in drainage together with sulfate, so stream chemistry records the process: base cations and sulfate rise together. At Hubbard Brook this is what depleted the soil’s exchangeable calcium. The budget treats 30 000 equivalents per year as fixed. A key exam idea is that this term is not a constant of nature. It declines as the exchanger is depleted, which is why the residual acid can grow even when deposition is constant.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: An annual budget is not a pulse
text:
An annual budget is not a pulse


The carbonate lecture added a single acid dose to a closed beaker: alkalinity fell by the dose, CT stayed fixed, and a pH followed.
The catchment budget is different:

it is a flux over a year, spread over 5.00 × 10⁸ L of water;
the water exchanges CO₂ with air and soil;
the lake is continuously flushed and replaced.

0.0200 meq/L is a flow-weighted annual average, not the result of pouring acid into a lake.


Same units, different meanings

eq/year: an amount per time (budget)
meq/L: a concentration (after dividing by water)
pH: a present state (needs CT and CO₂)

Before combining two numbers, check that they refer to the same boundary and time.



Students often carry the carbonate lecture’s model into the catchment without noticing that the boundary has changed. Water A and Water B were closed: nothing entered or left except the acid dose. A lake is an open, flushed system. Its water is replaced over its residence time, it exchanges carbon dioxide with the air, and inflow chemistry varies with season and flow. The annual budget averages over all of that. It is useful for comparing catchments and scenarios, but it does not tell you the pH on any particular day. The box is a checklist students can use in the exam: ask what kind of quantity each number is before you add, subtract or compare it.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Thread 3: alkalinity needs a reference




“Lower alkalinity” only means something compared with a reference.
Suppose that without the added acid, the catchment would export 50 000 eq/year of alkalinity: 0.100 meq/L.
The residual acid consumes alkalinity one-for-one:
50 000 − 10 000 = 40 000 eq/year = 0.0800 meq/L
As in the carbonate lecture, strong acid lowers alkalinity by exactly its amount in equivalents.


This is exercise 1, part two. The reference alkalinity export is stipulated, and it must be stated explicitly. Without a reference, a statement like the lake lost alkalinity has no number attached to it. The logic is the same as the carbonate lecture’s strong-acid rule: each equivalent of strong acid removes one equivalent of alkalinity. Here we apply it to annual amounts and then divide by water. The third bar anticipates the worked example: if the soils neutralised less, the alkalinity export would be lower. Ask students to connect this to the granite and limestone lakes from week 2: a granite catchment starts with a small reference alkalinity, so the same residual acid takes a much larger fraction of it.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Alkalinity alone does not give a pH
text:
Alkalinity alone does not give a pH




Model: carbonate system in equilibrium with a given CO₂ pressure, 25 °C, constants from the carbonate reference sheet.
With AT = 0.0800 meq/L:

in equilibrium with air: pH ≈ 7.1
with 10 × air CO₂, typical of soil water and groundwater: pH ≈ 6.1

Same alkalinity, one pH unit apart. To get a pH you need AT and CT or the CO₂ pressure.


This slide proves the notes’ warning with a calculation. For a fixed alkalinity, the pH depends on how much dissolved carbon dioxide is present, which depends on gas exchange. Stream water fed by groundwater is often supersaturated in carbon dioxide because soil respiration raises its partial pressure, so its pH is lower than the same water after it degasses in a lake. The two lines show that the difference between our base case and the reference alkalinity changes pH by only about 0.1 units at fixed CO2, much less than the effect of CO2 itself. The model ignores organic acids, which matter in brown Swedish waters. The point stands: alkalinity is a capacity, pH a state.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Which term controls the budget?




Worked example: suppose soils neutralise only 20 000 eq/year.

residual: 40 000 − 20 000 = 20 000 eq/year = 0.0400 meq/L
alkalinity: 50 000 − 20 000 = 30 000 eq/year = 0.0600 meq/L

Each 10 000 eq/year less neutralisation lowers alkalinity export by 0.0200 meq/L.
This is a sensitivity test: it shows which term matters, not which process actually changed.


This is the worked example from the notes. Change one term, hold the others fixed, and see how much the result moves. The line is straight because the budget is linear: every equivalent of acid not neutralised in the soil removes one equivalent of alkalinity from the lake. The calculation tells us the lake’s alkalinity is very sensitive to the soil term, which is exactly what made thin, granite-dominated catchments so vulnerable. It does not tell us why neutralisation might fall. Exhausted exchange sites, less weathering, more water bypassing the soil, or forestry removing base cations are all possible. Distinguishing them needs other measurements, such as soil base saturation trends and stream base cations.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Amount or dilution?




Exercise 2: double the water export to 1.00 × 10⁹ L/year, holding the acid amounts fixed.

residual amount: still 10 000 eq/year
residual concentration: 0.0100 meq/L

The concentration halved, but nothing chemical changed. That is dilution.
In a real catchment, more water also changes contact time, flow paths and weathering, so “everything else fixed” is an assumption.


This is exercise 2, and it is the same lesson as load versus concentration in the waste lecture and the very first unit. A wet year can lower concentrations simply by spreading the same amount over more water. A dry year can do the opposite. If you compared only concentrations between two years, you might wrongly conclude that the catchment’s chemistry had improved. The second caution is real hydrology. More water often means more flow through shallow soil layers and macropores, as in the soil lecture, which reduces contact with weathering minerals and exchange sites. Then the neutralisation term would also change. The demo at the end lets you compare these two cases directly.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Thread 4: when the balance tips, aluminium moves
text:
Thread 4: when the balance tips, aluminium moves




If acid input outruns neutralisation for long enough, alkalinity approaches zero and pH falls below about 5.5.
Then the soil’s aluminium buffer takes over, and Al³⁺ leaves with the drainage water. Free Al³⁺ rises about 1000-fold per pH unit.
The metals unit adds the next step: in brown, humus-rich water, organic ligands bind much of the aluminium, so the free ion, which harms fish gills, is lower than the total suggests.


This links the budget to biology. As long as the residual acid is small compared with the reference alkalinity, the lake keeps a positive alkalinity and a pH where aluminium stays mostly in the soil. Once the balance tips, aluminium dissolves in the soil and is carried to the stream. The figure is the gibbsite model from the soil lecture. The metals unit showed why total aluminium is not the whole story. Dissolved organic matter complexes aluminium, so the toxic inorganic fraction in a brown lake can be much lower than in a clear one at the same pH. In Swedish acidified lakes, fish deaths correlated better with inorganic aluminium than with pH alone. Speciation again decides the effect.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Check yourself


Acid input 40 000 eq/year, neutralisation 35 000 eq/year, water 5.00 × 10⁸ L/year. Residual acid in meq/L?
With reference alkalinity 50 000 eq/year, what alkalinity export (meq/L) follows from question 1?
A lake’s alkalinity export halves between a dry and a wet year, with the same deposition. Name two explanations and a measurement to tell them apart.
Can you state the lake’s pH from your answer to question 2? What else would you need?



Answers. One: the residual is 5000 equivalents per year, divided by 5.00 times ten to the eight litres gives 1.00 times ten to the minus five equivalents per litre, 0.0100 meq per litre. Two: 50 000 minus 5000 is 45 000 equivalents per year, which is 0.0900 meq per litre. Three: either dilution only, with the same annual alkalinity amount in twice the water, or a real fall in the annual amount, for example because wet-year water bypassed the soil. Measure flow and calculate annual loads: if the load is unchanged, it was dilution. Four: no. You need the dissolved inorganic carbon or the carbon dioxide pressure, and any organic acids.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Thread 5: a separate set of observations
text:
Thread 5: a separate set of observations


 A lake sediment core, Forlorn Lakes, Washington, USA. Photo: Molly McKnight, US Forest Service, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Now a different question in the same lake. Water just above the sediment is sampled before and during a period of oxygen depletion (constructed observations):



Indicator
Before
During




O₂ (mg/L)
8.0
0.20


filtered Fe (mg/L)
0.020
1.00


filtered PO₄-P (mg P/L)
0.010
0.200



These are observations, not model outputs. What chemistry could explain them?


Change gear. This is not part of the acid budget. It is a second, independent evidence set, so it needs its own boundary and its own explanation. Sediment cores like the one in the photo show layers of mineral and organic material deposited over years. Bacteria in the upper sediment consume oxygen while decomposing organic matter. In summer, when a lake is stratified, the bottom water is cut off from the atmosphere and its oxygen can run out. The numbers are invented for teaching but realistic in direction. Ask students to propose an explanation before showing the next slide. Most will recall the redox unit and suggest iron reduction. Then we test that idea.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: What changed, and by how much
text:
What changed, and by how much

Oxygen fell 40-fold while filtered iron rose 50-fold and phosphate-P 20-fold. All three changed together, in the same water, at the same time. That pattern is what a hypothesis has to explain.

Plotting on a log scale lets us compare changes of very different size. Oxygen dropped from 8.0 to 0.20 milligrams per litre, a factor of 40. Iron rose by a factor of 50, and phosphate-P by 20. The co-occurrence is the key observation. Remind students what the redox ladder from the redox unit predicts. After oxygen is used up, microbes turn to nitrate, then to manganese and iron oxides, then to sulfate. Rising dissolved iron fits that sequence. But a coincidence in time does not prove a mechanism. Two separate processes could be triggered by the same event, or a different water mass could have moved in. We first write the mechanism, then look for alternatives.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: A mechanism: iron reduction releases phosphate
text:
A mechanism: iron reduction releases phosphate

Under oxic conditions, an Fe(III) oxyhydroxide layer at the sediment surface holds phosphate. When O₂ runs out, Fe(III) is reduced and dissolves, and the phosphate it held is released. Phosphorus itself does not change oxidation state.

This is the classic iron–phosphate mechanism from the redox unit. Phosphate binds strongly to iron(III) oxyhydroxide surfaces. While the bottom water has oxygen, any iron(II) diffusing up from deeper sediment is oxidised at the surface and forms a fresh iron(III) layer, which acts as a lid for phosphate.
