When oxygen is gone, microbes use the iron(III) as an electron acceptor. The half-reaction is in the box. The solid dissolves, and its phosphate is released. Stress the last line: phosphate is not reduced. It is a passenger. This is the same idea as the waste lecture’s warning that metals held on iron hydroxide return when conditions change.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: The same chemistry, on a sea-wide scale
text:
The same chemistry, on a sea-wide scale


 Cyanobacteria bloom in the Baltic Sea, July 2025, Landsat. Image: NASA Earth Observatory, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

The deep Baltic Sea has large areas of oxygen-free bottom water.
There, iron-bound phosphate is released from sediments, as in our lake. This internal loading adds to the phosphorus from rivers and helps sustain summer cyanobacteria blooms like this one.
Cutting nutrient inputs from land is necessary, but the sediments keep releasing phosphate for years. Recovery is slow for the same reason as at Hubbard Brook: a stored inventory.


The Baltic is a large-scale version of our lake. Its deep basins are poorly ventilated because salty, dense water sits below fresher surface water, so oxygen-free bottoms are common and have expanded since the mid-twentieth century as nutrient inputs increased. Iron-bound phosphate released from those sediments contributes substantially to the phosphorus available for summer blooms of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Keep the numbers qualitative here; the point is the mechanism. Draw the parallel with the soil lecture. In both cases, decades of input built up a stored inventory, base-cation depletion in one case and phosphorus-rich sediments in the other, and that inventory delays recovery after the inputs are reduced.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Consistent is not proven

Our data are consistent with iron reduction, but they do not identify it uniquely. Each alternative predicts something different. A good explanation names the measurement that would tell them apart.

This is exercise 3. The observations fit the iron reduction mechanism, but they also fit other explanations. Mixing: if a different water mass, for example porewater-rich water stirred up from deeper sediment, moved past the sampling point, iron and phosphate would rise together without any new reaction. Conservative tracers, such as chloride or temperature, would change at the same time. Organic matter decomposition releases phosphate from biomass directly; then phosphate would rise with ammonium and carbon dioxide, even where iron stays low. Supporting evidence for iron reduction includes iron(II) speciation, porewater profiles with peaks just below the surface, and a fall in iron-bound phosphorus in the solid. Several processes can act together.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Keep forms and units aligned



Phosphate-P is reported as mass of phosphorus. 0.200 mg P/L = 6.46 µmol/L = 0.613 mg PO₄³⁻/L. Mixing the two bases gives a factor-3 error.
Filtered Fe is an operational fraction. It can include Fe(III) colloids and organic complexes, not just Fe²⁺.
eq/year (budget), meq/L (concentration) and pH (state) are three different kinds of quantity.

Before you combine two numbers, check they refer to the same water, time and fraction.


Quick conversion check
1.00 mg/L Fe ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 17.9 µmol/L
0.200 mg P/L ÷ 30.97 g/mol = 6.46 µmol/L
Molar ratio Fe : P released ≈ 18 : 6.5, about 3 : 1. Does that fit the Fe : P ratio of the sediment’s iron oxides? Only a solid-phase measurement can say.



These are the bookkeeping traps that ruin otherwise good arguments. Phosphorus is conventionally reported as phosphorus mass, so the phosphate ion mass is about three times larger. Always check which convention a dataset uses. Filtered iron passes through a filter, typically 0.45 micrometres, which lets through small colloids and organic complexes. It is not automatically dissolved iron(II), which is why a speciation measurement is part of the test. The molar ratio in the box is a useful habit: converting to moles lets you ask whether the amounts fit a proposed reaction. Whether three iron per phosphorus fits depends on how much phosphate the sediment’s iron oxides actually held, which needs a solid-phase measurement. Also, some released iron(II) may be reoxidised or precipitate as sulfide before sampling. The ratio is a check, not a proof.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Thread 6: the contaminant in the same lake
text:
Thread 6: the contaminant in the same lake




Activity C’s compound U behaves like this in a closed water–sediment system: half sorbed (Kd = 100 L/kg), half-life 10 days.
In the real lake, this is a separate argument with its own boundary:

outflow and inflow would add terms;
if sorbed U is buried, it leaves the active system without being destroyed;
anoxic sediment may change both Kd and the rate.

Keep the compound model and the budget in separate sections of your report.


The contaminant model from activity C is the last thread. It describes a closed system with fixed Kd and one first-order rate, and it accounts for every milligram. In a real lake, the boundary is open. Water flows out, carrying dissolved parent. Sediment accumulates and buries sorbed parent, which removes it from contact with the water without transforming it. And the redox change we just discussed can change both sorption, for example if the compound was bound to iron oxides, and degradation rates. The report template asks students to keep the compound model and the catchment and sediment arguments in clearly identified sections, so a reader can see which numbers come from which model.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Anatomy of a chemical explanation

Every strong argument in this course had these six parts. The test is what makes it science: a measurement that could have proved the claim wrong. The limits say what the numbers do not show.

This is the structure the integrated exercise and the exam expect. Walk through the example in the figure, which uses today’s worked case. The claim is a sentence a non-chemist could understand. The reaction chain shows how it happens. The balance gives a number, here 0.0600 meq per litre. The prediction says what else must be true if the claim holds; here, base-cation export should fall while sulfate stays the same. The test names a measurement that could contradict the prediction. And the limits state the boundaries: an annual budget, no pH without carbon data, other terms held fixed. Students should be able to fill these six boxes for any unit in the course.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Back to Sweden: what happened next
text:
Back to Sweden: what happened next


 Liming by helicopter, Kungsbacka, Sweden. Photo: Bulver, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

The 1972 argument was eventually accepted. International agreements cut sulfur emissions across Europe, and sulfur deposition over Sweden has fallen to a small fraction of its 1980s peak.
Many lakes are recovering, but slowly:

soils must rebuild exchangeable base cations by weathering;
forestry removes base cations in harvested wood;
thousands of lakes are still limed to bridge the gap.

The chemistry of every unit was needed to understand both the damage and the slow recovery.


Close the historical loop. Following the 1979 convention and later protocols, sulfur emissions in Europe fell dramatically, and sulfur deposition in Sweden is now far below its peak. Lake chemistry has responded: sulfate concentrations fell and alkalinity rose in many lakes. But recovery is slower than the cut in deposition, for the reasons this course has developed. Soil exchange sites lost base cations and refill slowly. Whole-tree harvesting removes additional base cations. Nitrogen deposition remains. Liming continues in many sensitive waters, as shown in the carbonate lecture. Students should see that the course’s chemistry is not abstract: it was the evidence base for one of Europe’s most successful environmental agreements.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Preparing for the exam

For any synthesis question, work through the same steps:

Draw the boundary. Which water, solid or air volume, and over what time?
List the quantities and their kind: amount, flux, concentration, state.
Write the reactions and check element and charge balance.
Close the budget in amounts or equivalents before converting.
Separate model predictions, constructed data and real observations.
Name an alternative explanation and the measurement that would distinguish it.
State the limits: what your numbers cannot tell you.


Course overview and unit list · Integrated exercises · Activity C report template

Give students a reusable procedure. These seven steps condense the habits from all units. Drawing the boundary first prevents most errors in this course: mixing an annual budget with a closed-water pulse, or a water concentration with a total inventory. Listing quantities by kind catches unit errors. Balancing reactions catches stoichiometry errors, like forgetting the second pair of hydrogen ions from pyrite. Closing budgets in amounts first avoids dilution traps. Separating model output from observations is required in the report. Naming an alternative and a test is what distinguishes an explanation from a story. And stating limits shows understanding, not weakness. Encourage students to practise on each unit’s exercises.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“0.0200 meq/L of residual acid gives pH X.” Not without CT, CO₂ and other acids.
“Lower concentration this year, so less acid.” Check the annual amount: dilution is not chemistry.
“Neutralisation is a fixed property of the catchment.” It draws on finite inventories that change.
“Fe and P rose together, so iron reduction released P.” Consistent is not proven; test alternatives.
“Phosphate-P and phosphate are the same number.” Factor of about 3.
“One model covers the whole lake.” The budget, the sediment and the contaminant need separate boundaries.


These mistakes collect the course’s main traps in their synthesis form. Ask students which unit each mistake comes from. The first comes from the carbonate unit: pH needs more than alkalinity. The second from the very first unit and the waste lecture: concentration is not load. The third from soils: inventories are finite. The fourth from redox, sharpened today: a pattern is not a mechanism. The fifth from units and forms, and the sixth from activity C: models have boundaries. If students can explain each correction with a number or a reaction, they are well prepared. Then use the interactive demo to check the budget reasoning one more time.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Explore: catchment acid budget


Compare less neutralisation with double water export. Which annual quantities change?



Compare less neutralisation with double water export. Which annual quantities change?

Use the reference presets, then change one variable. The complete exercise has model assumptions, a hand-check result, and a static reference for printing.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Summary







Thread
Key fact




Deposition
0.0200 HNO₃ + 2 × 0.0100 H₂SO₄ = 0.0400 eq m⁻² yr⁻¹ → 40 000 eq/year


Soils
neutralise 30 000 eq/year from finite inventories; base cations leave with SO₄²⁻


Budget
residual 10 000 eq/year ÷ 5.00 × 10⁸ L/year = 0.0200 meq/L


Alkalinity
needs a reference: 50 000 − 10 000 = 40 000 eq/year = 0.0800 meq/L


pH
not fixed by alkalinity: needs CT or CO₂ pressure (≈ 7.1 vs 6.1 here)


Sensitivity
20 000 neutralised → 0.0600 meq/L; double water → dilution only


Metals
below pH ≈ 5.5, Al³⁺ rises steeply; organic ligands lower the free ion


Sediment
O₂ ↓ 40×, Fe ↑ 50×, PO₄-P ↑ 20×: consistent with Fe(III) reduction, not proof


Mechanism
FeOOH + 3H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2H₂O; phosphate released, not reduced


Explanation
claim, reaction, balance, prediction, test, limits



Next: the course overview for exam preparation: revisit each unit’s summary slide and exercises. Then the integrated exercises, the notes and the activity C report.

This is the last summary of the course, so recite the whole chain. Emissions become acid deposition, counted in equivalents. Soils neutralise most of it from finite inventories, so their capacity can decline. The residual, divided by water export, lowers the lake’s alkalinity relative to a stated reference, but pH needs carbon dioxide and dissolved carbon too. If the balance tips, aluminium moves. A separate sediment observation set is consistent with iron reduction releasing phosphate, and the Baltic shows the same chemistry at sea scale. Every step needs a boundary, a balance and a test. For revision, use the overview page: each unit’s summary table and exercises cover the facts this synthesis relied on.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text: If a pollutant concentration falls downstream, has the pollutant been destroyed? Follow the amount before proposing a reaction.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Learning goals

Convert concentration to amount or load with explicit units.
Close a compartment balance and distinguish transfer from transformation.
Choose a system boundary and recognise when steady state is an assumption.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Define the quantity
Concentration divides amount by volume; it is not an inventory. Mass concentration might be mg/L, amount concentration mol/L, and an inventory mg or mol. Use a molar mass only when converting between mass and chemical amount. A sample with lower concentration can contain more solute if its volume is larger. Specify whether a result is reported as the element or as a compound: mg N/L and mg nitrate/L are different quantities.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Choose a boundary
A compartment is a specified volume such as a lake, a water sample, or the water plus sediment in a bottle. A flux crosses its boundary; a reaction can transform a species inside it. Write what lies inside the boundary before adding terms. Sorption removes a compound from water but does not remove it from a water-plus-sediment system. Transformation of a parent compound need not destroy its constituent elements.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Write a balance
For the amount \(M\) of a specified substance, \[\frac{dM}{dt}=\text{inputs}-\text{outputs}+\text{production}-\text{consumption}.\] Every term has amount/time units. For a well mixed constant-volume water body, an advective output is \(QC\), where \(Q\) is water flow and \(C\) is outlet concentration. The inflow and outflow volumes must also balance if volume stays fixed. A steady state sets accumulation to zero; it does not imply that input and output processes have stopped.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Separate mixing from reaction
When two waters mix without reaction or loss, add their inventories and divide by the combined volume. For flows at a junction, add loads and divide by total flow. This is a conservation prediction, not an equilibrium calculation. If the observed result differs, investigate sampling times, mixing, uncertainty, missing inputs, and chemical change. A concentration difference alone cannot isolate a reaction rate.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
A timescale is a model
The hydraulic replacement time is \(V/Q\) for constant volume and flow. It estimates a water-replacement scale, not the age of every molecule or the chemical lifetime of every solute. Under a well mixed model, flushing an initially present conservative solute with clean water gives an exponential decline. A reactive solute also depends on transformation, sorption, and exchange with other compartments.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Worked example
Mix 2.00 L at 3.00 mg/L with 1.00 L at 0.600 mg/L. The inventories are 6.00 and 0.600 mg. With additive volumes, no reaction, and no loss, the final inventory is 6.60 mg in 3.00 L, so the concentration is 2.20 mg/L. It is lower than 3.00 mg/L because of dilution; none of the tracked solute was destroyed.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 1: environmental composition, sources, sinks, and chemical processes.
USGS water chemistry: Background on water properties and chemical quantities.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
text:
1. Mixing without loss
Mix 4.00 L at 2.00 mg/L with 1.00 L of solute-free water. Find the inventory and final concentration. What caused the decrease?






Hint





Balance mg first, then divide by the final volume.









Worked solution





The initial and final inventory is 8.00 mg. Final concentration is 1.60 mg/L. Dilution lowers concentration without consuming solute.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
text:
2. A river load
A stream carries 0.200 m³/s at 0.500 mg/L. Calculate its solute load in g/s and kg/day. Use 1000 L/m³ and 86400 s/day.






Hint





Convert flow to L/s before multiplying.









Worked solution





The flow is 200 L/s, giving 100 mg/s = 0.100 g/s, or 8.64 kg/day. This assumes the flow and concentration remain constant over the day.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
text:
3. A two-phase bottle
A sealed bottle initially contains 10.0 mg of parent compound in water. Later, water contains 4.0 mg and sediment contains 5.0 mg. Sampling removes nothing. What amount is unaccounted for? Can you identify its fate?






Hint





Sum the measured parent inventories across both phases.









Worked solution





Measured parent totals 9.0 mg, leaving 1.0 mg unaccounted for. Transformation, unmeasured bottle-wall retention, and analytical error are candidates. The balance alone does not establish mineralisation or elemental loss.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
text:
4. Interpret the boundary
A lake concentration falls while its volume rises. What measurements would distinguish dilution, export, and chemical transformation?






Hint





Track volumes, flows, phase inventories, and chemical identities.









Worked solution





Measure volume and total inventory, inlet/outlet loads, relevant solid-phase amounts, and plausible transformation products over a consistent period. A concentration series alone does not close the balance.

title: Environmental amounts and balances exercises
section: Explore: a lake approaching steady state
text:
Explore: a lake approaching steady state
Predict what happens to the steady-state inventory if the solute input doubles, and what happens if the water flow doubles instead. Then change one input at a time and compare the curve, the time constant and the balance table.


Reference case: V = 1.0 × 10⁶ m³ and Q = 1.0 × 10⁴ m³/day give V/Q = 100 days. An input of 1.0 kg/day gives a steady inventory of 100 kg (0.10 mg/L); after 100 days the lake holds 63 kg.



E1. Choose Worked example. Read the balance table at steady state. Which fluxes are still running, and why does the inventory not change? Then choose Double the input and check the new steady inventory by hand.
E2. Reset, then raise the lake volume to 4 million m³ while keeping the flow and input fixed. What happens to the steady concentration, and what happens to the time needed to get there? Explain both with V/Q.
E3. Choose Flush with clean water, then Flushing plus reaction. How much of the 100 kg is left after one time constant in each case? Explain why seeing only the falling curve cannot tell you how much was flushing and how much was reaction.

Model conditions and hand check
The constructed lake has V = 1.0 × 10⁶ m³, Q = 1.0 × 10⁴ m³/day in and out, and an input of 1.0 kg/day of a conservative solute, starting clean. The replacement time is V/Q = 10⁶ / 10⁴ = 100 days. At steady state output equals input, so Q × C = 1.0 kg/day and C = 1.0 / 10⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m³ = 0.10 mg/L, an inventory of 100 kg. Starting from a clean lake, the inventory after one replacement time is 100 × (1 − e⁻¹) = 63 kg.
With a first-order reaction the two loss rates add: Q/V + k. For k = 0.010 per day this doubles the total loss rate, halving both the time constant (50 days) and the steady inventory (50 kg). Flushing 100 kg with clean water leaves 100 × e⁻¹ = 37 kg after 100 days by flushing alone, and 100 × e⁻² = 14 kg with the reaction added.
The lake is well mixed, so the outlet concentration equals the lake concentration. Volume, flow and input are constant, the inflow carries no other solute than the stated input, and the only reaction is first order. Sorption to sediment, exchange with air and seasonal changes in flow are not included.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
From chimney to lake

Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are emitted, transported by wind, oxidised to sulfuric and nitric acid, and then deposited in rain or directly onto surfaces. The catchment’s soils react with the acid before the water reaches the lake.

This is the whole lecture in one picture. Each arrow is a process we will look at, and each one changes what we can learn from a single measurement. Emission is controlled by fuel and technology. Transport by wind explains why the damage happened far from the sources. Oxidation turns gases that are not yet acids into strong acids. Deposition brings them down, either dissolved in precipitation or directly to leaves and soil. Finally the catchment soil, with its minerals and plants, modifies the acid before it reaches surface water. Keep the boundary idea from the first lecture in mind: we will draw a boundary around the catchment and do a budget.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Precursors are not yet acids

SO₂ and NO₂ must be oxidised first. NO₂ reacts with OH in daylight. SO₂ reacts more slowly with OH, but quickly inside cloud droplets with hydrogen peroxide. The net equation is bookkeeping, not the mechanism.

It is tempting to think of a chimney as releasing sulfuric acid. It mostly releases sulfur dioxide, and the acid is made in the air. For nitrogen, the main daytime route is nitrogen dioxide plus OH plus a collision partner, giving nitric acid; you met OH and M last lecture. For sulfur, the gas-phase route via OH works but is relatively slow, on the order of days to weeks. When clouds are present, sulfur dioxide dissolves in the droplets as bisulfite and is oxidised quickly by hydrogen peroxide. That is why sulfate formation is often fastest in clouds. The net equation at the bottom balances atoms but says nothing about which pathway operates or how fast.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Clouds and fog are chemical reactors
text:
Clouds and fog are chemical reactors


 Fog over a Swedish landscape. Photo: Robin Stumm, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

A cloud or fog is a huge number of tiny water droplets. Each droplet:

dissolves SO₂, H₂O₂ and acids from the surrounding air;
hosts fast aqueous oxidation of SO₂ to sulfate;
forms around a particle, often itself sulfate or nitrate.

Fog and cloud water can be more acidic than rain, because the droplets are small and hold less water per unit of dissolved acid. Forests in cloudy mountains catch this water directly.


Clouds are not just a delivery mechanism; they are where much of the chemistry happens. Droplets take up soluble gases, and the reaction of bisulfite with hydrogen peroxide is fast in the aqueous phase. Most cloud droplets do not evaporate into rain: they evaporate again, leaving behind a sulfate particle that is now larger. When droplets do fall, they carry the acid down. Fog and cloud water in contact with mountain forests can be several times more concentrated than rain, because the droplets contain little water. This occult or cloud deposition is easy to overlook if you only sample rain in an open bucket.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Two routes down: wet and dry
text:
Two routes down: wet and dry

Wet deposition arrives in rain, snow, fog or cloud water. Dry deposition is the direct uptake of gases and particles by surfaces, also in dry weather. A rain sample only measures the wet part.

Wet deposition is the easy part to measure: put out a clean collector, measure the volume of water and its concentration. Dry deposition is harder. Gases such as sulfur dioxide and nitric acid are taken up directly by leaves, needles and soil, and particles settle or are caught by surfaces. Forests are very efficient collectors because they have a large surface area. Dry deposition is usually estimated from air concentrations and models, or from throughfall measurements under the forest canopy. For our purposes the important point is logical: a rain sample cannot tell you the dry deposition, so a budget based only on rain is incomplete.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Measuring wet deposition


 Wet deposition sampler of the US National Atmospheric Deposition Program. The lid opens only when it rains. Photo: Mary O’Neill, USGS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

A wet-only collector opens its lid when it senses rain, so dry dust and gases are excluded. Each sample gives a volume and concentrations of ions such as SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺, Ca²⁺ and H⁺.
The wet flux is
F_{wet} = C_{rain} \times P
Crain in mol/L, P (rain depth) in L/m². Note that 1 mm of rain on 1 m² is 1 L.
Networks like this exist across Europe, coordinated by EMEP.


This is a standard wet-only sampler. Two buckets sit under a lid that moves to cover the dry bucket when it rains, so the wet bucket collects precipitation only. Samples are analysed for the major ions. The flux is concentration times precipitation amount. The unit trick to remember: one millimetre of rain on one square metre is one litre of water, so millimetres of rain are litres per square metre. European countries run similar networks under the EMEP programme, which grew out of the 1979 convention. These long records are how we know that sulfate deposition in Scandinavia has fallen since the 1980s.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Worked example: wet nitrate flux

Annual rain 0.600 m with nitrate 20.0 µmol/L throughout: 600 L/m² × 20.0 µmol/L = 0.0120 mol NO₃⁻ m⁻² yr⁻¹. This is an amount flux. Calling it an acid flux needs to know what came with the nitrate.

This is exercise 1. Convert the depth of rain into a volume per square metre: 0.600 metres over one square metre is 0.600 cubic metres, which is 600 litres. Multiply by the concentration, 20 micromoles per litre, to get 12 000 micromoles, or 0.0120 moles of nitrate per square metre per year. The assumption that the concentration is the same throughout the year is a simplification. Real samplers give a different concentration for every event, and the annual flux is the sum of concentration times volume for each event. Point out the last sentence on the slide: nitrate is an anion. Whether it arrived as nitric acid or as a neutral salt is a separate question.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Rain pH does not give the acid load
text:
Rain pH does not give the acid load




Two rain events both have pH 4.00, so [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴ mol/L.

1 mm: 1 L/m² × 10⁻⁴ mol/L = 0.100 mmol H⁺/m²
10 mm: 10 L/m² × 10⁻⁴ = 1.00 mmol H⁺/m²

Same pH, ten times the acid delivered. A concentration needs a water amount to become a load.
pH also counts only free H⁺, not acidity that appears later.


This is exercise 2, and it is the same lesson as the first lecture, now in the atmosphere. pH describes a concentration: the free hydrogen ion in the sample. The amount delivered to the ground also depends on how much water fell. The large event brought ten times as much hydrogen ion per square metre, even though a pH meter would read the same for both. We use the dilute approximation that hydrogen-ion activity equals concentration. The last point is important for the next slides: some acidity is not present as free hydrogen ion when it lands, but is generated later in the soil. A rain pH value cannot show that either.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Check yourself


20 mm of rain falls with 15 µmol/L sulfate. What is the sulfate input per m²?
Rain at pH 4.5 falls in a wet year; rain at pH 4.2 falls in a dry year. Which year brought more free H⁺? What do you need to know?
Why can a rain collector not measure the SO₂ taken up directly by a spruce forest?
Is SO₂ an acid when it leaves the chimney?



Answers. One: 20 millimetres is 20 litres per square metre; times 15 micromoles per litre gives 300 micromoles, or 0.300 millimoles of sulfate per square metre. Two: you cannot tell without the rain amounts. pH 4.2 means about twice the concentration of pH 4.5, so the wet year needs more than twice the rainfall to bring more hydrogen ion. Three: dry deposition happens directly to the needles, also in dry weather, and never passes through the collector. Four: not yet in the sense we mean. It is a precursor: it forms an acid only after oxidation, mainly in clouds or by OH. It is slightly acidic when it dissolves, but the strong acid is sulfuric acid.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Counting acid in equivalents


Acids differ in how many H⁺ each molecule can give. Count equivalents (eq): moles of H⁺ that can be neutralised.



Acid
eq per mol




HNO₃
1


H₂SO₄
2



Teaching catchment flux: 0.0200 mol HNO₃ + 0.0100 mol H₂SO₄ per m² per year
= 0.0200 × 1 + 0.0100 × 2 = 0.0400 eq m⁻² yr⁻¹




Equivalents let us add different acids on one scale: each equivalent can neutralise one mole of hydrogen ion, or consume one equivalent of alkalinity, a link to the carbonate lecture in week 2. Nitric acid gives one, sulfuric acid two, under the stated convention of complete neutralisation. The worked number is the flux for the teaching catchment that we will use for the rest of the lecture. Notice that it is based on supplied acid amounts, not on measured sulfate. The next slide shows why that distinction matters. Ask students: if I told you only the sulfate flux, could you compute the acid equivalents?

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Sulfate does not identify the acid
text:
Sulfate does not identify the acid

The same sulfate ion can arrive with 2 H⁺, with 2 NH₄⁺, or with base cations from dust or sea salt. Measured sulfate only fixes the anion. To find the acid, also measure H⁺, NH₄⁺ and the base cations.

This is the trap in exercise 4. A sulfate measurement tells you how much sulfate arrived, nothing more. If it came as sulfuric acid, it brings two hydrogen ions now. If it came as ammonium sulfate, the solution is close to neutral when it lands; but as we will see next, soil bacteria can later turn each ammonium into nitrate and two hydrogen ions. If it came with calcium from dust or with sodium and magnesium from sea spray, it brings no acid at all. Near the coast, a large part of sulfate is sea salt. So to report an acid dose you must measure the cations too, and think about what happens after deposition.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Ammonia: neutraliser now, acid later


 Tractor with a manure spreader, New York State, USA. Agriculture is the main source of ammonia. Photo: Pollinator, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Ammonia (NH₃) from manure and fertiliser is a base. In the air it neutralises acid:
\mathrm{NH_3+HNO_3\rightarrow NH_4NO_3}
So the rain becomes less acidic. But in soil, bacteria nitrify ammonium:
\mathrm{NH_4^++2\,O_2\rightarrow NO_3^-+2\,H^++H_2O}
Each NH₄⁺ can produce 2 H⁺ later, unless plants take it up first. Rain pH hides this potential acidity.


Ammonia is the main gaseous base in the atmosphere, and agriculture is its main source. It reacts with nitric and sulfuric acid to form ammonium salts, so it raises rain pH. That made rain look cleaner as sulfur emissions fell while ammonia stayed high. But ammonium is not chemically inert after deposition. If soil bacteria oxidise it to nitrate, two hydrogen ions are released for each ammonium. If plants take up the ammonium instead, the acidity is not produced. That is why we distinguish free hydrogen ion, which a pH meter sees, from potential acidity, which depends on what happens in the soil. Ammonia is also a nitrogen input that can over-fertilise ecosystems.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: From flux to a catchment budget
text:
From flux to a catchment budget


Teaching catchment (constructed):

area A = 1.00 × 10⁶ m² (1 km²)
water export = 5.00 × 10⁸ L/yr, about 500 mm of runoff
acid flux = 0.0400 eq m⁻² yr⁻¹

Annual input = flux × area = 0.0400 × 10⁶ = 40 000 eq/yr
Flow-weighted concentration = 40 000 / 5.00 × 10⁸ L = 0.0800 meq/L




Now apply the balance from lecture 1. Draw the boundary around the catchment. The input is the flux times the area. Converting that to a water concentration needs the annual water that leaves the catchment, here 500 million litres, corresponding to half a metre of runoff over one square kilometre. Dividing equivalents by litres gives an annual flow-weighted equivalent concentration. It is the average concentration you would see if every litre exported in the year carried an equal share. It is not a pulse into a closed lake, and it is not a pH. The next slide adds what the catchment soils do to this input.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
The annual budget with neutralisation

If catchment processes neutralise 30 000 eq/yr, the residual is 10 000 eq/yr: 10 000 / 5.00 × 10⁸ L = 0.0200 meq/L in the export. With only 20 000 eq/yr neutralised, it doubles to 0.0400 meq/L. A constructed budget, not a pH prediction.

This is the worked example from the notes and exercise 3. Subtract equivalents first, then divide by the annual water volume. The neutralisation term stands for weathering and cation exchange in the soil, which we discuss in two slides. Exercise 3 asks what happens with less neutralisation, 20 000 instead of 30 000: the residual doubles to 20 000 equivalents and the concentration doubles to 0.0400 milliequivalents per litre. Stress the two caveats. The numbers are constructed. And an equivalent concentration is not a pH; to get a pH you need the carbonate chemistry of week 2, and other ions. The budget tells us how much acid the water must carry, not how acidic it will be.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Load and concentration are different

Double the water export at the same deposition: the annual acid load stays 40 000 eq/yr, but the equivalent concentration halves to 0.0400 meq/L. A wet year can lower concentrations without any change in the acid input.

This is the question the week 1 demo asks, and the answer follows from the definitions. The load is set by the deposition flux and the area. Water only dilutes it. If you see lower concentrations in a wet year, do not conclude that deposition fell. Conversely, a dry year can raise concentrations without any increase in input. This is exactly the dilution-versus-destruction lesson from the Tisza case in the first lecture. Monitoring programmes therefore report both concentrations and fluxes, and they correct for water flow before claiming a trend. Ask students what measurement they would need to calculate a load from a stream concentration: the flow.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Why catchments respond differently

Between rain and lake, soils neutralise acid by mineral weathering and cation exchange, and plants take up nitrogen. Nitrification adds acid. Flow paths decide how much contact water has with soil.

The neutralisation term in our budget is not a single number of nature; it depends on the catchment. Weathering of minerals consumes hydrogen ions and releases base cations such as calcium and magnesium. It is slow on granite and gneiss, which cover much of Sweden, and fast on limestone. Cation exchange is fast: soil particles hold calcium and release it in exchange for hydrogen ions, but the store can be depleted after decades of acid input. Plants take up ammonium and nitrate, which affects acidity. Water that runs off quickly through the topsoil during snowmelt has little contact time, which is why spring floods can bring acid pulses to streams.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Europe cut its emissions


 Flue-gas desulfurisation equipment inside Lippendorf power station, Germany. Photo: High Contrast, CC BY 3.0 DE, Wikimedia Commons.

After the 1979 convention and its protocols, Europe reduced SO₂ emissions by well over three quarters since the 1980s: low-sulfur fuels, fewer coal plants, and flue-gas desulfurisation, which captures SO₂ with limestone.
Sulfate deposition in Scandinavia fell accordingly. Many lakes now show rising pH and alkalinity, but recovery is slow: soils lost base cations over decades. Nitrogen and ammonia have fallen much less.


Acid rain is one of the success stories of environmental policy, and chemistry was central to it. Flue-gas desulfurisation scrubs sulfur dioxide from exhaust with a limestone slurry, producing gypsum; the photo shows the machinery inside a German lignite power station. Together with cleaner fuels and the closure of old plants, this cut European sulfur emissions dramatically. The numbers vary by country and period, so the slide gives a rounded statement. The recovery of surface waters lags behind, because soils lost exchangeable base cations and need time to rebuild them by weathering. That is one reason Sweden still limes some lakes, the topic that opens the carbonate lecture in week 2.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Chimneys emit sulfuric acid.” They mostly emit SO₂; the acid forms by oxidation.
“Rain pH gives the acid load.” Multiply concentration by the water amount; pH misses potential acidity.
“A rain sample measures all deposition.” Dry deposition is missing.
“Every sulfate brings 2 H⁺.” Only if it arrives as H₂SO₄.
“Ammonia makes deposition harmless.” Nitrification can release 2 H⁺ per NH₄⁺ later.
“Lower concentration in a wet year means less deposition.” Water dilutes; the load may be unchanged.
“An equivalent concentration is a pH.” It needs carbonate chemistry to become one.


These errors appear often in exercises and in public discussion of acid rain. Ask students to fix each statement in one sentence. The first three are about where acids form and what a sample measures. The fourth and fifth are about counter-ions and the difference between free and potential acidity. The sixth is the dilution lesson from lecture 1 in a new context. The last one prepares for week 2. The budget in equivalents tells us how much acid-neutralising capacity is consumed, but the resulting pH depends on the carbonate system of the water, which is exactly what the alkalinity concept in the carbonate lecture describes.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Explore: deposition and dilution


Double water export. Which changes: annual load or equivalent concentration?



Double water export. Which changes: annual load or equivalent concentration?

Use the reference presets, then change one variable. The complete exercise has model assumptions, a hand-check result, and a static reference for printing.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Precursors
SO₂ and NOₓ are oxidised to H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ (OH; H₂O₂ in clouds)


Net equation
SO₂ + ½ O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ is bookkeeping, not mechanism


Wet deposition
flux = concentration × rain amount; 1 mm on 1 m² = 1 L


Dry deposition
gases and particles to surfaces; not in a rain sample


Rain pH
a concentration of free H⁺; same pH, more rain = more acid


Equivalents
HNO₃ 1 eq/mol, H₂SO₄ 2 eq/mol


Sulfate
with H⁺, NH₄⁺ or base cations: measure the cations


Ammonium
neutralises now; nitrification gives 2 H⁺ per NH₄⁺ later


Budget
40 000 eq/yr in; − neutralisation; ÷ water export = meq/L


Catchments
weathering, exchange, uptake and flow paths set the response



Next: molecules, radiation and climate. The same particles that carry acid also scatter sunlight. Then the exercises, notes and the week 1 demo.

 Summit caldera of Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, on 1 August 1991, six weeks after the climactic eruption of 15 June. Photo: T. J. Casadevall, USGS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


The summary table is the revision sheet. Recite the chain once: emission of precursors, oxidation to strong acids, wet and dry deposition, counting in equivalents with attention to counter-ions, and an annual budget for a catchment whose soils neutralise part of the input. Then return to the opening: Odén’s argument needed exactly this chain, from British and German chimneys to Swedish lakes. The photo is the teaser for the next lecture. In 1991 Mount Pinatubo injected so much sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere that the resulting sulfate particles cooled the planet for a year or two. Sulfate is not only an acid; it also changes how sunlight and heat move through the atmosphere.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text: Why does adding one gas affect outgoing radiation while adding another gas can have little direct infrared effect?

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Learning goals

Connect molecular absorption to changing dipole moment.
Distinguish spectral overlap, gas lifetime, and radiative influence.
Explain why atmospheric particles can have different effects from gases.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Absorption requires a matching transition
A molecule interacts with infrared radiation when the radiation matches an allowed rotational/vibrational transition. A vibration is infrared active when it changes the molecular dipole moment. The symmetric molecule CO₂ has infrared-active bending and asymmetric stretching modes; being symmetric does not mean every vibration is inactive. Homonuclear diatomics such as N₂ and O₂ lack ordinary dipole-active vibrational absorption and are weak direct greenhouse absorbers under ordinary atmospheric conditions.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Earth emits at different wavelengths
The warm surface emits strongly in the thermal infrared, whereas incoming sunlight is concentrated at shorter wavelengths. Absorbing and emitting gases alter how energy moves through the atmosphere and escapes to space. Absorption is wavelength dependent. The role of a gas depends on its bands, abundance, altitude, and overlap with other absorbers; one peak height is not a complete climate metric.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Read a deliberately simple spectrum
Use the supplied teaching spectrum below as a diagram of the logic, not a measured gas spectrum. At 0.55 µm the model transmits 0.95 of the incident light; at 10 µm it transmits 0.20. For this absorbing-only example, the absorbed fractions are \(1-T=0.05\) and \(0.80\). Real atmospheres also scatter and emit. Comparing transmission without the incident energy spectrum cannot give total absorbed power.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Persistence has several timescales
A first-order sink gives \(C(t)=C_0e^{-kt}\), a lifetime \(\tau=1/k\), and a half-life \(t_{1/2}=\ln2/k\). These are useful for a single isolated loss process. Carbon dioxide exchanges with ocean and land reservoirs on several timescales, so one exponential atmospheric lifetime does not describe all of its response. A gas’s chemical lifetime is also different from the time over which the climate system responds.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Particles absorb, scatter, and change clouds
text:
Particles absorb, scatter, and change clouds
Aerosols can scatter sunlight, absorb radiation, and affect cloud droplet formation. Their effect depends on composition, size, location, and the surrounding surface or cloud. A reflecting particle and an absorbing particle need not have the same influence. Oxidation can convert emitted gases to particles, linking air-pollution chemistry with radiation. Do not assign every aerosol a universal cooling sign or a gas-like persistence.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Worked example
For a constructed beam with 100 W/m² incident in one band, transmission 0.20 and no reflection imply 20 W/m² transmitted and 80 W/m² absorbed. This is a single-band beam calculation. It is not an estimate of whole-Earth forcing, which requires spectral integration and atmospheric structure.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 8: molecular absorption, spectral interpretation, and persistence.
NASA greenhouse mechanisms: Radiation and the role of greenhouse gases.
NASA aerosol and forcing explanation: The distinction between radiation changes and different atmospheric influences.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
text:
1. Compare wavelengths
For the two teaching bands in the notes, calculate absorbed fractions. Can you conclude that the gas absorbs more total energy in the 10 µm band without knowing the incident spectrum?






Hint





Absorbed power depends on both absorption fraction and incident power.









Worked solution





The fractions are 0.05 and 0.80 in the absorbing-only example. Total absorbed power also requires the incident energy in each band and their widths. Fractions alone cannot establish an integrated energy budget.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
text:
2. An infrared-active mode
Why is the statement “CO₂ is symmetric, so it cannot absorb infrared” incorrect? Contrast an active CO₂ mode with N₂ vibration.






Hint





Consider the changing dipole during vibration, not only the resting structure.









Worked solution





The CO₂ asymmetric stretch and bending motions change dipole moment and can absorb infrared. Ordinary N₂ vibration does not create that changing molecular dipole. Other weak absorption mechanisms do not reverse this basic comparison.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
text:
3. A constructed gas sink
A fictitious gas has a fixed first-order loss coefficient k = 0.0200 day⁻¹. Calculate its lifetime, half-life, and remaining fraction after 50.0 days.






Hint





Use 1/k, ln(2)/k, and exp(−kt).









Worked solution





Lifetime 50.0 days; half-life 34.7 days; remaining fraction e⁻¹ = 0.368. These describe the stated one-sink model, not CO₂ or a complete atmospheric transport system.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
text:
4. Compare two emissions
Two emitted gases have equal mass and different absorption bands and lifetimes. What information would you need to compare their climate effects?






Hint





Mass alone omits molecular number, radiation, chemistry, and timescale.









Worked solution





You need molecular masses, spectroscopic absorption, atmospheric abundance and overlap, chemical removal, distribution, and a stated comparison time horizon. Aerosol or chemical indirect effects can also matter. Equal emitted mass does not imply equal forcing.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises
section: Explore: how long a pulse stays in the air
text:
Explore: how long a pulse stays in the air
Predict which has more left after 100 years: a CO₂ pulse or a pulse of a gas with one sink and a 12-year lifetime. Then move the time and the lifetime and compare the two curves.


Reference case: after 100 years about 0.41 of a CO₂ pulse is still in the air, compared with less than 0.001 for a gas with one sink and a 12-year lifetime.



E1. Choose Lifetime 50, read at 50. Check the rate constant, half-life and fraction left by hand. Compare with exercise 3, which used days instead of years. Why are the numbers the same?
E2. Choose After 20 years, then Lecture comparison and After 500 years. At which times does the CO₂ pulse have more left than the 12-year gas? Use the table to say which part of the CO₂ pulse is responsible.
E3. Raise the one-sink lifetime until its curve is close to the CO₂ curve at 20 years. Then look at 500 years. Explain why no single lifetime can match the CO₂ curve at all times.

Model conditions and hand check
For one first-order sink, fraction left = e^(−t/τ), k = 1/τ and half-life = 0.693 τ. With τ = 50 years and t = 50 years: k = 0.0200 per year, half-life 34.7 years, fraction left e⁻¹ = 0.368. The fraction depends only on t/τ, so exercise 3’s 50 days and 50 days give the same numbers.
The CO₂ curve is the impulse-response fit of Joos et al. (2013), used in the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report: 0.217 + 0.224 e^(−t/394.4) + 0.282 e^(−t/36.54) + 0.276 e^(−t/4.304), with t in years. It gives about 0.60 left after 20 years, 0.41 after 100 years and 0.28 after 500 years. The 12-year gas has e^(−100/12) = 0.0002 left after 100 years.
The fit describes one small pulse added to present-day air, as simulated by carbon-cycle models. Its four parts are fitted terms, not separate measured reservoirs, and the constant part is only constant over the centuries the fit covers; weathering and carbonate reactions remove it over many thousands of years. The one-sink gas is constructed for comparison: no transport, no change in sink strength and no chemical side effects.

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
Why can two waters with the same pH respond differently to an acid input? Carbonate equilibria connect dissolved carbon, acid neutralisation, gas exchange, and mineral stability.
Start with carbonate species and alkalinity, then gas exchange and minerals. Work through the exercises, including a short R activity. The model and reference sheet supplies all constants and assumptions. Reading: vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition, chapters 10–11.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Calculate carbonate species ratios at a supplied pH and interpret a distribution diagram.
Distinguish pH, total dissolved inorganic carbon, alkalinity, and buffer capacity.
Explain why a strong-acid input and carbon dioxide uptake change water differently.
Apply a specified Henry coefficient and a simple calcite saturation test.
Use a supplied R calculation to plot species fractions, check it against a hand calculation, and explain what the plot cannot predict.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
Before starting
You need concentration units, an equilibrium expression, logarithms, and a balanced acid–base reaction. Recall that one millimole per litre is \(10^{-3}\) mol/L, and one micromole per litre is \(10^{-6}\) mol/L. Under our dilute-solution approximation, \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]\) when the numerical concentration is in mol/L. Thus pH 7 corresponds to \(10^{-7}\) mol/L, and lowering pH by one means ten times more hydrogen ion. The exact pH definition uses activity.
Try before reading further: does pH 8 tell you how many moles of acid a litre of water can neutralise? What additional information might you need?
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
A catchment connection
Acid deposition can change the acid input to a lake. Catchment minerals, soil exchange, organic acids, and biological activity also influence the water. Here we isolate carbonate chemistry first. All numerical waters are constructed teaching examples, not measurements from a real lake. The gas-exchange examples are separate boundary conditions, not an assumed continuation of the closed-water acid experiment.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
Interactive practice
Try the week 2 demo. Compare Water A and Water B, then explain the conserved carbon and changed alkalinity.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Opening the box

Last lecture we worked inside the dashed box: CT was fixed and carbon only changed form. Today we open two of the doors: gas exchange with the air and dissolution and precipitation of calcite. Each changes CT, alkalinity, or both, in a definite way.

Show the familiar diagram from the previous lecture. Inside the box we had a closed water, and strong acid only redistributed carbon among the three species. Real waters are open. Carbon dioxide can enter from the air or from respiration and leave again by degassing or photosynthesis. Calcite can dissolve from rocks and soils, or precipitate. The aim of today is bookkeeping: for each process, say what happens to total dissolved carbon and what happens to alkalinity. Once that is clear, pH follows from the tools of last lecture. By the end we will put all processes on one map.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Water meets air: Henry’s law




CO₂ molecules cross the water surface in both directions. At equilibrium the two fluxes are equal and
[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=K_H\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}
with K_H=0.034 mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹ at 25 °C and p in atm.
Henry’s law fixes only the CO₂* pool. Bicarbonate and carbonate ions cannot leave the water; they follow through the acid–base equilibria.


Henry’s law is a simple proportionality: the more carbon dioxide in the gas, the more dissolves. Check units with students: mol per litre per atmosphere times atmospheres gives mol per litre. Warn them that Henry coefficients are published in several conventions, some as pressure divided by concentration, so the number and the equation must come from the same source. We use the convention from the reference sheet. The most important sentence is the last one. Only the neutral dissolved carbon dioxide exchanges with the air. Bicarbonate is an ion; it stays in the water and is connected to carbon dioxide only through the equilibria we studied last time.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
A worked Henry calculation


Take p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=4.00\times10^{-4} atm (the exercise value):
[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=0.034\times4.00\times10^{-4}=1.36\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol/L}
That is 13.6 µmol/L. The atm units cancel.
The relation is linear: ten times more CO₂ in the gas gives ten times more CO₂*. Soil air often holds around 1% CO₂, so soil water can carry far more CO₂* than water at the surface.




This is exercise three, part one. Today’s atmosphere is a little above four times ten to the minus four atmospheres, about 420 parts per million, but the exercise uses a round supplied value so that everyone gets the same answer. Point to the three markers on the line. Pre-industrial air gave about 9.5 micromoles per litre. Soil air, enriched by root and microbial respiration, is typically ten to a hundred times richer in carbon dioxide than the atmosphere; one percent is a common round figure. Water that percolates through soil therefore picks up a lot of carbon dioxide. Keep that in mind: it is the start of the cave and kettle story.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: Henry gives CO₂*, not total carbon
text:
Henry gives CO₂*, not total carbon


If the same water is also specified to have pH 8.35, the ratio rule from last lecture gives the rest:
C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}](1+r_1+r_1r_2)
With r_1=100 and r_2\approx0.0105:
C_T\approx13.6\times102.05\approx 1388 µmol/L
The gas pool is only 1% of the dissolved carbon. Applying Henry’s law to CT would be off by a factor of 100.




This is exercise three, part three. Students must notice the word “specified”. Henry’s law alone does not tell us the pH; we supplied it as an extra piece of information. With the pH given, the proportions 1 to r1 to r1 r2 from last lecture convert the CO2-star pool into the total. At pH 8.35 almost all carbon is bicarbonate, so the total is about a hundred times the gas-controlled pool. The bar chart makes that visible: the slim blue sliver is all that Henry’s law describes. If you fix gas pressure, pH and total carbon independently, you will usually overconstrain the system and get a contradiction.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Why clean rain is acidic


Pure water in contact with air has no alkalinity. The only source of H⁺ is dissolved CO₂:
\mathrm{CO_2^*+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H^++HCO_3^-}
With no other ions, [H⁺] ≈ [HCO₃⁻], so
[\mathrm{H^+}]^2\approx K_1[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=10^{-6.35}\times1.36\times10^{-5}
[H⁺] ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L, pH ≈ 5.6.
This is why “acid rain” means rain below about 5.6.

 Raindrops on a puddle. Photo: Jean-Marie Vugnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


This short calculation explains a number students met in the pilot lecture and in the deposition unit. In pure water the charge balance is simply hydrogen ion equals bicarbonate, because there are no other ions and carbonate is negligible at this pH. Substituting into the first acid equilibrium gives hydrogen ion squared equals K1 times the dissolved carbon dioxide. With our constants and the exercise gas pressure the answer is pH 5.61; with today’s 420 parts per million it is 5.60. Natural rain varies around this value. Sulfuric and nitric acids from pollution push it lower, which is the acid deposition that damaged lakes and forests in the opening story of the last lecture.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
CO₂ uptake versus strong acid

Both inputs lower the HCO₃⁻ : CO₂* ratio, so both lower pH. But CO₂ adds carbon and leaves alkalinity unchanged, while strong acid removes alkalinity and leaves carbon unchanged.

Use the token picture the same way as last time. Start: ten bicarbonate and two CO2-star, so carbon twelve, alkalinity ten. Add three carbon dioxide molecules: carbon becomes fifteen, alkalinity is still ten, the ratio drops from five to two. Add three hydrogen ions instead: three bicarbonates become CO2-star, carbon stays twelve, alkalinity falls to seven, the ratio drops to 1.4. Both waters become more acidic, but by different bookkeeping. This is the key distinction for ocean acidification, for respiration in lakes, and for acid deposition. Ask students why the acid case has the lower ratio even though the same number of particles was added.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Why alkalinity ignores CO₂


Dissolved CO₂ that reacts makes one H⁺ and one HCO₃⁻ together:
\mathrm{CO_2+H_2O\rightarrow H^++HCO_3^-}
In A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}] they cancel: +1 − 1 = 0.
So added CO₂ can push pH down, but it never removes the reserve. The blue curve has no cliff; the red one does.




This is exercise three, part four, and the reason for the contrast in the last lecture’s ocean slide. Carbon dioxide is an acid only in a limited sense: every hydrogen ion it releases arrives together with a bicarbonate ion, which can take the hydrogen ion back. The alkalinity sum therefore does not change. The model curves start from Water A of last lecture. Adding one millimole per litre of strong acid uses up all its alkalinity and pH collapses to about four. Adding one millimole per litre of carbon dioxide doubles total carbon but only brings pH down to about 6.3. These are closed-bottle model results, not field data.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Which way does CO₂ move?


Compare the water’s own CO₂* with K_H\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} of the air above it:

Water higher: CO₂ escapes (degassing). CT falls, AT stays, pH rises.
Water lower: CO₂ enters (uptake). CT rises, pH falls.

Many lakes and streams, especially in the boreal zone, are supersaturated with CO₂. They receive CO₂-rich soil water and respiring organic matter, and release CO₂ to the air.

 Forest lake, Reivo nature reserve, Norrbotten. Photo: GeorgeInsjon, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Gas exchange always runs towards equilibrium with the air. Most water bodies are not at equilibrium, because the water was charged with carbon dioxide somewhere else, in soil or groundwater, or by respiration in the water itself. Northern lakes and streams are commonly net sources of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, fed by soil water and by decomposition of organic matter from their catchments; this is part of the next lecture. Photosynthesis works in the opposite direction: it removes carbon dioxide during the day and can raise pH. The key observation for the rest of today: when carbon dioxide leaves at constant alkalinity, pH rises, and so does carbonate ion.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Minerals: calcite dissolves and precipitates


\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+CO_3^{2-}}
In natural water, with dissolved CO₂:
\mathrm{CaCO_3+CO_2+H_2O\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+2HCO_3^-}
Each mole dissolved adds 1 mol CT and 2 eq alkalinity. Precipitation removes the same.
Read forward: CO₂-rich soil water dissolves limestone. Read backward: water that loses CO₂ deposits calcite.

 Calcite (CaCO₃) crystal, about 6 cm. Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.


This is the mineral door of the box. Write the simple dissolution first, then the version that includes carbon dioxide, which is how limestone weathering really happens. Count the bookkeeping: one calcium, two bicarbonates, so alkalinity rises by two equivalents and total carbon by one mole per mole of calcite. The second equation is reversible, and that is the whole story of today in one line. Forward, carbon dioxide-rich soil water attacks limestone and becomes hard. Backward, when that hard water loses carbon dioxide, the equilibrium shifts left and calcite comes out. Liming, from last lecture, is the forward reaction used deliberately.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: Is calcite stable here? The saturation state
text:
Is calcite stable here? The saturation state


\Omega=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{K_{sp}},\quad K_{sp}=3.3\times10^{-9}

Ω < 1: undersaturated, calcite can dissolve
Ω = 1: saturated, at equilibrium
Ω > 1: supersaturated, calcite can form

Use free ion concentrations. At fixed Ca²⁺ and CT, Ω rises about tenfold per pH unit in this range, because carbonate ion does.




The saturation state compares the actual ion product with the product at equilibrium. It is the mineral version of asking which direction a reaction can go. Use the free ion concentrations: ion pairs such as calcium sulfate reduce free calcium below the dissolved total. The plot fixes calcium at 0.5 millimoles per litre and total carbon at 1 millimole per litre and varies pH. Because carbonate is a small fraction that grows tenfold per pH unit below pK2, Omega does too. This water crosses saturation near pH 8.2. So anything that raises pH, such as losing carbon dioxide, can tip a water from dissolving calcite to depositing it. The strict expression uses activities; we use concentrations.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
A worked saturation comparison
Two water states, each with free Ca²⁺ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L:



State
Free CO₃²⁻ (mol/L)
Product
Ω




X
1.00 × 10⁻⁶
5.00 × 10⁻¹⁰
0.152


Y
1.00 × 10⁻⁵
5.00 × 10⁻⁹
1.52



X could dissolve calcite if calcite is present. In Y precipitation is favoured.
Ω does not give a rate or a final mass of calcite. Precipitation itself removes Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻, so Ω falls back towards 1 as calcite forms; the amount needs a mass balance.

This is exercise four. Multiply, divide by the solubility product, compare with one. A tenfold change in carbonate ion moves the water across saturation. Then discuss what the number cannot tell us. It cannot say how fast calcite forms, because precipitation needs nucleation sites and can be slow. It cannot say how much forms, because precipitation itself removes calcium and carbonate, lowers Omega and stops at saturation; a mass balance is needed for that. And it says nothing about dissolution if no calcite is present. Students also need to remember that replacing free calcium by total dissolved calcium overestimates Omega when ion pairs are important.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
The kettle, explained

Hard water starts near saturation. Heating drives CO₂ out, the carbonate equilibria shift, CO₃²⁻ rises and Ω passes 1. Calcite also becomes less soluble as temperature rises. The hot element provides the surface where crystals start.

Now the opening question has an answer. Follow the chain. Gases are less soluble in hot water, so heating drives carbon dioxide out as bubbles. With carbon dioxide leaving, the second equation on the minerals slide runs backward: bicarbonate re-forms carbon dioxide and carbonate ion. Alkalinity stays the same, but carbon falls, so pH and carbonate ion rise until the water is supersaturated. Calcite is unusual in being less soluble when hot, which adds to the effect. Crystals start on the heating element, where temperature is highest and a surface is available. Soft water from granite areas contains too little calcium and alkalinity to get far.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: A model: groundwater meets the air
text:
A model: groundwater meets the air




Constructed water: dissolves calcite to saturation under soil air at 0.01 atm CO₂. It ends up with AT ≈ 2.8 meq/L and Ca²⁺ ≈ 1.4 mmol/L, pH ≈ 7.3.
It then emerges and loses CO₂ towards the atmosphere (4.0 × 10⁻⁴ atm) at constant alkalinity:

pH rises to about 8.6
Ω rises to about 23

Nature’s kettle needs no heating, only degassing.


This model is generated by the figure script for this lecture, with our 25 degree constants and no temperature effect. It is constructed, but the numbers are realistic for limestone groundwater. In the soil, water is in contact with air that is rich in carbon dioxide, so it can dissolve a lot of calcite before reaching saturation. When the water emerges at a spring, in a cave or in a waterfall, it equilibrates towards the much lower carbon dioxide of the atmosphere. Alkalinity stays constant, carbon falls, pH rises by more than a unit, and Omega rises from one to over twenty. Turbulence speeds the degassing. The curve stops before any calcite forms; precipitation would then pull Omega back down.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Nature’s kettle: tufa at Plitvice


 Tufa coating submerged branches, Plitvice Lakes, Croatia. Photo: Alessandro Caproni, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

At the Plitvice Lakes in Croatia, water from limestone springs flows over a staircase of lakes and waterfalls.
Turbulent water loses CO₂, becomes supersaturated with calcite, and deposits it as tufa, a porous limestone. Mosses, algae and sunken branches provide surfaces; plants also take up CO₂.
Over thousands of years the tufa has built natural dams that hold the lakes in place.


Plitvice is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a spectacular example of exactly the model on the previous slide. Karst springs deliver hard water with high carbon dioxide. As it tumbles over falls and cascades, carbon dioxide escapes, pH and Omega rise, and calcite precipitates on surfaces. Mosses and algae help in two ways: they offer surfaces for crystals to start on, and their photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide. The barriers grow and the lakes are held behind them. Students can contrast this with the kettle: same chemistry, but degassing at constant temperature instead of heating. Similar deposits occur at many karst springs across Europe.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Underground: stalactites


Rainwater passes through soil, picks up CO₂ and dissolves limestone on its way down. When a drop reaches the open cave, it meets cave air with less CO₂ than the soil.
The drop degasses, Ω rises above 1, and a thin ring of calcite is left behind. Drop by drop this builds stalactites, and the water that falls builds stalagmites.
Growth is slow, often fractions of a millimetre per year, so speleothems are used as climate archives.

 Stalactites in a limestone cave, Mallorca, Spain. Photo: Killarnee, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The cave is the same chemistry once more, with a nice extra lesson. The dissolving part happens in the soil and rock above the cave, under high carbon dioxide; the depositing part happens where the drip water meets cave air. Growth rates vary widely, which is why I give only an order of magnitude. Because they grow slowly and in layers, and because their chemistry records conditions at the time of growth, cave formations are dated and used to reconstruct past climate. On Gotland, Lummelunda is a limestone cave students can visit. The general point: dissolution and precipitation of calcite are controlled by carbon dioxide as much as by calcium.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: Supersaturated is not the same as precipitating
text:
Supersaturated is not the same as precipitating


 Coccolithophore bloom colouring Hardangerfjord, Norway, 2020 (NASA Terra MODIS). Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Surface seawater is several times supersaturated with calcite, yet calcite does not simply fall out of the sea. Forming a new crystal needs a nucleation step, and ions such as Mg²⁺ slow crystal growth.
Organisms do it instead: plankton such as coccolithophores build calcite plates. Their blooms turn the sea milky blue.
CO₂ uptake lowers CO₃²⁻ and so lowers Ω, making shell building harder.


This slide connects the thermodynamic idea to kinetics and to the ocean. Omega above one says precipitation is favoured, but a crystal has to start somewhere, and in the open ocean spontaneous nucleation is very slow. Magnesium ions in seawater also inhibit calcite growth. Marine organisms overcome these barriers biologically, and most calcium carbonate in the ocean is made by organisms. The satellite image shows a coccolithophore bloom: the calcite plates scatter light and colour the water. This links back to the pteropod image of the last lecture. Ocean uptake of carbon dioxide keeps alkalinity but converts carbonate to bicarbonate, so Omega falls. Do not quantify seawater with our freshwater constants.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: All the processes on one map
text:
All the processes on one map







Process
CT
AT




CO₂ uptake, respiration
up
same


Degassing, photosynthesis
down
same


Strong acid
same
down

+1
+2

−1
