Dotted lines show pH. Know which arrow you are on before you calculate.


This map summarises the bookkeeping of the week. Each process moves the water in a fixed direction in the space of total carbon and alkalinity, and the background contours show where pH ends up. Carbon dioxide processes move horizontally. Strong acid moves straight down. Calcite moves along a slope of two. Photosynthesis and respiration are shown as pure carbon dioxide processes, which ignores small alkalinity changes from nutrient uptake. A field explanation must first decide which processes act and what is held fixed. Never fix total carbon in a calculation that also allows unlimited gas exchange; the reference sheet table lists what each example holds fixed. Real waters often move along several arrows at once.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Check yourself


A water’s CO₂* is 50 µmol/L. Air above it gives K_Hp=13.6 µmol/L. Which way does CO₂ move, and what happens to pH?
A lake takes up CO₂ from the air. What happens to CT, to AT, to pH?
Calcite dissolves into a closed bottle of water. By how much do CT and AT change per mole?
Ω = 0.4 in a stream with no calcite in its bed. Will the stream dissolve calcite?
Why is Henry’s law not enough to give pH on its own?



Answers. One: the water is supersaturated, so carbon dioxide escapes; at constant alkalinity pH rises. Two: total carbon rises, alkalinity is unchanged, pH falls. Three: plus one mole of carbon and plus two equivalents of alkalinity. Four: no; undersaturation means dissolution would be favoured if calcite were available, but there is none to dissolve. A thermodynamic driving force needs a reactant. Five: Henry’s law fixes only the carbon dioxide pool. To find pH you need one more piece of information, such as alkalinity or total carbon. Let students discuss question four in pairs; it catches many people.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

Applying Henry’s law to CT. It gives CO₂* only.
“CO₂ is an acid, so it lowers alkalinity.” H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ form together; AT is unchanged.
Fixing pCO₂, pH and CT independently. Usually two fix the third.
“Ω > 1, so calcite forms now.” Ω gives direction, not rate or amount.
Using total Ca for free Ca²⁺. Ion pairs lower the free ion.
Forgetting temperature. Gases and calcite are both less soluble in hot water.
Using freshwater constants for seawater.


Run through these quickly and ask for the reason behind each one. The second is the most important conceptual point of the lecture and is examined every year in some form. The third is the source of many contradictory calculations: in an open carbonate system, choosing two of gas pressure, pH, total carbon and alkalinity fixes the rest. The sixth reminds students that our constants are for 25 degrees; real waters are colder or hotter, and the direction of the temperature effect matters for kettles and for cold northern lakes. Ask students to add one more mistake from their own exercise work.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Explore: degassing and calcite saturation


Groundwater from soil air (0.010 atm) degasses to the air: pH rises from 7.26 to 8.65 and Ω from about 1 to about 23.



Follow groundwater from soil air to the open air at fixed alkalinity.

Start with the groundwater preset, which reproduces the “groundwater meets the air” model slide: saturated with calcite under soil air. Then press the degassed preset and ask students what changed. CO2-star falls by a factor of 25, total carbon falls, alkalinity and calcium stay fixed, and pH and Omega rise. Then try the exercise 3 preset to check the Henry calculation, and the rain preset to recover pH 5.6. Ask what would happen to Omega in a soft granite water with low alkalinity and calcium. The exercise page has the assumptions and a hand check.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Henry’s law
[CO₂*] = KH pCO₂; KH = 0.034 mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹ at 25 °C


Gas versus total
Henry fixes CO₂* only; CT needs pH or AT too


Clean rain
pure water + air CO₂ → pH ≈ 5.6


CO₂ uptake
CT up, AT unchanged, pH down, no alkalinity cliff


Strong acid
CT unchanged, AT down by the dose


Degassing
CT down, pH and CO₃²⁻ up


Calcite
dissolving adds 1 mol CT and 2 eq AT per mol


Saturation
Ω = [Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻]/Ksp; above 1 favours calcite forming


Kinetics
supersaturation can persist; surfaces and organisms help


Kettle, cave, tufa
CO₂ loss raises Ω until calcite precipitates



Next: Organic matter in water. Why are many Swedish lakes turning brown? Then the exercises and the reference sheet.

 Brown, humic river water, Korkeakoskenjoki, Finland. Photo: Anna Reponen, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Recite the bookkeeping once more. Gas exchange moves carbon but not alkalinity. Strong acid moves alkalinity but not carbon. Calcite moves both, one to two. Omega tells us whether calcite can dissolve or form, not how fast. The kettle, the cave and the tufa waterfall are one mechanism: carbon dioxide loss raises carbonate ion. The next lecture leaves carbonate chemistry and turns to the other big pool of carbon in natural water, dissolved organic matter. It also gives the reason many boreal lakes are supersaturated with carbon dioxide. The teaser photo shows a brown, humic forest river in Finland; its colour comes from organic matter washed in from soils and peat.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text: Why can ozone protect organisms in one atmospheric region and damage them near the ground? Explain the reactions and where they occur.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Learning goals

Combine reaction steps and identify a regenerated catalyst.
Distinguish photolysis, reaction, and transport.
Explain why the basic NO–NO₂ cycle alone does not yield sustained net ozone production.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Light selects reactions
Photolysis uses absorbed light to break or change a molecule. Photon energy is \(E=hc/\lambda\): shorter wavelengths carry more energy, but a reaction still requires absorption by the molecule. Light availability changes with altitude, clouds, and time. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation; at ground level it is an oxidising pollutant. The same formula does not mean the same environmental setting.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Make stratospheric ozone
A simplified formation sequence is \[\mathrm{O_2}+h\nu\rightarrow2\mathrm{O},\] \[\mathrm{O+O_2+M\rightarrow O_3+M}.\] M is a collision partner that removes excess energy. Ozone also undergoes photolysis and reactions with atomic oxygen. Abundance reflects a production–loss balance plus transport; a fast turnover need not imply a small steady inventory.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
A chlorine catalytic cycle
Consider \[\mathrm{Cl+O_3\rightarrow ClO+O_2},\] \[\mathrm{ClO+O\rightarrow Cl+O_2}.\] Adding the steps cancels Cl and ClO and gives \(\mathrm{O_3+O\rightarrow2O_2}\). Chlorine is regenerated and can repeat the sequence until another reaction interrupts it. This is a representative gas-phase cycle, not the full mechanism of the polar ozone hole; polar chemistry also involves particle surfaces and different catalytic cycles.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Tropospheric cycling
In the basic photochemical cycle, NO₂ photolysis forms NO and O; the O atom forms O₃ with O₂ and a collision partner. But \(\mathrm{NO+O_3\rightarrow NO_2+O_2}\) consumes that ozone. These steps alone form a cycle without sustained net production. Peroxy radicals from oxidation of volatile organic compounds or CO can instead convert NO to NO₂ without consuming ozone, allowing net ozone production in appropriate conditions.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Rates and lifetime
For a loss reaction \(X+\mathrm{OH}\rightarrow\) products, \(R=k[X][\mathrm{OH}]\). If OH is treated as constant, the pseudo-first-order loss coefficient is \(k'=k[\mathrm{OH}]\) and the chemical lifetime is \(1/k'\). This approximation isolates one sink. Deposition, transport, changing sunlight, and competing reactions alter the observed atmospheric persistence. A catalyst is regenerated in a sequence, not present in unlimited amount or active forever.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Worked example
Adding the two chlorine steps gives one ozone molecule and one atomic oxygen consumed for every two oxygen molecules produced. Cl and ClO cancel. Each completed cycle therefore removes one ozone molecule, but the number of cycles per chlorine atom depends on competing reactions and conditions. Stoichiometry by itself gives neither the cycle rate nor a global ozone loss.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapters 2–4: photolysis, one stratospheric catalytic cycle, and the NO–NO₂–ozone cycle.
NOAA ozone assessment: Formation, catalytic destruction, and the role of atmospheric region.
NASA photochemical explanation: How nitrogen oxides and organic chemistry participate in ground-level ozone formation.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
text:
1. Reaction bookkeeping
Add the two chlorine steps in the notes. Identify the catalyst, the intermediate, and the net reaction.






Hint





Cancel species occurring on both sides of the summed equation.









Worked solution





The net reaction is O₃ + O → 2 O₂. Cl is regenerated; ClO is the cycle intermediate. Neither appears in the net reaction.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
text:
2. A supplied rate
Take k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹ and constant OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³. Calculate k′ and the lifetime in seconds and days. Use 86400 s/day.






Hint





Multiply k by OH; invert the resulting s⁻¹ value.









Worked solution





k′ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. The lifetime is 1.0 × 10⁶ s, about 11.6 days for this one constant sink. It is an e-folding time, not a half-life.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
section: 3. Does the cycle make net ozone?
text:
3. Does the cycle make net ozone?
Sum the NO₂ photolysis, O₃ formation, and NO + O₃ reactions. Why can peroxy radicals change the outcome?






Hint





The third body and all nitrogen/oxygen intermediates cancel.









Worked solution





The basic cycle gives no net chemical change apart from energy conversion. A peroxy pathway can convert NO to NO₂ without using O₃, allowing the subsequent photolysis to contribute net ozone production.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
text:
4. Location and evidence
An ozone measurement rises at a surface station. Can you infer increased stratospheric ozone or identify a single emission source? Explain what else is needed.






Hint





A measurement is local; production and transport both matter.









Worked solution





No. Surface ozone depends on precursor chemistry, sunlight, deposition, mixing, and transported ozone. Altitude-resolved measurements, precursor observations, and meteorological information are needed. The molecular formula alone does not identify origin.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere exercises
section: Explore: OH and the lifetime of a gas
text:
Explore: OH and the lifetime of a gas
Predict what happens to the lifetime of gas X if the OH concentration doubles. Then predict how far X can travel if its reaction with OH is 100 times slower. Change one input at a time and keep apart the rate constant, the lifetime, and the half-life.


Reference case: k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹ and OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³ give k′ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹, a lifetime of 1.0 × 10⁶ s (11.6 days) and a half-life of 8.0 days.



E1. Choose Worked example, then Twice as much OH. By what factor did k′, the lifetime and the half-life change? Check the new lifetime by hand.
E2. Choose Slow reaction. Compare the lifetime with the transport times on the lecture slide. Why can a gas like this spread over the whole globe while the worked-example gas stays a regional problem?
E3. Choose Add deposition 0.1 per day. Why is the new lifetime shorter than both 11.6 days and 10 days? Explain why the two loss rate constants are added, not the two lifetimes.

Model conditions and hand check
For the worked example, k′ = k × [OH] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹²)(1.0 × 10⁶) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. The lifetime is 1/k′ = 1.0 × 10⁶ s, and dividing by 86400 s/day gives 11.6 days. The half-life is 0.693 × 11.6 = 8.0 days. With twice as much OH, k′ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ and the lifetime is 5.8 days. With deposition added, the loss rate constants add: 0.0864 + 0.100 = 0.186 per day, so the lifetime is 1/0.186 = 5.4 days.
OH is held at one constant value, taken as an average over day and night. The gas sits in one air parcel with no new emissions, so the amount left falls as e^(−t/τ). The other loss is a simple first-order process, such as deposition, given per day. The transport classes use the approximate times from the lecture: about a day to mix the lowest air layer, a few weeks to circle a hemisphere, and about a year to mix between hemispheres. Real OH varies with sunlight, season and place, and k depends on temperature.

title: Organic matter in water
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Where the organic matter comes from
text:
Where the organic matter comes from

Most dissolved organic matter in a boreal lake comes from land: decaying leaves, roots, soil humus and peat. It is coloured and rich in organic acids. A smaller part is made in the lake by algae and plants. That part is paler and is eaten quickly by bacteria.

Two broad sources. Material from the catchment is called terrestrial or allochthonous; material produced in the lake is aquatic or autochthonous. You do not need the Greek words, but students may meet them in reading. Catchments with a lot of peat and coniferous forest deliver the most coloured water, especially during snowmelt and autumn rain, when water flows through the upper, organic-rich soil layers. Algal organic matter matters more in nutrient-rich lakes and in the sea. Wastewater and farm runoff add organic matter too, often easily degradable. The point for today is that “organic matter” is a mixture whose properties depend on where it came from.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Not one molecule: a size continuum
text:
Not one molecule: a size continuum

Natural organic matter ranges from small acids to large particles. DOC (dissolved organic carbon) is the carbon in whatever passes the chosen filter; POC is what stays behind. DOC gives an amount of carbon, in mg C/L. It does not give a structure, a charge or a degradation rate.

This is the same lesson as the filter slide in the first water lecture, applied to carbon. Organic matter spans many orders of magnitude in size, from small acids such as acetate through humic and fulvic acids to colloids, cells and fragments. The boundary between dissolved and particulate is the filter we choose, often around 0.45 micrometres. To measure DOC, the filtered sample is acidified to remove inorganic carbon, then the organic carbon is oxidised and measured as carbon dioxide. The result counts carbon atoms only. Two waters with the same DOC can differ in colour, acidity, metal binding and how fast bacteria consume them. Always report the filter and method with a DOC value.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Organic acids carry charge


Humic substances carry carboxyl (–COOH) and phenolic (–OH) groups. Both are weak acids, so the ratio rule from the first water lecture applies:
\frac{[\mathrm{R\text{-}COO^-}]}{[\mathrm{R\text{-}COOH}]}=10^{\,\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}
At natural pH most carboxyl groups have lost H⁺; most phenolic groups have not.
So brown water contains many organic anions. They supply H⁺, which is why many humic lakes are naturally acidic, and they count in the charge balance.




Link straight back to the weak-acid split. The pKa values are illustrative: real humic material has a broad spread of sites, roughly from three to five for carboxyl and nine to ten or more for phenolic groups. Above about pH 5 most carboxyl groups are negatively charged. This has two consequences. First, these organic acids release hydrogen ions, and many brown lakes in Sweden have a natural pH between about 5 and 6 even without acid rain. Distinguishing natural organic acidity from anthropogenic acidification was a real practical problem during the acid rain period. Second, organic anions appear in the charge balance and can make a carbonate-only alkalinity calculation misleading.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Negative sites bind metals

Neighbouring negative groups can hold a metal ion such as Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺ or Al³⁺ in a complex. The metal stays in the filtered, “dissolved” fraction, but it is no longer a free ion. No electron moves: this is binding, not redox.

The fragment is schematic. Real humic matter is a mixture, not a single molecule, and you should never present a structural formula for it as if it were known. What matters is the arrangement of acid groups. Two or more groups on the same molecule can grip a metal ion from several sides, which makes the complex strong. Copper, lead, mercury and aluminium bind particularly strongly. The connection to the first water lecture is the filter diagram: complexes pass the filter and are counted in dissolved metal. They are not counted in the free-ion concentration. And remember the redox slide: binding changes the metal’s form without changing its oxidation state.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Same total, different free metal




Waters A and B both contain 2.00 µmol/L dissolved metal. Free metal is 0.500 in A and 0.100 µmol/L in B.

Bound in A: (2.00 − 0.500)/2.00 = 75.0%
Bound in B: (2.00 − 0.100)/2.00 = 95.0%

The free ion differs fivefold with identical totals. The free ion is often the best single guide to what organisms take up, so several regulators, including in the EU, adjust metal limits for DOC and pH.


This is exercise one. The arithmetic is trivial; the interpretation is the point. A total dissolved metal measurement would rank these two waters as identical. The free metal ion, which interacts most directly with uptake sites on gills and cell surfaces, is five times higher in A. That is why environmental quality standards for metals such as copper, nickel and lead are increasingly expressed in terms of bioavailability, adjusted for dissolved organic carbon, pH and hardness. Keep the claim modest: binding to organic matter generally lowers free-ion exposure, but organic matter can also carry metals further downstream as complexes. The metals lecture next week builds on this.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Colour: brown water absorbs blue light
text:
Colour: brown water absorbs blue light




Coloured organic matter absorbs strongly in the ultraviolet and blue, and less towards red. Water that removes blue and passes yellow-red looks brown.
Absorption falls roughly exponentially with wavelength. How steeply, and how much absorption per gram of carbon, depends on the source of the material.
The two constructed waters have the same DOC but differ fourfold in colour. Colour is a property, not a direct measure of carbon.


The curves are constructed, with round parameters of typical size. Point out the shape: very high absorption in the ultraviolet, falling steadily into the visible. Ultraviolet absorption at 254 nanometres or absorption at 420 nanometres are common routine measures of colour. Organic matter from peat and forest soils is rich in aromatic structures and absorbs strongly per unit carbon; algal material absorbs much less. So an absorbance measurement and a DOC measurement answer different questions. They are often correlated within one water body, but the ratio varies between waters and over time. Students should not convert colour into DOC with a universal factor.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Less light, shallower life




Light decreases exponentially with depth:
I(z)=I_0\,e^{-K_d z}
The attenuation coefficient Kd grows with colour. Plants and algae need roughly 1% of surface light.

clear lake, Kd = 0.3 /m: 1% at 15 m
brown lake, Kd = 3 /m: 1% at 1.5 m

Browning squeezes photosynthesis into a thin surface layer and lets less UV reach the water below.


The three lakes are constructed with round values, but the range is realistic between clear and very humic waters. The depth of one percent light is the logarithm of one hundred divided by Kd, about 4.6 divided by Kd. A tenfold increase in attenuation makes the lit layer ten times thinner. Consequences follow. Bottom plants and algae lose their light. The surface layer warms faster and the lake stratifies more strongly. Less ultraviolet penetrates, which protects some organisms but also reduces the natural disinfection of pathogens by sunlight. In a browning lake all these change together, which is why limnologists treat colour as a master variable.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Measuring colour in the field


 Secchi disk, Cochiti Lake, New Mexico, USA. Photo: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

A Secchi disk is lowered until it disappears. The depth is a simple measure of clarity, used in lake monitoring for over a century.
But clarity mixes several causes. Water can darken while DOC stays nearly constant, if:

the organic matter changes composition (more aromatic, more coloured);
iron increases: Fe(III) adds colour of its own and binds to organic matter;
particles increase.

Measure absorbance, DOC, iron and particles separately before choosing an explanation.


This connects to exercise four. A darkening water is an observation, not an explanation. In southern Sweden, studies of rivers have found that rising iron concentrations explain a substantial part of the colour increase, alongside the increase in organic matter itself. Whether iron or organic matter dominates differs between catchments. The practical lesson is to measure the candidate causes independently: absorbance spectra, DOC, total and filtered iron, and turbidity or suspended solids. Do not infer a source, a degradation rate or a toxicity from colour alone. The Secchi disk is cheap and robust, and long Secchi records are among the data that first revealed brownification.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Sunlight changes organic matter

Light absorbed by coloured organic matter breaks its light-absorbing groups. The water becomes paler, small molecules form that bacteria use readily, and some carbon is released as CO₂. A loss of colour therefore does not prove a loss of carbon.

Photochemistry is the flip side of colour: whatever absorbs light can be changed by it. Bleaching removes colour faster than it removes carbon, so in a sunlit surface layer colour can fall while DOC hardly changes. Part of the organic matter is broken into small molecules such as low molecular weight acids, which bacteria then consume, and a smaller part is converted directly to carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. Rates depend on sunlight, depth and the type of organic matter. Keep this qualitative. The take-home is the inverse of the previous slide: a change in colour and a change in carbon are separate observations and need separate measurements.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Organic matter consumes oxygen


Use CH₂O as a stand-in for simple organic matter:
\mathrm{CH_2O+O_2\rightarrow CO_2+H_2O}
1 mol C uses 1 mol O₂, so 12.0 g C uses 32.0 g O₂.
Worked example: complete aerobic oxidation of 3.00 mg C/L:
3.00 × 32.0/12.0 = 8.00 mg O₂/L
That is close to all the oxygen water holds: about 9 mg/L at 20 °C.




The reaction is the reverse of photosynthesis and is how bacteria get energy from organic matter. CH2O is a stoichiometric teaching formula, not the formula of humic substances, which are more reduced or more oxidised depending on their origin. With it, one carbon needs one oxygen molecule, and the mass ratio is thirty-two over twelve, about 2.67. The worked example from the notes shows the scale of the problem: a few milligrams of organic carbon per litre can in principle consume nearly all the dissolved oxygen. The chart is exercise two: a sealed litre at 9 milligrams per litre, with two milligrams of carbon, ends with 3.67.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Ultimate demand versus what you measure
text:
Ultimate demand versus what you measure




The 8.00 mg/L is an ultimate, stoichiometric demand. It assumes complete oxidation.
Real organic matter degrades at different speeds. If only 25% of 4.00 mg C/L is oxidised during an observation period:

consumed: 1.00 mg C → 2.67 mg O₂/L
complete oxidation would need 10.67 mg O₂/L

A 5-day test (BOD₅) measures the early part of the curve, not the ultimate demand.


This is exercise three. The curve is a constructed first-order decay with a round rate constant, chosen to make the shape visible. The difference between what has happened so far and what could happen eventually is important in practice. The standard biochemical oxygen demand test runs for five days in the dark at twenty degrees, and it measures only the readily degradable part. Humic organic matter from peat degrades much more slowly than algal material or sewage. So a brown lake can carry a large ultimate demand that a five-day test hardly sees. Also remember other oxygen consumers, such as nitrification of ammonium, which add to the demand.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
When demand outruns supply

In summer many lakes stratify: warm surface water floats on cold bottom water. The bottom water is cut off from the air, but organic matter keeps sinking into it. Oxygen falls, and microbes then use other electron acceptors: nitrate, manganese and iron oxides, and finally sulfate.

An oxygen budget needs sources as well as sinks. In the surface layer oxygen is resupplied from the air and by photosynthesis. Below the thermocline, neither works well, while sinking organic matter and the sediment keep consuming oxygen. When oxygen is gone, microbes use the next available electron acceptor, in the order shown, which is the order of decreasing energy yield; week four covers it in detail. Two consequences matter here. Iron(III) oxides dissolve, releasing iron and the phosphate that was attached to them. Sulfate reduction produces hydrogen sulfide, which is toxic. Browning can strengthen stratification and add organic matter, both of which favour low oxygen.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: A large-scale case: the Baltic Sea
text:
A large-scale case: the Baltic Sea


 Cyanobacteria bloom in the Baltic Sea, July 2025 (Landsat). NASA Earth Observatory, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

The Baltic has some of the largest low-oxygen bottom areas of any sea. Salty, dense water at depth is renewed only occasionally.
Nutrients feed algal and cyanobacterial blooms. When the organic matter sinks and decays it consumes oxygen. Without oxygen, iron oxides in the sediment dissolve and release phosphate, which feeds the next bloom.
The same chemistry as a stratified lake, on a regional scale.


The satellite image shows a summer cyanobacteria bloom swirling in the Baltic. The Baltic Sea is permanently stratified by salinity, with brackish water above and saltier water below, and the deep water is renewed only when occasional inflows of North Sea water arrive. Decades of nutrient input from agriculture and wastewater increased the production of organic matter, and its decay consumes oxygen in the deep basins. The release of phosphate from anoxic sediments, often called internal loading, is a feedback that keeps blooms going even after external inputs fall. Keep the numbers out of it; the mechanism is the point, and it is exactly the mechanism on the previous slide.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Check yourself


Two waters both have 6 mg/L DOC. Name three properties that could still differ.
Why can a humic lake have pH 5.5 without any acid rain?
Total dissolved copper is unchanged, but DOC doubles. What would you expect for free Cu²⁺?
Complete oxidation of 1.50 mg C/L of CH₂O-like substrate needs how much O₂?
Water becomes paler over a sunny summer. Has its DOC necessarily fallen?



Answers. One: colour or absorbance, acidity and charge, metal binding capacity, degradation rate, molecular size. Any three. Two: the organic matter itself contains carboxylic acids that release hydrogen ions. Three: more binding sites usually means more copper bound and less free copper, but the size of the effect depends on the binding chemistry and on pH, and some binding sites may already be occupied by other metals. Four: 1.50 times 32 over 12 gives 4.00 milligrams per litre. Five: no. Photobleaching removes colour faster than carbon. Measure DOC directly before concluding anything about carbon loss.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Back to browning: why, and so what?
text:
Back to browning: why, and so what?

Several drivers act together, and their importance differs between catchments. Recovery from acid rain is one of the best supported: as sulfate deposition fell, soil organic matter became more soluble. Each consequence on the right uses a chemical idea from today.

Return to the opening case. Research in Europe and North America has linked rising DOC to falling sulfate deposition: with less strong acid and less ionic strength in soil water, organic matter is more soluble and is washed out more easily. Climate also matters, through wetter autumns, milder winters and longer growing seasons, as do land use, including the expansion of spruce forests and ditching of peatlands, and rising iron. Read the consequences with the class and name the chemistry each uses: light absorption, oxygen stoichiometry, metal binding. This is an example of an environmental change produced by recovery from an earlier problem, a theme that returns later in the course.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Browning and drinking water


 Lake Bolmen at Piksborg, Småland. Photo: Eddie001, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Bolmen in Småland supplies drinking water to a large part of Skåne. Lakes like it are watched closely for colour and DOC.
More organic matter means:

more coagulant to remove colour and DOC;
organic matter that reacts with chlorine to form unwanted disinfection by-products;
organic matter left in pipes feeds bacterial regrowth.

So browning is a chemistry problem for water treatment, the topic of a later unit.


Bolmen, in southern Småland, is the raw-water source for a regional supplier that serves many municipalities in Skåne through a long tunnel. Treatment plants that take water from brown lakes have had to adapt their processes as colour has risen. The chemistry links directly to today: coagulation removes humic material partly through its charged acid groups; chlorine reacts with aromatic structures to form trihalomethanes and other by-products, which are regulated; and easily degradable DOC left after treatment can support bacterial growth in the distribution network. The water treatment unit later in the course develops these processes. The photo is an ordinary view of the lake.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“DOC is a substance.” It is the carbon in an operationally filtered fraction.
“Brown means more carbon.” Colour per unit carbon varies; iron adds colour.
“Dissolved metal is free metal.” Organic complexes pass the filter.
“More DOC means less dissolved metal.” It often means more dissolved but less free metal.
“CH₂O is the formula of humus.” It is a stoichiometric stand-in.
“BOD₅ is the total demand.” It measures the early, fast part.
“Paler water has lost carbon.” Photobleaching removes colour first.


These are the interpretation errors that come up most often, in exams and in real reports. Ask students to explain the fourth one. Organic matter can keep metals in solution as complexes and carry them downstream, so total dissolved metal can increase with DOC, while the free ion decreases. That is not a contradiction: it is the difference between total and species from the first water lecture. Remind students that every number in this lecture is either a constructed teaching example or a round illustrative value, and that the exercises state their assumptions explicitly. They should do the same in their own answers.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
section: Explore: oxygen demand in a sealed bottle
text:
Explore: oxygen demand in a sealed bottle


4.00 mg C/L has an ultimate demand of 10.67 mg O₂/L; at 0.10 per day, 4.20 mg O₂/L is used in 5 days.



Compare the ultimate demand with what a 5-day test sees.

Start with the exercise 3 preset: the curve is the constructed first-order decay from the “ultimate demand versus what you measure” slide. Point out that this pool needs more oxygen than a sealed bottle at 9 mg/L holds, so the oxygen runs out on day 18.6. Then compare the slow humic preset: same carbon, same ultimate demand, but a 5-day test sees almost nothing. Use the exercise 2 and worked example presets to check the stoichiometry. Ask students what a real lake has that the bottle lacks: reaeration and photosynthesis. The exercise page has the assumptions and a hand check.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Sources
boreal lakes: mostly from land (coloured); some from algae (pale)


DOC
carbon passing a stated filter; amount, not structure or reactivity


Acid groups
carboxyl mostly ionised at natural pH; humic lakes can be naturally acidic


Metal binding
complexes stay “dissolved”; free ion falls; total is not free


Colour
absorbs UV and blue; colour per unit C varies; iron adds colour


Light
I = I₀ e^(−Kdz); 1% light at about 4.6/Kd


Photochemistry
bleaching removes colour faster than carbon


Oxygen demand
CH₂O + O₂: 1 mol O₂ per mol C; 2.67 g O₂ per g C


Ultimate vs measured
complete oxidation versus what happens in the test period


Anoxia
stratification + organic matter → low O₂ → Fe, P and H₂S released



Next: Week 3, Metal speciation and mobility. Why does a Spanish river run red? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Iron-rich, acidic water of the Río Tinto, Spain. Photo: Carol Stoker, NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Recap the three roles of organic matter. As an acid it carries charge and binds metals. As a pigment it controls light. As a fuel it consumes oxygen and can drive water to anoxia, with consequences for iron, phosphorus and sulfide. All three are behind the browning of northern waters. Week three starts with metals, and builds directly on today’s distinction between total, complexed and free metal, and on the redox chemistry of iron. The teaser photo is the Río Tinto in southern Spain, coloured by iron from centuries of mining and very acidic. Next week explains how acidity, redox and binding control which metals stay dissolved and which precipitate.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Learning goals

Convert ionic concentrations to charge equivalents.
Distinguish analytical totals, free concentrations, and activities.
Use an equilibrium model without confusing thermodynamic possibility with reaction speed.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Water is a reaction medium
Dissolved ions are hydrated; their interactions depend on charge, solution composition, and temperature. A formula in an analytical table may denote an element total, a specific ion, or a reporting convention. Read the method and units before calculating. A filtered metal result does not necessarily mean free metal ion; small complexes and some colloids can pass the chosen filter.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Charge balance is a constraint
Bulk water must be electrically neutral. Sum positive and negative ionic charge equivalents, not masses: \[\Sigma_+=\sum_{z_i>0}z_ic_i,\qquad\Sigma_-=\sum_{z_i<0}|z_i|c_i.\] Using mmol/L gives meq/L. A calcium concentration of 0.500 mmol/L contributes 1.00 meq/L because calcium is divalent. A mismatch suggests omitted ions, unsuitable speciation, reporting errors, or analytical uncertainty; the water itself has not become macroscopically charged.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Concentration and activity
Thermodynamic equilibrium constants use dimensionless activities. For an aqueous solute, write \(a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ\), with \(c^\circ=1\) mol/L and activity coefficient \(\gamma_i\). In dilute teaching examples we take \(\gamma_i\approx1\), making numerical concentrations convenient. Ionic strength \(I=\tfrac12\sum c_i z_i^2\) weights squared charge; divalent ions can influence nonideality strongly. The dilute approximation should not be carried unexamined into seawater.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
A simple acid distribution
For \(\mathrm{HA\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-}\) in the concentration approximation, \[\frac{[A^-]}{[HA]}=10^{\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}.\] If these are the only forms, the deprotonated fraction is \(r/(1+r)\). At a prescribed pH one unit above the pKa, the ratio is ten and the fraction is \(10/11\). The pH must come from a measurement or an additional balance; a distribution formula does not by itself solve for pH.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
A small redox bridge
Oxidation loses electrons and reduction gains them. For example, \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+e^-\rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\) changes oxidation state; binding a ligand without electron transfer does not. Both pH and redox can change metal speciation. An equilibrium prediction tells which state is favoured under specified conditions. Kinetics, access to reactants, and transport determine whether the state is reached in the sampling period.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Worked example
A table reports Ca²⁺ = 0.500, Mg²⁺ = 0.250, Na⁺ = 0.500, HCO₃⁻ = 1.200, Cl⁻ = 0.400, and SO₄²⁻ = 0.200 mmol/L. Cations sum to \(2(0.500)+2(0.250)+0.500=2.000\) meq/L. Anions sum to \(1.200+0.400+2(0.200)=2.000\) meq/L. The signed imbalance is 0%. This is an intentionally simplified near-neutral ion set; minor H⁺/OH⁻ and other species are omitted. Closure is a useful check, not proof that every concentration or species assignment is correct.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium exercises
text:
1. Charge and mass units
A sample contains 40.08 mg/L calcium. Use molar mass 40.08 g/mol. Convert to mmol/L and meq/L.






Hint





A molar mass in g/mol has the same numerical value in mg/mmol.









Worked solution





Calcium is 1.000 mmol/L and contributes 2.000 meq/L. Milligrams cannot be added directly to milliequivalents.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium exercises
text:
2. A weak acid
For a fictitious HA with pKa 5.00 and total HA + A⁻ = 0.200 mmol/L, calculate the two concentrations at prescribed pH 6.00.






Hint





Calculate r = 10, then split the total in the proportion 1:10.









Worked solution





HA = 0.01818 mmol/L; A⁻ = 0.1818 mmol/L. Their sum is 0.200 mmol/L. These are equilibrium concentrations at supplied pH.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium exercises
text:
3. Ionic strength
A dilute solution contains 1.00 mmol/L Ca²⁺ and 2.00 mmol/L Cl⁻, with other ions negligible. Calculate ionic strength in mol/L.






Hint





Square the charge number in each contribution.









Worked solution





I = ½[(0.00100)(4) + (0.00200)(1)] = 0.00300 mol/L. This is not the total molar concentration or total dissolved mass.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium exercises
text:
4. A charge mismatch
An analysis has 2.00 meq/L cations and 1.64 meq/L anions. Calculate the signed imbalance. Should you change raw measurements until the table balances?






Hint





Use the stated denominator: sum of both charge totals.









Worked solution





The imbalance is +9.89%. Investigate units, omitted ions, methods, and uncertainty. Do not invent a correction or treat this teaching value as a universal acceptance threshold. Preserve original observations and document evidence for any correction.

section: Activity A: water table in R
text:
Activity A: water table in R
Download these files into one project folder:

water-ions.csv, the constructed original table.
corrections.csv, the evidence for one correction.
water-analysis.R, the supplied calculation.
water-report.Rmd, the report template.
Data dictionary, which defines the quantities.

Before running R, calculate the calcium contribution for sample A by hand. 20.04 mg/L divided by 40.08 mg/mmol gives 0.500 mmol/L; its divalent charge contributes 1.00 meq/L. Predict whether sample C balances if its sulfate value is only one tenth of sample A’s while its other entries match A.
Read the script in the editor. Then run from the activity folder:
source("water-analysis.R")
raw_balance
corrections
corrected_balance
water_plot
The script reuses read_csv(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise(), and ggplot(). Its new chemical operation is multiplying molar concentration by charge magnitude. if_else() separates positive and negative contributions without changing the raw table. The narrowly specified row replacement applies the supplied fictional lab record; you do not need to write a general data-cleaning program.
Explain the original charge discrepancy, inspect the correction evidence, and compare the waters after correction. Complete the report prompts. Restart R and Knit water-report.Rmd, or use rmarkdown::render("water-report.Rmd") from the same folder.






Expected checks and interpretation





Raw A has 2.00 meq/L cations and 2.00 meq/L anions; raw B has 0.500 of each. Raw C has 2.00 and 1.64, giving +9.89% imbalance. The supplied lab record corrects C sulfate from 1.9212 to 19.212 mg/L. After that documented correction, C matches A and all signed imbalances are zero to numerical precision.
The plot compares mmol/L, while the balance uses meq/L. Valence changes the conversion. The balance flags a mismatch; it does not identify the sulfate error without the extra record, nor prove all analyses correct after closure. There is no statistical treatment-group comparison here: A, B, and C are constructed sample identities, not replicate experiments.






Constructed ion concentrations after the documented correction; A and C coincide.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium exercises
section: Explore: charge balance and ionic strength
text:
Explore: charge balance and ionic strength
Predict what the charge balance shows if the sulfate entry is ten times too small, as in sample C. Then predict what adding sodium chloride does to the balance and to the activity of calcium. Change one input at a time.


Reference case: the worked ion table has 2.000 meq/L of cation charge and 2.000 meq/L of anion charge (0% imbalance), an ionic strength of 2.95 mmol/L, and activity coefficients of about 0.94 for single-charged and 0.79 for double-charged ions.



E1. Choose Worked example, then Sample C: sulfate error. Check the anion total and the +9.89% imbalance by hand. Which other single change to the table could produce the same imbalance, and why can the balance alone not tell you which entry is wrong?
E2. Reset, then raise the Ca²⁺ entry by 0.10 mmol/L. How much do the cation charge and the ionic strength change? Explain the factors 2 and 4 that appear.
E3. Choose Salty river and then Brackish. Why does the charge balance stay at zero while the activity coefficients fall? For which ions is γ ≈ 1 first a poor approximation?

Model conditions and hand check
The worked table (mmol/L) is Ca²⁺ 0.500, Mg²⁺ 0.250, Na⁺ 0.500, HCO₃⁻ 1.200, Cl⁻ 0.400 and SO₄²⁻ 0.200. Cations: 2(0.500) + 2(0.250) + 0.500 = 2.000 meq/L; anions: 1.200 + 0.400 + 2(0.200) = 2.000 meq/L. With sample C’s sulfate, 1.9212 mg/L ÷ 96.06 mg/mmol = 0.0200 mmol/L, anions are 1.640 meq/L and the imbalance is (2.000 − 1.640)/3.640 × 100 = +9.89%. The ionic strength of the worked table is ½(0.5 × 4 + 0.25 × 4 + 0.5 + 1.2 + 0.4 + 0.2 × 4) = 2.95 mmol/L.
Only the Ca²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ entries and the added NaCl can be changed; the other entries stay at the worked values. Added NaCl brings equal amounts of Na⁺ and Cl⁻. H⁺, OH⁻ and minor ions are left out, and every ion is treated as free (no complexes). Activity coefficients are estimated with the Davies equation at 25 °C, the same estimate as the lecture figure; it is not reliable much above an ionic strength of about 0.5 mol/L, so seawater is outside this model.

title: Chemical glossary
text:
Use these definitions with the model conditions in each unit. Similar words can describe different quantities; always check the phase and units.



Term
Meaning and explanation




Activity
Effective thermodynamic quantity relative to a standard state; concentration approximation.


Adsorption/sorption
Association with a surface or solid phase; phase balance. Sorption is the broader term used here.


Aerosol
Suspended solid particles or liquid droplets in air; deposition.


Alkalinity
An acid-neutralising balance in charge equivalents per volume; carbonate expression.


Bioavailability
Availability of chemical forms to a biological uptake or interaction process; speciation limits. It is not synonymous with a filtered total.


Buffer capacity
Resistance to a small pH change under specified conditions; distinction from alkalinity.


Cation exchange capacity
Exchange-site charge inventory per dry solid mass under stated conditions; CEC.


Charge equivalent
Amount weighted by ionic charge magnitude; charge balance.


Colloid
A small dispersed particle whose operational classification depends on method; particle transport.


Complex
A coordinated metal–ligand species; one-ligand model.


Concentration
Amount or mass per volume; inventory distinction.


Dissolved inorganic carbon
Carbon summed across the specified dissolved inorganic species; carbonate model.


Dissolved organic carbon
Organic carbon in a defined operational fraction; DOC.


Flux/load
Amount transferred per area per time or amount per time, respectively, with the convention stated; deposition budget.


Free ion
Uncomplexed aqueous ion in the stated model; metal total distinction.


Half-life
Time for half the tracked parent to transform under the specified kinetic model; first-order equation.


Henry coefficient
A convention-dependent gas–water equilibrium coefficient; units and pool.


Ionic strength
Half the sum of concentration times squared charge number; nonideality.


Kd
Solid-to-water distribution coefficient with the specified phase and concentration units; linear model.


Koc
Organic-carbon-normalised sorption coefficient for an appropriate model; conditional use.


Kow
Octanol–water distribution of a specified molecular form; property limitations.


Ligand
A binding partner coordinating a metal; free and total ligand.


Mineral saturation
Comparison of the free-ion activity product with equilibrium; calcite example.


Oxidation/reduction
Loss/gain of electrons; balanced half-reactions.


pH
Negative base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity; dilute approximation.


Photolysis
Light-driven molecular change following absorption; atmospheric chemistry.


Speciation
Distribution among chemical forms under stated conditions; ratios and fractions.


Steady state
Zero net accumulation despite continuing processes; balance.


Transformation
Change of chemical identity; parent and product distinction.

title: Environmental Chemistry
text:
How do molecular properties and reactions decide what happens to substances in air, water and soil? This 7.5 ECTS course follows chemistry from the atmosphere through lakes and rivers to soils and contaminants.
Course book: vanLoon and Duffy, Environmental Chemistry: A Global Perspective, 4th edition (2017). See course content and reading.

title: Environmental Chemistry
text:
Topics
Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Each topic has a lecture, notes and exercises.

Week 1: Environmental balances and atmosphere: amounts and balances, atmospheric reactions and ozone, acid deposition, molecules and climate.
Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry: water composition, carbonate species and alkalinity, gas exchange and minerals, organic matter in water.
Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox and treatment: metal speciation, sorption, redox cycles, water treatment.
Week 4: Soils, waste and contaminants: soil chemistry, mine waste and leachate, organic contaminants.
Week 5: Connected systems: a case that links air, catchment and water.
