title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
About this lecture


In August 2022, hundreds of tonnes of dead fish washed up along the Oder, the river between Poland and Germany. Investigators had to work out what was in the water. Their answer combined several factors: unusually salty water from industrial discharges, low flow, heat, and a bloom of a toxic alga that thrives in salty water.
Every step of that investigation started from a water analysis: a table of numbers.
Today you will learn to:

read what each number means (total, species, filtered);
check a table with charge balance;
decide when activity matters, and split a weak acid at a given pH.


 Dead fish on the Oder, August 2022. Photo: Hanno Böck, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.


Open with the Oder disaster because it shows that water chemistry is not abstract. In the summer of 2022 a very large fish kill spread along the Oder. The official investigations pointed to a combination of causes rather than one poison: high salt content from discharges, low water levels, high temperatures, and a bloom of the golden alga Prymnesium parvum, which produces toxins and grows well in brackish water. So far in the course we have followed chemicals through the air and the climate system. From today we move into water. This first water lecture gives the tools for reading any water analysis. The next two lectures apply them to carbonate chemistry.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Water is a reaction medium




Water molecules are polar: the oxygen end is slightly negative, the hydrogen ends slightly positive. That is why salts dissolve: each ion is wrapped in a hydration shell of oriented water molecules.
A dissolved ion is therefore not alone. It interacts with water, with other ions and with any molecule that can bind it.
So a water sample is a mixture of reacting species. Before we calculate anything, we need to know which of those species a laboratory number actually describes.


Start from the molecular picture. Sodium chloride dissolves because water’s partial charges stabilise the separated ions. Around a cation the water oxygens point inward; around an anion the hydrogens point inward. The sizes in the sketch are schematic. The important consequence for us is that dissolved substances react and interact. Calcium can pair with sulfate, iron can bind to organic molecules, carbon dioxide can react with water to form bicarbonate. A laboratory measurement rarely captures one of these forms on its own. That leads to the first practical question of the lecture: when a report says “iron, 0.3 milligrams per litre”, what exactly has been measured?
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: What does one number in a water table mean?
text:
What does one number in a water table mean?




Ask three questions of every entry:

Is it an element total or one species?
Whole water or a filtered fraction? “Dissolved” usually means “passed a 0.45 µm filter”.
Is the mass reported as the element (mg Fe/L) or as a compound (mg CaCO₃/L)?

A filtered total can include complexes and small colloids, not only free ions.


Walk through the diagram from top to bottom. The whole sample contains free hydrated ions, ions bound to dissolved ligands, small colloids and larger particles. A filter is a method decision, not a law of nature: the particles stay behind, everything else passes and is analysed together. The laboratory then reports one number, usually the total of the element in the filtrate. That number is not the concentration of the free ion, which is often the form that matters for toxicity. The third question catches a frequent error: hardness and alkalinity are often reported as milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre, which is a different number from milligrams of calcium.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Mass, moles and charge

Laboratories report mg/L, but chemistry counts particles and charges. Divide by molar mass to get mmol/L. Multiply by the size of the charge to get milliequivalents (meq/L).
A calcium result of 40.08 mg/L is 1.000 mmol/L, but 2.000 meq/L, because each Ca²⁺ carries two charges.

This conversion is the first calculation on any ion table, and it is where many mistakes happen. A molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as milligrams per millimole, so dividing milligrams per litre by molar mass gives millimoles per litre directly. Milligrams of different ions cannot be added in any meaningful way, because a milligram of sodium contains far more ions than a milligram of sulfate. Equivalents count charge, so they can be added and compared across ions. Exercise one is exactly this calculation. Ask students to convert 22.99 milligrams per litre of sodium in their heads before showing the right-hand box.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Charge must balance


Bulk water is electrically neutral. For each ion, multiply its concentration by the size of its charge. Then add up the cations and, separately, the anions. The two totals must be equal.
Worked example (mmol/L): Ca²⁺ 0.500, Mg²⁺ 0.250, Na⁺ 0.500; HCO₃⁻ 1.200, Cl⁻ 0.400, SO₄²⁻ 0.200.
Cations: 1.000 + 0.500 + 0.500 = 2.000 meq/L. Anions: 1.200 + 0.400 + 0.400 = 2.000 meq/L.




Electroneutrality is one of the most reliable constraints in water chemistry. A litre of water cannot carry a measurable net charge: the electrostatic energy would be enormous. So every positive charge in the table must be matched by a negative charge. The worked example is the simplified ion set from the notes. Notice that the divalent ions count twice: 0.500 millimoles per litre of calcium supplies a full milliequivalent. Hydrogen and hydroxide ions are left out because at near-neutral pH they are tiny compared with the major ions. Ask students what the right-hand column would look like if somebody had forgotten to double the sulfate.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: When the balance does not close
text:
When the balance does not close




Three constructed samples from the R activity. A and B balance. Sample C does not:
\text{imbalance}=\frac{\text{cations}-\text{anions}}{\text{cations}+\text{anions}}\times100
=\frac{2.00-1.64}{3.64}\times100=+9.89\%
A positive sign means anions are missing. The water itself is not charged. Something in the analysis or the table is wrong or incomplete.


Use a consistent sign convention; ours is cations minus anions, divided by the sum. A gap tells us that the table does not describe the water correctly. Possible reasons include an ion that was not measured, a unit or transcription error, a species assigned the wrong charge, or ordinary analytical uncertainty. Many laboratories have an acceptance range for this imbalance, but there is no universal threshold, and we do not use one here. Ask the class: sample C has positive imbalance, so is something too large among the cations or too small among the anions? Either is possible. The balance tells us that something is wrong, not what.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Find the cause; never fudge the data
text:
Find the cause; never fudge the data


 USGS hydrologist collecting a water-quality sample, Mississippi River at Baton Rouge. Photo: Scott Dennis/USGS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

In sample C, sulfate was entered as 1.9212 mg/L. The laboratory record shows the decimal point was misplaced: the true value is 19.212 mg/L.

1.9212 mg/L → 0.040 meq/L
19.212 mg/L → 0.400 meq/L

The missing 0.36 meq/L is exactly the gap. After the documented correction all three samples balance.
Never adjust raw numbers until a table balances. Keep the original, record the evidence, then correct.


This is a constructed laboratory record, used in the R activity. The point is professional practice. A charge balance can flag a problem but it cannot tell you which number is wrong. Here a separate record identifies a transcription error, and the corrected value closes the gap exactly. Without that record, you would report the imbalance and investigate, not invent a value. The R script keeps the original table and applies the correction as a separate, documented step, which is how real data handling should work. Closure after correction is a consistency check. It does not prove every number in the table is right, because two errors could cancel.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Same ions, different waters




After the correction, sample C coincides with A. Sample B is a much more dilute water: every ion is lower.
The plot shows mmol/L, the number of ions. The charge balance used meq/L. For divalent Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ the two differ by a factor of two.
Comparing waters is easier once the table has been checked. A salty river like the Oder in 2022 would stand out immediately in Na⁺ and Cl⁻.


This is the plot from the R activity. Students should recognise that the visual comparison is only trustworthy after the table has passed its checks: before the correction, sample C appeared to have almost no sulfate. Remind them which unit is on the axis. When they write the report, they need to state whether they are comparing amounts of ions or amounts of charge. The link back to the Oder is qualitative. In a salt-polluted river the sodium and chloride entries would be many times higher than in an ordinary river. That leads to the next question: when water becomes salty, do our simple concentration calculations still hold?
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Ions feel each other




In dilute water each ion acts almost on its own. In salty water, each ion is surrounded by a slight excess of opposite charge, an ionic atmosphere. That shielding makes the ion behave as if it were less concentrated.
Equilibrium constants are therefore written with activities:
a_i=\gamma_i\,c_i/c^\circ
γ is the activity coefficient; c° = 1 mol/L. When γ ≈ 1, activity ≈ concentration.


Give the physical picture before the formula. An ion surrounded by other ions is partly screened from its surroundings, so it is less able to react or to escape than its concentration suggests. The activity coefficient measures this effect. Thermodynamic equilibrium constants, such as acid constants and solubility products, are strictly defined with activities. In our dilute teaching examples we use concentrations, which amounts to assuming gamma is one. That is an approximation, and students need to know when it is acceptable. The positions of the ions in the sketch are schematic: the real atmosphere is a small statistical excess of opposite charge, not a fixed shell.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Ionic strength measures how crowded the water is
text:
Ionic strength measures how crowded the water is


I=\tfrac12\left(c_1z_1^2+c_2z_2^2+c_3z_3^2+\dots\right)
one term for every ion in the water.
The charge is squared, so divalent ions count four times as much per mole.
Worked example: 1.00 mmol/L Ca²⁺ and 2.00 mmol/L Cl⁻:
I = ½ (1.00 × 4 + 2.00 × 1) = 3.00 mmol/L = 0.00300 mol/L.
This is not the total concentration (3.00 mmol/L of ions is a coincidence here) and not the mass of salt.




Ionic strength is the single number that summarises how strongly the ions in a solution interact. Squaring the charge reflects that electrostatic effects grow strongly with charge. Work the example from exercise three slowly. The calcium contributes four millimoles per litre to the sum, the chloride two, and half of six is three. Point out the coincidence: here the ionic strength happens to equal the total ion concentration in number, but that is not true in general. For a sulfate salt it would not be. The worked ion table from earlier in the lecture has an ionic strength close to 0.003 mol per litre as well, which is typical for a moderately hard freshwater.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: How big is the activity correction?
text:
How big is the activity correction?

Estimated with the Davies equation. At I = 0.003 a monovalent ion has γ ≈ 0.94 and a divalent ion γ ≈ 0.79. In brackish water such as the central Baltic, divalent ions fall to roughly γ ≈ 0.35. Freshwater calculations tolerate γ ≈ 1; salty water does not.

The curves come from the Davies equation, a standard estimate for dilute to moderately salty water. Its details are not examinable; the message is. In a soft lake the correction for single-charged ions is a few percent, small compared with other uncertainties in a teaching model. Divalent ions are already about twenty percent off in a moderately hard water. In brackish or salt-polluted water the correction becomes large, and seawater needs dedicated models and constants. That is why this course states the dilute-freshwater approximation every time we use it, and why constants from freshwater must never be carried unexamined into seawater or into a salt-polluted river like the Oder in 2022.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: A simple acid: the ratio rule
text:
A simple acid: the ratio rule


For a weak acid \mathrm{HA\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-}:
\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}=10^{\,\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}

pH = pKa: ratio 1, half each
pH = pKa + 1: ratio 10, A⁻ fraction 10/11 = 0.909
pH = pKa − 1: ratio 0.1, A⁻ fraction 0.091

The fraction of A⁻ is r/(1+r), with r the ratio.




This is the second tool of the lecture and it returns in almost every later unit. Taking the logarithm of the acid equilibrium expression gives the ratio rule: every pH unit above the pKa multiplies the ratio of base to acid form by ten. A ratio is not a fraction. At one unit above the pKa, the ratio is ten to one, so the fraction of A-minus is ten parts out of eleven, or 0.909, not 0.9 and not ten. The curve is the same calculation repeated at many prescribed pH values. The horizontal axis is a pH that we choose. Nothing in this formula predicts what the pH of a water will be.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Worked example: splitting a total


A fictitious acid HA has pKa = 5.00. The total HA + A⁻ is 0.200 mmol/L. The pH is measured as 6.00.

Ratio: r=10^{6.00-5.00}=10
Split the total 1 : 10, that is into 11 parts
HA = 0.200/11 = 0.01818 mmol/L
A⁻ = 0.200 × 10/11 = 0.1818 mmol/L

Check: 0.01818 + 0.1818 = 0.200.
The pH was given. A distribution formula does not produce a pH; that needs a measurement or another balance.




This is exercise two. Take students through the steps in order and insist on the check that the parts add back to the total. Common slips are to use the ratio as if it were the fraction, or to give A-minus as 0.18 and HA as 0.02 without noticing that the total is then wrong in the third figure. Stress the final sentence. A student who is asked “what is the pH of this water” cannot answer from the pKa and total alone. In the next lecture, alkalinity provides the extra balance that does determine pH in carbonate waters.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Why the split matters: ammonia and fish
text:
Why the split matters: ammonia and fish




Ammonium is a weak acid:
\mathrm{NH_4^+\rightleftharpoons NH_3+H^+},\quad pK_a\approx9.25\ (25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})
The uncharged NH₃ passes easily through fish gills and is the main toxic form. The ion NH₄⁺ is far less harmful.
Same total ammonia, but NH₃ rises tenfold per pH unit: about 1% at pH 7.25, 9% at pH 8.25. Water-quality limits for ammonia therefore depend on pH and temperature.


This is the reason environmental chemists care about weak-acid splits. The total ammonia in a river comes from wastewater, agriculture and decay. Its toxicity depends on how much is in the neutral form, which can cross biological membranes. The ratio rule tells us directly that each pH unit changes the toxic fraction tenfold. In productive, warm rivers, daytime photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide and can raise pH, increasing the neutral fraction at the warmest time of day. Temperature also shifts the pKa. The same total ammonia result can therefore be harmless in one water and toxic in another, which is why guidelines are tabulated against pH and temperature.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Check yourself


Convert 24.31 mg/L Mg²⁺ (molar mass 24.31 g/mol) to mmol/L and meq/L.
A table gives 1.50 meq/L cations and 1.50 meq/L anions. Does that prove every value is correct?
Which has the larger ionic strength: 1 mmol/L NaCl or 1 mmol/L MgSO₄?
An acid has pKa 4.00. At pH 6.00, what fraction is in the A⁻ form?
“Dissolved iron is 0.30 mg/L, so the free Fe³⁺ is 0.30 mg/L.” What is wrong?



Answers. One: 1.000 millimoles per litre and 2.000 milliequivalents per litre. Two: no. Closure is a consistency check; compensating errors or a missing pair of ions could still be hidden. Three: magnesium sulfate. Sodium chloride gives one millimole per litre, magnesium sulfate gives one half of four plus four, which is four millimoles per litre. Four: the ratio is one hundred, so the fraction is one hundred out of one hundred and one, about 0.990. Five: the filtered result is an element total that includes complexes and colloids, and free ferric iron is extremely low at natural pH. Give students two minutes before revealing answers.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: A different kind of change: redox
text:
A different kind of change: redox

In a redox reaction an electron moves and an oxidation state changes: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺. In complexation a ligand binds but no electron moves: Fe³⁺ stays +3. Both change the free-ion concentration, for different reasons. Both pH and redox conditions control metal speciation.

Up to now everything was acid–base or simple counting. A short bridge to redox, which is developed fully in week four. Make the distinction sharp. Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. Iron(II) becoming iron(III) is oxidation, and it needs an electron acceptor such as dissolved oxygen. Binding to a ligand changes how the iron exists in solution, but the iron keeps its oxidation state. Students often call any change in a metal’s form “oxidation”. Ask them to classify three examples: copper binding to organic matter, ferrous iron meeting oxygen, and calcium pairing with sulfate. Only the second is redox.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Redox you can see: iron in a stream
text:
Redox you can see: iron in a stream


 Ochre stream, Wooldale, West Yorkshire, England. Photo: Humphrey Bolton, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Groundwater without oxygen can carry dissolved Fe²⁺, which is colourless. When it emerges and meets air:
\mathrm{4Fe^{2+}+O_2+10H_2O\rightarrow4Fe(OH)_3(s)+8H^+}
Iron(III) is almost insoluble near neutral pH, so an orange-brown oxide coats the stream bed.
The reaction also releases H⁺: oxidising iron is an acid source, which matters for mine drainage in week 3.


This is a very common sight in old mining areas and in wetlands. The groundwater feeding such streams has lost its oxygen underground, so iron is present in the soluble ferrous form. At the surface oxygen arrives, iron is oxidised, and ferric hydroxide precipitates as the orange deposit called ochre. Balance the equation with the class if time allows: four irons each lose one electron, one oxygen molecule accepts four. The hydrogen ions on the right show that iron oxidation and precipitation acidify the water. We will meet this reaction again in acid mine drainage and in water treatment, where it is used deliberately to remove iron.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Favoured is not the same as fast
text:
Favoured is not the same as fast




Equilibrium tells you which state is favoured under given conditions. Kinetics tells you how fast it is reached.

Organic matter and O₂ react strongly downhill, yet leaves survive in a lake for months: the barrier is high without microbes.
Fe²⁺ oxidation by O₂ is fast near neutral pH but very slow in acidic water.

An equilibrium model predicts the destination, not the travel time.


This is one of the most important habits of mind in environmental chemistry. A thermodynamic calculation, including every equilibrium calculation in this course, tells us which direction a reaction can go and where it would end. It does not tell us how long it takes. Many environmentally important systems are far from equilibrium because the reactions are slow or need a catalyst, often microbes. The iron example is well known: at pH around seven, ferrous iron exposed to air oxidises within minutes to hours, but in strongly acidic water it can persist for a long time. When a field observation disagrees with an equilibrium prediction, ask first whether there was enough time.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Back to the Oder: reading the analysis
text:
Back to the Oder: reading the analysis




Investigators worked through questions like these:

What was measured? Conductivity, major ions, oxygen, pH, nutrients, algae.
Charge and salt: high Na⁺ and Cl⁻ meant high ionic strength. Freshwater constants and γ ≈ 1 no longer apply.
Speciation: pH and temperature control toxic forms such as NH₃.
Rates: a bloom developed over weeks of low, warm flow.

No single number explained the fish kill. A checked, interpreted analysis did.


Return to the opening case and show that each tool of the lecture had a role. The six steps on the left are a checklist students can use on any water analysis, including in the exercises. We do not quote specific measured values from the Oder because they varied along the river and in time; the qualitative chain is well established. The salt, the alga and the hot, low-flow conditions acted together. This is a good example of why environmental chemistry rarely finds one cause. The chemistry tells you which explanations are consistent with the data and which measurements would separate them.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

Adding mg/L of different ions. Convert to meq/L before comparing charge.
Forgetting the charge. 1 mmol/L Ca²⁺ is 2 meq/L, and its charge counts four times in ionic strength.
“Dissolved” means free ion. A filtered total includes complexes and colloids.
Forcing a balance. Investigate an imbalance; correct only with evidence.
Ratio equals fraction. A ratio of 10 is a fraction of 10/11.
A distribution formula gives pH. The pH must be measured or found from another balance.
Equilibrium means it happens. It tells you the direction, not the speed.


Go through the list and ask students to give a one-sentence reason for each. The first two are calculation errors that cost marks in every exam. The third and fourth are interpretation errors that also happen in professional work: reporting filtered metal as if it were the bioavailable free ion, and “cleaning” data until it looks right. The last three are conceptual. Students will meet the sixth one again in the carbonate lecture, where alkalinity provides the missing balance. Encourage students to use this list as a self-check while working through the exercises and the R activity.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
section: Explore: charge balance and ionic strength
text:
Explore: charge balance and ionic strength


Worked ion table: 2.000 meq/L cations and 2.000 meq/L anions; ionic strength 2.95 mmol/L; γ about 0.94 and 0.79.



Change table entries and add salt; compare the charge balance with ionic strength and activity.

Begin with the worked example: both charge totals are 2.000 milliequivalents per litre and the ionic strength is close to 0.003 mol per litre, as on the earlier slides. Then choose the sample C sulfate error and ask students why the imbalance is positive and what it does and does not tell us. Back at the worked example, add salt. Sodium chloride brings equal positive and negative charge, so the balance stays closed, but the ionic strength climbs and the activity coefficient of divalent ions falls to about 0.35 in brackish water. That is the Oder message: a table can balance perfectly and still be far outside the range where gamma equals one. The exercise page has the full ion table, the model conditions and a hand check.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




A water-table entry
element total or species; filtered or whole; reported as element or compound


Units
mg/L ÷ molar mass = mmol/L; × |charge| = meq/L


Charge balance
total cation charge = total anion charge (meq/L); an imbalance flags errors or missing ions


Data practice
keep raw values; correct only with documented evidence


Ionic strength
I = ½ (c₁z₁² + c₂z₂² + …); divalent ions weigh four times


Activity
a = γc; γ ≈ 1 only in dilute water; salty water needs a correction


Weak acid
[A⁻]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa); fraction = r/(1 + r)


Ammonia
NH₃ (toxic form) rises tenfold per pH unit below pKa ≈ 9.25


Redox
electron transfer changes oxidation state; binding does not


Equilibrium vs kinetics
direction and end point versus speed



Next: Carbonate species and alkalinity. Why did acid rain kill fish in some Swedish lakes but not others? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Forest damaged by acid deposition, Jizera Mountains, Czech Republic. Photo: Lovecz, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Recap with the chain of questions. What was measured. Convert to charge. Check the balance. Decide whether activity matters. Split weak acids at the measured pH. Ask whether a predicted state is reached fast enough to matter. The next lecture applies charge balance and the acid ratio rule to the most important acid–base system in natural water, dissolved carbon dioxide, bicarbonate and carbonate. The teaser photo is from the acid rain period in central Europe. The next lecture explains why lakes receiving the same acid rain could respond so differently, and alkalinity, a quantity built directly on today’s charge balance, is the answer.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
text:
1. Two equal metal totals
Waters A and B each contain 2.00 µmol/L dissolved total metal. Free metal is 0.500 µmol/L in A and 0.100 µmol/L in B. Assume only free and organically complexed forms. Find bound fractions.






Hint





Subtract free from total, then divide by total.









Worked solution





A is 75.0% bound; B is 95.0% bound. The free-ion amounts differ by a factor of five despite identical totals. This simplified partition does not by itself give a toxicity endpoint.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
text:
2. Oxygen inventory
In a sealed litre of water, oxygen starts at 9.00 mg/L. Completely oxidise 2.00 mg C/L of CH₂O-like substrate, with no other oxygen terms. Calculate residual O₂.






Hint





Demand is carbon mass × 32/12.









Worked solution





Demand = 5.33 mg O₂/L; residual = 3.67 mg/L. The calculation assumes the complete aerobic oxidation can occur and ignores gas exchange and competing processes.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
text:
3. Incomplete degradation
Only 25% of a 4.00 mg C/L CH₂O-like pool is oxidised during an observation period. Calculate model oxygen consumption. Can you report it as the ultimate demand?






Hint





Apply the accessible fraction before the stoichiometric ratio.









Worked solution





Oxidised carbon = 1.00 mg C/L, so consumption is 2.67 mg O₂/L. Complete oxidation of the entire pool would require 10.67 mg O₂/L. The period-specific consumption is not the ultimate demand.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
text:
4. Interpret a dark-water change
Water becomes darker while DOC changes little. What chemical explanations and measurements would you consider?






Hint





Carbon quantity and optical properties are different observables.









Worked solution





Changes in molecular composition, chromophoric groups, particle content, or iron-associated colour could alter absorption per unit carbon. Compare spectra/absorbance, DOC, filtration, iron, and pH. Do not infer a unique source, degradation rate, or toxicity from colour alone.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water exercises
section: Explore: oxygen demand in a sealed bottle
text:
Explore: oxygen demand in a sealed bottle
Predict how much of the ultimate oxygen demand of 4.00 mg C/L is used in a 5-day test, and whether 9.00 mg/L of oxygen is enough to oxidise all of it. Change one input at a time.


Reference case: 4.00 mg C/L has an ultimate demand of 10.67 mg O₂/L. With a rate of 0.10 per day, 4.20 mg O₂/L (39%) is used in 5 days, and a bottle starting at 9.00 mg/L runs out of oxygen on day 18.6.



E1. Choose Exercise 2: sealed litre. Check the ultimate demand and the oxygen left after complete oxidation against your answer to exercise 2.
E2. Choose Exercise 3: 5-day test, then Slow humic carbon. The carbon amount and ultimate demand are the same. Why does the 5-day result differ so much, and what does that mean for a brown lake?
E3. Reset, then move the measurement day until about 25% of the demand is used. Compare the oxygen used with your answer to exercise 3. Then move to day 40: why does the oxygen used stop at 9.00 mg/L instead of reaching 10.67?

Model conditions and hand check
Ultimate demand = carbon × 32.0/12.0. For 3.00 mg C/L this gives 8.00 mg O₂/L; for 2.00 mg C/L, 5.33 mg O₂/L, leaving 9.00 − 5.33 = 3.67 mg/L; for 4.00 mg C/L, 10.67 mg O₂/L. With a first-order rate of 0.10 per day, the oxygen used by day \(t\) is \(10.67\,(1-e^{-0.10t})\), which is 4.20 mg/L on day 5 and reaches 25% (2.67 mg/L) after about 2.9 days.
The organic matter is represented by CH₂O, so 1 mol C uses 1 mol O₂. The rate constant is a constructed round value, not a measured property of any water. The bottle is sealed and dark: no reaeration, no photosynthesis and no other oxygen users such as nitrification. When the oxygen is used up the aerobic model stops; reactions with other electron acceptors are not modelled.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text: How can two waters contain the same dissolved total metal while differing in free metal, light penetration, and oxygen demand?
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish organic carbon amount from its molecular composition and reactivity.
Explain metal binding and light attenuation without treating all organic matter as identical.
Calculate an idealised oxygen demand and state its limits.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Operational fractions
Organic matter contains many molecules and particles with different sizes and functional groups. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is an operationally measured carbon amount after the specified separation; particulate organic carbon is associated with the retained fraction. Neither result gives a unique molecule, ligand concentration, or biodegradation rate. Record the filter and analytical method. Some colloidal material may appear in an operationally dissolved fraction.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Functional groups create reactivity
Carboxyl, phenolic, and other binding groups can lose protons and bind metals. Their charge and availability change with pH. Binding can keep a metal in a filtered fraction while lowering its free-ion concentration. Organic matter can also promote colloidal transport. Greater DOC therefore does not automatically mean lower total dissolved metal or no metal exposure; kinetics, uptake routes, and ligand chemistry matter.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Colour changes the light field
Chromophoric organic matter absorbs parts of the light spectrum. Darker water can reduce light penetration and alter where photochemical reactions occur. Not all DOC absorbs equally: colour per unit carbon varies with composition and processing. Absorbance is therefore a property measurement, not a direct universal conversion to DOC. Photochemical change can transform molecules without immediately removing all carbon from water.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Organic oxidation consumes oxygen
Use \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) as a stoichiometric representation of a simple organic substrate: \[\mathrm{CH_2O+O_2\rightarrow CO_2+H_2O}.\] One mole of its carbon consumes one mole of O₂ in complete aerobic oxidation. This is a teaching carbon-oxidation model, not the molecular formula of all natural organic matter. Real demand depends on oxidation state, biodegradability, timescale, and other oxygen-consuming processes such as nitrification.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Link to anoxia and sediment
When oxygen demand exceeds replenishment, oxygen can decline. Other electron acceptors may then support microbial oxidation. Reduction of iron-bearing solids can change sorption surfaces and release associated solutes. Reaeration, mixing, and photosynthesis can offset demand, so an organic-carbon increase is not itself a complete oxygen budget. Measure both the sources and sinks on an appropriate timescale.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Worked example
Assume 3.00 mg C/L of an added CH₂O-like substrate is completely oxidised aerobically. With molar masses 12.0 g/mol for carbon and 32.0 g/mol for O₂, the demand is \(3.00(32.0/12.0)=\mathbf{8.00}\) mg O₂/L. That is an ultimate stoichiometric demand for this substrate. It is not a measured five-day biochemical oxygen demand, nor a prediction that all of a lake’s DOC is consumed immediately.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 12: organic-matter fractions, binding, light, and oxygen demand.
USGS organic-matter processes: Adsorption, biodegradation, and chemical controls on organic-matter transport.
Canada copper chemistry: How water chemistry and organic binding modify metal exposure; use the chemistry discussion, not regulatory thresholds.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
About this lecture


In 1985 scientists of the British Antarctic Survey reported that springtime ozone over Antarctica had fallen dramatically. Satellites soon mapped an ozone hole larger than the continent. Two years later, the Montreal Protocol began phasing out the chemicals behind it.
Yet on hot summer days, health agencies across Europe warn of too much ozone at ground level.
Same molecule. Protective high up, harmful near the ground. Why?
Today you will learn to:

see how light selects which reactions can happen;
combine steps into a catalytic cycle and cancel intermediates;
explain why NO₂ and sunlight alone do not build up ozone;
turn a rate constant into a lifetime.


 Antarctic ozone hole, 22 September 2012; blue and purple mark the lowest ozone. Image: NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Last lecture we treated a lake or river as a compartment with inputs, outputs and reactions. Today the compartment is the atmosphere, and the reactions are driven by sunlight. Start with the ozone story. The discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985 surprised even the scientists who had predicted chlorine-driven ozone loss, because the loss was so large and so concentrated. Contrast it with summer smog, when ground-level ozone irritates lungs and damages crops. By the end of the lecture students should be able to explain both with a few reaction steps and one idea: which reactions can happen depends on where you are, because light and reaction partners change with altitude.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Same molecule, two places

Temperature falls with height through the troposphere, then rises again in the stratosphere, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet light there and warms the air. Most ozone sits at about 15–35 km. A small amount near the ground is the ozone we breathe.

The left panel uses the standard atmosphere, a reference profile of temperature with altitude. The temperature turns around at about 11 kilometres: that is the tropopause. Above it, the stratosphere warms with height. That warming is itself a chemical signature: ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet light and converts it to heat. The right panel is a schematic of the ozone profile. Most of the ozone is in the stratosphere. The amount near the ground is small, but it is in contact with lungs and leaves. The two regions have different light, different temperatures and different reaction partners, so the chemistry differs as well.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Light selects which reactions can happen
text:
Light selects which reactions can happen




A photon’s energy is
E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
Shorter wavelength, more energy. Per mole of photons, E ≈ 119 600 / λ(nm) kJ/mol.
To split O₂ (bond 498 kJ/mol) a photon needs λ < 240 nm: hard ultraviolet, available only high in the atmosphere.
NO₂ can be split by near-UV light below about 400 nm, which reaches the ground.


Photolysis means using absorbed light to break a molecule. The energy per photon is Planck’s constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Multiplying by Avogadro’s number gives energy per mole of photons, which we can compare with bond energies. The oxygen double bond needs about 498 kilojoules per mole, so only photons shorter than about 240 nanometres can split it. Those photons are absorbed high in the atmosphere and never reach the ground. The bond holding the extra oxygen atom in nitrogen dioxide is much weaker, so near-ultraviolet sunlight at ground level can break it. That single difference explains why ozone is made in different ways in the stratosphere and near the ground.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Energy is not enough: the molecule must absorb
text:
Energy is not enough: the molecule must absorb




A photon can only drive a reaction if the molecule absorbs it. Energy above the bond energy is necessary but not sufficient.
O₂ absorbs the shortest UV. O₃ absorbs strongly between about 200 and 310 nm, the range that damages DNA.
So the ozone layer is a filter: it removes almost all UV-C and most UV-B before sunlight reaches the ground.


Photon energy only tells us what is possible. A reaction also requires that the molecule absorbs at that wavelength. Oxygen absorbs the hardest ultraviolet. Ozone has a strong absorption band in the ultraviolet, from about 200 to about 310 nanometres. That is why it matters so much: those wavelengths damage DNA and proteins. UV-C is removed completely, UV-B mostly, and UV-A mostly reaches the ground. When ozone thins, it is the UV-B that increases at the surface. Keep the idea of absorption bands in mind: it returns in the climate lecture, where infrared absorption decides which gases are greenhouse gases.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
How ozone is made

\mathrm{O_2}+h\nu\rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{O}\qquad\qquad \mathrm{O+O_2+M\rightarrow O_3+M}
M is any collision partner, usually N₂ or O₂. It carries away the extra energy and is not consumed. This is the first half of the Chapman mechanism (1930).

This is the simplified formation sequence. In the first step, a hard ultraviolet photon splits an oxygen molecule into two oxygen atoms. In the second step, an oxygen atom combines with an oxygen molecule. The new ozone molecule is formed with too much energy and would fall apart, unless it collides with another molecule that takes the excess energy away as heat. That third body is written M. It appears on both sides of the equation, so it is not consumed: it only enables the reaction. Because the second step needs collisions, it depends on air density. The sequence is named after Sydney Chapman, who proposed it in 1930.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Ozone is made and destroyed all the time
text:
Ozone is made and destroyed all the time

O and O₃ convert into each other quickly: each round absorbs a UV photon and turns it into heat. Real loss happens only when O meets O₃. The ozone amount is a balance of production, loss and transport, just like the lake balance in the last lecture.

Once ozone is made, it is split again by ultraviolet light, giving an oxygen atom, which quickly forms ozone again. This fast back-and-forth is how the ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet and warms the stratosphere. It does not change the total of O plus O3, which chemists call odd oxygen. The total changes only through the slow source, oxygen photolysis, and the slow sink, oxygen atom plus ozone. This is the balance equation from the last lecture in a new setting. Fast turnover does not mean a small inventory: the amount of ozone is set by the ratio of production to loss, plus transport by winds.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: How we measure the ozone layer
text:
How we measure the ozone layer


 Launching an ozonesonde at the South Pole Station. Photo: NOAA Photo Library, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

An ozonesonde is a small balloon-borne instrument that measures ozone as it rises to about 30 km. It gives the profile in the previous figure.
Ground spectrometers and satellites measure the total column: all the ozone above a point. It is reported in Dobson units. A typical column is about 300 DU, equal to a layer of pure ozone only about 3 mm thick at ground pressure.
The “ozone hole” is defined as columns below 220 DU.


Measurements anchor the chemistry. Ozonesondes are launched on weather balloons and report ozone concentration every few metres of altitude. Spectrometers on the ground and on satellites measure how much ultraviolet light is absorbed and convert that to a total column. One Dobson unit corresponds to a layer of pure ozone one hundredth of a millimetre thick at standard temperature and pressure. So the entire ozone layer, compressed to the pressure at sea level, would be about three millimetres thick. That thin a layer protects all life at the surface from the most damaging ultraviolet. The Antarctic ozone hole is the area where the column falls below 220 Dobson units.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: A shortcut for ozone loss: catalysis
text:
A shortcut for ozone loss: catalysis

A chlorine atom attacks O₃; the ClO formed meets an O atom and gives Cl back. Chlorine is a catalyst: it is regenerated and can repeat the cycle many times until another reaction stops it.

The Chapman sink alone predicts more ozone than is observed. Additional loss comes from catalytic cycles involving nitrogen oxides, hydrogen radicals and halogens. Here is the chlorine cycle. In the first step chlorine reacts with ozone and forms chlorine monoxide. In the second, chlorine monoxide reacts with an oxygen atom and releases the chlorine atom again. Follow the chlorine: it goes round the loop and comes back unchanged. That is what makes it a catalyst. Each trip destroys one ozone molecule and one oxygen atom. A single chlorine atom can go round many times before it is captured into a less reactive form. That is why small amounts of chlorine can matter.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Bookkeeping: cancel the intermediates


Write the steps and add them:
\mathrm{Cl+O_3\rightarrow ClO+O_2} \mathrm{ClO+O\rightarrow Cl+O_2}
Sum: Cl + O₃ + ClO + O → ClO + O₂ + Cl + O₂
Cancel what appears on both sides:
\mathrm{O_3+O\rightarrow 2\,O_2}


Catalyst: Cl. Consumed in step 1, regenerated in step 2.
Intermediate: ClO. Formed in step 1, consumed in step 2.
Neither appears in the net reaction.

The net reaction says what one cycle does. It does not say how fast the cycle runs or how many times one Cl atom goes round. That needs kinetics.


This is exercise 1, done together. Add the two steps as if they were algebraic equations. Species that appear on both sides cancel. The catalyst is the species that is used first and returned later; the intermediate is the one that is made first and used later. Both cancel, which is why neither shows up in the net reaction. A frequent mistake is to read the net equation as a complete description. It tells us the stoichiometry of one cycle only. To estimate ozone loss you would need the rates of each step, the concentrations of chlorine and of the oxygen atoms, and the competing reactions that remove chlorine.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Where the chlorine came from

CFCs are so unreactive that they survive for decades in the lower atmosphere. They slowly reach the stratosphere, where hard UV splits off Cl. Most chlorine is then stored in reservoirs (HCl, ClONO₂), until the polar winter releases it.

Chlorofluorocarbons were valued precisely because they are unreactive: non-toxic, non-flammable propellants and refrigerants. That same stability means nothing removes them in the troposphere. OH does not attack them and they are not washed out by rain. Over years they mix up into the stratosphere. Only there is the ultraviolet hard enough to break a carbon–chlorine bond and release a chlorine atom. In 1974 Molina and Rowland pointed out this pathway; with Paul Crutzen, who studied nitrogen oxide catalysis and did his doctorate at Stockholm University, they received the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Most stratospheric chlorine is stored in reservoirs that do not destroy ozone, so the cycle runs slowly. The polar winter changes that.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Why a hole over Antarctica?


 Polar stratospheric clouds over Oslo, Norway. Photo: Havardtl, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

In the dark polar winter the stratosphere becomes cold enough for polar stratospheric clouds.
On their particle surfaces, the reservoirs HCl and ClONO₂ react to form Cl₂. When the sun returns in spring, light splits Cl₂ into Cl atoms and catalytic loss runs fast.
This is a different mechanism from the simple cycle: it needs surfaces and different ClO cycles. Gas-phase chemistry alone did not predict it.


The photo shows polar stratospheric clouds, also called nacreous or mother-of-pearl clouds, occasionally seen in Scandinavia in winter. They form only at very low temperatures, which are common in the Antarctic winter stratosphere and less common in the Arctic. Reactions on these cloud particles convert chlorine from the safe reservoirs into chlorine gas. Nothing happens during the polar night. When sunlight returns in September and October, chlorine gas is photolysed and chlorine atoms destroy ozone quickly. The main polar cycles involve the ClO dimer rather than oxygen atoms, which are scarce. That is why our simple cycle is representative, not the full polar mechanism. The Montreal Protocol has reduced stratospheric chlorine, and recovery is expected over the coming decades.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Check yourself


Why can ozone be made from O₂ in the stratosphere but not directly from O₂ at ground level?
In the cycle NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂, then NO₂ + O → NO + O₂: what is the catalyst, what is the intermediate, and what is the net reaction?
M appears on both sides of O + O₂ + M → O₃ + M. Why is it written at all?
True or false: “A catalyst lasts forever.”



Answers. One: splitting oxygen needs photons shorter than about 240 nanometres, which are absorbed high up and do not reach the ground. Two: nitric oxide is the catalyst, nitrogen dioxide is the intermediate, and the net reaction is again O3 plus O gives two O2. This is the nitrogen oxide cycle that Crutzen described. Three: M removes the excess energy; without the collision the new ozone falls apart, so the rate depends on air density. Four: false. A catalyst is regenerated in each cycle, but other reactions can capture it, as when chlorine is stored in HCl. It is not present in unlimited amount.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Down to the ground: summer smog
text:
Down to the ground: summer smog


 Photochemical smog over Mexico City, seen from the air. Photo: Fidel Gonzalez, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Near the ground there is no hard UV, so O₂ is not split. Ground-level ozone must be made another way.
Its ingredients are nitrogen oxides (NO + NO₂ = NOₓ, mainly from combustion), volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or CO, and sunlight.
Ozone then irritates airways and damages crops and forests. Episodes are worst in hot, sunny, still weather, as in many European heatwaves.


Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant: it is not emitted, it is made in the air. The ingredients are nitrogen oxides from traffic and combustion, reactive organic compounds from fuels, solvents and vegetation, or carbon monoxide, and sunlight. The photo shows the brown haze of photochemical smog over a large city, where all three ingredients meet. In Europe, high ozone episodes occur during hot, sunny summers with weak winds. Ozone also travels: much of the ozone measured in Scandinavia is formed elsewhere and transported. The next two slides show which reactions link NOx and ozone, and why the organic compounds are needed.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: NO₂ and light alone: a null cycle
text:
NO₂ and light alone: a null cycle

Sunlight splits NO₂; the O atom makes O₃. But NO then uses up that O₃ again. Add the three steps and everything cancels: no net ozone. In sunlight the three species reach a balance set by light and concentrations.

This is exercise 3. Write the three reactions and add them. Nitrogen dioxide is split by near-ultraviolet sunlight into nitric oxide and an oxygen atom. The oxygen atom forms ozone, exactly as in the stratosphere. But nitric oxide reacts quickly with ozone and makes nitrogen dioxide again. Every species cancels, so the cycle redistributes nitrogen between NO and NO2 and holds some ozone at a steady level, without building it up over time. This is why freshly emitted NO near a busy road actually lowers ozone locally: it titrates it. To get net ozone production, something else must turn NO into NO2 without consuming ozone.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Peroxy radicals break the null cycle
text:
Peroxy radicals break the null cycle

When OH attacks a VOC or CO, peroxy radicals (HO₂, RO₂) form. They convert NO to NO₂ without using O₃. Light then splits that NO₂, and the O atom becomes a new ozone molecule. Each NO can go round many times.

Here is the key extra step. The hydroxyl radical attacks an organic compound or carbon monoxide, and with oxygen this produces peroxy radicals: HO2 in the case of carbon monoxide, RO2 for organic compounds. A peroxy radical oxidises nitric oxide to nitrogen dioxide. Unlike the null cycle, no ozone was used to do that. When the nitrogen dioxide is photolysed, the oxygen atom forms ozone that is not consumed again. The nitrogen oxides act almost like a catalyst: NO goes round many times, and each round adds ozone. That is why controlling ground-level ozone needs control of both NOx and VOCs, and why it peaks in sunny weather.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: OH sets the pace: rate and lifetime
text:
OH sets the pace: rate and lifetime


For a loss reaction X + OH → products, the rate is
R = k[\mathrm{X}][\mathrm{OH}]
Hold OH constant: k' = k[\mathrm{OH}], lifetime \tau = 1/k'.
Worked example. k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹, OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³:

k′ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹
τ = 1.0 × 10⁶ s ≈ 11.6 days
half-life = 0.693 τ ≈ 8.0 days





OH, the hydroxyl radical, is the main oxidant of the lower atmosphere, often called its detergent. It reacts with most organic compounds, CO, methane and many pollutants. This is exercise 2. If the OH concentration is treated as constant, the second-order rate law becomes pseudo-first order with rate constant k-prime. Its inverse is the lifetime, the time for the amount to fall to about 37 percent. Point out the units: cubic centimetres per molecule per second, times molecules per cubic centimetre, gives per second. The lifetime is an e-folding time, not a half-life. It includes only this one sink. Deposition, photolysis or transport would make the real persistence shorter.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Lifetime decides how far a gas travels
text:
Lifetime decides how far a gas travels

Compare a gas’s lifetime with transport times. OH lasts about a second and never leaves the air parcel where it formed. A gas lasting days to weeks is a regional problem. Methane and CFCs live long enough to spread over the whole globe.

This connects chemistry with transport. Mixing through the lowest kilometre or two of air takes about a day. Wind carries air around the globe in a hemisphere in a few weeks. Exchange between the hemispheres takes about a year. Compare these with chemical lifetimes. OH is so reactive that it is destroyed within about a second, so its concentration reflects only local production. The exercise gas, with a lifetime of about twelve days, will spread across a region but not evenly around the world. Methane, with a lifetime of about a decade, and CFCs, around a century, become well mixed globally. That is why CFCs from the Northern Hemisphere could destroy ozone over Antarctica.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Back to a surface station


 Mobile air quality monitoring station in Zürich, Switzerland. Photo: Balise42, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Ozone measured at a ground station rises. Can you conclude that stratospheric ozone increased, or name the source?
No. Surface ozone reflects:

local production from NOₓ + VOC + sunlight;
local loss by NO and by deposition to surfaces;
transport of ozone formed elsewhere, and mixing from above.

You would need precursor measurements, weather data and altitude-resolved ozone.


This is exercise 4 and it closes the story. A rise in ground-level ozone is a local measurement with several possible causes. Sunny weather speeds production. Lower NO emissions nearby can actually raise ozone, because less ozone is titrated. Air masses can bring ozone formed hundreds of kilometres away, and occasionally air from the upper troposphere or stratosphere mixes down. The molecular formula is identical whatever its origin, so the measurement alone cannot name a source. This is the same lesson as the river last week: a concentration at one point needs a balance of production, loss and transport before you interpret it.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Ozone is good” or “ozone is bad.” It depends on where it is.
“Enough photon energy means the reaction happens.” The molecule must also absorb that wavelength.
“M is a reactant.” It is a collision partner; it is not consumed.
“The net equation shows the mechanism and the rate.” It shows stoichiometry only.
“NO₂ + sunlight makes ozone pile up.” Alone, it is a null cycle; peroxy radicals are needed.
“The lifetime is the half-life.” τ = 1/k′; the half-life is 0.693 τ.
“A catalyst works forever.” Reservoir species capture it.


These are the errors that appear most often for this topic. Go through them and ask students to give the correct statement in their own words. The first one is the theme of the whole lecture. The second and third concern the meaning of photolysis and of the third body. The fourth is about what an overall equation does and does not tell you; this matters for every mechanism in the course. The fifth is the tropospheric ozone point. The sixth is a units and definitions issue: lifetime and half-life differ by a factor of about 0.69. The last one explains why chlorine does not destroy all ozone.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
section: Explore: OH and the lifetime of a gas
text:
Explore: OH and the lifetime of a gas


Worked example: k = 1.0 × 10⁻¹², OH = 1.0 × 10⁶ molecules/cm³, lifetime 11.6 days, half-life 8.0 days.



Change OH, the rate constant and an extra sink, and see how far the gas can travel.

Start with the worked example and confirm the numbers from the “OH sets the pace” slide: k-prime one times ten to the minus six per second, lifetime 11.6 days, half-life 8.0 days. Ask students to predict before each click. Twice as much OH halves the lifetime, because only the product k times OH matters. Making the reaction a hundred times slower gives about three years, long enough to mix between the hemispheres, like the long-lived gases on the transport slide. Adding deposition shows that parallel sinks add their rate constants, so the lifetime becomes shorter than either sink alone would give. The exercise page has the model conditions and a hand check.

Next: atmospheric deposition and acidity. OH also turns SO₂ and NO₂ into acids, and rain brings them down. Then the exercises and notes.

 Bełchatów coal power station, Poland. Photo: Petr Štefek, CC BY 2.5, Wikimedia Commons.


The summary table is the revision sheet. Recite the chain once. Light selects reactions, through both energy and absorption. In the stratosphere, oxygen photolysis makes ozone, and catalysts such as chlorine destroy it; the polar hole needs cold cloud surfaces and returning sunlight. Near the ground, nitrogen dioxide photolysis makes ozone, but net production needs peroxy radicals from organic compounds or carbon monoxide. OH controls lifetimes, and lifetime controls how far a gas travels. The photo is the teaser for the next lecture. The same OH radical that sets lifetimes also oxidises sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide from power stations and traffic into sulfuric and nitric acid.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
2. Same pH, different acid response
Two constructed waters start at pH 7.50. Water A has \(C_T=1.00\) mmol/L; water B has \(C_T=0.100\) mmol/L. At this pH the fractions are \(\alpha_0=0.066023\), \(\alpha_1=0.932598\), \(\alpha_2=0.001379\).

Calculate initial alkalinity from the carbonate-only expression. Include water ions: \([\mathrm{H^+}]=3.1623\times10^{-8}\) mol/L and \([\mathrm{OH^-}]=3.1623\times10^{-7}\) mol/L.
Add 0.0500 mmol/L of a strong monoprotic acid to each, with negligible dilution. Calculate each new alkalinity. No gas exchange, mineral reaction, or biological transformation occurs. What happens to \(C_T\)?
A calculation satisfying both balances gives final pH values 7.235 for A and 6.252 for B. Explain the difference without assuming initial pH measures the acid-neutralising inventory.
Can you obtain the final pH by subtracting 0.0500 from 7.50? Explain the units.







Hint





First put all concentrations in mol/L. Multiply the carbonate concentration by two in the alkalinity expression. A mole of monoprotic strong acid supplies one equivalent. To express eq/L as meq/L, multiply by 1000.









Worked solution





For A, the bicarbonate and carbonate contribution is \((0.932598+2\times0.001379)\times10^{-3}\) eq/L. The water-ion term is \(2.8461\times10^{-7}\) eq/L. The resulting initial alkalinities are approximately 0.9356 meq/L for A and 0.09382 meq/L for B.
The acid supplies 0.0500 meq/L. Final alkalinities are therefore 0.8856 and 0.04382 meq/L. Carbon stays dissolved in this closed model, so each \(C_T\) is conserved; a larger fraction becomes CO₂*.
B loses about 53% of its initial alkalinity, compared with about 5.3% for A. Its larger pH fall is consistent with its smaller carbonate inventory. Alkalinity is not identical to local buffer capacity, but here the two waters have the same initial species fractions and different carbon amounts.
A pH difference is logarithmic and dimensionless; an acid dose has amount-per-volume units. Direct subtraction cannot satisfy the chemical balances. A numerical solver is not required for this exercise.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
section: 3. Use Henry’s law for the correct pool
text:
3. Use Henry’s law for the correct pool
A separate water equilibrates with a large gas reservoir having a supplied \(p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=4.00\times10^{-4}\) atm. Use \(K_H=0.034\) mol L\(^{-1}\) atm\(^{-1}\).

Calculate \([\mathrm{CO_2^*}]\) and show the unit cancellation.
Is that enough information to calculate pH or \(C_T\)?
If the equilibrated water is also specified to have pH 8.35, calculate \(C_T\).
In another water, CO₂ enters while no acid, mineral, or biological process acts. Explain why the alkalinity stays constant even though pH can decrease.







Worked solution





\([\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=0.034\times4.00\times10^{-4}=1.36\times10^{-5}\) mol/L = 13.6 µmol/L. The atm units cancel. This specifies the gas pool only. Another independent carbonate constraint is needed to calculate pH and total carbon.
With pH 8.35 supplied, \(C_T=13.6(1+100+1.04713)\) µmol/L, or approximately 1.388 mmol/L. Henry’s law alone did not give that total.
Dissociation of the added CO₂ produces hydrogen ion and bicarbonate together; their contributions cancel in alkalinity. Gas transfer adds carbon rather than strong-acid equivalents. At fixed alkalinity the pH generally falls as CO₂ enters. An imposed pH of 8.35 is a specified state, not the predicted endpoint of every water exposed to this gas.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
4. Check calcite saturation
Two separate water states each have free calcium \(5.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. Free carbonate is \(1.00\times10^{-6}\) mol/L in state X and \(1.00\times10^{-5}\) mol/L in state Y. Use \(K_{sp}=3.3\times10^{-9}\).
Calculate \(\Omega\) for each. Identify which could dissolve available calcite and which could precipitate it. Can you infer a precipitation rate or final mass? Explain why replacing free calcium with dissolved total calcium might matter.






Worked solution





The products are \(5.00\times10^{-10}\) and \(5.00\times10^{-9}\). Thus \(\Omega_X=0.152\) and \(\Omega_Y=1.52\). X is undersaturated and could dissolve calcite if it is present. Y is supersaturated, so precipitation is thermodynamically favoured, but may be delayed by kinetics or nucleation. Neither ratio gives a rate or final mass. Ion pairs and complexes can make free calcium smaller than total dissolved calcium.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
section: 5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
text:
5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
This task reuses objects, arithmetic, tables, and labelled plots from introductory computing. The small addition is a regular pH grid. No statistical fit is needed: these are predictions from equilibrium expressions.
Download speciation.R and report.Rmd into the same folder. Open that folder as your working project. The script needs ggplot2; rendering the report also needs rmarkdown, as in introductory computing. Open the script in the editor before running it.

Predict and inspect
Before running the script, sketch the expected dominance near pH 4, 8, and 12. The script starts with these calculations:
pH <- seq(4, 12, by = 0.05)
r1 <- 10^(pH - 6.35)
r2 <- 10^(pH - 10.33)
denominator <- 1 + r1 + r1 * r2
seq() creates regularly spaced values. Each vector operation evaluates the chemical expression at every pH value. ^ means a power. The script divides the three proportions by denominator and puts them in a table. Its remaining code arranges that table for the familiar ggplot() and geom_line() functions.
Run from the folder holding both files:
source("speciation.R")
head(speciation)
speciation_plot
Compare the plot with the prediction and with the hand calculation in question 1.



Three carbonate species fractions at prescribed pH, calculated from the supplied equilibrium model.




Check and explain

In the report template, select the pH 8.35 row and compare its fractions with your hand calculation. Explain any difference due to rounding.
Check that fractions stay between zero and one and sum to one.
Explain what happens to concentrations if \(C_T\) doubles at each prescribed pH.
Explain why moving along the horizontal axis does not simulate adding a specified dose of acid to a closed sample.
Replace the template prompts with your prediction, calculation, chemical interpretation, and assumptions. Restart R, then Knit the saved report, or run rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd") from its folder.







Worked interpretation





CO₂* dominates at low pH, bicarbonate in the middle, and carbonate at high pH. At pH 8.35, the model fractions agree with question 1. The sum is one to numerical precision, and every fraction lies between zero and one. Doubling \(C_T\) at fixed pH doubles the concentrations, while leaving these model fractions unchanged.
The horizontal axis supplies pH independently at each point. An acid-dose experiment must instead conserve carbon and satisfy the changed alkalinity. The curve alone does not supply that second constraint or predict a final pH. The model assumes equilibrium, 25 °C, and dilute freshwater; it omits ion pairing and other acid–base systems.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
6. Explain a catchment observation
A lake’s pH decreases after a disturbance. Suggest two chemically distinct processes from this unit that could cause a decrease, and identify additional measurements that would help distinguish them. State one limitation of interpreting only pH. Do not claim a cause from a single observation.






Worked explanation





Strong-acid input and net CO₂ uptake can both lower pH. In the isolated model, strong acid lowers alkalinity while CO₂ uptake conserves it and increases dissolved inorganic carbon. Paired pH, alkalinity, and inorganic-carbon or dissolved-CO₂ measurements would help assess these possibilities. Calcium and mineral context could reveal additional reactions. A real catchment can have several processes acting together; pH alone does not identify the cause or neutralising inventory.
