At 25 °C, use pK₁ = 6.35, pK₂ = 10.33, Kw = 10⁻¹⁴, KH = 0.034 mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹ and Ksp = 3.3 × 10⁻⁹ in dilute freshwater, with concentrations in place of activities. The water is at equilibrium with the gas. Alkalinity is held fixed, so gas exchange changes only total inorganic carbon. Calcium is set separately and taken as the free ion (no ion pairs). No calcite dissolves or precipitates, so Ω above 1 shows only that calcite forming is favoured, not how fast or how much. Temperature effects are not modelled.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
About this lecture


In the 1970s and 1980s, acid rain from European industry fell on southern Scandinavia. Thousands of lakes lost their fish. Yet other lakes that received the same rain hardly changed.
The difference was not the rain. It was the chemistry already dissolved in the water, above all its dissolved inorganic carbon.
Today you will learn to:

name the three dissolved carbon species and predict which dominates at a given pH;
tell a fraction apart from an amount;
use alkalinity, the water’s acid-neutralising reserve, to predict how pH responds to acid.

Last lecture you met charge balance and a simple acid distribution. Today you apply both to the most important acid–base system in natural water.

 Forest damaged by acid deposition, Jizera Mountains, Czech Republic. Photo: Lovecz, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Open with the story, not the equations. Acid deposition damaged forests across central Europe and acidified lakes across southern Norway and Sweden. The striking fact is the patchiness: two lakes a few kilometres apart could receive the same acidic rain, and one lost its fish while the other barely changed. By the end of the lecture students should be able to explain that difference with one quantity, alkalinity, and to understand why it is not the same thing as pH. Mention that this lecture is the first of a pair. The second deck adds gas exchange and minerals. Everything today is a closed-water model at 25 °C.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: A puzzle from the Swedish forests
text:
A puzzle from the Swedish forests


 Forest lake, Norra Kvill National Park, Småland. Photo: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Much of Sweden sits on granite and gneiss. These rocks weather slowly and release few dissolved ions. Lakes on them are clear and soft: they contain little dissolved material.
Where the bedrock or soil contains limestone (calcium carbonate), the water carries much more dissolved calcium and carbonate species.
Both kinds of lake received similar acid deposition. The soft-water lakes acidified. The limestone lakes did not.
Question for this lecture: what is it about dissolved carbonate that lets a lake absorb acid?


Ask students to look at the photo: a beautiful, clear forest lake. Clarity here is partly a sign of low dissolved content. Explain that the bedrock sets the starting composition of the water. Granite is mostly silicate minerals that weather slowly; limestone dissolves comparatively quickly and supplies calcium and carbonate species. Do not explain the mechanism yet. Pose the question and leave it open: the rest of the lecture builds the tools to answer it. If students already say “buffering”, ask them what is doing the buffering and how much of it there is. That is exactly the distinction between pH and alkalinity we will make.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Two lakes, two ion signatures

Each column adds up charge (µeq/L). Cations and anions must balance, as in the last lecture. In the limestone lake, most negative charge is carried by bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). In the granite lake, bicarbonate is almost absent and sulfate from acid rain dominates.

These are constructed compositions, but in the typical range for a soft-water lake and a hard-water lake. Point out three things. First, the scales differ by about a factor of ten: the limestone lake simply contains much more dissolved material. Second, in the limestone lake bicarbonate is the dominant anion. Third, in the granite lake sulfate, largely from deposition, takes the place of bicarbonate, and a little free hydrogen ion appears among the cations. Remind students of the charge balance from the previous lecture: every column pair must sum to the same charge. We will return to this figure when we define alkalinity, because alkalinity can be read from exactly this kind of balance.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Sweden’s response: add limestone


 Forest liming by helicopter, Kungsbacka, Sweden. Photo: Bulver, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Since the late 1970s, Sweden has spread finely ground limestone (CaCO₃) on thousands of lakes, streams, wetlands and forest soils. Sweden has run one of the largest liming programmes in the world.
Liming does not remove the acid rain. It adds something to the water that takes up hydrogen ions.
To understand why it works and how much is needed, we need to know:

what forms carbon takes when it is dissolved;
how those forms trade hydrogen ions;
how to count the water’s capacity to neutralise acid.



Liming is a large and long-running chemical intervention, and a good example of chemistry used for management. Lime is spread from boats, from helicopters as in this photo, or on wetlands upstream so that it dissolves gradually. Ask the class: why would adding a rock help? Some will say “it is basic”. Push further: what does basic mean in terms of species, and how much rock is enough? Those questions motivate the three numbered steps. We answer the dosing question near the end of the lecture with a back-of-the-envelope calculation.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: A laboratory version of the puzzle
text:
A laboratory version of the puzzle

Two constructed waters both start at pH 7.50. Water A contains ten times more dissolved inorganic carbon than Water B. Each receives the same small dose of strong acid, with negligible dilution.
Predict before we calculate: which pH falls more? What does a pH reading alone leave out?

This is the lake puzzle stripped down to its chemistry: same starting pH, different carbon inventory, same acid input. Give students thirty seconds to commit to a prediction, and ask for a show of hands. Many will say they change equally, because they have learned that pH describes acidity. The model assumptions: closed water, so no gas exchange; no minerals, organic acids or other buffers; 25 °C; background counter-ions keep the solution electrically neutral. This is not a recipe for preparing either water. We return to these two beakers with numbers about two thirds of the way through the lecture.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Where dissolved carbon comes from

Carbon enters water from the air (carbon dioxide), from rocks (carbonate minerals) and from organisms (respiration). Once dissolved, it is shared between three forms that convert into each other by gaining or losing H⁺. Today we work inside the dashed box.

Give the big picture once so that later details have a place. Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves. Carbonate minerals dissolve or precipitate. Organisms respire carbon dioxide into the water or remove it by photosynthesis. Inside the water, three forms interconvert very quickly by proton exchange. In this lecture we hold the total amount of dissolved carbon fixed, a closed system, and study only the exchange inside the box. The next deck opens the box: gas exchange with the atmosphere and the calcite mineral. Separating these processes is a key skill. Many wrong environmental explanations mix up “carbon changed form” with “carbon was added or lost”.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
One element, three dissolved forms

C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
CT is the total dissolved inorganic carbon. CO₂* groups dissolved CO₂ with the small amount of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). When one species converts to another, carbon is redistributed, not removed.

Show the structures so the formulas become molecules. CO2 is neutral and linear. Bicarbonate carries one negative charge and still has one hydrogen it can lose. Carbonate carries two negative charges. The star in CO2-star is a bookkeeping convention: true carbonic acid is a small fraction of the dissolved pool, so we group it with dissolved CO2 and treat the sum as one species. C_T is the conserved quantity in a closed water. Stress the sentence at the bottom. When acid converts bicarbonate to CO2-star, the carbon is still in the bottle. That will matter when we explain why the two waters behave differently.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: Each step trades a hydrogen ion
text:
Each step trades a hydrogen ion
\mathrm{CO_2^*+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H^++HCO_3^-}\qquad pK_1=6.35 \mathrm{HCO_3^-\rightleftharpoons H^++CO_3^{2-}}\qquad pK_2=10.33

Low pH (many H⁺) pushes both equilibria to the left; high pH pushes them to the right. Natural freshwaters (pH ≈ 6–8.5) sit mostly in the bicarbonate region.

These are effective constants for 25 °C dilute freshwater, taken from the reference sheet. The first reaction is shorthand: it combines dissolution, hydration and acid dissociation. It is not an elementary step. The predominance bar is the one picture to remember. Below pK1 the neutral CO2 pool dominates. Between the two pK values bicarbonate dominates. Above pK2 carbonate dominates. Adding acid pushes species left: hydrogen ions are bound into bicarbonate and CO2-star instead of staying free. That binding is the molecular meaning of buffering. Point out that ordinary lakes and rivers sit in the green region, so bicarbonate is the workhorse species of freshwater chemistry.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: From an equilibrium expression to a ratio
text:
From an equilibrium expression to a ratio


K_1=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}
Rearrange, and use [\mathrm{H^+}]\approx10^{-\mathrm{pH}} mol/L:
\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}=\frac{K_1}{[\mathrm{H^+}]}=10^{\,\mathrm{pH}-6.35}

pH 6.35: ratio 1 (equal amounts)
pH 7.35: ratio 10
pH 8.35: ratio 100

The ratio depends only on pH, not on how much carbon there is.




This is the most useful single calculation in the lecture, and it can be done in your head. Dividing K1 by the hydrogen-ion concentration gives the ratio of the two neighbouring species. In logarithmic form it is a straight line of slope one: every pH unit multiplies the ratio by ten. Have students say the ratios aloud for pH 5.35 and 8.35. Emphasise the last line. The ratio contains no information about the total amount of carbon, which is the seed of today’s main point. We use the approximation that hydrogen-ion activity equals its concentration, appropriate for dilute freshwater. The reference sheet states it explicitly.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: Add the second step and normalise
text:
Add the second step and normalise


r_1=10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35},\qquad r_2=10^{\mathrm{pH}-10.33}
The three species stand in proportion
[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]:[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]:[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]=1:r_1:r_1r_2
Worked example, pH 8.35: r_1=100, r_2=0.01047, so 1 : 100 : 1.047.
Divide each by the sum, 102.047, to get fractions α:
α₀ = 0.0098 · α₁ = 0.9799 · α₂ = 0.0103
Check: they sum to 1.




Chain the two ratios. Bicarbonate relative to CO2-star is r1. Carbonate relative to bicarbonate is r2. So carbonate relative to CO2-star is r1 times r2. Dividing by the sum converts the proportions to fractions that add to one. These are written alpha-zero, alpha-one and alpha-two after the number of protons lost. At pH 8.35, almost all carbon is bicarbonate and the other two are about one percent each. This pH is near the bicarbonate maximum, halfway between the two pK values on the log scale. Students will repeat this exact calculation in exercise 1. Encourage them to always check that the fractions sum to one.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
The distribution diagram

Repeat the calculation at every pH and you get this diagram. Where curves cross, pH = pK. Each species dominates across about four pH units. The x-axis is a prescribed pH, not an amount of acid added and not time.

This is the same calculation as the previous slide, repeated across the pH axis by the R script in the activity. Read it with the students. Find pH 8.35 and confirm the green curve is near 0.98. Find the crossing points: at pH 6.35 CO2-star equals bicarbonate, and at 10.33 bicarbonate equals carbonate. At each crossing the two species are equal, but neither is exactly one half, because the third species is still present in a small amount. A common misreading treats the x-axis as acid added or as time. It is neither: each vertical slice is a separate water with that pH. To find what pH a water reaches after acid, we need alkalinity.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Where real waters sit

Clean rain (about 5.6) is acidic just from dissolved CO₂. Most lakes and rivers lie between 6.5 and 8.3, where bicarbonate dominates. Surface seawater is near 8.1. An acidified soft-water lake can fall below pH 5, where nearly all carbon is CO₂*.

Anchor the abstract diagram in real waters; the ranges are approximate. Rain in equilibrium with atmospheric carbon dioxide is around pH 5.6 even without pollution, so acid rain means rain well below that. Most freshwaters and the surface ocean sit in the bicarbonate region. An acidified lake at pH 4.5 to 5 has almost no bicarbonate left. Students should notice that this is the same situation as the granite lake’s ion bar, where bicarbonate had nearly vanished. The diagram explains which species is present. It does not yet explain why one water reaches pH 5 and another stays at 7.5. For that we need amounts.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Check yourself

Use the distribution diagram and the ratio rule. No calculator needed.

At pH 5.35, what is [HCO₃⁻] / [CO₂*]?
At pH 10.33, which two species are equal? Is either exactly half of CT?
A lake is at pH 7.35 with CT = 0.50 mmol/L. Roughly how much of the carbon is bicarbonate?
True or false: “At pH 8 a water has a lot of bicarbonate.”



Answers. One: 0.1, so one bicarbonate for every ten CO2-star. Two: bicarbonate and carbonate are equal at pK2. Neither is exactly one half, because a small CO2-star fraction remains, though at this pH it is tiny. Three: the ratio is ten, so about ten elevenths, roughly 0.45 mmol/L of bicarbonate. Four is the trap. At pH 8 a large fraction of the carbon is bicarbonate, but whether that is a lot depends on how much carbon there is. Use the trap to move to the next slide: fractions are not amounts.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: Fractions do not give the amount
text:
Fractions do not give the amount




Both waters are at pH 7.50, so they have identical fractions: about 93% bicarbonate and 7% CO₂*.
But the amount of bicarbonate is

Water A: 0.93 mmol/L
Water B: 0.093 mmol/L

pH sets the shape of the column; CT sets its height. Each bicarbonate ion can take up one H⁺. Water A has ten times as many to offer.


This is the turning point of the lecture. A pH measurement fixes the proportions but not the amount. Only the amount of bicarbonate and carbonate determines how much acid can be absorbed before the species run out. Make the physical picture concrete: each bicarbonate ion is a site that can bind one incoming hydrogen ion. Water A has ten times as many of those sites per litre. In the lake story, the granite lake is Water B, or worse, and the limestone lake is Water A. We now need a quantity that counts these sites properly, including the fact that carbonate can take up two hydrogen ions. That quantity is alkalinity.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Alkalinity counts the acid-neutralising capacity

A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}]
Units: equivalents per litre (eq/L). Water A at pH 7.50: AT = 0.9356 meq/L. Water B: 0.0938 meq/L.

Alkalinity counts how many hydrogen ions the water can take up before its carbonate species are pushed all the way to CO2-star. Bicarbonate takes up one, carbonate two, hydroxide one. Free hydrogen ions are already there and count negatively. CO2-star is the reference state and counts zero. That is why the units are equivalents, not moles. The two waters’ values follow directly from their fractions and C_T; check the numbers with the class. This carbonate-only definition ignores borate, organic acids, phosphate and other contributors. It is appropriate for our dilute freshwater model but needs checking for real samples, as the reference sheet notes.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Alkalinity is the charge-balance gap




Charge balance forces
A_T\approx(\text{total base cations})-(\text{total strong-acid anions})
Base cations: Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺, K⁺. Strong-acid anions: SO₄²⁻, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻.

Weathering of limestone adds Ca²⁺ with HCO₃⁻: alkalinity rises.
Acid deposition adds SO₄²⁻ with H⁺: alkalinity falls.

The lake’s acid reserve is set by its catchment.


Return to the two lakes from the start. Because cations and anions balance, whatever positive charge from calcium, magnesium, sodium and potassium is not matched by sulfate, chloride and nitrate must be matched by bicarbonate and carbonate, minus free hydrogen ion. That excess is alkalinity. This view links today to last lecture’s charge balance. It also explains the catchment story chemically. Limestone weathering supplies calcium balanced by bicarbonate. Sulfuric acid deposition supplies sulfate balanced by hydrogen ion, which consumes bicarbonate. In the granite lake the base cations barely exceed the strong-acid anions, so alkalinity is near zero or negative. The deposition unit develops this budget further.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Three quantities, three questions





Quantity
Answers the question




pH
How acidic is the water now?


Alkalinity AT
How much strong acid can it neutralise?


Buffer capacity β
How much acid moves pH by one unit, here?



At pH 7.50, Water A’s buffer capacity is about ten times Water B’s.




Students often merge these three ideas into the word “buffering”. Separate them clearly. pH is a state: the current hydrogen-ion level. Alkalinity is an inventory: the total acid-neutralising capacity. Buffer capacity is a local slope: how much acid is needed per unit pH change at the current state. The plot shows buffer capacity across pH for both waters. It peaks near the pK values and has a minimum near pH 8.3. Water A’s curve lies about ten times above Water B’s in the freshwater range, because buffer capacity scales with C_T. We will not ask students to calculate beta by hand; the figure is for interpretation.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Acid consumes alkalinity, not carbon

For a strong-acid dose q (eq/L) in our closed water: \;A_{T,\text{after}}=A_{T,\text{before}}-q\; and C_T is unchanged.
Do not subtract an acid dose from a pH value. pH must be recalculated from the new AT and CT.

Walk through the cartoon. Three hydrogen ions arrive. Three bicarbonate ions become CO2-star. Carbon is conserved, twelve before and twelve after. Alkalinity falls by exactly three. The pH falls because the bicarbonate-to-CO2-star ratio fell, and we know from the ratio rule how to turn a ratio into a pH. The key bookkeeping statement is the equation: strong acid lowers alkalinity one-for-one and leaves C_T unchanged in a closed water. The typical error is to treat pH as additive: pH is a logarithm of a concentration that is itself set by equilibria, so a dose cannot simply be subtracted from it.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Finding the new pH




At fixed CT, alkalinity rises steadily with pH. Each alkalinity value has exactly one pH.

Start at pH 7.50 on the curve.
Lower AT by 0.050 meq/L.
Read off the new pH.

The same step down is a small fraction of Water A’s alkalinity and a large fraction of Water B’s (note the log axis).


This is the graphical solution to the problem. For a fixed C_T, alkalinity is a monotonic function of pH, so we can invert it: given the new alkalinity, there is one pH. The arrows show the move for each water. On a logarithmic axis, an equal absolute step down looks tiny near the top of Water A’s curve and large on Water B’s. You do not need to implement a numerical solver; the supplied final pH values were found exactly this way by the instructor script. The exam-relevant skill is the bookkeeping, alkalinity minus dose with C_T fixed, plus the ability to explain why the pH outcome differs.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Return to the two waters










Constructed water
CT (mmol/L)
AT before (meq/L)
AT after (meq/L)
Final pH




A
1.00
0.9356
0.8856
7.235


B
0.100
0.09382
0.04382
6.252




Water A lost about 5% of its alkalinity and dropped 0.27 pH units.
Water B lost about 53% and dropped 1.25 pH units: over ten times more H⁺.

Same starting pH, same dose, very different outcome. The difference is the carbon inventory, which a pH reading cannot show.

Go back to the predictions students made with the two beakers. The numbers resolve the puzzle. The dose consumed a small part of A’s alkalinity and more than half of B’s. A pH drop of 1.25 means the free hydrogen-ion concentration rose by a factor of about eighteen. These are model results from the stated assumptions, not field data. In exercise 2 students reproduce the alkalinity changes by hand and interpret the supplied final pH values. If time allows, ask: what single measurement would have warned you that Water B was vulnerable? The answer is alkalinity, or C_T, not pH.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
The whole acid response

Keep adding acid. Water B’s pH collapses once its small alkalinity is used up (about 0.09 mmol/L). Water A holds above pH 6 until roughly 0.6 mmol/L, then also falls once its reserve runs out near 0.94.

This curve extends the single dose to a whole titration, model pH against cumulative strong acid. Both curves show the same shape: a gentle slope while bicarbonate remains, then a cliff when alkalinity reaches zero. The position of the cliff equals the starting alkalinity. Translate back to the lakes. Years of acid deposition act like a slow titration. A soft-water lake with a small reserve reaches its cliff quickly and drops into the pH range harmful to fish and invertebrates. Low pH also releases toxic aluminium from soils, covered in the metals unit. A limestone lake has a reserve large enough that it never gets there.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Why liming works


\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)+2H^+\rightarrow Ca^{2+}+CO_2^*+H_2O}
Each mole of dissolved calcite neutralises 2 equivalents of acid, adding 2 eq of alkalinity.
Back of the envelope: raise a 1.0 × 10⁶ m³ lake from AT = 0.044 to 0.20 meq/L.

Needed: 0.156 meq/L = 0.078 mmol/L CaCO₃
= 7.8 g CaCO₃ per m³ → ≈ 8 tonnes, if all dissolves

Real liming uses more, because not all the lime dissolves and the lake water is gradually replaced: hydraulic residence time, as in unit 1.

 Calcite (CaCO₃) crystal, about 6 cm. Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Now we can answer the question from the start. Calcite dissolves by taking up two hydrogen ions per formula unit, so it adds two equivalents of alkalinity per mole. The calculation uses Water B’s post-acid alkalinity as the starting point and a target of 0.2 meq/L, a typical liming goal for restoring sensitive species, chosen here as round numbers. Molar mass of calcium carbonate is about 100 g/mol, so 0.078 mmol/L is about 7.8 mg/L, or 7.8 grams per cubic metre. In practice more is needed. Dissolution is incomplete, and the lake is flushed by inflowing acidic water. That is why liming has to be repeated, and it ties back to residence time from the first lecture.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: The same chemistry, on a bigger stage
text:
The same chemistry, on a bigger stage


 NOAA illustration, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO₂ emissions.
Adding CO₂ raises CT but not alkalinity:
\mathrm{CO_2+H_2O+CO_3^{2-}\rightarrow 2HCO_3^-}
pH falls (by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times) and carbonate ion is consumed. Shell-building organisms such as pteropods find it harder to build and keep calcium carbonate.
This is not the same as adding strong acid. Next lecture shows why.


Show that the tools from today apply directly to a global problem. Ocean uptake of carbon dioxide adds carbon without adding or removing alkalinity, which is different from our strong-acid case where alkalinity fell and C_T stayed fixed. The result is still a lower pH and less carbonate ion, which matters for organisms that build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. The pteropod image is a widely used NOAA illustration of shell dissolution under lower pH. The numbers quoted are rounded, well-established figures. Do not develop ocean chemistry further here: seawater needs other constants and includes borate. The contrast between CO2 uptake and strong-acid addition is the opening of the next deck.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Same pH means same water.” pH fixes the fractions, not the amounts.
“Acid destroys carbonate carbon.” In a closed water it only converts HCO₃⁻ to CO₂*. CT is unchanged.
“Subtract the dose from the pH.” Subtract the dose from alkalinity, then find the pH.
“At pH = pK each species is 50%.” The two neighbours are equal; the third species is still present.
“Alkalinity is how basic the water is.” It is a capacity in eq/L, not a pH. Acidic waters can have positive alkalinity.
“The distribution diagram shows a titration.” Its x-axis is prescribed pH, not acid added.


These are the errors that appear most often in exercises and exams for this topic. Go through them quickly and ask students to say why each is wrong in their own words. The fifth one is subtle: a water at pH 6.5 can still have positive alkalinity, because bicarbonate is present in substantial amounts. Alkalinity becomes zero only around pH 4.5 for typical freshwater carbon contents, when nearly all carbon is CO2-star. This is why alkalinity titrations end near that pH. Encourage students to use this list as a self-check while doing the exercises.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Explore: carbonate response to acid


Compare Water A and Water B: same initial pH and acid dose, different carbon inventories.



Compare Water A and Water B: same initial pH and acid dose, different carbon inventories.

Use the reference presets first and confirm the table values from the “Return to the two waters” slide. Then change one variable at a time. Raise C_T in Water B until it behaves like Water A. Increase the dose until Water A’s alkalinity is exhausted and watch the pH cliff. Ask students to explain each change in words before reading the plot. The exercise page has the model assumptions, a hand-check result and a static reference for printing.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




CT
CO₂* + HCO₃⁻ + CO₃²⁻; conserved when species interconvert


Ratio rule
[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]/[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35}; one pH unit = factor 10


Fractions α
from pH alone; sum to 1; curves cross at pH = pK


Freshwater
pH 6.5–8.3: bicarbonate dominates


Amount
concentration = α × CT; pH does not give CT


Alkalinity AT
HCO₃⁻ + 2CO₃²⁻ + OH⁻ − H⁺ (eq/L): acid-neutralising capacity


Charge balance
AT ≈ base cations − strong-acid anions


Strong acid
AT falls by the dose; CT unchanged; pH recalculated


Lakes
granite → small AT → acidifies; limestone → large AT → resists


Liming
CaCO₃ adds 2 eq alkalinity per mol



Next: gas exchange and minerals. What happens when the water meets the air, and why does a kettle scale up? Then the exercises and the reference sheet.

 Limescale (CaCO₃) from a kettle. Photo: Alexander Davronov, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The summary table is the revision sheet. Recite the chain once. pH gives the fractions. C_T turns fractions into amounts. Alkalinity counts acid-neutralising capacity. Strong acid lowers alkalinity one-for-one with C_T fixed, and pH follows. Then connect back to the opening: lakes on granite have a small reserve and acidified, lakes on limestone have a large one and resisted, and liming adds the missing reserve. The limescale photo is the teaser for the next deck. Heating drives carbon dioxide out of hard water, the carbonate equilibria shift, and calcite precipitates on the kettle element. Explaining that needs gas exchange and mineral saturation, the topics of the next lecture.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Use 25 °C, dilute freshwater, and concentrations in mol/L. Approximate activities by concentrations, with standard-state factors implicit in the numerical equilibrium expressions. Ignore ion pairs, organic acids, phosphate, borate, and other acid–base systems. These choices are unsuitable for seawater or concentrated solutions.








Quantity
Teaching value
Meaning




\(pK_1\)
6.35
First dissociation of the combined dissolved carbon dioxide pool


\(pK_2\)
10.33
Bicarbonate dissociation


\(K_w\)
\(1.0\times10^{-14}\)
Numerical water ion product in this concentration approximation


\(K_H\)

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Species and equilibria
Write \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\) for \(\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\). It is a combined pool, not the chemical formula of a single molecule. Most of this pool is dissolved molecular carbon dioxide under these conditions. The effective first dissociation incorporates hydration:
\[\mathrm{CO_2^* + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-},\qquad
K_1=10^{-6.35}.\]
\[\mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + CO_3^{2-}},\qquad
K_2=10^{-10.33}.\]
In the first expression, the water term represents the net reaction of dissolved carbon dioxide; the notation groups hydrated and unhydrated forms together.
The total dissolved inorganic carbon in this model is
\[C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}].\]
No carbon leaves this sum merely because it changes species. Mineral reactions, gas exchange, or biological transformations can change the dissolved total.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
section: Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
text:
Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
Dividing the equilibrium expressions gives
\[r_1=\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35},\qquad
r_2=\frac{[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-10.33}.\]
The proportions of the three species are \(1:r_1:r_1r_2\). Therefore
\[\alpha_0=\frac{1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_1=\frac{r_1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_2=\frac{r_1r_2}{1+r_1+r_1r_2}.\]
Each \(\alpha\) is dimensionless and each concentration is \(\alpha_i C_T\). The fractions sum to one. In this model the fractions depend on pH and the constants; \(C_T\) sets the concentration scale. A distribution curve supplies possible compositions at prescribed pH values. It does not solve for pH.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Alkalinity and buffering
The carbonate-only total alkalinity is
\[A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}],\qquad
[\mathrm{OH^-}]=K_w/[\mathrm{H^+}].\]
Use mol of charge equivalents per litre (eq/L); \(1\) meq/L is \(10^{-3}\) eq/L. Bicarbonate contributes one equivalent per mole, carbonate two. Real freshwater can have additional alkalinity contributions, so this expression must be checked before applying it to measurements. The USGS carbonate-speciation guidance explains the importance of other acid-neutralising species.
Alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance relative to the carbon dioxide reference state. pH describes hydrogen-ion activity at the present state. Local buffer capacity describes the amount of acid or base required for a small pH change under specified conditions. These are related, but are different quantities.
For a strong-acid addition \(q\) eq/L with negligible dilution and no other reaction, \(A_{T,\mathrm{after}}=A_{T,\mathrm{before}}-q\). In a closed water with no mineral or biological reactions, \(C_T\) stays constant. Added acid redistributes carbon toward \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\). The final pH must satisfy both the carbon balance and the new alkalinity.
crumbs: Week 2: Aquatic composition and carbonate chemistry

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Gas and mineral boundaries
For water equilibrated with a large gas reservoir, use the specified convention
\[[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=K_H p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}.\]
Here partial pressure is in atm. Applying this coefficient to total inorganic carbon would be incorrect. Gas uptake by itself changes \(C_T\) but conserves \(A_T\) in our model. At fixed alkalinity it generally lowers pH. Fixing gas pressure, pH, and \(C_T\) independently would usually overconstrain the model.
For calcite, \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+CO_3^{2-}}\). Use the free-ion concentrations to estimate
\[\Omega=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{K_{sp}}.\]
\(\Omega<1\) indicates undersaturation; dissolution is thermodynamically favoured if calcite is available. \(\Omega>1\) indicates supersaturation; precipitation can be favoured, but kinetics and nucleation can delay it. \(\Omega=1\) is saturation. Dissolving one mole of calcite adds one mole to dissolved inorganic carbon and two equivalents to alkalinity. This process is excluded from the closed acid example.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
About this lecture


In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius in Stockholm did long calculations by hand on one question: how would Earth’s temperature change if the amount of carbon dioxide in the air changed? He estimated several degrees of warming for a doubling.
Air is about 99% nitrogen and oxygen. CO₂ is only a few hundredths of a percent. How can such a small amount matter?
Today you will learn to:

explain why CO₂ and H₂O absorb infrared while N₂ and O₂ do not;
read a transmission spectrum and compute absorbed power for one band;
tell lifetime, half-life and climate response apart;
explain why particles can cool or warm.

Last lecture: sulfate in rain. Today: sulfate, and gases, in the light.

 Svante Arrhenius (1859–1927), Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1903. Photogravure, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Arrhenius is known to chemists for the Arrhenius equation and for his theory of electrolytic dissociation, which won the 1903 Nobel Prize. In 1896 he also published a long calculation of how changes in carbonic acid, as CO2 was then called, would affect the temperature of the ground. His numbers were rough, but the physical idea was right, and his estimate for doubling CO2 is not far from modern ones. Today we explain the chemistry behind that idea: why some molecules interact with the infrared radiation that Earth emits and others do not, how to read a spectrum, and why both lifetime and particles matter. This is the last lecture of week 1.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Two kinds of light

The Sun’s surface is about 5800 K; it emits mostly visible and near-infrared light. Earth’s surface, about 288 K, emits thermal infrared peaking near 10 µm. The two ranges hardly overlap, so a gas can be transparent to sunlight but absorb Earth’s heat.

Every warm object emits radiation, and its temperature sets the wavelengths. These curves come from Planck’s law, each scaled to its own peak so the shapes can be compared. The hotter Sun peaks at about half a micrometre, in the visible. The much cooler Earth peaks around ten micrometres, in the thermal infrared, invisible to us. Because the two curves barely overlap, we can treat incoming shortwave and outgoing longwave radiation separately. That is the key to the greenhouse effect: a gas that is transparent to sunlight but absorbs in the thermal infrared lets energy in more easily than it lets energy out.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: How the atmosphere intercepts outgoing heat
text:
How the atmosphere intercepts outgoing heat

Sunlight warms the surface. The surface emits infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb part of it and re-emit in all directions, some back down. Energy finally escapes from higher, colder layers, which emit less. More absorber raises that escape level, and the surface warms.

Walk through the picture from left to right. Most sunlight passes through the clear atmosphere and is absorbed at the surface. The warm surface emits infrared. Greenhouse gas molecules absorb that infrared and quickly pass the energy to neighbouring molecules by collisions, warming the air. The air itself emits infrared in all directions, so part returns to the surface. The radiation that reaches space at absorbing wavelengths comes from high, cold layers, and a cold layer emits less. Adding more absorber moves that emission level higher and colder, so to stay in balance the surface and lower atmosphere must warm. In the window region, surface radiation escapes directly.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Why N₂ and O₂ do not absorb, but CO₂ does
text:
Why N₂ and O₂ do not absorb, but CO₂ does

A vibration absorbs infrared only if it changes the molecule’s dipole moment. N₂ and O₂ stay symmetric when they stretch. CO₂ has no dipole at rest, but its asymmetric stretch and bend create one while they vibrate.

Infrared light is an oscillating electric field. It can push on a molecule only if the molecule’s charge distribution oscillates too: the dipole moment must change during the vibration. In nitrogen and oxygen the two atoms are identical, so stretching the bond never creates a dipole. That is why ninety-nine percent of the air is essentially transparent to thermal infrared. Carbon dioxide is linear and symmetric at rest, so it has no permanent dipole. But in the asymmetric stretch the carbon moves towards one oxygen, and in the bend the molecule is no longer straight; both create an oscillating dipole. Water is bent and has a permanent dipole, so it absorbs strongly at many wavelengths.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Where each gas absorbs

The CO₂ bend at about 15 µm sits close to the peak of Earth’s emission. Water vapour absorbs widely. Between about 8 and 13 µm little absorbs: the atmospheric window. A gas absorbing in the window has more effect than one absorbing where others already do.

This is a schematic of band positions, not a measured spectrum. Water vapour absorbs in a band near six micrometres and across the far infrared through its rotations. Carbon dioxide has the strong bending band near fifteen micrometres and the asymmetric stretch near 4.3 micrometres, where Earth emits little. Ozone absorbs near 9.6 micrometres and methane near 7.7. The window between about eight and thirteen micrometres is where surface radiation escapes most freely. Overlap matters: adding a gas at wavelengths already absorbed by water vapour changes less than adding one in the window. Altitude matters too. So a single peak height is not a climate metric.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Reading a simple spectrum




A transmission spectrum shows the fraction T of light that passes at each wavelength. If nothing is reflected, the absorbed fraction is 1 − T.



Wavelength
T
Absorbed




0.55 µm
0.95
0.05


10 µm
0.20
0.80



These are invented teaching values, not a real gas. The fraction alone does not give the energy absorbed.


This is the deliberately simple spectrum from the notes. The model gas is almost transparent in visible light and absorbs most radiation in a band near ten micrometres. Reading it is straightforward: absorbed fraction equals one minus transmission, assuming no reflection or scattering. Exercise 1 then asks the important follow-up question: does the gas absorb more energy at ten micrometres? Not necessarily. You also need to know how much energy arrives in each band and how wide the bands are. A large fraction of a weak beam can be less energy than a small fraction of a strong one. That leads to the worked beam calculation on the next slide.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: One beam, one band: a worked example
text:
One beam, one band: a worked example

A constructed beam of 100 W/m² in one band meets a layer with T = 0.20 and no reflection: 20 W/m² pass and 80 W/m² are absorbed. This is a single-band calculation, not Earth’s energy balance, which needs all wavelengths, emission and atmospheric structure.

This is the worked example from the notes. Multiply the incident power by the transmission to get the transmitted power, and subtract to get the absorbed power. Students should be able to do this in their heads. Stress what the calculation leaves out. A real atmosphere emits as well as absorbs, so the absorbed energy does not simply disappear; it is re-radiated. There are many wavelengths, each with its own transmission and incident power, and they must be summed. The atmosphere also has layers at different temperatures. Climate models do exactly this summation for thousands of wavelengths and many layers. Our single beam is the building block.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Check yourself


Why does O₂, the second most abundant gas, contribute almost nothing to infrared absorption?
CO₂ is a symmetric molecule. Why can it still absorb infrared?
In the teaching spectrum, the gas absorbs 80% at 10 µm and 5% at 0.55 µm. Does it absorb more energy at 10 µm?
A 50 W/m² beam meets a layer with T = 0.60 and no reflection. How much is absorbed?



Answers. One: O2 is a homonuclear diatomic; its stretch never changes the dipole moment, so it has no ordinary infrared-active vibration. Two: its asymmetric stretch and bend create a changing dipole during the vibration, even though the molecule has no dipole at rest. Three: not necessarily. We need the incident energy in each band and the band widths. For sunlight the visible band carries a lot of energy; for Earth’s emission the infrared does. This is exercise 1. Four: 50 times 0.60 gives 30 transmitted, so 20 watts per square metre are absorbed.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: How long does a gas stay?
text:
How long does a gas stay?




For a single first-order sink with rate constant k:

amount left: C = C_0e^{-kt}
lifetime τ = 1/k (37% left)
half-life = ln 2 / k = 0.693 τ

Worked example, fictitious gas with k = 0.0200 per day:

lifetime 50.0 days
half-life 34.7 days
left after 50.0 days: 0.368



This is exercise 3, and it reuses the tools from the atmospheric reactions lecture. A single first-order sink gives an exponential decline. The lifetime is the inverse of the rate constant; after one lifetime about 37 percent remains. The half-life is shorter by a factor of 0.693. In the exercise, k is 0.0200 per day, so the lifetime is 50 days and the half-life about 35 days. These numbers describe a fictitious gas with one constant sink. Real greenhouse gases are removed by chemistry, by uptake into oceans and soils, or by both, and the next slide shows why carbon dioxide does not fit this simple picture.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
CO₂ has no single lifetime

CO₂ is not destroyed in the air; it is redistributed to the ocean surface, plants and soils, and slowly the deep ocean. Each takes CO₂ at its own pace. A model fit used by the IPCC leaves about 20% of a pulse in the air after centuries. A gas like methane, destroyed by OH, behaves more like one exponential of about a decade.

Compare the two curves. The dashed curve is a single sink with a lifetime of about twelve years, similar to methane’s, whose main sink is reaction with OH. After a few decades it is essentially gone. The solid curve is an impulse response fit to carbon-cycle models, published by Joos and colleagues in 2013 and used in the IPCC fifth assessment. It falls quickly at first, as the surface ocean and land take up carbon, then slowly, and a fraction remains for many centuries until slow processes such as carbonate dissolution and weathering act. This is the compartment balance from lecture 1 again: CO2 is transferred between reservoirs, not destroyed.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Watching the build-up


 Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, among old lava flows. Photo: Brian Vasel/NOAA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Since 1958, CO₂ has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa, far from local sources. The record, begun by Charles David Keeling, shows:

a seasonal cycle: northern plants take up CO₂ in summer and release it in winter;
a steady rise, from about 315 ppm in 1958 to above 420 ppm today. Before industrialisation it was about 280 ppm.

Because CO₂ is long-lived, it is well mixed: one remote station tracks the global trend.


The Mauna Loa record is the most famous environmental chemistry time series. The site was chosen because it is high, remote and surrounded by bare lava, so local vegetation and pollution have little influence. The seasonal wiggle is a balance signal: the Northern Hemisphere biosphere takes up carbon during the growing season and releases it in winter. The rise is the accumulation from fossil-fuel burning and land-use change, partly offset by ocean and land uptake. Connect to the transport slide from the atmospheric reactions lecture: because the lifetime of CO2 in the air is much longer than the mixing time, one remote station is representative of the global background.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Equal mass is not equal effect
text:
Equal mass is not equal effect

Two gases are emitted in equal mass. To compare their climate effects you need: the number of molecules (molar mass), their absorption bands and overlap, how long they stay, any chemical or particle side effects, and the time horizon of the comparison.

This is exercise 4. Equal mass does not mean equal numbers of molecules: methane’s molar mass is 16 grams per mole, carbon dioxide’s 44, so a kilogram of methane holds about 2.7 times as many molecules. Absorption differs per molecule and depends on where the bands fall and what else already absorbs there. Lifetime decides how long the effect lasts. Some gases also have indirect effects: methane oxidation produces ozone and water vapour in the stratosphere, and sulfur dioxide forms particles. Finally, any comparison needs a stated time horizon. A short-lived gas looks more important over 20 years than over 100 years. That is why policy uses metrics with an explicit horizon.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Particles: not just another gas


 Summit caldera of Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, on 1 August 1991, six weeks after the climactic eruption of 15 June. Photo: T. J. Casadevall, USGS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

In June 1991 Mount Pinatubo sent millions of tonnes of SO₂ into the stratosphere. It was oxidised to sulfate particles, the same chemistry as in the deposition lecture.
The particle veil scattered sunlight back to space, and global average temperature fell by roughly half a degree for about a year or two. Then the particles settled out.
Particles act through size, composition and location, not through infrared absorption bands, and they last days to a few years, not centuries.


Pinatubo is the natural experiment that tested climate models. The eruption injected sulfur dioxide high into the stratosphere, where it was oxidised to sulfuric acid droplets that spread around the globe. Because there is no rain in the stratosphere, they remained for over a year. They reflected sunlight, and global surface temperatures fell measurably before recovering as the particles were removed. Contrast with greenhouse gases. Particles mainly interact with sunlight rather than with Earth’s infrared, their effect depends on size and composition, and their lifetime is short: days in the lower atmosphere, a year or two in the stratosphere. So aerosols cannot be treated like long-lived gases.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Three ways particles change radiation

Bright particles such as sulfate scatter sunlight: cooling. Dark black carbon absorbs it: warming of the air layer and of snow it lands on. Particles also seed cloud droplets; more particles give more, smaller droplets and a brighter cloud.

The three panels are three distinct pathways, and they can have opposite signs. Scattering by sulfate and sea salt sends part of the sunlight back to space, a cooling effect. Black carbon from incomplete combustion absorbs sunlight and warms the layer of air where it sits; when it lands on snow or ice it darkens the surface and speeds melting, which matters in the Arctic and in Scandinavian mountains. The cloud pathway is the most uncertain. Every cloud droplet forms on a particle. With the same amount of water spread over more particles, droplets are smaller and more numerous, and the cloud reflects more sunlight. Do not assign every aerosol a universal cooling sign.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Seeing the cloud effect from space
text:
Seeing the cloud effect from space


 Ship tracks in low clouds over the North Atlantic off Spain and Portugal, 22 January 2018. Image: Jeff Schmaltz, NASA MODIS, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

The bright lines are ship tracks. Exhaust particles from ships seed extra cloud droplets, so the cloud along each ship’s path becomes brighter than the cloud around it.
The ship emits SO₂ and soot; the chemistry turns gases into particles, and the particles change the clouds.
Since 2020, international rules have cut the sulfur content of ship fuel sharply, and ship tracks have become less frequent. A cleaner-air policy can therefore slightly reduce a cooling effect.


This satellite image shows the cloud pathway directly. Low marine clouds are sensitive to the number of particles available as droplet seeds. Along each ship’s path the exhaust adds particles, the droplets become smaller and more numerous, and the cloud reflects more sunlight, so the tracks appear as bright lines. The International Maritime Organization reduced the permitted sulfur content of ship fuel in 2020, and studies have reported fewer ship tracks since then. This is an example of a trade-off students should understand: removing sulfur improves air quality and reduces acid deposition, but also removes some reflective particles. It is not a reason to keep pollution, but it must be counted.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Back to Arrhenius’s question


 Svante Arrhenius. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

How can a few hundredths of a percent of CO₂ change the climate? Now we can answer with molecules:

N₂ and O₂ have no changing dipole; they are transparent to Earth’s infrared.
CO₂ bends and absorbs near 15 µm, close to the peak of Earth’s emission.
Absorption makes energy escape from higher, colder layers.
CO₂ is not destroyed; a large fraction stays for centuries.

Particles and short-lived gases add effects of both signs, on shorter timescales.


Return to the opening question and answer it in four steps, using only today’s chemistry. The bulk of the air does nothing to infrared because of molecular symmetry. Carbon dioxide does, through its bending vibration, at wavelengths where Earth emits strongly. More absorption raises the level from which energy escapes to space, and a colder emitting level requires a warmer surface to stay in balance. And because carbon dioxide is redistributed between reservoirs rather than destroyed, each emission keeps acting for centuries. Arrhenius did not know all of this in 1896, but his basic reasoning about absorption and balance stands.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“CO₂ is symmetric, so it cannot absorb infrared.” Its bend and asymmetric stretch change the dipole.
“The most abundant gases matter most.” N₂ and O₂ are almost inactive in the infrared.
“A bigger absorption peak means a bigger climate effect.” Overlap, altitude, incident energy and lifetime also matter.
“Absorbed fraction = absorbed energy.” Multiply by the incident power in each band.
“CO₂ has a lifetime of X years.” It has several timescales; part stays for centuries.
“Aerosols always cool.” Black carbon warms; effects depend on composition and location.
“Equal mass, equal effect.” Molecules, bands, lifetime and time horizon differ.


These are the most frequent errors on this topic. Have students explain each correction in their own words. The first two are about the dipole rule and are the core chemistry of today. The third and fourth are about reading spectra correctly. The fifth is a frequent statement even in the media; the answer is that the airborne fraction of a CO2 pulse declines over several timescales, and a substantial part stays for many centuries. The sixth separates scattering from absorbing particles. The last one sums up exercise 4. Encourage students to use this list as a self-check before the week 1 exercises.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Explore: how long a pulse stays in the air
text:
Explore: how long a pulse stays in the air


After 100 years about 0.41 of a CO₂ pulse is still in the air; a 12-year gas has almost none left.



Compare one first-order sink with the several timescales of CO₂.

Start with the lecture comparison: the same curves as the CO2 impulse slide, read at 100 years. Then use the lifetime 50, read at 50 preset to repeat exercise 3; the fraction left depends only on time divided by lifetime, so years or days give the same 0.368. Move the time slider and point to the table: the fast part is gone within a decade or two, the medium part within a century or two, and about a fifth stays for centuries. Ask a student to find a single lifetime that matches CO2 at 20 years, then look at 500 years. It fails, which is the message: CO2 has no single lifetime because it is redistributed, not destroyed.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Two kinds of light
Sun about 5800 K, peak near 0.5 µm; Earth about 288 K, peak near 10 µm


Greenhouse effect
gases absorb and re-emit infrared; escape from higher, colder layers


Dipole rule
IR-active vibration changes the dipole; N₂, O₂ inactive


CO₂ modes
bend near 15 µm, asymmetric stretch near 4.3 µm; symmetric stretch inactive


Bands
overlap with H₂O and the 8–13 µm window decide added effect


Transmission
absorbed fraction = 1 − T; energy needs incident power


Lifetime
τ = 1/k, half-life = 0.693 τ, for one first-order sink


CO₂
several timescales; about 20% of a pulse stays for centuries


Particles
scatter (cool), absorb (warm), brighten clouds; short-lived



Next: aquatic composition and equilibrium, the start of week 2: from air to water. Then the exercises and notes.

 Dalälven river at Forsbo, Möklinta, Sweden. Photo: Q1959, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The summary table is the revision sheet for today. Recite the chain once: two kinds of light; the dipole rule decides which molecules absorb Earth’s infrared; band position and overlap decide how much an addition matters; absorbed energy needs incident power; lifetime and reservoirs decide how long an emission acts; and particles act on sunlight and clouds, with either sign and short lifetimes. That completes week 1: amounts and balances, atmospheric reactions, deposition and climate. The photo is the teaser for week 2. We now move from the air into water. Rivers and lakes carry what the atmosphere delivers, and the next lecture teaches how to read a water analysis.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text:
1. Wet input
Rainfall is 0.600 m/year and nitrate is 20.0 µmol/L throughout. Calculate nitrate input per square metre per year. Use 1 m³ = 1000 L.






Hint





A metre of rain over one square metre is one cubic metre.









Worked solution





600 L/m²/year × 20.0 µmol/L = 0.0120 mol nitrate/m²/year. This is a nitrate amount flux. Calling it an acid-equivalent flux requires the form and transformations to be specified.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text:
2. Rain pH
Two rain events both have pH 4.00 but depths of 1.00 and 10.0 mm. In the dilute approximation, calculate free-H⁺ input per m² for each. Does this include all titratable acidity?






Hint





1 mm over 1 m² is 1 L; [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴ mol/L.









Worked solution





Inputs are 0.100 and 1.00 mmol H⁺/m². The larger event carries ten times the free hydrogen-ion amount. Other acid–base species and dry deposition are not included.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text:
3. Change the catchment budget
Use the worked budget but reduce neutralisation from 30000 to 20000 eq/year. Keep annual water export fixed. Find the residual equivalent load concentration.






Hint





Subtract equivalents before dividing by the annual volume.









Worked solution





Residual = 20000 eq/year. Dividing by 5.00 × 10⁸ L/year gives 4.00 × 10⁻⁵ eq/L = 0.0400 meq/L. It is not a pH and is not a closed-water pulse.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text:
4. A sulfate result
A rain sample contains sulfate. What additional evidence is needed before reporting a strong-acid dose from that result?






Hint





Counterions and subsequent transformations affect acidity.









Worked solution





Measure or constrain acidity/alkalinity, major cations including ammonium, other anions, precipitation volume, and dry deposition as relevant. Sulfate may arrive partly as neutral salts. Nitrification, uptake, and catchment reactions can change the net acid budget.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity exercises
text:
Explore: deposition and dilution
Predict what happens if annual water export doubles while deposition flux and catchment area stay fixed. Change one input at a time and distinguish flux, annual load, and the equivalent concentration.


Reference case: 40000 eq/year of acid input gives 0.0800 meq/L before neutralisation at 500 million L/year water export.



E1. Choose Worked example, then Double water export. Which annual amounts stay fixed? Check the equivalent concentration by hand.
E2. Reset, then double catchment area while keeping water export fixed. Explain why this is a different comparison from doubling both area and water.
E3. Set both acid inputs to zero. Explain why water volume cannot create an acid input.

Model conditions and hand check
The constructed inputs are 20.0 mmol HNO₃ and 10.0 mmol H₂SO₄ per m² per year. At the stated full-neutralisation endpoint, their equivalent flux is (20 + 2 × 10)/1000 = 0.0400 eq/m²/year. Across 1.00 km² this gives 40000 eq/year. Dividing by 500 million L/year gives 0.0800 meq/L; doubling that water export gives 0.0400 meq/L at the same annual load.
These are supplied acid inputs, not sulfate or nitrate measurements treated as free acid. All input is assumed to reach the annual exported water, with no storage, neutralisation, or other sinks. This is an annual equivalent budget, not a closed-lake pulse or a pH prediction. Area and water export are independent controls only for the stated sensitivity comparison.
More guided comparisons for week 1.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text: How does an atmospheric emission become an acid input to a catchment, and why does rain pH alone not give the annual acid load?

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Learning goals

Trace oxidation and wet/dry transfer from air to a catchment.
Convert a deposition flux to amount and charge equivalents.
Distinguish free hydrogen ion, potential acidity, and net catchment response.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Oxidation creates new species
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are precursors, not simply bottles of sulfuric and nitric acid dispersed in air. Oxidation occurs through several gas and aqueous pathways. One useful nitrogen pathway is \(\mathrm{NO_2+OH+M\rightarrow HNO_3+M}\). A net sulfur oxidation can be represented as \(\mathrm{SO_2+\tfrac12O_2+H_2O\rightarrow H_2SO_4}\); this is bookkeeping, not an elementary rate law.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Wet and dry pathways
Wet deposition transfers substances in rain, snow, fog, or cloud water. Dry deposition transfers gases and particles to surfaces without precipitation. Aerosols are suspended particles or droplets; some are emitted and others form by chemical reactions. A low rain concentration during a wet year can still correspond to a large wet flux. Dry deposition requires separate information and cannot be inferred just from a rain sample.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Count acid equivalents carefully
In a stated complete neutralisation convention, HNO₃ supplies one equivalent per mole and H₂SO₄ supplies two. Actual deposited sulfate or nitrate need not arrive as free acid: accompanying cations, ammonium, and biological transformations matter. Ammonia can neutralise atmospheric acid; later nitrification of ammonium can generate acidity. Do not assign two free hydrogen ions to every measured sulfate regardless of its chemical form.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Connect flux to a receiving volume
text:
Connect flux to a receiving volume
For a uniform flux \(F\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ and catchment area \(A\), the annual input is \(FA\). Converting that input to an equivalent water concentration requires a receiving water volume and assumptions about retention, export, and mixing. In the recurring teaching catchment, use area \(1.00\times10^6\) m² and annual water export \(5.00\times10^8\) L. This defines an annual flow-weighted concentration, not a sudden dose to a closed lake.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Why catchments respond differently
Weathering, mineral availability, soil exchange, plant uptake, and flow paths modify the relationship between atmospheric input and lake chemistry. pH describes the current hydrogen-ion activity; alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance. A buffered catchment can receive acid while showing a modest pH change. Measurements should therefore link atmospheric fluxes with water flow, alkalinity, and major ions rather than treating pH as a complete budget.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Worked example
Assume the catchment receives \(0.0200\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ of HNO₃ and \(0.0100\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ of H₂SO₄, with full neutralisation of both protons in the stated accounting convention. The acid-equivalent flux is \(0.0200+2(0.0100)=0.0400\) eq m⁻² yr⁻¹. Over \(1.00\times10^6\) m², that is 40000 eq/year. If an identified catchment neutralisation process consumes 30000 eq/year and no other acid terms act, the residual is 10000 eq/year. Dividing by \(5.00\times10^8\) L/year gives 0.0200 meq/L of residual equivalent load. This budget is constructed; it does not predict pH without carbonate and other constraints.

text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapters 5–7: acid formation and wet/dry fluxes.
EPA acid deposition: Wet/dry transfer and precursor oxidation.
EPA effects of acid rain: Links between deposition, catchment buffering, and aquatic response.
