title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
About this lecture


In January 2000 a tailings dam at a gold mine near Baia Mare, Romania, failed. About 100 000 m³ of cyanide-laden water entered the rivers and travelled down the Someș, the Tisza and the Danube. Fish died along hundreds of kilometres.
Downstream, the measured cyanide concentration fell. Was the poison destroyed, or only spread out?
Today you will learn to:

tell concentration apart from amount and load;
draw a boundary and write a balance;
separate mixing, transfer and reaction;
estimate a timescale from volume and flow.

This is the first lecture of the course. Every later unit uses these tools.

 Dead fish collected on the Tisza after the 2000 cyanide spill, Hungary. Photo: Délmagyarország/Karnok Csaba, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Welcome to the course. Start with the story. In early 2000 a dam holding mining waste near Baia Mare failed, and water contaminated with cyanide flowed into the river system that drains into the Tisza and then the Danube. The images of dead fish were shown across Europe. The question for today sounds simple: when the measured concentration downstream was lower, had nature removed the cyanide? To answer, we need to count amounts, not just read concentrations, and we need to decide where we draw the line around our system. These are the habits that every later lecture relies on, from lake acidification to contaminant fate.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
A concentration falls downstream. Why?

A lower number at station B has at least three explanations. Water joined the river (dilution). The substance moved into sediment or air (transfer). Or it reacted to something else (transformation). Only the third is chemical destruction, and even then the atoms remain.

This slide sets the question for the whole lecture. Draw students’ attention to the dots. In the dilution panel the number of dots is unchanged; only the water volume grew. In the transfer panel the dots are still in the system, but some now sit in the sediment or have escaped to the air. Only in the transformation panel do the original molecules disappear, and they are replaced by products. A concentration measurement at A and at B cannot by itself tell these three cases apart. Our job today is to find the extra information that can: volumes, flows, other compartments and products.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Concentration is not amount

Amount = concentration × volume. A dilute large sample can hold more solute than a concentrated small one. Also state what you count: mg of nitrate and mg of nitrogen are different numbers for the same water.

Concentration is amount divided by volume. It describes how crowded the solute is, not how much exists. Sample 2 has a fifth of the concentration of sample 1 but twice the solute, because its volume is ten times larger. The box on the right is a common reporting trap. Nitrate results are reported either as mass of nitrate ion or as mass of nitrogen. The molar mass of nitrate is about 62 grams per mole and nitrogen contributes 14 of those, so the two numbers differ by a factor of about 4.4. Always check the label, mg NO3 per litre or mg N per litre, before comparing data from different sources.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Load: amount carried per time


 A US Geological Survey streamgage that records river flow. Photo: U.S. Geological Survey, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

A river does not hold a fixed amount; it carries one. The rate is the load:
\text{load} = Q \times C
Worked example. A stream carries Q = 0.200 m³/s at C = 0.500 mg/L.

Q = 200 L/s
load = 200 L/s × 0.500 mg/L = 100 mg/s = 0.100 g/s
per day: 0.100 g/s × 86 400 s = 8.64 kg/day

A load needs both a concentration and a flow measurement.


For a flowing water, the useful quantity is the load: amount per time. It is concentration times flow. This is why monitoring stations such as this streamgage measure water flow continuously, and why chemistry samples are taken at gauged sites. Walk through the units: convert cubic metres to litres first, then milligrams per second, then grams per day. The daily figure assumes flow and concentration stay constant over the day, which is rarely true in a real river. Students repeat this in exercise 2. Point out that a river with low concentration but very high flow can carry a larger load than a polluted small stream.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Choose the boundary first

A compartment is a volume you define: a lake, a sample bottle, or water plus sediment. A flux crosses the boundary. A reaction happens inside it. Sorption to sediment is an output from the water, but only an internal move for the lake as a whole.

Before writing any balance, write down what is inside your boundary. The same physical process can be a loss or no loss at all, depending on that choice. If the boundary is drawn around the water only, sorption to the sediment removes the compound and appears as an output. If the boundary includes the sediment, sorption just moves the compound from one part of the system to another, and the total is unchanged. Neither choice is wrong. Problems arise when the boundary is not stated, and someone reports “removal” that is really a transfer. Many disagreements in environmental reports come down to unstated boundaries.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Write the balance

For a well-mixed water body of constant volume, the outflow term is Q × C: outflow water times the outlet concentration. Inflow and outflow water must also balance if the volume stays fixed.

This is the general balance, written in words: the change of the amount per unit time equals inputs minus outputs plus production minus consumption. Inputs and outputs cross the boundary. Production and consumption are reactions inside it. Check that every term has the same units, amount per time. If one term is in milligrams per litre and another in kilograms per day, something is missing, usually a volume or a flow. For a well mixed lake, the outlet concentration equals the lake concentration, so the advective output is flow times lake concentration. We will use exactly this form when we discuss flushing and steady state.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Transfer or transformation?




A sealed bottle starts with 10.0 mg of a parent compound in water. Later the water holds 4.0 mg and the sediment 5.0 mg.

Water alone: 6.0 mg “lost”.
Water + sediment: only 1.0 mg missing.

The missing 1.0 mg may be transformation, loss to the bottle wall, or analytical error. The balance tells you how much to explain, not what happened to it.


This is exercise 3, and it shows why the boundary matters. If you only measure the water, it looks as if most of the compound has gone. Once the sediment is measured, most of it is accounted for, and the real question shrinks to one milligram. That remaining milligram is not automatically degradation. It could be stuck to the glass, it could be a measurement error of ten percent, or it could have been transformed. To claim transformation you need positive evidence, such as measured products. Also note that transformation of the parent does not destroy its elements. A balance on carbon or chlorine atoms is a different balance from one on the parent molecule.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
section: Steady state does not mean nothing happens
text:
Steady state does not mean nothing happens

A constructed lake (V = 10⁶ m³, Q = 10⁴ m³/day) receives 1.0 kg/day of a conservative solute. The inventory rises and levels off when output = input. At steady state the amount stops changing, but both fluxes keep running.

Steady state is one of the most misunderstood words in this course. It means that accumulation is zero: the amount in the compartment no longer changes. It does not mean that inputs have stopped. In this constructed lake, one kilogram enters every day and one kilogram leaves every day at steady state. The level of 100 kilograms is set by the balance: input divided by flow gives the steady concentration, 0.1 milligram per litre, times the volume. Ask students: if the input doubled, what would the steady inventory be? It doubles. Also note that real lakes are often not at steady state, so treat it as an assumption to be checked, not a fact.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Mixing without reaction




Mix 2.00 L at 3.00 mg/L with 1.00 L at 0.600 mg/L.

amounts: 6.00 mg + 0.600 mg = 6.60 mg
volume: 3.00 L
concentration: 6.60 / 3.00 = 2.20 mg/L

Add amounts, then divide by total volume. Never average concentrations.
All conservative mixtures of two waters fall on a straight mixing line. A point off the line needs another explanation.


This is the worked example from the notes. The concentration fell from 3.00 to 2.20 milligrams per litre, yet no solute was lost: all 6.60 milligrams are in the mixture. The method is always the same: convert to amounts, add, divide by total volume. A simple average of the two concentrations would give 1.80, which is wrong because the volumes differ. The mixing line is a powerful field tool. Plot measured concentration against the fraction of each water, often estimated from a conservative tracer such as chloride. If the sample lies below the line, something removed solute, or the sampling, timing or measurement needs checking.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Rivers mix by load

At a junction, add loads, then divide by total flow. The tributary is four times more concentrated, yet the mixed river is only 0.80 mg/L. Nothing reacted; the solute was diluted.

The same logic applies to flowing water, with flows in place of volumes and loads in place of amounts. The main river carries 20 grams per second and so does the tributary. Below the junction 40 grams per second flow in 50 cubic metres per second, which gives 0.80 milligrams per litre. Remind students that one milligram per litre equals one gram per cubic metre, which makes the unit arithmetic clean. In the Tisza case, every tributary and the Danube itself added water to the plume. That alone lowered concentration a great deal, without any chemical destruction.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Check yourself


Mix 4.00 L at 2.00 mg/L with 1.00 L of clean water. What is the final concentration? Was solute destroyed?
A lake is at steady state. Does that mean no pollutant enters it?
A report says “60% of the pesticide was removed from the pond water within a week.” What would you ask before calling it degradation?
Is 5 mg NO₃⁻/L more or less nitrogen than 5 mg N/L?



Answers. One: 8.00 milligrams in 5.00 litres gives 1.60 milligrams per litre; nothing was destroyed, it is dilution. This is exercise 1. Two: no, steady state only means inputs and outputs balance, so the amount does not change. Three: ask about the boundary. Was the sediment measured? Were plants, the air and the container considered? Were products measured? Was the water volume constant? Four: less. Five milligrams of nitrate contains only about 1.1 milligrams of nitrogen, whereas 5 milligrams of nitrogen per litre corresponds to about 22 milligrams of nitrate per litre.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
section: How long does the water stay?
text:
How long does the water stay?


 Lake Vättern with the island of Visingsö, Sweden, from the air. Photo: acediscovery, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

The hydraulic replacement time is
\tau = V / Q
Lake Vättern, Sweden’s second-largest lake: V ≈ 77 km³, outflow Q ≈ 40 m³/s.
τ ≈ 77 × 10⁹ m³ ÷ 40 m³/s ≈ 1.9 × 10⁹ s ≈ 60 years.
A conservative pollutant that enters Vättern today can stay for decades. A small forest pond may be replaced in days.


The ratio of volume to flow gives a timescale: how long the outflow would take to replace the lake’s water. For Vättern, with its large volume and modest outflow through Motala ström, the answer is around 60 years. These are rounded values; the exact figure depends on the source. The message is that big, slowly flushed lakes have long memories. That is why persistent pollutants are a special concern there. Be careful with the interpretation: tau is a replacement scale for the water. It is not the age of every water molecule, and it is not the chemical lifetime of a solute that also reacts or sorbs.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Flushing and reaction act together

Clean water flushes a well-mixed lake: a conservative solute falls as C = C_0e^{-t/\tau}. After one τ about 37% remains, not zero. A solute that also reacts with rate constant k disappears faster: the two loss rates add, 1/τ + k.

Under the well-mixed model, flushing an initially contaminated lake with clean water gives an exponential decline. After one replacement time, about 37 percent is left, because new clean water mixes with the old water rather than pushing it out like a piston. If the solute also reacts with a first-order rate constant, the losses add: the total rate constant is one over tau plus k. In the plot k equals one over tau, so the reactive solute falls twice as fast. Here is the important consequence: if you only see the concentration fall, you cannot know how much was flushing and how much was reaction without knowing tau.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
section: Back to the Tisza: a pulse moving downstream
text:
Back to the Tisza: a pulse moving downstream

A constructed 100 kg pulse of a conservative tracer. As tributaries join, flow rises and the pulse spreads out. The peak falls about 50-fold, yet the area under each curve times Q gives 100 kg at every station.

Now return to the opening case with a model. This is not the measured Tisza plume. It is a constructed pulse that cannot react at all. Each curve is what a sampler at one station would see as the pulse passes. The peak concentration collapses downstream for two physical reasons: more water joins the river, and the pulse is stretched along the channel. But if you multiply flow by concentration and add up over the whole passage, you recover the same 100 kilograms each time. This is the test that separates dilution from destruction. For the real cyanide plume, some cyanide was also lost by reaction and volatilisation, but much of the drop was dilution.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
section: Closing the balance in the field

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“The concentration fell, so the pollutant was destroyed.” Check dilution and transfer first.
“Average the concentrations.” Add amounts or loads; then divide by total volume or flow.
“Steady state means no input.” It means input and output balance.
“τ = V/Q is how long every molecule stays.” It is a replacement scale for the water, not a chemical lifetime.
“Removed from the water” = “gone.” Name the boundary; sorption may be internal transfer.
“mg/L nitrate equals mg/L N.” State the basis; they differ by a factor of about 4.4.


These are the errors that appear most often in exercises and in real environmental reports. Ask students to explain in their own words why each statement is wrong. The first is the central lesson of the lecture. The second is an arithmetic error that only works when the volumes are equal. The third and fourth concern the meaning of words: steady state and residence time sound like they describe processes stopping or molecules waiting, but they describe balances. The fifth is about boundaries. The last is about units, and it causes real confusion when comparing data sets from different countries or laboratories.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
section: Explore: a lake approaching steady state
text:
Explore: a lake approaching steady state


The constructed lake: V/Q = 100 days; 1.0 kg/day gives a steady 100 kg (0.10 mg/L).



Change the input, the flow and the reaction, and watch the lake’s balance respond.

Start with the worked example from the steady-state slide and read the balance table: at steady state input and outflow are both 1 kilogram per day and the change is zero. Ask students to predict before each click. Double the input: the steady level doubles, the time constant does not change. Double the flow instead: the steady level halves and the lake gets there twice as fast. Raise the volume: the steady concentration stays at input over flow, only the approach is slower. Then use the two flushing presets to connect to the flushing slide: about 37 percent left after one time constant, and the reaction adds to the flushing loss. The exercise page has the hand check and the model assumptions.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Amount
concentration × volume; state the basis (mg N or mg NO₃⁻)


Load
flow × concentration; 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³


Boundary
decides whether a process is an output or an internal transfer


Balance
change in M per time = I − O + P − R; same units in every term


Steady state
accumulation zero; fluxes still run


Mixing
add amounts or loads, then divide; points off the mixing line need explaining


Timescale
τ = V/Q; about 37% of a conservative solute left after one τ


Losses add
flushing (1/τ) and reaction (k) combine


Opening case
falling concentration downstream: mostly dilution unless the load also falls



Next: reactions in the atmosphere. The air is a compartment too, and there light drives the reactions. Then the exercises and notes.

 Antarctic ozone hole, 22 September 2012. Image: NASA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


The summary table is the revision sheet. Recite the chain once. Convert concentrations to amounts or loads. Draw a boundary. Write the balance with consistent units. Ask whether a change is dilution, transfer or transformation, and what measurement would tell them apart. Then return to the opening: the falling cyanide concentration along the Tisza and Danube was largely dilution, so the load, not the concentration, is the quantity to follow. The image is the teaser for the next lecture. In the atmosphere we apply the same balance thinking, but now sunlight drives chemical production and loss, and ozone is both made and destroyed.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
1. Close the annual budget
Calculate residual acidity and reference-adjusted alkalinity export for the base case. Report annual equivalents and meq/L.






Hint





Work in annual equivalents before converting to a flow-weighted concentration.









Worked solution





Residual acidity = 10000 eq/year, or 0.0200 meq/L. Alkalinity export = 50000 − 10000 = 40000 eq/year, or 0.0800 meq/L. No pH follows without additional constraints.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
2. Change water export
Double water export to 1.00 × 10⁹ L/year, holding acid and neutralisation amounts fixed only for this sensitivity exercise. Find residual acid-equivalent concentration. Is it reasonable to assume all real catchment processes stay unchanged?






Hint





Divide the same annual residual by the new annual volume.









Worked solution





Residual concentration is 0.0100 meq/L. In a real catchment, higher water flow could change weathering contact, retention, and transport. The fixed-flux sensitivity is an explicit mathematical assumption, not a universal hydrological response.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
3. Interpret sediment indicators
Use the supplied oxygen, Fe, and phosphate-P comparison. State a balanced iron reduction half-reaction, explain possible P release, and name an alternative explanation.






Hint





The iron-bearing carrier changes; phosphate need not undergo redox.









Worked solution





FeOOH + 3 H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2 H₂O. Reduction/dissolution can release sorbed phosphate. Mixing with a separate Fe/P-rich porewater source, desorption changes, or other minerals could contribute. Measure Fe(II), porewater gradients, and phase inventories to distinguish them.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
4. A reproducible chemical argument
Write a short report using activity C and the catchment/sediment evidence. Include one reaction, one hand-checked balance, one model figure, and an explanation of what is still uncertain.






Hint





Use the downloadable activity C report; distinguish invented observations from model outputs.









Worked solution





A sound response reports the base-case 0.0200 meq/L acid residual, distinguishes annual export from closed-water pH, explains a plausible Fe–P mechanism without claiming proof, and labels the contaminant plot as a separate first-order model. It states fixed boundaries and proposes a discriminating measurement rather than treating model curves as field measurements.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
Assemble the short report
Use the activity C report template and its supporting files. Keep the compound model and catchment/sediment arguments in clearly identified sections. Include the completed prediction, hand calculation, model checks, figure interpretation, catchment equivalent budget, and a redox hypothesis with a discriminating observation. A classmate should be able to render the report from the saved files and understand which numbers are inputs, predictions, or constructed observations.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises
text:
Explore: the annual catchment budget
Predict how less accessible neutralisation differs from more annual water export. Close the annual acid-equivalent balance before interpreting a concentration or trying to explain a pH observation.


Reference catchment: 40000 eq/year acid input minus 30000 eq/year neutralised leaves 10000 eq/year residual acid.



E1. Choose Worked catchment. Show that annual acid actually neutralised plus residual acid equals acid input. Calculate the reference-adjusted alkalinity.
E2. Compare Less neutralisation with Double water export. Identify which annual amounts change and which concentration changes are dilution alone.
E3. Choose Capacity exceeds input, then Exceed reference alkalinity. Explain why unused capacity is not automatically credited as extra alkalinity, and why a negative alkalinity balance is not a negative solute concentration.

Model conditions and hand check








Quantity
Worked catchment
Less neutralisation




Acid input
40000 eq/year
40000 eq/year

30000 eq/year
20000 eq/year

10000 eq/year

40000 eq/year

The explicit reference alkalinity export is 50000 eq/year. In the worked case, residual acid is 0.0200 meq/L. Accessible neutralisation capacity caps how much added acid can react; unused capacity is not an additional source in this reference comparison. Other annual terms stay fixed when one slider changes. This is an annual flow-weighted budget, not a dynamic lake or a closed-water pulse. Predicting pH also requires carbon, gas exchange, and acid–base constraints.
More guided comparisons for week 5.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text: Which linked chemical explanation survives the available balances, and which parts remain hypotheses?

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Learning goals

Combine deposition, neutralisation, and water export in one equivalent budget.
Use several indicators to assess a coupled sediment-redox explanation.
Write a reproducible chemical explanation that separates model predictions from observations.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
The annual catchment budget
Reuse the constructed catchment: area \(1.00\times10^6\) m², annual water export \(5.00\times10^8\) L, and acid-equivalent input 40000 eq/year. A stipulated mineral/soil neutralisation term consumes 30000 eq/year. With no other acid terms in this teaching budget, residual export is 10000 eq/year or 0.0200 meq/L. Do not silently add unmeasured retention or biological terms to force agreement.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: An alkalinity comparison needs a reference
text:
An alkalinity comparison needs a reference
For an explicit comparison, suppose reference annual alkalinity export is 50000 eq/year under the same water export, and the added residual acidity decreases it by 10000 eq/year. Alkalinity then changes from 0.100 to 0.0800 meq/L. This does not fix pH: dissolved inorganic carbon, gas exchange, and other acid–base systems are still needed. An annual flow-weighted export is not the same boundary condition as the closed-water acid pulse in the carbonate unit.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
A separate sediment observation set
A second constructed comparison samples water immediately above sediment before and during oxygen depletion. O₂ changes from 8.0 to 0.20 mg/L; filtered Fe from 0.020 to 1.00 mg/L; filtered phosphate-P from 0.010 to 0.200 mg P/L. These are invented observations, not outputs of a fitted reaction model. They are consistent with reduction of an iron carrier phase and associated phosphate release, but do not identify that mechanism uniquely.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Keep forms and units aligned
Phosphate-P is reported as elemental phosphorus mass, not phosphate-ion mass. Filtered Fe is not automatically free Fe²⁺. Annual acidity is an equivalent flux; pH is a present activity measure. Before combining evidence, state whether measurements refer to matching water masses, times, and operational fractions. A neat numerical correlation can be chemically meaningless if quantities or boundaries differ.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Build an explanation with a test
text:
Build an explanation with a test
An explanation should give the proposed reaction chain, a supporting balance or calculation, a prediction, and a measurement that could distinguish alternatives. For the catchment, compare neutralisation, alkalinity export, major ions, and flow. For sediment, test Fe(II), mineral phases, porewater gradients, and solute fluxes. Alternative sources and mixing belong in the interpretation when the available observations cannot rule them out.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Worked example
If neutralisation were only 20000 instead of 30000 eq/year, the residual input would be 20000 eq/year = 0.0400 meq/L at the stated export. Under the same 50000 eq/year reference alkalinity, export would be 30000 eq/year = 0.0600 meq/L. This is a sensitivity calculation: it shows which term controls the budget. It does not establish which catchment process changed or predict a unique pH.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Specify the species
A dissolved metal may be a hydrated ion, a hydrolysis product, a ligand complex, or an operationally included small colloid. A species balance sums forms of the same element. Complexation changes coordination and can change charge; it does not require electron transfer. Fe(II) to Fe(III), in contrast, changes oxidation state. Use oxidation state and species identity separately.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
A transparent binding model
Take one complex, \(\mathrm{M+L\rightleftharpoons ML}\), and use the concentration-based teaching constant \(\beta=[ML]/([M][L])\). With ligand in sufficiently large excess, prescribe free \([L]\) and write \[M_T=[M]+[ML]=[M](1+\beta[L]).\] Then \([M]=M_T/(1+\beta[L])\). If binding appreciably depletes ligand, a second balance \(L_T=[L]+[ML]\) is needed. Substituting total ligand for free ligand without checking this approximation can overestimate binding.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
pH changes coordination
Water ligands can lose protons, schematically \(\mathrm{M^{2+}+H_2O\rightleftharpoons MOH^++H^+}\). Rising pH often favours hydrolysis; it can also deprotonate organic ligands, changing their binding capacity. The competing trends depend on the specific metal and ligand. An acidic shift can release metal from a surface or ligand without requiring oxidation of the metal.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Test mineral saturation with free ions
text:
Test mineral saturation with free ions
For the fictitious hydroxide \(\mathrm{M(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons M^{2+}+2OH^-}\), saturation requires \([M^{2+}][OH^-]^2=K_{sp}\) in the dilute approximation. The free-ion saturation concentration is \(K_{sp}/[OH^-]^2\). Complexation can increase the dissolved total compatible with this free-ion limit. If the solution is supersaturated, a reaction may be favoured, but the rate and final state still require kinetics and balances.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Mobility and exposure are separate questions
text:
Mobility and exposure are separate questions
Strong dissolved binding can reduce free-ion concentration while allowing metal to travel with mobile water or colloids. Conversely, binding to immobile solids can retain metal locally. Biological exposure depends on metal form, competition, uptake mechanism, and reaction rates. A simple free-ion calculation is a chemical comparison, not a universal toxicity or risk model.



Model free-metal fraction at prescribed free-ligand concentrations.

section: Activity C: a fate model in R
text:
Activity C: a fate model in R
Download compounds.csv, fate.R, and fate-report.Rmd into one folder. Read the input dictionary. Reuse readr, dplyr, ggplot2, and the R Markdown workflow. The new mathematical operation is exp(), the inverse of the natural logarithm.
The script creates a regular daily table for the two cases and evaluates:
remaining_fraction = exp(-k_per_day * time_days)
total_parent_mg = initial_parent_mg * remaining_fraction
water_mg_l = total_parent_mg / (water_volume_l + kd_l_kg * dry_solid_kg)
These lines are expressions used inside mutate() in the supplied script. The starting mass is already distributed between phases at time zero. The coefficient k applies equally to parent in water and solids; this assumption is what lets total parent follow one exponential.

Predict which compound has more parent in water initially. Calculate U’s day-20 state by hand before running the code.
Run source("fate.R"), inspect fate, and print fate_plot.

Explain why a smaller water concentration does not automatically mean a shorter half-life, less total parent, or lower biological risk.
Complete the report, restart R, and Knit it from saved inputs. Use its final section to make the separate catchment and sediment arguments in the integrated case.







Expected model results





At day zero, U has 0.500 mg/L water parent and V has 0.9091 mg/L, because their Kd values differ. At day 20, U has 0.250 mg total parent, split equally between phases, giving 0.125 mg/L water concentration. At day 30, U has 0.125 mg total and 0.0625 mg/L water concentration; V has 0.500 mg total and 0.4545 mg/L water concentration.
The two parent phase inventories sum to the declining total. Total parent plus the transformed-parent accounting term equals the initial mass. The latter term records loss of parent identity, not a measured product mass or proof of mineralisation. These are model predictions under supplied constants, not a fit, a statistical comparison, or field evidence.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Learning goals

Relate ionisation and neutral partitioning to the stated environmental conditions.
Combine a two-phase balance with a supplied first-order parent-loss model.
Distinguish partitioning, persistence, exposure, and biological effect.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Structure affects phase preference
Nonpolar regions, hydrogen-bonding groups, size, and charge influence interactions with water and organic phases. The octanol–water coefficient \(K_{ow}\) compares concentrations of a specified form at equilibrium in two phases; log Kow is its base-ten logarithm. It is not a half-life or a toxicity measurement. Hydrophobic neutral compounds may associate strongly with organic matter, but uptake, metabolism, and environment still affect exposure.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Ionisation changes the problem
For a monoprotic organic acid HA, the neutral fraction is \[f_{HA}=\frac{1}{1+10^{\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}}.\] Rising pH shifts it toward A⁻. The neutral form and ion can have different sorption and uptake behaviour; a coefficient measured for neutral molecules may not describe the combined pool. Charged compounds can also bind strongly through ion exchange or specific interactions, so “ionised means no sorption” is not a valid general rule.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Use organic-carbon normalisation cautiously
For a suitable neutral organic solute in an organic-carbon-dominated sorption regime, use the approximation \(K_d=f_{oc}K_{oc}\), with organic-carbon fraction \(f_{oc}\) in kg organic C per kg dry solid and \(K_{oc}\) in L/kg organic C. This is a conditional approximation, not a rule for all ions, minerals, soot, or concentrations. Combining it with a water–solid mass balance predicts distribution only within those conditions.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
A first-order parent-loss model
With constant \(k\) and no new parent input, \[M(t)=M_0e^{-kt},\qquad k=\ln2/t_{1/2}.\] Mass here tracks the parent compound. Products may remain and need not be harmless or fully mineralised. A measured water decline could also result from sorption, volatilisation, or export; it does not establish this transformation model without supporting evidence. Rate coefficients depend on conditions and the process represented.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
State the coupled teaching model
In activity C, a closed water–solid system equilibrates rapidly at fixed Kd. Parent transformation acts with the same specified first-order coefficient in both phases, so the total parent mass follows one exponential. Then \(C_w(t)=M(t)/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). There is no volatilisation, inflow, or outflow. If only dissolved parent degraded or exchange were slow, this model would need a different kinetic balance.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Worked example
For fictitious neutral compound U, take \(M_0=1.00\) mg, \(V_w=1.00\) L, \(m_s=0.0100\) kg, \(K_d=100\) L/kg, and half-life 10.0 days. Initially half the parent is in water and \(C_w=0.500\) mg/L. After 20.0 days the total parent is 0.250 mg; water and solid each contain 0.125 mg, so \(C_w=\mathbf{0.125}\) mg/L. The missing 0.750 mg parent has transformed under this stipulated model. It has not simply moved to the sorbed parent pool.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
About this lecture


Every summer, cyanobacteria blooms swirl across the Baltic Sea. Below them, the deep water of the central Baltic holds one of the largest areas of oxygen-free bottom water made by human activity anywhere in the world.
Cutting nutrient inputs from land has helped, but slowly. One reason: the sea floor itself releases phosphate when oxygen disappears.
Today you will learn to:

balance redox reactions by counting electrons;
use the sequence of electron acceptors as a guide, not a timetable;
explain how iron reduction releases phosphate without any phosphorus redox.

Last lecture: phosphate binds to iron oxides. Today: what happens when those oxides dissolve.

 Phytoplankton bloom swirling in the Baltic Sea, July 2025, seen by a Landsat satellite. Image: NASA Earth Observatory (Michala Garrison), public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


Open with the satellite image. The swirls are cyanobacteria, which bloom in late summer in the Baltic Proper and Gulf of Finland. Their growth depends strongly on phosphate, because many of them can fix nitrogen gas. Under the bloom is a less visible problem: large areas of deep water with little or no oxygen. Since the 1980s the riparian countries have reduced nutrient loads, especially phosphorus from wastewater. Yet the sea has responded slowly. A large part of the explanation is chemistry at the sediment surface, where iron, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon are linked by electron transfer. The last lecture showed phosphate binding to iron oxides. Today we see what happens to that binding when the iron is reduced.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Why the deep Baltic runs out of oxygen
text:
Why the deep Baltic runs out of oxygen

Fresh river water floats on top of salty water from the North Sea. A halocline separates them and blocks mixing. Organic matter sinks through it and decays, using oxygen that cannot be replaced from the air. Salty inflows that refresh the deep water are rare.

Explain the physics first, because it sets up the chemistry. The Baltic is brackish: rivers supply fresh water at the surface, and denser salt water enters only through the narrow Danish straits. The density difference creates a sharp salinity jump, the halocline, at a depth of very roughly 60 to 80 metres in the central Baltic. Wind mixes the surface layer, but not across the halocline. Below it, oxygen is consumed by bacteria decomposing sinking algae and is only replaced when a large inflow of salty, oxygen-rich North Sea water pushes into the deep basins. Such major inflows happen irregularly, sometimes with gaps of a decade. Between them, the deep water gradually loses its oxygen.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: What happens when the oxygen is gone?
text:
What happens when the oxygen is gone?

In a cut-off bottom water, chemistry changes in a typical order: first oxygen falls, then nitrate, then dissolved iron and phosphate rise, and finally hydrogen sulfide appears. Nobody added phosphate. Why this order, and where does the phosphate come from?

This figure is constructed, with relative units, to show the typical order rather than real data from a particular station. Read it left to right. Oxygen declines first. Once it is low, nitrate declines. Then dissolved iron(II) and phosphate rise together. Later, hydrogen sulfide appears, and dissolved iron falls again. Ask students to note two puzzles. First, why does each substance wait for the one before it? Second, phosphate has no reason to change oxidation state, so why does it rise at the same time as iron? The rest of the lecture answers both. Remind them that real basins overlap these stages, because of mixing and patchy sediments.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Redox is electron bookkeeping

Every redox reaction pairs an electron donor, which is oxidised, with an electron acceptor, which is reduced. Electrons lost = electrons gained. CH₂O is a bookkeeping formula for organic matter, with carbon at oxidation state 0.

Start with the familiar reaction, aerobic respiration, split into two half-reactions. In the first, organic carbon goes from oxidation state zero to plus four in carbon dioxide and releases four electrons. In the second, oxygen accepts those four electrons, each oxygen atom going from zero to minus two. When the half-reactions are added, the electrons cancel. This is the rule for every redox reaction: the donor’s loss equals the acceptor’s gain. CH2O is not a real molecule in sediments. It is a convenient formula with the average oxidation state of carbon in carbohydrates. Microbes carry out these reactions to gain energy; chemistry tells us which are possible and in what proportions, not how fast they go.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Oxidation states you will need





Element
Species

C
CH₂O / CO₂ / CH₄

NH₄⁺ / N₂ / NO₃⁻
−III / 0 / +V


Fe

+II / +III

+V (stays)

Rules: H is +I, O is −II (except in O₂), and the states add up to the charge of the species.
Example, nitrate: N + 3(−II) = −1, so N = +V.
Each change of one unit is one electron per atom.
Notice phosphorus. In natural waters it stays at +V. If phosphate moves during a redox change, something else was reduced.


This is a refresher slide, to be used as a reference during the rest of the lecture. Work one example aloud, nitrate: three oxygens at minus two give minus six, the ion has charge minus one, so nitrogen must be plus five. Ask students to do sulfate themselves. The table already holds the key to the second puzzle from the time series. Phosphorus stays at plus five in phosphate. Phosphate rose when oxygen disappeared, but phosphorus itself was not reduced. So the phosphate must have been released from something that was. That something is iron, as we will see. Keep the table visible when balancing reactions later.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: When oxygen runs out: the redox ladder
text:
When oxygen runs out: the redox ladder

Microbes use the acceptor that gives the most energy first. As it runs low, the next one takes over. That explains the order in the bottom-water series. It is a guide, not a timetable: steps overlap in space and time.

This is the central concept of the lecture. Organic matter is the common electron donor. Several acceptors can take its electrons, and they yield different amounts of energy to the microbes. Oxygen gives the most, then nitrate, then manganese and iron oxides, then sulfate, and finally carbon dioxide itself in methanogenesis. Microbes that use a higher-energy acceptor tend to outcompete the others while it lasts. Each step also leaves evidence: what disappears and what appears. Stress the caveat in the notes. The thresholds depend on pH, on which minerals are present, and on local conditions. Different processes run side by side in neighbouring microsites. Use the ladder to make predictions, then check them with measurements.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
The ladder in the mud




In a sediment, the ladder is laid out in depth. Oxygen often disappears within millimetres. Below it, nitrate, then dissolved manganese and iron, then sulfide and methane.
The steps overlap and their depths change with season and with how much organic matter arrives.
When the bottom water itself loses its oxygen, the upper rungs vanish and iron reduction reaches the sediment surface.


The time series showed the ladder in time; a sediment shows it in space. These profiles are constructed, but the order is typical of lake and coastal sediments. Oxygen diffusing from the water is consumed so fast that it often penetrates only a few millimetres. Nitrate is consumed just below. Manganese and iron(II) appear deeper, where their oxides are being reduced, and sulfide and methane deeper still. Peaks occur because dissolved products diffuse up and are re-oxidised where the acceptor above is still present. The crucial point for the Baltic: as long as the bottom water has oxygen, a thin layer of iron(III) oxide stays at the sediment surface. When oxygen vanishes, the iron-reduction zone moves up to the surface.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: You can see the ladder in a jar
text:
You can see the ladder in a jar


 Upper part of a Winogradsky column: purple sulfur bacteria in bands above dark, sulfide-rich mud. Photo: kOchstudiO, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

A Winogradsky column is a sealed tube of pond mud with a little added carbon and sulfate, left in the light for weeks.
Oxygen enters only at the top, so microbes sort themselves into layers:

the top stays oxic;
in the middle, coloured bands of bacteria live on sulfide rising from below;
the bottom turns black with iron sulfide formed by sulfate reduction.

The same zones exist in every sediment, compressed into a few centimetres.


This classroom experiment is a good way to make the ladder visible. Students can set it up in a lab session. Mud, a source of organic carbon such as shredded paper, and a sulfate source such as gypsum or egg yolk are packed into a tube and left near a window. Over weeks, oxygen is used up everywhere except near the top. Sulfate reducers at the bottom produce sulfide, which reacts with iron to form black iron sulfide. Purple and green sulfur bacteria grow in bands where light and sulfide meet. The exact colours vary from column to column, which is itself a lesson: the sequence is robust, the details are local.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Nitrogen: one element, many oxidation states
text:
Nitrogen: one element, many oxidation states

\mathrm{NH_4^++2O_2\rightarrow NO_3^-+2H^++H_2O}
Nitrification uses oxygen and releases acid. For 0.100 mmol/L NH₄⁺: 0.200 mmol/L O₂ (6.40 mg/L) and 0.200 mmol/L H⁺, so alkalinity falls by 0.200 meq/L. Nitrogen changes form but stays in the water.

Nitrogen spans eight units of oxidation state, from minus three in ammonium to plus five in nitrate. Nitrification, carried out by bacteria and archaea, oxidises ammonium to nitrate with oxygen. Check the balance with the class: eight electrons lost per nitrogen, and two O2 molecules accept eight electrons. The calculation is exercise 1. Two moles of oxygen per mole of ammonium is a large oxygen demand, about six and a half milligrams per litre for a modest ammonium concentration. The two protons consume alkalinity, as in the carbonate lecture. Most importantly, nitrification does not remove nitrogen from the water. Only the reverse direction, down the ladder to nitrogen gas, does that.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Balancing denitrification


\mathrm{4NO_3^-+5CH_2O+4H^+\rightarrow2N_2+5CO_2+7H_2O}

N: +V → 0, gains 5 e⁻ each; 4 NO₃⁻ accept 20 e⁻.
C: 0 → +IV, loses 4 e⁻ each; 5 CH₂O donate 20 e⁻.
Atoms: 4 N, 5 C, 14 H, 17 O on each side. Charge: 0 = 0.

Donor ratio: 1.25 mol C per mol nitrate. For 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate: 0.100 mmol/L C (1.20 mg C/L) and 0.0400 mmol/L N₂.




Balance by electrons first, then atoms, then charge. Each nitrogen falls from plus five to zero and gains five electrons. Each carbon rises from zero to plus four and loses four. The smallest whole numbers that make the electrons match are four nitrates and five CH2O, twenty electrons each way, which the bar chart shows. Then fill in protons and water to balance hydrogen and oxygen, and check the charge: minus four plus four on the left, zero on the right. The ratio of 1.25 carbon per nitrate is exercise 2. This net reaction ignores growth of new biomass and intermediates such as nitrite. Denitrification needs low oxygen, nitrate and an electron donor. It is how sediments, wetlands and treatment plants remove nitrogen as gas.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Check yourself

Use oxidation states and electron counting.

What is the oxidation state of S in SO₄²⁻, and of Fe in FeOOH?
How many electrons does one Fe(III) gain when FeOOH becomes Fe²⁺? How many does one sulfate gain when it becomes HS⁻?
Oxidise 0.050 mmol/L NH₄⁺ fully to nitrate. How much O₂ is used?
True or false: “Phosphate rose in anoxic bottom water, so phosphorus was reduced.”



Answers. One: sulfur is plus six, because four oxygens give minus eight and the ion is minus two. Iron in FeOOH is plus three. Two: one electron for iron, from plus three to plus two. Eight for sulfur, from plus six to minus two. That is why sulfate reduction needs much more organic matter per sulfur than iron reduction does per iron. Three: two oxygen per ammonium, so 0.100 millimoles per litre, or 3.2 milligrams per litre. Four is false. Phosphorus stays at plus five. Its release must come from a change in something it was attached to. The next slides show what.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Iron: a solid that dissolves when reduced
text:
Iron: a solid that dissolves when reduced


 Iron-rich mine water emerging from underground coats a slope with orange iron(III) oxide, Great Allegheny Passage, Pennsylvania. Photo: daveynin, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

\mathrm{FeOOH(s)+3H^++e^-\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2H_2O}
Check: 1 Fe, 2 O, 4 H on each side; charge +2 = +2. Fe(III) gains one electron.
Fe(III) oxides are almost insoluble at natural pH. Fe²⁺ is soluble. So reduction turns a solid into a solute.
The reverse happens wherever Fe²⁺-rich water meets air: orange Fe(III) oxide precipitates.


This is exercise 3. Verify the half-reaction with the class: iron, oxygen and hydrogen balance, and the charges are plus three minus one on the left and plus two on the right. What makes iron special in environmental chemistry is the solubility contrast between its two oxidation states. Iron(III) forms oxyhydroxides that are practically insoluble at the pH of most natural waters, as we saw in the metals and surfaces lectures. Iron(II) stays dissolved. So reducing iron dissolves the solid. The photo shows the opposite direction: groundwater rich in dissolved iron(II) reaches the surface, meets oxygen, and the iron is oxidised and precipitates as orange oxide. The same switch runs at the sea floor.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Phosphate rides on iron

With oxygen, a thin Fe(III) oxide layer at the sediment surface sorbs phosphate moving up from decaying matter. Without oxygen, the iron is reduced, the layer dissolves, and Fe²⁺ and phosphate both escape. Phosphorus stays +V: its carrier changed oxidation state.

This is the answer to the second puzzle. In the surfaces lecture we saw that iron oxides hold phosphate strongly by inner-sphere binding. While the bottom water has oxygen, the iron(III) layer at the sediment surface acts as a lid: phosphate released by decomposition deeper in the sediment is caught as it diffuses up. When the bottom water becomes anoxic, iron reduction reaches the surface, the oxide dissolves, and the phosphate held on it is released along with iron(II). Phosphorus never changes its oxidation state. This is why Fe and phosphate rise together in the time series. The release from sediments is called internal loading, as opposed to the external load from rivers and wastewater.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Sulfur: the bottom of the ladder
text:
Sulfur: the bottom of the ladder

With oxygen, nitrate and iron oxides used up, microbes reduce sulfate, abundant in seawater. Toxic H₂S builds up in the deepest Baltic basins. Sulfide also binds iron as black FeS, so when oxygen returns, less iron is free to recapture phosphate.

Seawater, even the brackish Baltic, contains much sulfate, so once the higher acceptors are exhausted, sulfate reduction becomes a major pathway. Check the half-reaction: sulfur goes from plus six to minus two, eight electrons. Hydrogen sulfide is toxic to animals, and in the deep basins of the central Baltic it has accumulated at times to form true dead zones. Sulfide also reacts with iron(II) to form insoluble iron sulfides, which make anoxic mud black. That has a long-lasting effect. Iron locked up as sulfide is no longer available to form a new oxide layer when oxygen returns, so the sediment’s ability to trap phosphate is weakened. Reoxygenation does not simply reverse anoxia.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Reading redox evidence


Observation: dissolved Fe and phosphate rise while O₂ declines above a sediment.
Coupled explanation: organic matter uses up O₂, then Fe(III) oxides are reduced, releasing Fe²⁺ and the phosphate they held.
Why correlation is not proof: mixing with another water mass, other minerals dissolving, or a new phosphate source could give the same pattern.
Tests: Fe(II) measured directly, solid-phase iron and phosphorus in the sediment, porewater profiles, and fluxes over time.




This is exercise 4, and the skill is reasoning from evidence. The coupled explanation is the one we built today, and it is often right. But a good scientist asks what else could produce the same pattern. A different, phosphate-rich water mass could have mixed in. Calcium phosphate minerals could dissolve. Fresh organic matter could release phosphate as it decomposes. To test the iron explanation, measure iron(II) itself, look for loss of iron(III) and of iron-bound phosphorus in the surface sediment, and use porewater profiles like this one to calculate fluxes across the sediment surface. A single electrode reading of redox potential is rarely enough to identify which processes are active in a natural sample.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Back to the Baltic: a self-reinforcing loop
text:
Back to the Baltic: a self-reinforcing loop

More phosphate feeds more blooms, more sinking organic matter, more oxygen loss, and more phosphate release. That is why internal loading can keep the Baltic eutrophic long after external loads are cut.

Now put the pieces together into the loop that is often called the Baltic’s vicious circle. Phosphate in the surface water feeds blooms, especially of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, which need phosphorus but can take nitrogen from the air. The blooms sink and decompose below the halocline, using oxygen. Anoxic sediments release iron-bound phosphate. Some of that phosphate is mixed back up to the surface and fuels the next bloom. Each step is chemistry we have covered this week: speciation, surfaces, redox. The external load from land and wastewater sets the overall level, and reducing it is the only lasting solution, but the internal loop explains the long delay in the sea’s response.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Can the loop be broken?


Inflows of oxygen-rich North Sea water, like the large one in December 2014, can ventilate the deep basins for a while. Iron oxide re-forms and traps some phosphate. But the effect fades, and sulfide-bound iron is not fully restored.
Cutting external loads is the lasting solution. Since the 1980s, better wastewater treatment around the Baltic has removed much of the phosphorus that rivers and cities once delivered.
How treatment plants do that, and where the phosphorus ends up, is the next lecture.

 Summer bloom around Gotland in the central Baltic Sea, July 2018. Image: Jeff Schmaltz, NASA (MODIS), public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


End the story with the management question. Major inflows are natural events. When salty, oxygen-rich water reaches the deep basins, the upper rungs of the ladder return, iron is re-oxidised and some phosphate is trapped again. Studies after the 2014 inflow showed that the improvement was partial and temporary. The deep water lost its oxygen again within a few years in many areas, and iron tied up as sulfide could not all return to the cycle. The more reliable lever is the external load. Phosphorus removal at wastewater treatment plants has been one of the main measures. The satellite image shows the scale of the problem: blooms covering much of the central Baltic around Gotland in a single summer.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Phosphate was released, so phosphorus was reduced.” P stays +V; its iron carrier was reduced.
“Nitrification removes nitrogen.” It changes NH₄⁺ to NO₃⁻; only denitrification sends N to the air.
“The redox ladder is a fixed timetable.” It is a guide; steps overlap.
“Balance atoms and you are done.” Check electrons and charge too.
“One redox-potential reading identifies the process.” Use several indicators.
“Adding oxygen reverses everything.” Sulfide-bound iron and slow reactions leave a legacy.


These are the errors that appear most often in this unit. The first two are conceptual and come up every year in exams. Ask students to explain each in their own words with an example from the Baltic. The third and fifth are about evidence: the ladder makes predictions, but measurements decide. The fourth is procedural: a reaction can have balanced atoms and still violate the electron or charge balance, which signals an error. The last links to management. Reoxygenation helps, but it does not instantly restore the earlier state, because some changes, such as iron sulfide formation and burial, are slow to reverse.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Explore: the electron-acceptor ladder


Reference case: 0.500 mmol C/L decomposed uses up O₂, nitrate and the Fe(III) oxide, releasing 0.020 mmol/L phosphate.



Decompose more organic matter: which acceptor goes next, and when does phosphate appear?

Start with Oxygen still present and drag the organic matter slider slowly to the right. Ask students to call out which acceptor will be used next before it happens. The slope of each line comes from electron counting: oxygen takes four electrons, nitrate five, iron one, sulfate eight, while each carbon gives four. That is why the iron oxide disappears so quickly and sulfate lasts so long. Point out that phosphate is released only when the iron step starts, although phosphorus is never reduced. The Denitrification preset reproduces the 1.25 carbon per nitrate result. Low-sulfate lake water shows methane forming once sulfate is gone. Stress that the model runs the ladder strictly in order, while real sediments overlap the steps.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Redox
donor is oxidised, acceptor is reduced; electrons lost = gained


Balancing
electrons first, then atoms, then charge


Redox ladder
O₂ → NO₃⁻ → Mn(IV) → Fe(III) → SO₄²⁻ → CO₂; a guide, not a timetable


Sediments
the ladder in depth; O₂ often gone within millimetres


Nitrification
NH₄⁺ + 2O₂ → NO₃⁻ + 2H⁺ + H₂O; uses O₂, consumes alkalinity


Denitrification
1.25 mol CH₂O-C per mol NO₃⁻; N leaves as N₂


Iron
FeOOH + 3H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2H₂O; solid becomes solute


Phosphate
released with the iron carrier; P stays +V


Sulfur
SO₄²⁻ → HS⁻ (8 e⁻); FeS locks up iron


Baltic
stratification + blooms + internal loading form a loop



Next: Water pollution and treatment chemistry. How do we take nitrogen and phosphorus out of wastewater, and where do they go? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Surface aerator in the aeration tank of an activated sludge plant. Photo: Marcos von Sperling, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The table is the revision sheet. Recite the chain: organic matter supplies electrons; acceptors are used roughly in order of energy yield; each step leaves evidence. Nitrogen can be converted to nitrate with oxygen, or removed as gas without it. Iron reduction dissolves iron oxides and releases the phosphate they held, which is the key to internal loading in the Baltic. Sulfate reduction produces sulfide, which is toxic and binds iron. The teaser photo shows an aeration tank in a wastewater treatment plant. There, engineers run the same reactions on purpose, switching oxygen on and off to make microbes nitrify and denitrify. That is the next lecture.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
1. Exchange amount
A 0.100 kg soil has CEC 20.0 cmolc/kg. If all sites were occupied by Mg²⁺, how many moles of Mg would occupy them?






Hint





Convert cmol of charge to mol of charge, then divide by two.









Worked solution





Total charge = 20.0 × 0.01 × 0.100 = 0.0200 mol charge. Mg²⁺ amount = 0.0100 mol. This is an idealised capacity state, not an aqueous concentration.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
2. Base saturation
A soil has CEC 12.0 cmolc/kg and base-cation occupation 9.00 cmolc/kg. Calculate base saturation. Does the result specify soil-water pH?






Hint





Divide occupied base charge by total exchange charge.









Worked solution





Base saturation = 75.0%. It does not uniquely set pH; mineralogy, exchange selectivity, solution composition, other acid–base reactions, and the measurement method matter.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
3. A carbonate inventory
A soil contains 0.0100 mol accessible CaCO₃. For a specified complete neutralisation endpoint, take CaCO₃ + 2 H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂* + H₂O. How much acid can this inventory consume?






Hint





Use the two-equivalent coefficient for the stated endpoint.









Worked solution





The stoichiometric inventory is 0.0200 mol H⁺ equivalents. Real protection also depends on dissolution rate, accessibility, gas exchange, and the actual final state.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
4. Compare two soils
Two soils have equal pH but one is rich in organic matter and exchange-active clay while the other is coarse quartz sand. What would you measure before predicting their responses to an acid input?






Hint





Measure inventories and pathways, not only pH.









Worked solution





Compare CEC under stated conditions, base saturation, carbonate and weatherable minerals, organic matter, water flow, and aluminium/iron chemistry. Equal pH is not evidence of equal buffering or solute retention.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
Explore: same pH, different reserves
Predict which soil is first to release aluminium when both receive 5.0 cmolc/kg of acid: Soil A (sandy podzol) or Soil B (clay loam), both at pH about 5. Then change one inventory at a time.


Reference case: Soil B (CEC 20.0, base cations 14.2 cmolc/kg, base saturation 71 %) after 5.0 cmolc/kg of acid keeps 9.2 cmolc/kg of base cations (46 %). Soil A (CEC 3.0, base cations 1.7 cmolc/kg) runs out after 1.7 cmolc/kg, so the remaining 3.3 cmolc/kg is buffered by aluminium.



E1. Choose Soil B, then Soil A. For each, how much acid can be neutralised before aluminium takes over? Check the base saturation after 5.0 cmolc/kg of acid by hand.
E2. Choose Exercise 2 and confirm your base saturation. Then raise CEC while keeping the base cations fixed. Which changes: base saturation, the reserve, or both?
E3. Choose Soil A, limed. How many cmolc/kg does 2.0 cmol/kg of CaCO₃ add, and why is it twice the number of moles? Which reserve is used first in this model?

Model conditions and hand check
The two soils are the constructed Soil A and Soil B from the lecture. Acid is counted in cmolc/kg and consumed in a fixed order: accessible CaCO₃ first (2 equivalents per mole, CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂* + H₂O), then exchangeable base cations (one equivalent of bases leaves per equivalent of acid), and then aluminium. CEC is held constant; the sites given up by base cations are taken by Al³⁺ and H⁺. Slow weathering, uptake by plants, rates, flow paths and pH are not modelled. For Soil B after 5.0 cmolc/kg: 14.2 − 5.0 = 9.2 cmolc/kg of base cations remain, and base saturation falls from 14.2/20.0 = 71 % to 9.2/20.0 = 46 %. If those 5.0 cmolc/kg left as Ca²⁺, that is 2.5 cmol Ca/kg. Soil A has only 1.7 cmolc/kg, so 3.3 cmolc/kg of the same acid is buffered by aluminium.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text: Why can two soils at the same pH differ in their response to acid or a contaminant input?

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Learning goals

Connect mineral and organic surfaces with exchange and buffering.
Calculate charge-based exchange inventories.
Explain why retention capacity does not determine transport by itself.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Several reacting phases
Soil contains minerals, organic matter, water, gas, and organisms. Water composition reflects contact with those phases and the time available for reaction. Soil pH measures a state under a specified method; it does not inventory exchange sites or neutralising minerals. Texture, mineralogy, organic matter, and flow paths therefore matter even when two pH measurements are equal.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Cation exchange conserves charge
A negatively charged exchange site can hold cations. A schematic exchange is \(\mathrm{2XNa+Ca^{2+}\rightleftharpoons X_2Ca+2Na^+}\), with X denoting one negative site charge. Exchange transfers ions between water and sites without destroying the element. A divalent ion occupies two monovalent charge equivalents. Selectivity depends on the exchanger, ion activities, and competing ions.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Interpret exchange capacity
Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is commonly reported as cmol of charge per kg dry soil, written cmolc/kg. One cmolc is 0.01 mol of charge equivalents. Permanent mineral charge and pH-dependent sites contribute differently, so method and pH matter. Base saturation expresses the fraction of exchange capacity occupied by specified base cations; it does not mean the solution has that same ion ratio.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Acid inputs meet a finite inventory
text:
Acid inputs meet a finite inventory
Protons can displace cations, protonate organic and oxide sites, and dissolve minerals. A carbonate-bearing soil can consume acidity through mineral dissolution. An acid soil lacking carbonate may rely more on exchange, weathering, and aluminium chemistry. Some neutralisation reactions mobilise metals or change nutrient availability. A measured resistance to one short acid pulse does not guarantee indefinite protection under continued inputs.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Retention and preferential flow
A soil with many potential sites may still transmit solute through fast pathways with limited solid contact. Waterlogged microsites can change redox and the stability of iron phases. Colloids may transport sorbed substances, while erosion moves the solids themselves. To explain movement, combine chemical partitioning with water flow, residence time, and particle transport. Avoid using CEC as a universal sorption coefficient for anions or neutral organic compounds.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Worked example
A dry soil has CEC 10.0 cmolc/kg. In 0.200 kg, the exchange charge inventory is \(10.0\times0.01\times0.200=\mathbf{0.0200}\) mol of charge. If half is occupied by Ca²⁺, calcium carries 0.0100 mol charge and corresponds to 0.00500 mol Ca, not 0.0100 mol Ca. This capacity accounting is not a prediction that all that calcium immediately enters porewater.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapters 17–18: reacting soil phases, charge-based exchange, acid inventories, and transport limitations.
FAO soil chemical properties: The meaning of exchange capacity and the role of organic matter.
USDA CEC teaching note: Charge sites in clay and organic matter.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
About this lecture


In August 2015, a clean-up crew at the abandoned Gold King Mine in Colorado accidentally released about 3 million gallons (roughly 11 000 m³) of acidic, metal-rich mine water. The Animas River turned orange for many kilometres. Within days the colour had moved downstream and faded.
The water looked clean again. But where had the metals gone?
Today you will learn to:

explain why mineral surfaces carry pH-dependent charge;
close a water–solid mass balance with Kd;
recognise finite capacity and competition;
ask whether particles retain a contaminant or carry it.

Last lecture: iron and aluminium hydrolyse and precipitate. Today: what their solids do.

 The Animas River between Silverton and Durango, within a day of the Gold King Mine release, August 2015. Photo: Riverhugger, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Open with the image. The Gold King Mine release is one of the best-documented mine-water spills, because it happened during an EPA operation and was monitored intensively. The orange colour is iron(III) oxyhydroxide, the solid that forms when acidic iron-rich water is diluted and its pH rises, exactly the hydrolysis we discussed in the metals lecture. Within days the plume passed and the river looked normal. That is the puzzle for today. Metals do not disappear. If they are no longer in the water, they are somewhere else: on particles, in the river bed, or further downstream. To answer where, we need the chemistry of surfaces.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Removed, or only moved?


After the plume passed, dissolved metal concentrations at Durango fell back towards earlier levels within days to weeks.
Much of the metal load had travelled attached to iron oxyhydroxide particles. Many of those particles settled on the river bed and in reservoirs downstream.
So a water sample can look clean while the system still holds the metal.
Question for this lecture: when a contaminant leaves the water, has it been removed, or has it only moved onto a surface that may move again?

 Water monitoring in the Animas River at Durango, Colorado, 14 August 2015. Photo: Eric Vance, US EPA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


This slide states the main question. Monitoring after the spill showed that concentrations in the water fell quickly as the plume passed, while much of the metal had been carried on particles. Those particles settled along the river and in downstream reservoirs. Later reports discussed whether high spring flows could stir up those deposits again. We do not need the details of the monitoring programme. The chemical lesson is general. Sorption and settling transfer a contaminant from water to solid. The total in the system is unchanged. Whether that is good news depends on whether the solid stays put. Ask students what they would need to measure to tell the difference, and keep their answers for the end of the lecture.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: From dissolved to particulate: a continuum
text:
From dissolved to particulate: a continuum

There is no sharp line between dissolved and particulate. Colloids, about 1 nm to 1 µm across, stay suspended for a long time. A 0.45 µm filter cuts through the colloid range, so “dissolved” includes some colloids and “particulate” includes others.

Show the scale. Ions and small molecules are below a nanometre. Humic molecules, iron oxide nanoparticles and clay platelets fill the colloid range. Bacteria, silt and sand are larger. The filter used to define dissolved sits inside this continuum at 0.45 micrometres. That number is a convention, not a natural boundary. Colloids matter because they are small enough that gravity hardly settles them, but large enough to carry many binding sites. A metal on a colloid can pass a filter and be reported as dissolved, or be retained and reported as particulate, depending on the colloid’s size. This is why a filtered result must always be read together with the method.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Small particles have enormous surfaces

For a sphere, the surface per gram scales as 1/diameter. A gram of 10 nm particles has about 10 000 times the surface of a gram of fine sand. Fresh iron oxyhydroxides are made of such tiny crystals, so a few grams carry hundreds of square metres of reactive surface.

This is geometry, not chemistry. The figure uses smooth spheres of mineral density 2.65 grams per cubic centimetre, so the numbers are idealised. Each factor of ten smaller in diameter gives ten times more surface per gram. Real clays and fresh iron oxyhydroxides have even more surface than spheres of the same size, because they are platy or porous; freshly precipitated ferrihydrite is commonly reported at a few hundred square metres per gram. The point for environmental chemistry: binding happens at surfaces, so the fine fraction of a sediment or soil does most of the binding even when it is a small fraction of the mass. The orange floc in the Animas was exactly this kind of high-surface material.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: Oxide surfaces gain and lose protons
text:
Oxide surfaces gain and lose protons

\mathrm{>SOH+H^+\rightleftharpoons>SOH_2^+}\qquad\mathrm{>SOH\rightleftharpoons>SO^-+H^+}
Here >S means a surface metal atom, such as Fe at the edge of an oxide. At low pH the surface is positive; at high pH it is negative.

At the surface of an oxide, the metal atoms cannot complete their coordination with the solid, so they bind hydroxyl groups from water. These surface hydroxyls are amphoteric: they can take up a proton or give one away, just like the bound water of a hydrolysing metal ion in the last lecture. The notation with the greater-than sign means “attached to the solid surface”. Be clear that S stands for a surface site, not for sulfur. At low pH most groups are protonated and the surface is positive. At high pH most have lost a proton and the surface is negative. In between, the positive and negative groups balance.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Surface charge depends on pH




At one pH the positive and negative sites balance: the point of zero charge. For iron oxides it typically lies roughly between pH 7 and 9.

Below it: positive surface, attracts anions such as phosphate and arsenate.
Above it: negative surface, attracts cations such as Cu²⁺ and Pb²⁺.

Most natural waters sit near or below this pH, so iron oxides are good at holding phosphate.


The curve is a constructed two-constant model with zero charge at pH 8, typical of iron oxides. Read it from left to right. Strongly positive at low pH, zero near 8, negative at high pH. The point of zero charge differs between minerals: silica is negative over almost the whole natural range, while iron and aluminium oxides are positive in many acidic and neutral waters. Use this to predict electrostatic attraction. Phosphate, an anion, is attracted to iron oxides in ordinary waters. Metal cations are attracted more strongly as pH rises. Keep in mind that charge is only part of the story; the next slides add specific bonding.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: Sorption edges: cations and anions behave oppositely
text:
Sorption edges: cations and anions behave oppositely

Metal cations bind more as pH rises; oxyanions bind more as pH falls. Each change happens over one or two pH units, a sorption edge. Acid can therefore release metals from oxides, while rising pH can release phosphate.

These are constructed curves with the typical shapes seen in laboratory experiments with iron oxides. The fraction of a metal cation such as lead that is sorbed rises steeply over a narrow pH range. The fraction of an oxyanion such as phosphate or arsenate falls at high pH. This explains two field observations. First, acidification releases metals from particles, which was one of the mechanisms in the last lecture’s exercise. Second, when the pH of lake water rises during intense photosynthesis, phosphate can be released from sediment particles. Note that the cation edge lies below the zero-charge pH: specific bonding lets cations bind even where the surface is not yet negative.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: Clays: permanent charge and cation exchange
text:
Clays: permanent charge and cation exchange

In clay minerals, some Si⁴⁺ and Al³⁺ in the crystal is replaced by ions of lower charge. The layers keep a negative charge that does not depend on pH. It is balanced by cations such as Ca²⁺, Na⁺ and K⁺, which can be exchanged for others.

Clays add a second kind of surface charge. During formation, some silicon is replaced by aluminium and some aluminium by magnesium in the crystal lattice. Each replacement leaves one unit of negative charge in the layer. That charge is permanent: it does not depend on pH, unlike the oxide surfaces we just saw. Cations sit between the layers and on the outer surfaces to balance it, and they are held mainly electrostatically, so other cations can replace them. The exchange is charge for charge: one calcium replaces two sodium. This cation exchange capacity is central in soil chemistry, which we meet in week 4. It also explains why clay-rich sediments hold metal cations.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
More than charge: inner-sphere binding

Outer-sphere ions keep their water shell and are held by charge alone; they exchange easily. Inner-sphere complexes form a direct bond with surface oxygen, by ligand exchange. They are much stronger and can form even on a surface of the same charge.

Electrostatics is the first approximation. The second is chemistry. An outer-sphere ion, such as sodium, stays fully hydrated and sits near the surface because of opposite charge. Change the ionic strength and it leaves. An inner-sphere complex is a real coordination bond: the sorbing ion replaces a surface hydroxyl or water and bonds directly to the surface metal through oxygen. Phosphate on iron oxide is the classic case, often sharing two surface oxygens. Copper and lead also bind inner-sphere. This is why phosphate binds strongly, why it competes with arsenate for the same sites, and why sorption edges for cations appear below the zero-charge pH. Specific binding is the link between surface chemistry and coordination chemistry.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: A number for sorption: the distribution coefficient
text:
A number for sorption: the distribution coefficient


For low concentrations, sorbed and dissolved amounts are often roughly proportional:
q=K_d\,C_w

q: sorbed per dry solid (mg/kg)
Cw: in water (mg/L)
Kd: distribution coefficient (L/kg)

Kd belongs to one system: this solute, this solid, this water, this pH. It is not a molecular constant.




After the mechanisms we need a number we can calculate with. The distribution coefficient is the simplest one: the ratio of sorbed concentration to dissolved concentration at equilibrium. Check the units carefully: milligrams per kilogram divided by milligrams per litre gives litres per kilogram. A large Kd means the solute strongly prefers the solid. The warning is important. Kd measured for lead on one sediment at pH 7 tells you little about lead on another sediment at pH 5, because the edges we just saw move it by orders of magnitude. Use a Kd only for the conditions it was measured under, and only at low concentrations where the relationship is linear.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Close the two-phase balance


In a closed bottle, all the solute is either in water or on solid:
M_T=C_wV_w+q\,m_s=C_w(V_w+K_dm_s)
C_w=\frac{M_T}{V_w+K_dm_s}
