Both terms in the denominator are in litres. Kdms acts like an extra volume the solute can spread into. The sorbed fraction is Kdms/(Vw + Kdms).




Derive the equation with the class. Total mass equals mass in water plus mass on solid. Substitute the Kd relation for q, factor out the water concentration, and divide. A useful picture: Kd times solid mass has units of litres, so the solid behaves like an extra, invisible volume of water. If that extra volume equals the real water volume, half the solute is sorbed. The curve shows how the water concentration falls as solid is added, for two Kd values. Note that it is not linear: doubling the solid does not halve the concentration. The model assumes equilibrium, a closed bottle, and no degradation or loss to the walls.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
section: Worked example: one bottle, three cases
text:
Worked example: one bottle, three cases


1.00 mg solute, 1.00 L water, 0.0100 kg dry solid, Kd = 100 L/kg.

Kdms = 1.00 L, so Cw = 1.00/2.00 = 0.500 mg/L
water 0.500 mg; solid 0.500 mg; q = 50.0 mg/kg

Double the solid: Cw = 1/3.00 = 0.333 mg/L, solid 0.667 mg.
pH change lowers Kd to 10: Cw = 1/1.10 = 0.909 mg/L. Desorption, with no new solute added.




Work the first case slowly. Kd times solid mass is 100 times 0.01, so one litre. The denominator is two litres, giving half a milligram per litre in water. Multiply back to masses and check that they sum to one milligram. The sorbed concentration is 50 milligrams per kilogram. The other two bars are exercises 1 and 3. Doubling the solid does not halve the water concentration; it reduces it to one third. A tenfold drop in Kd, for example after a pH change, pushes 91 percent of the solute back into the water. The water concentration nearly doubled although nothing was added. That is how a contaminated sediment can become a source.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Check yourself

Use the two-phase balance and the surface-charge picture.

2.00 mg solute, 1.00 L water, 0.0500 kg solid, Kd = 20 L/kg. What is Cw, and what fraction is sorbed?
Is an iron oxide surface at pH 5 more likely to hold phosphate or Cu²⁺ by charge alone?
A sediment is acidified. Predict what happens to sorbed lead.
Why can’t a Kd measured at pH 7 simply be used at pH 5?



Answers. One: Kd times solid mass is one litre, so Cw is 2.00 divided by 2.00, one milligram per litre, and half is sorbed. Two: phosphate. At pH 5 the iron oxide surface is positive, below its zero-charge point, so it attracts anions. Three: lead sorption falls as pH falls, across the cation edge, so lead is released to the water. Four: Kd is not a constant. It depends on pH through surface charge and the sorption edge, and could change by orders of magnitude between pH 7 and 5. Use question four to lead into the limits of the linear model.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Surfaces fill up




A linear Kd has no limit. Real surfaces have a finite number of sites. The Langmuir model levels off at a capacity qmax:
q=\frac{q_{max}\,b\,C_w}{1+b\,C_w}
Example: qmax = 20.0 mg/kg on 0.0100 kg of solid gives at most 0.200 mg sorbed. That solid cannot hold 1.00 mg, whatever Kd says.
Other solutes compete for the same sites: phosphate and arsenate, for example.


This is exercise 2. The linear model was fine at low concentrations, but it predicts that a surface can hold unlimited amounts if the water concentration keeps rising. The Langmuir model adds a ceiling. At low concentration it behaves like Kd equal to qmax times b, here 100 litres per kilogram, the same start as the dashed line. At high concentration it approaches qmax. Multiply the capacity by the solid mass to get the most the solid can hold: 0.2 milligrams. Competition matters too. Phosphate and arsenate bind to the same iron oxide sites, so adding phosphate fertiliser can release arsenic. A Kd measured at low loading or without competitors can overestimate retention.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Particles move

Sorption moves a contaminant from water to a solid. What happens next depends on the solid. Particles that settle can retain metal in the bed. Floods can stir the bed up again. Colloids stay suspended and can carry sorbed metal far downstream.

Now connect the chemistry to transport. Sorption on a large, settling particle removes metal from the flowing water, but deposits it in the bed sediment, where it can stay for years. A flood or a dredging operation can resuspend the bed and return the particles to the water. Sorption on colloids does the opposite of retention: the colloid moves with the water, so the sorbed metal travels too, sometimes faster than a dissolved solute that interacts with the stationary bed. To claim removal, you must name the destination of the solid and say how long it stays there. A falling water concentration alone is not enough.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Back to the Animas


 Where Cement Creek joins the Animas River, November 2015. The stones are coated with orange iron oxyhydroxide. Photo: US EPA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

Now we can answer the opening question.

As the acidic mine water mixed with river water, its pH rose and iron precipitated as fine oxyhydroxide.
Those particles had large surfaces that sorbed other metals.
Many particles settled along the bed and in reservoirs. The metals were moved, not destroyed.
High flows can resuspend them.

This creek carried mine drainage long before 2015. The spill was a sudden pulse in a chronic problem.


Close the loop. The release was acidic water rich in iron and other metals. Dilution raised the pH, iron hydrolysed and precipitated, and the fresh oxyhydroxide had the large, reactive surface that we calculated earlier. Other metals sorbed onto it, and much of the metal load then travelled and settled with those particles. That explains why the water cleared quickly while metal remained in the river system. The photo shows Cement Creek, which receives drainage from several old mines, including Gold King, and has been orange for decades. The spill drew attention, but the chronic inputs from many abandoned mines in the area are the larger, long-term load. Monitoring the bed and floods matters as much as monitoring the water.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
A filtered sample loses metal




Constructed data: downstream, the filtered metal falls from 8.0 to 2.0 µg/L, but the unfiltered total hardly changes.
The metal did not vanish. It moved onto particles that the filter held back, while they still travel with the river.
To decide between retention and transport, measure:

particle load and size fractions;
flow, to turn concentrations into loads;
metal in bed sediment over time.



This is exercise 4. The pattern of a falling filtered concentration and a steady total concentration is a fingerprint of sorption onto suspended particles. In terms of the bottle model, the water-phase concentration dropped because more solid surface became available, perhaps from a tributary or from fresh precipitation. But unless the particles settle, the metal leaves the reach with the water just as before. The numbers here are constructed for teaching. Ask students what would change in the figure if the particles settled before the downstream station. The answer: the total bar would drop too, and the bed sediment would gain metal. Only measurements of the solids can show that.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Lower concentration in the water means removal.” Check where the solute went.
“Dissolved means below 0.45 µm, so it is truly dissolved.” Colloids pass filters too.
“Kd is a constant of the chemical.” It belongs to one solid, one water, one pH.
“Doubling the solid halves the concentration.” Use the full denominator, Vw + Kdms.
“Sorption is forever.” pH, competition and redox can release it.
“Surfaces only attract opposite charges.” Inner-sphere binding is chemical, not only electrostatic.


Go through the list and ask students for a counterexample from today for each. The first is the central idea of the lecture. The second reminds them that filtration is a method, not a definition of chemistry. The third and fourth are the most common calculation errors in the exercises. The fifth points to the next lecture. When iron oxides are reduced in sediments without oxygen, the solid dissolves and everything sorbed on it is released, even though no pH change or competition occurred. That is how the Baltic Sea’s sediments release phosphate, and it is our next topic. The last mistake explains why phosphate binds so firmly to iron oxides.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Explore: the two-phase bottle


Worked example: 1.00 mg, 1.00 L water, 0.0100 kg solid, Kd = 100 L/kg gives 0.500 mg/L.



Double the solid, or let a pH change lower Kd: where does the solute go?

Start with the worked example and confirm the numbers from the “one bottle, three cases” slide. Before pressing Double the solid, ask the class to predict the new water concentration; many will say a quarter of a milligram per litre. The curve shows why it is a third: the water volume stays in the denominator. Then press the pH-change preset and point out that the solid gives solute back to the water although nothing was added. Drag the solid slider to zero to show that without a surface everything stays dissolved. Remind students that the model is linear and has no capacity limit. The exercise page has the hand check and the model conditions.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Summary









Concept
Key fact




Colloids
about 1 nm–1 µm; the 0.45 µm filter cuts through them


Surface area
per gram scales as 1/diameter; fine particles dominate binding


Oxide surfaces
>SOH gains or loses H⁺; positive at low pH, negative at high pH


Zero charge
iron oxides roughly pH 7–9; attract anions below, cations above


Sorption edges
cations bind more as pH rises; oxyanions as pH falls


Clays
permanent negative charge; exchangeable cations


Inner-sphere
direct bond by ligand exchange; strong and specific


Distribution coefficient
q = KdCw (L/kg); valid for one system


Two-phase balance
Cw = MT/(Vw + Kdms); total conserved


Capacity
sites are finite: at most qmax × ms


Transport
settling retains, floods resuspend, colloids carry



Next: Redox and environmental cycles. What happens to iron oxides, and the phosphate they hold, when oxygen runs out? Then the exercises and the notes.

 Phytoplankton bloom swirling in the Baltic Sea, July 2025, seen by a Landsat satellite. Image: NASA Earth Observatory (Michala Garrison), public domain, Wikimedia Commons.


The table is the revision sheet. Run through the chain once more. Small particles have large surfaces. Surfaces carry charge that depends on pH, plus specific binding sites. A distribution coefficient summarises the result for one system, and a mass balance tells you how much is in the water and how much on the solid. Capacity and competition set limits. Finally, sorbed material is only as immobile as the particle that carries it. The teaser image shows cyanobacteria blooms in the Baltic Sea. Their fuel includes phosphate released from bottom sediments when iron oxides dissolve under low oxygen. That is redox chemistry, and it is the next lecture.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text: Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text:
1. Sum the reactions
Combine the two pyrite/iron stages and show the final oxygen and water coefficients.






Hint





Add equations and cancel Fe²⁺.









Worked solution





FeS₂ + 15/4 O₂ + 7/2 H₂O → Fe(OH)₃ + 2 SO₄²⁻ + 4 H⁺. Fe, S, O, H, and charge balance. The product charge is −4 + 4 = 0.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text:
2. A shortfall
The worked pyrite inventory reacts fully, but only 0.0150 mol accessible CaCO₃ is available. Calculate the residual acid equivalents for the stated endpoint.






Hint





Subtract two equivalents per mole of accessible calcite from the generated amount.









Worked solution





Acid generated = 0.0400 mol eq; neutralised = 0.0300 mol eq; residual = 0.0100 mol eq. Final pH still requires a water volume and the remaining acid–base equilibria.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text:
3. Concentration versus load
Discharge A is 10.0 L/s with dissolved Fe 2.00 mg/L. Discharge B is 40.0 L/s with Fe 1.00 mg/L. Which exports more iron?






Hint





Multiply each concentration by its own flow.









Worked solution





A exports 20.0 mg/s, B 40.0 mg/s. B has lower concentration but twice the load. These are dissolved loads and do not include suspended iron solids.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text:
4. Long-term claim
A treated waste initially gives neutral-pH water. What evidence is needed before concluding that future metal and acid release will stay low?






Hint





Consider remaining reactive inventories, access, rate, and stability.









Worked solution





Check remaining sulfide and neutralising minerals, oxygen/water access, weathering rates, pH/redox changes, flow, dissolved/solid inventories, and relevant-duration leach observations. One initial pH does not establish long-term stability.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry exercises
text:
Explore: acid potential versus neutralisation
Predict what happens to a heap that drains at neutral pH today if the same calcite can neutralise only one equivalent per mole instead of two. Does the acid potential change, or only how long the drainage stays neutral? Change one input at a time.


Reference case: one tonne of waste with 1 % pyrite has an acid potential of 333 eq H⁺. With 7.5 kg reachable CaCO₃ at the CO₂* endpoint (150 eq) and an oxidation rate of 0.02 per year, the calcite is used up after about 30 years and 183 eq of acid remain to drain out.



E1. Choose Worked example. Check the acid potential, the CaCO₃ needed and the year the calcite runs out by hand. Then double the oxidation rate. Which numbers change, and which stay fixed?
E2. Compare Near-neutral endpoint and Half the calcite coated. Why do they give the same curves although the reasons are chemically different?
E3. Choose Calcite-rich heap, then lower the reachable share of calcite until the drainage eventually turns acidic. Explain why a neutral leachate alone could not tell this heap apart from the worked example.

Model conditions and hand check
The constructed case is one tonne of waste with 1.0 % FeS₂ by mass: 10 000 g / 120 g/mol = 83.3 mol FeS₂. At 4 H⁺ per FeS₂ the acid potential is 333 eq/t, with 167 mol sulfate. Neutralising it needs 333 / 2 = 167 mol CaCO₃ = 16.7 kg/t at the CO₂* endpoint, or 33.3 kg/t at the near-neutral endpoint. The waste holds 7.5 kg/t CaCO₃ = 75 mol, worth 150 eq/t at the CO₂* endpoint. Cumulative acid generated is 333 × (1 − e^(−0.02 t)); it reaches 150 eq when t = −ln(1 − 150/333) / 0.02 ≈ 30 years. After all pyrite has reacted, 333 − 150 = 183 eq/t of acid remain.
Assumptions: pyrite oxidises completely to sulfate and Fe(OH)₃ (4 H⁺ per FeS₂), at a first-order rate chosen for illustration only. Calcite is the only neutraliser, and the reachable part reacts as fast as acid forms until it is used up; the rest never reacts. Each mole of CaCO₃ neutralises 2 eq (CO₂* endpoint) or 1 eq (near-neutral, HCO₃⁻ stays in solution). Rates of calcite dissolution, oxygen supply, flow paths, other minerals and dilution are omitted. The curves are amounts per tonne, not concentrations or pH.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text: Why can a waste material continue producing acidity after the initial dissolved acid has been washed away?

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Learning goals

Balance sulfide oxidation and subsequent iron hydrolysis.
Distinguish present pH from potential acid-generating inventory.
Close a neutralisation budget and track the residual solids.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Expose a reactive mineral
Breaking and moving sulfide-bearing material changes access to oxygen and water. Pyrite oxidation can be represented by \[\mathrm{FeS_2+\tfrac72O_2+H_2O\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2SO_4^{2-}+2H^+}.\] This first stage yields iron(II), sulfate, and acidity. Microbial and mineral-surface processes can affect rates. The presence of pyrite does not by itself give a discharge concentration without reaction extent, flow, and neutralisation terms.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: Iron oxidation can release more acid
text:
Iron oxidation can release more acid
Iron(II) can oxidise and precipitate as an idealised hydroxide: \[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}+\tfrac14O_2+\tfrac52H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s)+2H^+}.\] Adding this step to the initial pyrite oxidation gives four H⁺ equivalents per mole of pyrite for this endpoint. Real iron solids differ in hydration and crystallinity; the hydroxide notation is a teaching representation. Removing orange iron precipitate is not necessarily the end of acid generation.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Neutralisation is another reaction
For the specified CO₂* endpoint, \[\mathrm{CaCO_3+2H^+\rightarrow Ca^{2+}+CO_2^*+H_2O}.\] An inventory of calcite can consume acidity, but access, surface coatings, and dissolution rate can limit the realised effect. At other solution conditions, bicarbonate can remain and alter the net stoichiometric accounting. Always state the endpoint rather than treating one acid-neutralisation coefficient as independent of the chemical state.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Present acidity and future generation
A leachate pH is a snapshot. Remaining sulfide can continue oxidising; remaining minerals can continue neutralising. A high-flow period can dilute concentrations while exporting a large load. Assess acid generation, neutralisation inventories, and water flow together. Laboratory extraction conditions and duration should be reported because a short leach test may not represent long-term exposure.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Immobilisation can be reversible
Iron precipitates can retain metals or phosphate, but changed pH or redox can destabilise the retention. A waste treatment that transfers contaminants into solids needs a statement about the conditions keeping those solids stable. The same logic applies beyond mine waste: organic wastes can impose oxygen demand, and mixed wastes can change pH, ligand concentrations, and redox. Leachate chemistry is controlled by reactions as well as original composition.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Worked example
Assume 0.0100 mol FeS₂ oxidises completely to sulfate and Fe(OH)₃ as represented above. It generates 0.0400 mol acid equivalents and 0.0200 mol sulfate. Neutralising that acidity to the stated CO₂* endpoint needs 0.0200 mol CaCO₃, or 2.00 g with supplied molar mass 100 g/mol. This is a stoichiometric comparison, not a field treatment dose: rates, mixing, other reactions, and residuals are omitted.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Reading
vanLoon and Duffy, 4th edition. Chapter 19: one sulfide-waste example, neutralisation, and phase stability.
EPA mine-drainage chemistry: Stoichiometric acid generation and the role of iron oxidation/precipitation.
BLM passive-treatment technical note: How flow, neutralisation, and residual phases constrain treatment.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
About this lecture


Last lecture ended in the Baltic Sea: phosphate from land feeds blooms, blooms use up oxygen, and anoxic sediments release more phosphate. The lasting way to break that loop is to cut what flows in.
Since the 1970s, Swedish towns have built wastewater treatment plants that remove most of the phosphorus and, at large plants, much of the nitrogen before the water reaches the sea.
Today you will learn to:

match a pollutant’s form to a treatment mechanism;
tell transfer from transformation;
calculate sequential stages, which multiply;
track the side effects: oxygen, alkalinity and by-products.

Your tools: precipitation (metals), surfaces, and redox from this week.

 Surface aerator in the aeration tank of an activated sludge plant. Photo: Marcos von Sperling, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Pick up the thread from the redox lecture. Internal loading explains why the Baltic responds slowly, but the external load sets the level, and municipal wastewater was once one of the largest point sources of phosphorus. Sweden introduced chemical phosphorus removal at most municipal plants in the 1970s, and large coastal plants later added nitrogen removal. The photo shows an aeration tank, the heart of biological treatment. Today’s lecture is not about plant engineering or dosing. It is about the chemistry behind treatment, using the tools from this week: hydrolysis and precipitation from the metals lecture, sorption from surfaces, and electron transfer from redox. The guiding question is always: where does the pollutant go?
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
section: Removed from the water, but where?
text:
Removed from the water, but where?


 Secondary clarifier at a wastewater treatment plant, Harelbeke, Belgium. Photo: Annabel, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Each person sends roughly 2 g of phosphorus a day to the sewer. For a city of a million people, that is several hundred tonnes a year.
A modern plant removes well over 90 % of it from the water. But phosphorus is an element. It cannot be destroyed.
Question for this lecture: for each pollutant, which process changes its chemical form, and which only moves it into another stream, such as sludge or gas, that still has to be managed?


Make the scale concrete. The per-person figure is a rough round number from human excretion and household products; plants use their own measured loads. Multiplied by a large city and a year, it becomes hundreds of tonnes of an element that cannot be destroyed, only moved. The photo shows a clarifier, a settling tank where the biological sludge separates from the treated water. The clear water flows over the edge; the solids settle and are pumped away. That separation is where much of the phosphorus, and many metals, leave the water. Pose the lecture question and ask students to keep a mental ledger for every process: what goes in, what comes out, and in which stream.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
section: Start with the form of the pollutant
text:
Start with the form of the pollutant

A treatment process works on a form, not on an element. Particles can be settled or filtered; dissolved ions need reaction or sorption; nitrogen needs microbes; microorganisms need disinfection. Every row ends in a destination.

This table is the organising idea of the lecture. Before choosing a process, identify the form of the target. Particles respond to gravity and filters. Colloids are too small to settle on their own and first need coagulation. Dissolved phosphate and metals must be converted to a solid or bound to one. Ammonium and nitrate need biological transformation. Organic matter is oxidised by microbes. Microorganisms are inactivated by disinfection. Notice the right-hand column: every mechanism has a destination. Three of the rows end in sludge. That is why one overall removal percentage can never describe a plant: the percentage depends on the form, and it hides where the material went.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
A wastewater treatment train

Water passes a series of stages. Each stage sends something out of the water line: grit and sludge to the sludge line, N₂ and CO₂ to the air. The sludge is digested to biogas and stabilised solids.

Walk through the simplified layout from left to right. Screens and grit chambers remove large objects and sand. Primary settling removes settleable particles. The biological stage has an anoxic tank and an aerated tank, with nitrate-rich water recycled from the aerated tank back to the anoxic one. Secondary settling separates the microbes, most of which are returned to keep the biology going. Iron salts are dosed to precipitate phosphate, often with final filtration. The two outputs that are easy to overlook are the gases, nitrogen and carbon dioxide, and the sludge line, which collects most of the phosphorus and metals. Real plants differ, for example in where the iron is dosed, but the logic of streams is the same.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Transfer or transformation?

Transfer keeps the element and changes its place: water to sludge, water to air. Transformation changes the chemical form. Only a transformation to a harmless form, or a transfer to a safe, managed stream, counts as treatment.

This is the main distinction of the lecture, and it maps directly onto the question we asked. On the left, settling, precipitation, sorption and stripping move an element from the water to a solid or to air. The element still exists and must be managed in its new stream. On the right, nitrification, denitrification, organic oxidation and disinfection change chemical form. Some transformations solve the problem: nitrate to nitrogen gas, which is most of the air. Others do not: ammonium to nitrate leaves the nitrogen in the water. Disinfection inactivates microbes but can create by-products, a new problem. Ask students to classify each process in the treatment train on the previous slide.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Coagulation: making colloids settle

Colloids in water are usually negatively charged and repel each other, so they stay suspended. Adding Fe³⁺ or Al³⁺ produces hydroxide flocs that neutralise the charge and sweep particles together. The flocs settle as sludge.

This brings together the metals and surfaces lectures. Natural colloids, clays and organic matter, mostly carry negative surface charge at the pH of natural water, so they repel each other and stay dispersed. Adding iron(III) or aluminium salts does two things. The positively charged hydrolysis species neutralise the colloid charge, so particles can stick together. And iron or aluminium hydroxide precipitates as a fluffy, high-surface floc that traps particles as it forms, called sweep flocculation. The same flocs sorb phosphate and some dissolved organic matter. Remember the hydrolysis reaction from the metals lecture: every iron(III) that becomes hydroxide releases three protons. That is the next slide.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Coagulants consume alkalinity




\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+3H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s)+3H^+}
Each Fe³⁺ releases 3 H⁺. A dose of 0.0200 mmol/L Fe³⁺ gives 0.0600 mmol/L H⁺: alkalinity falls by 0.0600 meq/L.
A hard water hardly notices. A soft water with 0.20 meq/L loses all its alkalinity at about 0.067 mmol/L Fe (3.7 mg/L), and its pH collapses.
Real dosing needs the actual water, but the bookkeeping is the carbonate lecture’s.


This is exercise 2. The reaction is a simplified representation: the real precipitate and the real net reaction depend on pH and on the other ions present. But the proton bookkeeping holds. Three protons per iron means three equivalents of alkalinity consumed per mole of iron. Link to the carbonate lecture. Strong acid lowers alkalinity one for one, and the pH response depends on how much alkalinity there was. In hard water the dose is a small fraction of the reserve. In soft water, common in much of Sweden, a realistic coagulant dose can consume all of it, so plants add lime or another base to keep the pH in the range where the hydroxide precipitates. The two waters are constructed for illustration.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Phosphate leaves as a solid


 Jar-test stirrer with beakers of sample water, used to compare coagulant doses. Photo: Organic sweet, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Simplified:
\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+PO_4^{3-}\rightarrow FePO_4(s)}
In practice phosphate is caught in a mixed iron hydroxide–phosphate solid, partly by precipitation and partly by sorption on the fresh hydroxide surface. Plants usually need more than one Fe per P.
Either way, the phosphorus is transferred to sludge. A jar test finds the dose that works for a particular water.


Chemical phosphorus removal combines two mechanisms from this week. Some phosphate precipitates with iron directly. Much of it sorbs to the freshly formed iron hydroxide, the same inner-sphere binding we saw in the surfaces lecture. That is why the iron dose is usually larger than the simple one-to-one formula suggests: part of the iron forms hydroxide, which provides the surface. The photo shows a jar test, the standard laboratory method for choosing a coagulant dose. Identical jars of the water receive different doses, are stirred, and are left to settle; you compare clarity and residual phosphate. Note the connection to the Baltic: this iron-bound phosphate is stable only while the sludge stays oxic.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Sequential stages multiply


Each stage acts on what enters it, not on the original amount.
M_{water}=M_0(1-f_1)(1-f_2)
Worked example: 10.0 mg of an element. Stage 1 transfers 60.0 %: 6.00 mg to sludge, 4.00 mg left. Stage 2 transfers 50.0 % of that: 2.00 mg more to sludge, 2.00 mg in the effluent.
Overall: 80.0 %, not 60 + 50 = 110 %. Check: 8.00 + 2.00 = 10.0 mg.




This is the worked example from the notes. The common error is to add the percentages, which can give more than one hundred percent and hides where the material goes. Multiply the fractions that remain instead: 0.4 times 0.5 is 0.2, so 20 percent stays in the water and 80 percent was transferred. Then close the balance by streams: sludge plus effluent equals what came in. Exercise 1 asks the same with two stages of 30 percent each, starting from 100 milligrams: 0.7 times 0.7 is 0.49, so 49 milligrams remain and 51 percent was removed. The example assumes no gas or chemical-product stream, which is true for phosphorus and metals but not for nitrogen.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Check yourself

Classify, then calculate.

Three stages each remove 50 % of what enters. What fraction of the original remains in the water?
A plant turns all its NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻. Has it removed nitrogen?
Is chemical phosphorus removal a transfer or a transformation? Where does the P go?
How much alkalinity does 0.0500 mmol/L Fe³⁺ consume, if it all forms Fe(OH)₃?



Answers. One: one half cubed, so one eighth, 12.5 percent, remains; 87.5 percent was transferred, not 150 percent. Two: no. Every nitrogen atom is still in the water, now as nitrate. That is exercise 3, and it leads into the next slides. Three: a transfer. Phosphorus stays at oxidation state plus five and moves into the sludge as an iron-bound solid. Four: three times 0.05, so 0.150 milliequivalents per litre. Ask students which of the four answers needed a mass balance and which needed stoichiometry. Most real treatment questions need both.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Biological treatment burns organic matter


In the aerated tank, microbes oxidise dissolved organic matter:
\mathrm{CH_2O+O_2\rightarrow CO_2+H_2O}
This is the respiration of the redox lecture, run on purpose. Air is blown in to supply the oxygen; that is a large part of a plant’s energy use.
Part of the carbon leaves as CO₂ (transformation). Part becomes new microbial biomass, which settles as sludge (transfer).

 Aeration tank of a sewage treatment plant in Bengaluru, India. Photo: Vraj Acharya, WELL Labs, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.


The activated sludge process uses a dense, recycled population of microbes to oxidise the organic matter in sewage. Chemically it is aerobic respiration, organic carbon donating electrons to oxygen, exactly as in the redox lecture, except that engineers supply the oxygen by blowing air through the tank. If the organic matter reached a lake untreated, the same reaction would consume the lake’s oxygen. Here it happens in a tank where oxygen is supplied. The carbon has two fates. Some is oxidised to carbon dioxide and leaves as gas. Some is built into new cells; the excess is wasted as sludge. So even biological treatment produces a solid stream to manage.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
section: Nitrogen: changing form is not removal
text:
Nitrogen: changing form is not removal

Nitrification (aerated tank) turns NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻ using 2 O₂ per N; 1.00 mmol/L NH₄⁺ gives 1.00 mmol/L NO₃⁻, still in the water. Denitrification (anoxic tank) turns nitrate into N₂ gas, using organic matter from the sewage as the electron donor.

This is exercise 3 in practice. Nitrification alone converts ammonium, which is toxic to fish and consumes oxygen in rivers, into nitrate. That is useful, but the nitrogen count in the water is unchanged. To remove nitrogen, the plant must also denitrify. The common layout puts the anoxic tank first, where it receives the raw sewage with its organic carbon, and recycles nitrate-rich water back from the aerated tank. In the anoxic tank, microbes use nitrate instead of oxygen to oxidise the organic matter, exactly the denitrification reaction we balanced last lecture, with 1.25 moles of carbon per mole of nitrate. The nitrogen leaves as N2 gas, harmless in air.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Disinfection has a different target

Disinfection inactivates microorganisms; it does not remove dissolved chemicals. Chlorine also reacts with natural organic matter, forming by-products such as trihalomethanes. The target and the side products must be judged separately.

Disinfection is mainly a drinking-water topic, though some wastewater is also disinfected. The point for chemistry is that disinfection has a different target from everything else in the lecture. It kills or inactivates pathogens, which is essential for public health, but it does not remove nitrate, metals or most organic contaminants. Chlorine is a strong oxidant and reacts with natural organic matter, the brown humic material from week 2, forming chlorinated by-products. Trihalomethanes are the best known and are regulated in drinking water. That is why drinking-water plants try to remove organic matter by coagulation before chlorinating. Other disinfectants, such as UV light and ozone, have their own trade-offs.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
section: Treatment changes chemistry beyond its target
text:
Treatment changes chemistry beyond its target


 Water tower at the Flint water treatment plant, Michigan. Photo: US EPA, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

In 2014, Flint, Michigan, switched its drinking-water source to the Flint River and treated it at the city’s own plant, without adding a corrosion inhibitor.
The new water was more corrosive. In homes with lead service pipes, the protective scale inside the pipes was destabilised, and lead levels in tap water rose.
The treatment met its targets for microbes and particles. It failed on the chemistry it did not track.


Flint is a well-documented, sobering example of treatment chemistry with unintended consequences. Keep to the chemistry. In April 2014 the city switched from water purchased from Detroit to the Flint River, treated locally. The treated water was more corrosive to pipes, and no orthophosphate corrosion inhibitor was added. Lead service lines, which connect older homes to the main, had a mineral scale that had kept lead mostly out of the water. Under the new chemistry the scale dissolved and broke away, and lead concentrations at the tap rose in many homes. The city returned to Detroit water in October 2015. There were serious public-health consequences and legal proceedings, which are beyond this course.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Why the lead came out

Lead pipes are protected by a thin scale of lead carbonate and phosphate minerals. Its stability depends on pH, alkalinity, chloride and orthophosphate, all set by treatment. Change the water and the scale can dissolve (free Pb²⁺) or flake off (lead particles). This is the metals lecture: the solubility of a solid, controlled by water chemistry.

Connect Flint to this week’s chemistry. The scale inside an old lead pipe is a set of sparingly soluble lead minerals, mainly carbonates and, where phosphate is dosed, phosphates. Their solubility depends on the pH, the alkalinity and the ligands in the water, exactly the free-ion and saturation reasoning from the metals lecture. Orthophosphate dosing helps form lead phosphate solids of very low solubility. A change in source water without matching corrosion control shifted that equilibrium. Lead then reached the tap both as dissolved ions and as particles that broke away from the pipe wall, which is why sampling must catch both. The lesson for treatment: every chemical change at the plant reaches every pipe downstream.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Back to the phosphorus




A constructed plant with three stages acting on what is left:

primary settling: 30 % → 70 % left
biological uptake: 40 % → 42 % left
iron precipitation: 90 % → 4.2 % left

Overall 95.8 % transferred, and 95.8 % of the phosphorus is now in sludge. The balance closes: 30.0 + 28.0 + 37.8 + 4.2 = 100.


Return to the opening question with the tools of the lecture. The stage percentages are round constructed numbers, chosen to be in a plausible range, not data from a real plant. Multiply what remains: 0.7 times 0.6 times 0.1 is 0.042. So 4.2 percent of the incoming phosphorus reaches the sea, and the other 95.8 percent is in three sludge streams. Close the balance by adding all four parts. This is the answer to “where did it go”: treatment did not destroy any phosphorus; it moved almost all of it from water heading to the Baltic into a solid stream that the plant must manage. That leads to the last chemical question of the lecture.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Sludge: problem and resource


Sludge collects what the water lost: phosphorus and nitrogen, organic matter, and also metals and some persistent organic contaminants that sorb to solids.

As a resource: phosphorus is a limited fertiliser raw material. Sludge can return it to farmland, or P can be recovered from it.
As a risk: metals such as cadmium and sorbing organic pollutants travel with it.

Whether sludge is spread, burned or deposited, the mass balance continues.

 A plant that burns sewage sludge for energy, Industriepark Höchst, Frankfurt, Germany. Photo: Norbert Nagel, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.


Finish the mass-balance story. Because so many processes transfer material into solids, sludge concentrates both valuable and harmful substances. Phosphorus is mined from a limited number of phosphate rock deposits, so recycling it from sludge has become a policy goal in Sweden and the EU. At the same time, cadmium, other metals and sorbing organic contaminants such as some PFAS are also concentrated in sludge, which is why spreading on farmland is regulated and debated. Incineration destroys organic contaminants but leaves the metals and phosphorus in the ash. The point is not to decide the policy, but to see that every option is another step in the same mass balance, which continues into soils, the topic of week 4.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

“Removal means destruction.” Most removal is transfer to sludge or gas.
“Add the stage percentages.” Multiply the fractions remaining.
“Nitrification removes nitrogen.” It changes NH₄⁺ to NO₃⁻; denitrification removes N as N₂.
“Filtration treats everything.” Dissolved nitrate and neutral organic molecules pass a filter.
“Disinfection cleans the water chemically.” It targets microbes and can form by-products.
“A coagulant only affects particles.” It consumes alkalinity and changes pH.


Go through the list and ask students to give the counterexample from today for each. The fourth is exercise 4. A water with suspended clay, dissolved nitrate and a neutral organic contaminant needs at least three mechanisms: filtration or coagulation for the clay, biological or other treatment for nitrate, and contaminant-specific sorption or destruction for the organic compound, each with its own residual stream. The last mistake is the Flint lesson in small form: any chemical added at a plant changes the water’s whole chemistry, not just the target. This course gives you the balances and mechanisms; real treatment design and dosing need the actual system and its operating data.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Explore: where the phosphorus goes


Three stages transferring 30 %, 40 % and 90 % of what enters leave 4.2 % of the phosphorus in the effluent; 95.8 % is in sludge.



Follow the phosphorus through three stages and close the balance.

Start with the Phosphorus plant preset, the constructed plant from “Back to the phosphorus”, and confirm 30, 28, 37.8 and 4.2 milligrams. Point at the third metric: adding the percentages gives 160 percent, which is impossible. Then use the worked example and exercise 1 presets. Ask students to predict before each change: which stage should be improved by five percentage points to cut the effluent most? The last stage wins because the fraction it leaves is the smallest factor. Stress that every milligram taken out of the water appears in a sludge bar. The exercise page has the model assumptions and a hand check.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Start with the form
particles, colloids, ions, molecules and microbes need different mechanisms


Transfer vs transform
transfer moves an element to sludge or gas; transformation changes its form


Coagulation
Fe³⁺/Al³⁺ hydroxide flocs neutralise and sweep colloids into sludge


Coagulant acidity
Fe³⁺ + 3H₂O → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3H⁺: 3 meq alkalinity per mmol Fe


Phosphorus
precipitated and sorbed with iron; moved to sludge, not destroyed


Sequential stages
remaining = M₀(1 − f₁)(1 − f₂) …; never add percentages


Biological oxidation
CH₂O + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O; part of the carbon becomes sludge


Nitrogen
nitrification changes form; denitrification sends N to the air as N₂


Disinfection
targets microbes; chlorine + organic matter → by-products


Side effects
pH, alkalinity and corrosion control decide whether pipes release lead



Next: Soil chemistry and retention. What happens to the phosphorus, metals and organic matter when they reach soil? Then the exercises and the notes.

The table is the revision sheet for treatment chemistry. The chain to remember: identify the form; choose a mechanism; name the destination; close the balance. Most treatment is transfer, and transfers multiply through a series of stages. Biological treatment transforms carbon and nitrogen, using the same electron bookkeeping as the redox lecture. Coagulants and disinfectants have side effects that must be tracked: alkalinity and pH, by-products, and corrosion. This also closes week 3. Metals, surfaces, redox and treatment are one story about where elements go and in what form. Next week takes the same questions into soils, where sludge, deposition and weathering meet, and where sorption, exchange and redox control what stays and what leaches.
crumbs: Week 3: Metals, surfaces, redox, and treatment
